subject: science
statement: A handspan is a standard unit because everyone has a hand.
why: Students observe that everyone can use their hand to measure and assume the result is universally valid.
fix: Handspans vary in size between different people, so they cannot be used for accurate, universal measurement.

probe.question: If you and your teacher both measure the same table using handspans, will the number of handspans be the same?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because we are both measuring the same table.

root_belief: self is the universal standard

subject: science
statement: 100 cm is longer than 1 metre because 100 is a larger number than 1.
why: Students focus on the numerical value rather than the unit scale.
fix: 100 cm and 1 metre represent the exact same physical length; they are just different ways of saying it.

probe.question: Which is longer: a 100 cm stick or a 1 metre stick?
probe.wrong_answer: The 100 cm stick.

root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

subject: science
concept: Aligning zero mark with object start
statement: If the zero mark of a ruler is broken, you cannot measure anything with it.
why: Students believe the starting point must always be the literal '0' digit on the tool.
fix: You can start from any full mark (like 1 cm) and subtract that value from the final reading.

probe.question: How would you measure a pencil if the first 2 cm of your ruler are broken?
probe.wrong_answer: I cannot use this ruler to get a correct measurement.

root_belief: damaged tools are useless

subject: science
statement: It doesn't matter where your eyes are as long as you can see the mark on the ruler.
why: Students do not realize that perspective changes the alignment of the object and the scale.
fix: The eye must be placed vertically above the point where the measurement is to be taken to avoid parallax error.

probe.question: Where should your eye be while taking a reading on a scale?
probe.wrong_answer: Anywhere, as long as I can see the ruler clearly.

root_belief: observation is independent of position

subject: science
statement: A curved line can be measured by placing a straight ruler directly along the curve.
why: Students try to force the tool they have to fit the shape of the object.
fix: A thread is used to trace the curve first, and then the thread's length is measured on a straight ruler.

probe.question: How would you measure the length of a curved snake drawn on paper?
probe.wrong_answer: By keeping the ruler straight over the snake.

root_belief: tools only work for their visual shape

subject: science
statement: Any motion that is not in a straight line is circular motion.
why: Students overgeneralize the category of 'circular' to include all curves.
fix: Circular motion specifically requires the object to remain at a fixed distance from a center point.

probe.question: Is a car turning a random corner always in circular motion?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is not going straight.

root_belief: visual similarity implies category membership

subject: science
statement: Motion is only periodic if it happens very fast.
why: Students associate 'repetition' with high frequency or speed, like a vibrating string.
fix: Periodic motion is defined by the regularity of the interval, not the speed; the Earth's orbit is periodic even if it takes a year.

probe.question: Is the movement of the hour hand of a clock periodic?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it moves too slowly to be repeating.

root_belief: human time scales define physical properties

subject: science
statement: An object can only have one type of motion at a time.
why: Students find it difficult to decompose complex movements into multiple categories.
fix: Objects can exhibit multiple motions, like a rolling ball which has both rectilinear and circular (rotational) motion.

probe.question: What kind of motion does a sewing machine needle have while the wheel is turning?
probe.wrong_answer: Only periodic motion.

root_belief: one object has one single property

subject: science
statement: A spinning top is in circular motion.
why: Students confuse the rotation of an object around its own axis with the circular path of an object around a center.
fix: In circular motion, the whole object moves along a circular path; a spinning top is rotating around an internal axis.

probe.question: If a boy is spinning in one spot, is he in circular motion?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because he is moving in a circle.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: A pendulum's motion is circular because it moves in an arc.
why: Students see the curved path and ignore the repeating back-and-forth nature.
fix: A pendulum is periodic because it repeats its motion along the same path in equal intervals of time.

probe.question: Why is a swinging bell considered periodic motion?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it moves in a circle.

root_belief: visual similarity implies category membership

subject: science
statement: Motion only exists if the object is getting further away from you.
why: Students define motion relative to themselves as the observer rather than a fixed reference point.
fix: Motion is any change in the position of an object with time, regardless of the direction relative to the observer.

probe.question: If a ball is thrown towards you, is it in motion?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is coming closer, not going away.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
concept: Metre is the SI unit of length
statement: The SI unit for measuring the distance between cities is the Kilometre.
why: Students confuse the 'most common' or 'convenient' unit with the 'standard' (SI) unit.
fix: The SI unit of length is always the Metre; Kilometre is a multiple of the SI unit used for convenience.

probe.question: What is the SI unit of length used to measure the distance between Delhi and Mumbai?
probe.wrong_answer: Kilometre.

root_belief: convenience equals standard

subject: science
statement: We see objects because our eyes send out rays of light to touch them.
why: Students feel that vision is an active process directed by the observer.
fix: We see objects only when light from a source falls on them and then travels to our eyes.

probe.question: Can you see a book in a room that is completely dark?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if I open my eyes wide enough.

root_belief: perception is an active outward process
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's research on children's ideas

subject: science
statement: The Moon is a luminous object because it glows brightly at night.
why: The Moon appears to be a source of light in the night sky.
fix: The Moon is non-luminous; it only reflects the light of the Sun that falls on it.

probe.question: Why does the Moon shine?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it produces its own light like a bulb.

root_belief: bright things are sources

subject: science
statement: Transparent objects like clear glass do not reflect any light and are invisible.
why: Because light passes through them, students think they have no interaction with light.
fix: Even transparent objects reflect a small amount of light, which is why we can see the surface of glass.

probe.question: Why can you see a glass window even though it is clear?
probe.wrong_answer: You can't see the glass, you only see the frame.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Light can bend around corners to reach the other side of a wall.
why: Students observe that a room gets bright even if the bulb is in the hallway.
fix: Light only travels in straight lines; it reaches other areas by reflecting off walls and floors.

probe.question: If you look through a bent pipe at a candle, will you see the flame?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because light flows through the pipe.

root_belief: light behaves like a fluid

subject: science
statement: A shadow is a physical thing or a reflection that exists on its own.
why: Shadows move with the person, making them seem like an attached property or object.
fix: A shadow is simply the absence of light in a region where an opaque object blocked it.

probe.question: What is a shadow made of?
probe.wrong_answer: It is made of black air or a dark reflection.

root_belief: shadow is an independent object

subject: science
statement: Shadows can be seen even if there is no screen or surface behind the object.
why: Students think the shadow is 'cast' into the air.
fix: A shadow can only be seen when it falls on a surface like the ground, a wall, or a screen.

probe.question: If you hold a bird in the high sky, will you see its shadow on the ground?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the shadow stays right under the bird in the air.

root_belief: effects exist without a medium

subject: science
statement: The image in a pinhole camera is upright because light goes straight through the hole.
why: Students assume the image must look exactly like the object in orientation.
fix: Light from the top of the object travels in a straight line through the pinhole to the bottom of the screen, creating an inverted image.

probe.question: What happens to the image of a candle in a pinhole camera?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays upright because the hole is too small to flip it.

root_belief: images must look like the object

subject: science
statement: Only mirrors and very shiny metals reflect light.
why: Students associate 'reflection' only with seeing a clear image of themselves.
fix: All objects we see reflect light; mirrors reflect it in a way that forms an image, while others scatter it.

probe.question: Does a piece of white paper reflect light?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because you cannot see your face in it.

root_belief: only perfect effects are real

subject: science
statement: The shadow of an object is always the same size as the object itself.
why: Students often see their own shadows on the ground and assume a 1:1 size ratio.
fix: The size of a shadow changes depending on the distance between the light source, the object, and the screen.

probe.question: What happens to a shadow's size if you move the object closer to the torch?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays the same size as the object.

root_belief: size is an intrinsic fixed property

subject: science
statement: Translucent materials block all light but are just 'weak' opaque objects.
why: Difficulty in distinguishing between 'partial' passage and 'no' passage of light.
fix: Translucent materials allow light to pass through them partially, but we cannot see clearly through them.

probe.question: Can light pass through a sheet of oiled paper?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is blocked because the paper is thick.

root_belief: categories are binary

subject: science
statement: A mirror image is just a person standing behind a transparent glass.
why: The depth perception in a mirror makes it look like there is space behind the glass.
fix: A mirror is an opaque object with a polished surface that reflects light back into the same room.

probe.question: Is a mirror transparent, translucent, or opaque?
probe.wrong_answer: Transparent, because you can see 'into' it.

root_belief: what is seen is physically there

subject: science
statement: Light travels further at night than during the day.
why: Beams of light (like car headlights) are much more visible at night.
fix: Light travels the same way regardless of the time; it is just easier to see the contrast against a dark background.

probe.question: Does a torch beam go a longer distance at night?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the sun isn't there to stop it.

root_belief: visibility distance equals travel distance

subject: science
statement: Electricity flows from the battery to the bulb through a single wire and stops there.
why: Students see a single wire in some diagrams or think of electricity like water from a tap.
fix: Electricity must return to the source; it requires a complete, unbroken loop from one terminal to the other.

probe.question: If you connect one wire from the positive terminal of a cell to the tip of a bulb, will it glow?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the electricity reaches the bulb.

root_belief: only one connection is needed for effect
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's research on children's ideas

subject: science
statement: The bulb consumes electricity, so less current returns to the battery than what left it.
why: Students confuse energy (which is transformed) with current (which is conserved).
fix: The amount of current flowing into the bulb is exactly equal to the amount flowing out of it.

probe.question: Compare the current in the wire before the bulb and the wire after the bulb.
probe.wrong_answer: The current after the bulb is less because the bulb used it.

root_belief: electricity is a substance that gets used up

subject: science
statement: Electricity travels from both terminals of the battery and meets at the bulb to make it light up.
why: The symmetrical appearance of circuits leads students to believe in a 'clashing' model.
fix: Current flows in one continuous direction around the loop, from positive to negative.

probe.question: How does electricity move from a cell to a bulb?
probe.wrong_answer: It comes from both sides and crashes in the bulb.

root_belief: two opposing forces meet to create an effect

subject: science
statement: The bulb only has one terminal at the bottom tip.
why: The metal casing of the bulb is often mistaken for a holder rather than a functional terminal.
fix: An electric bulb has two terminals: the metal tip at the base and the metal casing around the base.

probe.question: Where should the two wires from a cell be connected to a bulb?
probe.wrong_answer: Both wires should touch the bottom tip of the bulb.

root_belief: only the most prominent part is functional

subject: science
statement: All non-metal materials are perfect insulators and can never conduct electricity.
why: Textbooks emphasize metals as conductors, leading to overgeneralization about non-metals like graphite or impure water.
fix: While most non-metals are insulators, some like graphite (pencil lead) and certain liquids can conduct electricity.

probe.question: Will a circuit work if you use a pencil lead (graphite) to bridge a gap?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is not a metal.

root_belief: a category property applies to every member

subject: science
statement: A switch stores electricity when it is in the OFF position.
why: Students use everyday language like 'storing' or 'stopping' and imagine the switch as a dam.
fix: A switch simply creates a gap in the circuit; it does not store any electricity.

probe.question: What happens to the electricity when the switch is turned off?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays inside the switch waiting to be released.

root_belief: stopping flow means accumulation at the barrier

subject: science
statement: Two cells in a torch will work regardless of which way their ends are facing.
why: Students may not realize that the orientation of terminals determines the direction of potential.
fix: Cells must be connected in series with the positive terminal of one touching the negative terminal of the next.

probe.question: If you put two cells in a torch with both positive ends facing each other, will it light up?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, as long as there are two cells, it will work.

root_belief: quantity of components matters more than arrangement

subject: science
statement: The glass of the bulb is what produces the light.
why: The glass is the largest and most visible part of the bulb that appears to glow.
fix: The light is produced by the thin wire inside called the filament when it becomes hot.

probe.question: Which part of the bulb actually glows?
probe.wrong_answer: The glass outer cover.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Air is a good conductor because electricity travels through it during lightning.
why: Students observe lightning and conclude that air must always allow electricity to pass.
fix: Air is generally an insulator; lightning only occurs when the electrical pressure is extremely high.

probe.question: If there is a small gap between two wires in a circuit, will the bulb glow?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because electricity can travel through the air.

root_belief: extreme cases represent the normal state

subject: science
statement: A battery is like a reservoir full of electricity that flows out like water.
why: The water-pipe analogy is often taken too literally by students.
fix: A battery is a source of energy that pushes charges already present in the wires.

probe.question: Where does the electricity come from when a circuit is closed?
probe.wrong_answer: It is stored inside the battery and flows out into the wires.

root_belief: objects are containers for substances

subject: science
statement: A thicker wire will always make a bulb glow brighter than a thinner wire.
why: Students associate 'bigger' or 'thicker' with 'more power' or 'easier flow'.
fix: In simple Class 6 circuits, the thickness of short connecting wires does not visibly change the bulb's brightness.

probe.question: If you replace a thin copper wire with a very thick one, what happens to the bulb?
probe.wrong_answer: It will glow much brighter because more electricity can fit.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: science
statement: A circuit is closed as long as the wires are touching the bulb anywhere on its surface.
why: Students do not realize that specific internal paths exist within the bulb.
fix: A circuit is only closed if the wires are connected to the two specific terminals of the bulb.

probe.question: If you touch both wires to the glass part of the bulb, will it glow?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the wires are touching the bulb.

root_belief: contact with the whole is contact with the part

subject: science
statement: All metals are attracted to magnets.
why: Students observe iron objects being attracted and generalize this property to all shiny metallic objects.
fix: Only specific metals like iron, nickel, and cobalt are magnetic; others like aluminum, copper, and gold are not.

probe.question: Will a magnet pick up an aluminum soda can or a copper wire?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they are both metals.

root_belief: all members of a category share one property

subject: science
statement: If you break a magnet in half, you get one North pole piece and one South pole piece.
why: Intuition suggests that if a whole has two ends, cutting it separates those ends into independent parts.
fix: Breaking a magnet creates two smaller magnets, each with its own North and South pole.

probe.question: If you break a bar magnet in the middle, what poles will the two new pieces have?
probe.wrong_answer: One piece will be only North and the other only South.

root_belief: parts of a whole are independent units
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
statement: The center of a bar magnet is the strongest part.
why: Students often believe the center of an object is its most important or powerful point.
fix: The magnetic strength is maximum at the poles (ends) and minimum at the center.

probe.question: Where will a bar magnet pick up the most iron filings?
probe.wrong_answer: In the middle of the bar.

root_belief: center is the most important part

subject: science
statement: If an object is attracted to a magnet, it must be a magnet itself.
why: Students confuse the property of being magnetic (material) with being a magnet (source).
fix: Magnetic materials like iron are attracted to magnets, but only another magnet can be repelled.

probe.question: An iron nail is pulled toward a magnet. Does this prove the nail is a magnet?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because attraction only happens between two magnets.

root_belief: symmetric interaction implies identical properties

subject: science
statement: A compass needle points North because it is attracted to the North Star.
why: Students associate the word 'North' with the most famous northern celestial object they know.
fix: A compass needle aligns with the Earth's magnetic field, which acts like a giant hidden magnet.

probe.question: Why does a compass needle point North even during the day when stars aren't visible?
probe.wrong_answer: It can still feel the pull of the North Star through the sky.

root_belief: visible or famous objects cause effects

subject: science
statement: Magnets work like glue or sticky tape.
why: Students use everyday experiences with adhesives to explain non-contact forces.
fix: Magnetism is a force that acts even without touching; it is not a physical sticky substance.

probe.question: Can a magnet attract a pin through a thin piece of paper?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the 'stickiness' cannot go through the paper.

root_belief: forces require physical contact to work

subject: science
statement: A large magnet will always attract a small magnet, even if like poles are facing.
why: The belief that size or strength overrides the fundamental rules of magnetic poles.
fix: No matter the size, like poles will always repel each other.

probe.question: What happens if you push the North pole of a huge magnet toward the North pole of a tiny magnet?
probe.wrong_answer: The big one will pull the small one because it is stronger.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: science
statement: A magnet's power gets used up over time like a battery.
why: Analogy with other portable sources of 'power' or 'energy' that deplete with use.
fix: A magnet does not lose its strength by being used; it only loses it if heated, dropped, or hammered.

probe.question: If I use a magnet to pick up 100 pins every day, will it eventually stop working?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it will run out of magnetism.

root_belief: properties are finite consumable substances

subject: science
statement: Only iron is magnetic; other metals like nickel are not.
why: Iron is the most common magnetic material mentioned in textbooks and daily life.
fix: While iron is common, nickel and cobalt are also naturally magnetic metals.

probe.question: Which of these is magnetic: Iron, Nickel, or both?
probe.wrong_answer: Only iron.

root_belief: one example represents the whole class

subject: science
statement: Heating a magnet makes it stronger because it gives it more energy.
why: Generalization that adding heat energy always increases the 'power' of a physical property.
fix: Heating a magnet actually destroys its magnetic alignment, making it lose its magnetism.

probe.question: What happens to a magnet if you heat it strongly over a flame?
probe.wrong_answer: It becomes a much stronger magnet.

root_belief: more energy always increases desired properties

subject: science
statement: The compass needle is moved by the wind inside the casing.
why: Students look for a visible, mechanical cause for the movement of the needle.
fix: The compass casing is sealed; the needle moves due to the invisible magnetic field of the Earth.

probe.question: How does the needle move if the compass is inside a glass box?
probe.wrong_answer: Air currents inside the box push it.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Magnetism is the same thing as static electricity.
why: Both phenomena involve attraction and repulsion without physical contact.
fix: Magnetism is a property of certain materials like iron, while static electricity involves charges on surfaces.

probe.question: Will a magnet attract a plastic comb that has been rubbed on hair?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they both have attraction forces.

root_belief: similar effects must have the same cause

subject: science
statement: Heat and temperature are the same thing.
why: In everyday language, we use these words interchangeably to describe how hot something is.
fix: Heat is the energy that flows between objects, while temperature is a measure of how hot or cold an object is.

probe.question: If you have a cup of water and a bucket of water both at 50 degrees Celsius, do they have the same amount of heat?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because their temperatures are the same.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: Cold is a substance that flows into objects to make them cooler.
why: When we touch ice, we feel a sensation of 'coldness' entering our hand.
fix: Cold is not a thing; it is just the absence of heat. Heat always flows from a hotter object to a colder one.

probe.question: When you put an ice cube in warm juice, what is moving?
probe.wrong_answer: The cold is moving from the ice into the juice.

root_belief: properties are physical substances
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
statement: Metal objects are naturally colder than wooden objects.
why: Metal feels colder to the touch than wood when both are in the same room.
fix: Both are at the same room temperature, but metal is a good conductor and carries heat away from your hand faster.

probe.question: If a metal chair and a wooden chair have been in the same room for two days, which one is at a lower temperature?
probe.wrong_answer: The metal chair.

root_belief: what you feel is the absolute truth

subject: science
statement: Woolen clothes produce heat to keep us warm.
why: We feel warm immediately after putting on a sweater, suggesting the sweater is a source of heat.
fix: Wool is an insulator; it does not produce heat but traps the heat produced by our body and prevents it from escaping.

probe.question: If you wrap a thermometer in a wool sweater, will the temperature reading rise?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the wool generates heat.

root_belief: passive objects are active agents

subject: science
statement: Heat cannot travel through a vacuum because there are no particles.
why: Students overgeneralize the need for a medium in conduction and convection to all forms of heat transfer.
fix: Heat can travel through a vacuum via radiation, which does not require any material medium.

probe.question: How does the sun's heat reach the Earth through the empty space of the universe?
probe.wrong_answer: It travels through air particles in space.

root_belief: all processes require a physical medium

subject: science
statement: Heat only travels in the upward direction.
why: Students observe that hot air and steam always rise, leading to a rule that heat only goes up.
fix: While convection currents move upwards, heat can travel in any direction through conduction and radiation.

probe.question: If you hold your hand to the side of a hot candle flame, why do you still feel heat?
probe.wrong_answer: You only feel it because the air is moving sideways.

root_belief: one observation is a universal rule

subject: science
statement: Land breeze blows during the day because the land is hot.
why: Students associate 'land' with the heat of the sun during the day.
fix: Land breeze blows at night when the land cools down faster than the sea, causing air to move from land to sea.

probe.question: At what time of day would you feel a breeze blowing from the land toward the sea?
probe.wrong_answer: In the afternoon when the sun is brightest.

root_belief: hot things always cause the effect

subject: science
statement: Black clothes 'attract' heat like a magnet attracts iron.
why: The word 'absorb' is often misinterpreted as an active 'pulling' force.
fix: Black surfaces do not pull heat; they simply reflect very little and convert more of the incident light/radiant energy into heat.

probe.question: Why does a black shirt feel hotter in the sun than a white shirt?
probe.wrong_answer: Because black color pulls the sun's rays toward it.

root_belief: passive absorption is active attraction

subject: science
statement: In conduction, particles move from the hot end of a rod to the cold end.
why: Students confuse the flow of energy with the flow of matter (like in convection).
fix: In solids, particles only vibrate in their fixed positions and pass energy to neighbors; they do not travel.

probe.question: How does heat reach the other end of a metal spoon in hot tea?
probe.wrong_answer: The hot atoms travel through the spoon to the handle.

root_belief: transfer requires movement of the carrier
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
statement: Insulators like blankets block 'cold' from entering.
why: Students perceive the environment as 'attacking' with cold, and the blanket as a shield.
fix: Blankets are insulators that prevent the heat of the body from escaping to the colder surroundings.

probe.question: If you put an ice cream box inside a thick blanket, what happens?
probe.wrong_answer: The blanket warms up the ice cream.

root_belief: cold is an active substance

subject: science
statement: A laboratory thermometer should be taken out of the liquid to read it correctly.
why: Students apply the rule for clinical thermometers (which have kinks) to laboratory thermometers.
fix: A laboratory thermometer must be read while its bulb is still in contact with the substance because it lacks a kink.

probe.question: Why did your reading of the boiling water drop as soon as you lifted the thermometer?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the water on the bulb evaporated instantly.

root_belief: a rule from one context works everywhere

subject: science
statement: Speed is the same thing as the distance an object travels.
why: Students often ignore the time component and only look at how far an object went to judge speed.
fix: Speed is the distance covered divided by the time taken; it is a rate, not just a length.

probe.question: Car A travels 10km in 1 hour. Car B travels 10km in 2 hours. Which has more speed?
probe.wrong_answer: They have the same speed because they both went 10km.

root_belief: confusing a rate with a quantity

subject: science
statement: Only objects that move very fast have speed.
why: In everyday language, 'speed' is often used as a synonym for 'high velocity'.
fix: Every moving object has a speed, whether it is a crawling snail or a jet plane.

probe.question: Does a slow-moving tortoise have speed?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is too slow to have speed.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: To calculate speed, you should divide the time taken by the distance covered.
why: Students often memorize formulas incorrectly or assume the order of numbers in a word problem dictates the division.
fix: Speed is always distance divided by time (S = D/T).

probe.question: If a bus travels 100 km in 2 hours, what is its speed?

root_belief: mathematical operations are interchangeable

subject: science
statement: A heavier pendulum bob will swing faster and have a shorter time period.
why: Intuition suggests that heavier objects fall or move faster due to gravity.
fix: The time period of a simple pendulum depends only on its length, not on the mass of the bob.

probe.question: If you replace a plastic bob with a metal bob of the same size, what happens to the time period?
probe.wrong_answer: The time period will decrease because the metal bob is heavier.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

subject: science
statement: Increasing the amplitude (swing distance) of a pendulum increases its time period.
why: Students think that because the bob has to travel a longer distance, it must take more time.
fix: For small angles, the time period remains constant regardless of the amplitude.

probe.question: If you pull a pendulum back further, how does the time for one swing change?
probe.wrong_answer: It will take more time because it has further to travel.

root_belief: more distance always means more time

subject: science
statement: A steeper line on a distance-time graph means the object is moving 'higher' or 'upward'.
why: The visual 'upward' direction of the line is interpreted as physical height.
fix: A steeper slope on a distance-time graph indicates a higher speed, not a change in altitude.

probe.question: What does a very steep line on this graph tell you about the object's motion?
probe.wrong_answer: It is climbing a very steep mountain.

root_belief: visual height represents physical height

subject: science
statement: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the object is moving at a constant speed.
why: Students often confuse 'constant speed' (straight diagonal line) with 'constant position' (horizontal line).
fix: A horizontal line means the distance is not changing, so the object is at rest (zero speed).

probe.question: A graph shows a flat horizontal line at 5 meters. How fast is the object moving?
probe.wrong_answer: It is moving at a steady, constant speed.

root_belief: straight lines always mean constant motion

subject: science
statement: Uniform motion means the object is moving in a straight line at any speed.
why: Students focus on the 'uniformity' of the path rather than the 'uniformity' of the speed.
fix: Uniform motion specifically means moving at a constant speed along a straight line.

probe.question: If a car goes around a circular track at a constant 40 km/h, is it in uniform motion?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the speed is not changing.

root_belief: one attribute defines the whole concept

subject: science
statement: One oscillation is the movement from one side of the swing to the other side.
why: Students perceive a single 'stroke' of motion as a complete event.
fix: One oscillation is the complete to-and-fro motion from one point back to the same point in the same direction.

subject: science
statement: The line that is physically higher on the graph always represents the faster object.
why: Students look at the Y-axis value (position) instead of the rate of change (slope).
fix: Speed is represented by the slope; a lower line can represent a faster object if it is steeper.

probe.question: Line A is at the top of the graph but flat. Line B is at the bottom but very steep. Which is faster?
probe.wrong_answer: Line A because it is higher up on the distance scale.

root_belief: higher position means a larger value

subject: science
statement: You can calculate speed by dividing kilometers by minutes without any conversion.
why: Students ignore the standard pairing of units (km with hours, meters with seconds).
fix: Units must be consistent; speed is usually expressed in km/h or m/s.

probe.question: If a car travels 5 km in 10 minutes, is its speed 0.5 km/h?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, 5 divided by 10 is 0.5.

subject: science
concept: Current flows only in closed path
statement: Electric current is consumed or used up by the bulb in a circuit.
why: Students observe the bulb glowing and think it 'eats' the energy like food.

subject: science
concept: Current flows only in closed path
statement: In an open circuit, current travels from the battery to the switch and stops there.
why: Students view electricity as a fluid that moves through pipes until it hits a dead end.

subject: science
statement: The short, thick line in a cell symbol represents the positive terminal.
why: Students often associate 'thickness' or 'heaviness' with 'positive' or 'more'.

subject: science
statement: A battery is just another name for a single electric cell.
why: In everyday language, people call a single AA cell a 'battery'.
fix: A battery is a combination of two or more cells connected together, usually in series.

probe.question: What do you call a combination of four cells?

subject: science
statement: All wires get equally hot when the same current flows through them.
why: Students ignore the material properties and focus only on the source of electricity.
fix: The amount of heat produced depends on the material, length, and thickness of the wire.

subject: science
concept: Fuse wire has low melting point

why: Students think safety involves moderation rather than breaking the circuit.

subject: science
concept: Fuse wire has low melting point
statement: A thicker fuse wire is always safer than a thin one.
why: Students associate 'thick' with 'strong' and 'safe'.

subject: science
statement: The magnetic effect of current only works if the wire is touching the compass.
why: Students often believe forces require direct physical contact.

probe.question: Will a compass move if it is placed 1cm away from a current-carrying wire?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it must touch the wire

subject: science
statement: An electromagnet is just a permanent magnet that uses electricity to start.
why: Students confuse the temporary nature of electromagnets with permanent magnets.
fix: An electromagnet only acts as a magnet as long as the electric current is flowing through its coil.

probe.question: What happens to the iron nail's magnetism when you disconnect the battery?

subject: science
concept: Hammer hits gong due to magnetism

why: Students focus on the visible movement and assume electricity acts as a physical push.

subject: science

subject: science
statement: Electricity and magnetism are the same thing because they both involve 'attraction'.

subject: science
statement: Light can bend around corners like sound does.
why: Students observe light filling a room even if the source is hidden.

probe.question: If you place a cardboard with a tiny hole between a candle and your eye, but move the hole slightly to the left, can you still see the flame?

subject: science
statement: The image in a plane mirror is located on the surface of the glass.
why: The mirror surface is the physical boundary where the reflection occurs.
fix: The image is formed behind the mirror at the same distance as the object is in front.

probe.question: If you stand 2 meters away from a mirror, where is your image located?

root_belief: what you see is where it is

subject: science
statement: Lateral inversion means the image is upside down.
why: Confusion between the terms 'inversion' and 'lateral inversion'.

probe.wrong_answer: It raises its hand but appears upside down.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
concept: Virtual images cannot be on screens
statement: Virtual images are not real and cannot be seen by the human eye.
why: The word 'virtual' is interpreted as 'imaginary' or 'non-existent' in everyday language.
fix: Virtual images are real optical phenomena that we can see, but they cannot be projected onto a screen.

subject: science
statement: A concave mirror always makes things look bigger.
why: Students often only use concave mirrors (like makeup mirrors) at very close distances.
fix: Concave mirrors can form smaller, same-sized, or larger images depending on the object's distance.

probe.question: What happens to the size of the image in a concave mirror as you move very far away from it?

root_belief: one observation applies to all cases

subject: science
statement: A prism adds colors to white light.
why: The prism is seen as the 'source' of the colors because white light looks 'pure'.

probe.question: Where do the colors of a rainbow come from when light passes through a prism?

root_belief: the tool creates the effect

subject: science
statement: If you walk away from a plane mirror, your image gets smaller.
why: Objects further away look smaller due to perspective, so students assume the image itself shrinks.

probe.question: If you move 5 meters back from a mirror, does the actual height of your image change?

root_belief: appearance is the same as physical reality

subject: science
concept: Real images can be on screens

probe.question: If a concave mirror forms a real image but you remove the screen, does the image still exist in space?

subject: science
statement: All lenses are used to magnify objects.

probe.question: Does a concave lens make a distant building look larger or smaller?

root_belief: all members of a category are identical

subject: science
statement: We see objects because our eyes send out rays to them.
why: The active feeling of 'looking' at something suggests the eye is the source of the action.

probe.question: How do you see a book in a dark room when you turn on a torch?

root_belief: perception is an active outward process

subject: science
statement: Convex mirrors are used in cars because they make images larger.
why: Students assume 'better' mirrors must magnify things.
fix: Convex mirrors are used because they provide a wider field of view, even though images appear smaller.

probe.question: Why does a car's side mirror say 'Objects in mirror are closer than they appear'?

root_belief: bigger is always better

subject: science
statement: Newton's disc turns white because the colors hide behind each other.

probe.question: Why does the seven-colored disc look white when rotated fast?

subject: science
statement: Force is something an object 'has' or 'contains' like an ingredient.
why: Students observe moving objects and think the force is inside them keeping them going.

probe.question: If a ball is rolling on a floor, does it 'carry' force with it?

subject: science
concept: Force can change speed or direction
statement: If an object is at rest, there are no forces acting on it.

probe.question: A book is lying still on a table. Are any forces acting on it?

root_belief: no motion means no force

subject: science
statement: Only living things like humans or animals can exert a force.
why: In everyday life, 'force' is often used as a synonym for effort or will.

probe.question: When you lean against a wall, does the wall exert a force on you?

subject: science
statement: Friction only acts on objects that are already moving.
why: Students think friction is just the 'rubbing' they feel during motion.

probe.question: You try to push a heavy box but it doesn't move. Is friction acting?

root_belief: friction is a result of motion only

subject: science
concept: Gravity acts on all objects with mass
statement: Gravity only acts on objects when they are falling through the air.
why: Students see gravity's effect most clearly when an object is dropped.
fix: Gravity acts on all objects at all times, whether they are falling, flying, or sitting on the ground.

subject: science
concept: Pressure equals Force divided by Area

why: The words are used interchangeably in common conversation.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
concept: Pressure equals Force divided by Area
statement: A larger area always results in more pressure.
why: Students often associate 'larger' or 'more' with a greater effect.
fix: Pressure is inversely proportional to area; for the same force, a larger area results in less pressure.

probe.question: Why do heavy trucks have many wide tires?

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: science
statement: Liquid pressure only acts downwards towards the bottom of the container.
why: Students relate liquid pressure to the weight of the water, which pulls down.
fix: Liquids exert pressure in all directions—sideways and upwards too—at any given depth.

probe.question: If you poke a hole in the side of a water bottle, why does water come out?

root_belief: gravity only acts downwards

subject: science
concept: Atmosphere exerts pressure in all directions
statement: Air cannot exert pressure because it is weightless and invisible.
why: Air feels like 'nothing' to students, and they don't feel the weight of the atmosphere.
fix: Air has mass and weight; the huge column of air above us exerts a large pressure in all directions.

probe.question: Why does a suction cup stick to a wall?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it has glue or it is sticky, not because of air.

root_belief: invisible things have no physical properties

subject: science
concept: Atmosphere exerts pressure in all directions
statement: We don't feel atmospheric pressure because it is very weak.
why: Students assume that if they don't feel a sensation, the magnitude must be zero or low.
fix: Atmospheric pressure is very high, but we don't feel it because the pressure inside our bodies balances it.

probe.question: Is the air pressure on your head more than, less than, or equal to the weight of an elephant?

subject: science
concept: Opposite forces subtract for net force
statement: If two people push an object from opposite sides, the object must stop moving.
why: Students think 'opposite' always means 'cancellation' regardless of the magnitude.

subject: science
statement: Magnetic force only works if the magnet is touching the object.

probe.question: Can a magnet move a paperclip without touching it?

subject: science
statement: Perfectly smooth surfaces have zero friction.
why: Students believe that if they cannot see or feel roughness, it does not exist.

probe.question: If we polish two metal blocks until they look like mirrors, will there be no friction between them?

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Friction only acts on objects that are already moving.

subject: science
statement: Friction always acts in the opposite direction of the object's motion.

subject: science
statement: A larger surface area in contact creates more friction.

subject: science
statement: Friction depends only on the weight of the object.

probe.question: If you press a book hard against a vertical wall, does the friction depend only on the book's weight?

subject: science
statement: Static friction has a single fixed value for a given surface.

probe.question: If the maximum static friction is 10N and you push with 2N, what is the friction force?

subject: science
concept: Rolling friction is less than sliding

probe.question: Why does a ball rolling on a level floor eventually stop if no one touches it?

subject: science

subject: science

subject: science

statement: Sound travels fastest in air because air is thin and offers less resistance.
