concept: Metal transfer from anode to cathode
statement: In electroplating, the metal atoms travel through the air or jump directly between plates.
why: Students struggle to visualize the role of the solution in transporting ions.
fix: Metal ions from the solution deposit on the cathode, and the anode dissolves to replenish the solution.

probe.question: How does copper get from one plate to the other in a copper sulfate solution?
probe.wrong_answer: It moves through the water without changing into anything else.

root_belief: Matter moves directly from source to destination

subject: science
statement: Liquids conduct electricity using free electrons just like copper wires.
why: Students carry over the model of metallic conduction to all states of matter.
fix: Liquids conduct electricity through the movement of ions, not free electrons.

probe.question: What carries the electric charge through a salt solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Electrons flowing through the liquid.

root_belief: Mechanism in one state applies to all states

subject: science
statement: Iron is coated with zinc because zinc is 'stronger' than iron.
why: Students use everyday meanings of 'strong' to explain protection.
fix: Zinc is used because it is more reactive and prevents the iron underneath from rusting.

probe.question: Why do we plate iron bridge girders with zinc?
probe.wrong_answer: To make the iron harder and harder to break.

root_belief: A word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
concept: Tap water and salt solutions conduct
statement: Adding sugar to water makes it a good conductor because the sugar dissolves.
why: Students confuse 'dissolving' with 'ionizing'.
fix: Sugar dissolves as molecules, not ions, so sugar solution does not conduct electricity.

probe.question: Will a circuit be completed if you use a sugar solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the sugar has dissolved in the water.

root_belief: Dissolving always produces mobile charged particles

subject: science
statement: Electricity 'creates' the metal that is deposited on the electrode.
why: The appearance of new solid metal seems like creation from energy.
fix: Electricity only provides the energy to move existing metal ions from the solution to the electrode.

probe.question: Where does the copper on the spoon come from during electroplating?
probe.wrong_answer: The electricity turns into copper when it hits the spoon.

root_belief: Energy can be directly converted into matter

subject: science
statement: The magnetic needle moves because the liquid itself becomes a magnet.
why: Students misattribute the magnetic field of the wire to the liquid in the beaker.
fix: The needle moves because the current in the wire wrapped around the compass creates a magnetic field.

probe.question: Why does the compass needle deflect when the tester leads are dipped in lemon juice?
probe.wrong_answer: Because lemon juice is magnetic when electricity is in it.

root_belief: The nearest object is the cause of the effect

subject: science
statement: Chromium plating is done to make the whole object out of chromium.
why: Students don't distinguish between a surface coating and the bulk material.
fix: Only a thin layer of chromium is deposited to save costs while providing shine and rust resistance.

probe.question: Is a 'chrome' bicycle handle made entirely of chromium?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, that is why it is so shiny and doesn't rust.

root_belief: The surface represents the whole object

subject: science
statement: The liquid in the beaker is just there to hold the electrodes and doesn't participate.
why: The liquid looks unchanged to the naked eye during the early stages.
fix: The electrolyte is essential as it provides the ions that carry the current and provide the metal for plating.

probe.question: Can we use plain distilled water for copper plating if the copper plates are present?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the water just needs to let the electricity pass between plates.

root_belief: If a substance doesn't disappear, it isn't reacting

subject: science
statement: Rubbing creates new charges inside an object that were not there before.
why: Students often think friction 'generates' electricity like a factory rather than moving existing particles.
fix: Rubbing only transfers existing electrons from one object to another; no new charge is created.

probe.question: If you rub a glass rod with silk, where does the positive charge on the rod come from?
probe.wrong_answer: The friction creates the positive charge inside the rod.

root_belief: matter can be created through physical action

subject: science
statement: Charged objects only attract other things; they do not repel.
why: In everyday life, students see static 'cling' (attraction) more often than active repulsion.
fix: Objects with the same type of charge will push away or repel each other.

probe.question: What happens if two balloons are both rubbed with the same woolen cloth and brought near each other?
probe.wrong_answer: They will stick together because they are both charged.

root_belief: electricity is a force of attraction only

subject: science
statement: Lightning is a form of fire or burning gas in the sky.
why: Lightning is bright and hot, leading to a visual association with fire.
fix: Lightning is a massive flow of electric charge (discharge) between clouds or cloud and ground.

probe.question: What is lightning made of?
probe.wrong_answer: It is a streak of fire caused by clouds catching flame.

root_belief: bright hot things must be fire

subject: science
statement: A lightning conductor attracts lightning to the building to stop it from hitting other places.
why: The word 'conductor' and its position on top of buildings suggest it acts like a magnet for lightning.
fix: A lightning conductor provides a safe, low-resistance path for the charge to flow into the ground, protecting the structure.

probe.question: Does a lightning rod increase the chance of your house being hit?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it pulls lightning toward the house.

root_belief: safety devices work by attracting the danger

subject: science
concept: Crust is made of tectonic plates
statement: The Earth's tectonic plates float on a continuous ocean of liquid lava.
why: Diagrams in textbooks often show a bright red mantle, which students interpret as liquid water-like magma.
fix: The mantle is mostly solid rock that can flow very slowly over millions of years; it is not a liquid ocean.

probe.question: What is directly underneath the tectonic plates?
probe.wrong_answer: A sea of liquid melted fire or lava.

root_belief: solid things must float on liquid to move
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

subject: science
statement: An earthquake of magnitude 7 is only slightly stronger than one of magnitude 6.
why: Students assume the Richter scale is linear, like a ruler or a marksheet.
fix: The Richter scale is logarithmic; an increase of 2 in magnitude means 1000 times more destructive energy.

probe.question: How much more powerful is a magnitude 8 earthquake compared to a magnitude 6?
probe.wrong_answer: It is about 2 units or 20% stronger.

root_belief: all scales increase linearly

subject: science
statement: A charged object cannot attract a neutral (uncharged) object.
why: Students believe that for an electrical force to exist, both objects must already have their own charge.
fix: A charged object can attract an uncharged object by inducing a temporary separation of charges in it.

probe.question: Why does a charged comb pick up tiny bits of uncharged paper?
probe.wrong_answer: The paper must have been secretly charged before the comb touched it.

root_belief: interactions require both parties to have the same property

subject: science
concept: Crust is made of tectonic plates
statement: Tectonic plates are the same thing as the continents.
why: Maps often show plates and continents together, and students only see the land above water.
fix: Tectonic plates are huge slabs of the crust that carry both continents and the ocean floor.

probe.question: Do tectonic plates exist under the Atlantic Ocean?
probe.wrong_answer: No, plates are just the land masses like Asia and Africa.

root_belief: only visible parts of a system exist

subject: science
statement: Seismographs are used to predict exactly when an earthquake will happen in the future.
why: Confusion between 'recording' an event and 'predicting' an event, similar to weather forecasts.
fix: Seismographs only record the waves of an earthquake that is already happening; we cannot yet predict earthquakes.

probe.question: What is the main purpose of a seismograph?
probe.wrong_answer: To give a warning several days before an earthquake starts.

root_belief: scientific instruments are for prediction

subject: science
statement: Static electricity is a 'different' kind of electricity than the one in our wires.
why: The different names ('static' vs 'current') and different sources (rubbing vs batteries) suggest two different substances.
fix: All electricity involves the same electric charges; 'static' just means the charges are not flowing in a continuous circuit.

probe.question: Is the charge on a rubbed balloon the same as the charge moving through a bulb's wire?
probe.wrong_answer: No, static electricity is a different natural force.

root_belief: different names mean different substances

subject: science
concept: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection
statement: The angle of incidence is the angle between the mirror surface and the incoming light ray.
why: Students often measure from the mirror surface because it is the most visible physical boundary.
fix: The angle of incidence is always measured between the incident ray and the normal, not the surface.

probe.question: If a light ray strikes a mirror at an angle of 20 degrees to the surface, what is the angle of incidence?
probe.wrong_answer: 20 degrees

root_belief: Surface is the primary reference frame

subject: science
concept: Laws apply to each point on a rough surface
statement: The laws of reflection do not apply to rough or irregular surfaces.
why: The irregular appearance of the surface makes students think the physical laws of light no longer apply.
fix: Laws of reflection apply to every single point on a rough surface, but the normals at different points are not parallel.

probe.question: Does the law 'angle of incidence = angle of reflection' hold true for light hitting a wooden table?
probe.wrong_answer: No

root_belief: Irregularity implies a lack of physical laws

subject: science
statement: Rough objects like paper or walls do not reflect light at all.
why: Students associate reflection only with mirrors and shiny objects that produce clear images.
fix: All objects reflect light; otherwise, we would not be able to see them.

probe.question: Why can you see a non-shiny book on your desk?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it is not reflecting any light.

root_belief: Only shiny objects reflect light

subject: science
statement: Our eyes send out invisible rays that allow us to see objects.
why: Everyday experience of looking makes it feel like the eye is actively doing something to the object.
fix: We see objects because they reflect light into our eyes, not because our eyes send light out.

probe.question: How do we see a tree during the day?
probe.wrong_answer: Our eyes send out rays that touch the tree.

root_belief: Perception is an active outward process

subject: science
statement: The pupil is a solid black spot or bead inside the eye.
why: The pupil looks like a solid black circle rather than an empty hole.
fix: The pupil is actually a small opening in the iris that allows light to enter the eye.

probe.question: What would happen if you tried to touch the pupil of an eye?
probe.wrong_answer: You would touch a solid black bead.

root_belief: Openings are perceived as solid objects

subject: science
statement: The lens inside the human eye is a rigid piece of glass-like material.
why: Students compare the eye lens to glass lenses in spectacles which are hard and rigid.
fix: The eye lens is a flexible, jelly-like material that changes shape to focus on objects at different distances.

probe.question: How does the eye lens change when looking at a nearby object?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays the same because it is made of hard material.

root_belief: Biological parts behave like rigid hardware

subject: science
statement: Rods and cones in the retina both help us see colors in bright light.
why: Students assume all sensory cells in the retina perform the same basic task of seeing.
fix: Cones are sensitive to bright light and color, while rods are sensitive to dim light.

probe.question: Which cells help us see in a very dark room?
probe.wrong_answer: Cones

root_belief: Related components have identical functions

subject: science
statement: Persistence of vision is a defect where the eye takes too long to clear an old image.
why: The term persistence is often used in everyday language to describe a delay or a stubborn error.
fix: Persistence of vision is a feature that allows us to see continuous motion by retaining an image for a fraction of a second.

probe.question: Why do movies look like they are moving instead of a series of still photos?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the eye is too slow to see the gaps.

root_belief: Processing delays are always system failures

subject: science
concept: Number of images depends on angle
statement: Two parallel mirrors produce a large but limited number of images.
why: It is difficult for students to conceptualize an infinite number of images in a finite space.
fix: Two parallel mirrors theoretically form an infinite number of images because light reflects back and forth indefinitely.

probe.question: If you stand between two parallel mirrors, how many images of yourself will you see?
probe.wrong_answer: Exactly ten.

root_belief: Physical infinity cannot exist in reality

subject: science
concept: Cornea is the transparent front part
statement: The cornea is only a protective layer and does not help in focusing light.
why: The cornea is the outermost part, so students assume its only role is to prevent injury.
fix: The cornea is the first and main part of the eye that refracts light to help focus it.

probe.question: Which part of the eye does the most work in bending light rays?
probe.wrong_answer: The lens only, as the cornea is just a cover.

root_belief: Outer layers serve only protective purposes

subject: science
concept: Blind spot has no sensory cells
statement: The blind spot is the part of the eye that is covered when we blink.
why: The word blind is associated with closing eyes or the inability to see anything at all.
fix: The blind spot is a specific point on the retina where the optic nerve leaves the eye and no light-sensitive cells exist.

probe.question: Can you see an image if it falls on the blind spot of your retina?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, but only if your eyes are open.

root_belief: Scientific terms mean their everyday literal sense

subject: science
statement: If a person can see distant stars clearly, they cannot have any eye defects.
why: Students believe that if the eye can perform one difficult task, it must be healthy.
fix: A person might see distant objects clearly but struggle with near objects, which is still an eye defect.

probe.question: If a student can read the blackboard from the back of the class but not a book, is their vision perfect?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they can see far away.

root_belief: One successful function implies total health

subject: science
concept: Incident ray, reflected ray, normal in same plane
statement: The reflected ray can be in a different plane than the incident ray and the normal.
why: Textbook diagrams are 2D, leading students to ignore the 3D nature of light rays.
fix: The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same flat plane.

probe.question: Can the reflected ray pop out of the plane formed by the incident ray and the normal?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if the mirror is tilted.

root_belief: Three-dimensional constraints are ignored in diagrams

subject: science
concept: Vitamin A is essential for eye health
statement: Eating carrots is the only way to get enough Vitamin A for eye health.
why: Carrots are the most famous example of eye-healthy food in popular culture.
fix: While carrots are good, Vitamin A is also found in green leafy vegetables, milk, eggs, and papaya.

probe.question: What is the only food you should eat to improve night vision?
probe.wrong_answer: Carrots

root_belief: One specific food is the sole nutrient source

subject: science
statement: The Moon produces its own light like a bulb.
why: The Moon appears very bright in the dark sky, leading students to think it is a source of light.
fix: The Moon is a non-luminous object that only reflects the sunlight falling on it.

probe.question: If the Sun were to suddenly disappear, would we still see a bright Moon at night?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the Moon has its own light.

root_belief: Objects that shine produce light
source_hint: HBCSE diagnostic studies on celestial objects

subject: science
statement: Moon phases are caused by the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.
why: Students confuse phases with lunar eclipses because both involve darkness on the Moon.
fix: Phases occur because we only see the part of the Moon's illuminated half that faces Earth as it orbits us.

probe.question: What causes the change in the shape of the Moon every night?
probe.wrong_answer: The Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, casting a shadow.

root_belief: Shadows cause all darkness in space

subject: science
statement: Stars go away or disappear during the daytime.
why: Stars are not visible during the day due to the Sun's glare, so students assume they are gone.
fix: Stars are always in the sky, but they are hidden during the day by the bright light of the Sun.

probe.question: Where do the stars go when the Sun rises?
probe.wrong_answer: They move to the other side of the Earth or disappear.

root_belief: What you cannot see does not exist
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
statement: The Pole Star is the brightest star in the night sky.
why: Because the Pole Star is famous and important for navigation, students assume it must be the brightest.
fix: The Pole Star is only of average brightness; Sirius is actually the brightest star in the night sky.

probe.question: How can you identify the Pole Star in the sky?
probe.wrong_answer: By looking for the single brightest point of light in the sky.

root_belief: Importance implies intensity

subject: science
statement: Stars actually move across the sky from East to West.
why: We see stars rising in the East and setting in the West, just like the Sun.
fix: Stars appear to move because the Earth is rotating on its axis from West to East.

probe.question: Why do stars change their position in the sky during the night?
probe.wrong_answer: Because stars are revolving around the Earth.

root_belief: Perception is reality

subject: science
statement: The Sun is not a star because it looks different and is much larger.
why: The Sun appears as a huge, hot disc while stars appear as tiny twinkling dots.
fix: The Sun is a medium-sized star that only looks large because it is much closer to Earth than other stars.

probe.question: Is the Sun a star?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the Sun is a sun and stars are those tiny things at night.

root_belief: Apparent size is actual size

subject: science
statement: Shooting stars are actual stars falling from the sky.
why: The term 'shooting star' suggests a star is moving or falling.
fix: Shooting stars are actually meteors—small pieces of rock entering Earth's atmosphere and burning up.

probe.question: What is a shooting star made of?
probe.wrong_answer: It is a star that has lost its balance and fallen.

root_belief: Everyday language is scientifically accurate

subject: science
statement: Stars in a constellation are all at the same distance from Earth.
why: They appear to be on a flat 2D plane (the sky) forming a pattern.
fix: Stars in a constellation are at vastly different distances from us; they only look close together from our perspective.

probe.question: Are the stars in the Big Dipper close to each other in space?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they are a group located in the same spot in the universe.

root_belief: Visual proximity implies physical proximity

subject: science
statement: Planets twinkle just like stars do.
why: Planets look like bright dots in the sky, so students group them with stars.
fix: Planets do not twinkle because they are much closer and appear as tiny discs rather than point sources of light.

probe.question: How can you tell a planet apart from a star in the night sky?
probe.wrong_answer: You can't, because both of them twinkle at night.

root_belief: Distant lights are all the same

subject: science
statement: Earth is the only planet that has a moon.
why: Students often refer to Earth's satellite as 'The Moon' and don't realize other planets have them too.
fix: Many planets in our solar system, like Jupiter and Saturn, have many natural satellites (moons).

probe.question: Do other planets have moons?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only Earth has a moon to give it light at night.

root_belief: Local experience is universal

subject: science
statement: The Moon changes shape because clouds cover parts of it.
why: Clouds often block the moon, and students associate covering an object with changing its visible shape.
fix: Moon phases are independent of weather; they are caused by the Moon's position relative to the Sun and Earth.

probe.question: If there were no clouds for a whole month, would the Moon still change shape?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it would stay a full circle the whole time.

root_belief: Visible changes are due to local obstructions
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
statement: Stars are smaller than the Sun and the Moon.
why: Stars appear as tiny specks, while the Sun and Moon appear much larger in the sky.
fix: Most stars are actually much larger than the Sun and millions of times larger than the Moon.

probe.question: Which is actually larger: the Sun or the stars we see at night?
probe.wrong_answer: The Sun is much larger than those tiny stars.

root_belief: Apparent size is actual size

subject: science
statement: Planets move in perfect circles around the Sun.
why: Simplified diagrams in textbooks often show orbits as perfect circles.
fix: Planetary orbits are actually elliptical (oval-shaped), not perfect circles.

probe.question: What is the shape of the path a planet takes around the Sun?
probe.wrong_answer: It is a perfect circle.

root_belief: Simplified diagrams are literal

subject: science
statement: Displacement and distance are always the same value.
why: Students ignore the path taken and only look at the total length covered in everyday contexts.
fix: Distance is the total path length, while displacement is only the straight-line distance between the start and end points.

probe.question: An athlete runs one full lap of a 400m circular track. What is their displacement?
probe.wrong_answer: 400 meters

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: Displacement cannot be zero if an object has moved.
why: In everyday language, 'displaced' means something was moved from its original spot and stayed elsewhere.
fix: If the initial and final positions are the same, the displacement is zero regardless of the distance traveled.

probe.question: You go to school and come back home. What is your net displacement?
probe.wrong_answer: The distance from home to school and back.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
concept: Velocity is displacement per unit time
statement: Velocity is just another word for speed.
why: In common conversation, speed and velocity are used interchangeably.
fix: Velocity is speed with a specific direction; it changes if either the speed or the direction changes.

probe.question: A car travels at 50 km/h North and another at 50 km/h South. Do they have the same velocity?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because both are going at 50 km/h.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
concept: Velocity is displacement per unit time
statement: If an object's speed is constant, its velocity must be constant.
why: Students focus on the numerical value (magnitude) and ignore the directional component of velocity.
fix: Velocity changes if the direction of motion changes, even if the speed remains the same.

probe.question: A car turns a corner at a constant speed of 20 km/h. Is its velocity constant?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the speed is not changing.

root_belief: one property defines the whole concept

subject: science
concept: Acceleration is change in velocity over time
statement: Acceleration only means an object is speeding up.
why: The word 'accelerate' in cars and daily life specifically refers to increasing speed.
fix: Acceleration is any change in velocity, which includes speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction.

probe.question: A car applies brakes to slow down. Is it accelerating?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is decelerating, which is not acceleration.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
concept: Acceleration is change in velocity over time
statement: Zero acceleration means the object is not moving.
why: Students confuse the rate of change of motion with the motion itself.
fix: Zero acceleration means the velocity is constant; the object could be moving at a very high speed.

probe.question: A spaceship moves in deep space at 10,000 km/h with its engines off. What is its acceleration?

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: science
statement: Negative acceleration always means the object is moving backwards.
why: Students associate the negative sign with the direction of the velocity rather than the change in velocity.
fix: Negative acceleration means the acceleration vector points in the opposite direction of the chosen positive axis; it often means slowing down.

probe.question: If a car moving East (positive) slows down, what is the sign of its acceleration?
probe.wrong_answer: Positive, because it is still moving East.

root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

subject: science
statement: A distance-time graph shows the actual physical path of the object.
why: Students interpret the shape of the line as a map of the road or track.
fix: The graph shows how distance changes over time, not the spatial direction of the movement.

probe.question: A distance-time graph shows a hill shape. Does this mean the object went up a hill?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the object moved upwards and then downwards.

root_belief: what you see is what it is

subject: science
statement: A horizontal line on a velocity-time graph means the object is at rest.
why: Students carry over the rule from distance-time graphs where a flat line means no movement.
fix: A horizontal line on a v-t graph means the velocity is constant and not zero.

probe.question: A v-t graph shows a straight horizontal line at v = 5 m/s. Is the object moving?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is stationary.

root_belief: a rule from one context works everywhere

subject: science
statement: The equations of motion can be used for any moving object.
why: Students apply formulas without checking the underlying assumptions or constraints.
fix: The three equations of motion (v=u+at, etc.) only apply when acceleration is uniform (constant).

probe.question: Can we use s = ut + 1/2 at^2 for a car whose acceleration is changing every second?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, as long as we know the average acceleration.

root_belief: a rule from one context works everywhere

subject: science
statement: An object in uniform circular motion has zero acceleration because its speed is constant.
why: Students believe acceleration only exists if the speedometer reading changes.
fix: In circular motion, the direction changes constantly, which means the velocity changes, so there is acceleration.

probe.question: A stone is whirled in a circle at a constant speed of 2 m/s. Is it accelerating?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the speed is not increasing or decreasing.

root_belief: one property defines the whole concept

subject: science
concept: Area under v-t graph is displacement
statement: The area under a graph is always measured in square meters (area units).
why: Students confuse the geometric calculation of area with the physical quantity it represents.
fix: The area under a graph represents the product of the quantities on the x and y axes; for a v-t graph, this is displacement (meters).

probe.question: What does the area under a velocity (m/s) vs time (s) graph represent?
probe.wrong_answer: The surface area of the path.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: If an object is at rest, no forces are acting on it.
why: Students only recognize active forces like pushing and ignore passive forces like gravity or normal force.
fix: An object at rest has multiple forces acting on it, but their vector sum (net force) is zero.

probe.question: A book is lying on a table. What forces are acting on it?
probe.wrong_answer: No forces are acting on it because it is not moving.

root_belief: What you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: An object needs a continuous force to keep moving at a constant velocity.
why: In daily life, friction always slows things down, making it seem like force is required for motion.
fix: Force is only needed to change velocity; an object will continue moving at a constant speed in a straight line if net force is zero.

probe.question: A spacecraft is moving in deep space far from stars. What force is needed to keep it at 100 km/s?
probe.wrong_answer: A constant force is needed to maintain that speed.

root_belief: Motion implies a continuous cause

subject: science
statement: Inertia is a force that keeps things moving.
why: Students treat inertia as an 'internal force' or impetus that an object carries.
fix: Inertia is not a force; it is an inherent property of matter that describes its resistance to changes in motion.

probe.question: Why does a ball keep rolling after you stop pushing it?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the force of inertia is still pushing it forward.

root_belief: A word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: Heavier objects have more inertia only when they are moving.
why: Students associate inertia with the difficulty of stopping something, rather than the difficulty of starting it.
fix: Inertia depends only on mass and is present whether the object is at rest or in motion.

probe.question: Does a heavy boulder have inertia while it is sitting still on the ground?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it only gets inertia once it starts moving.

root_belief: Properties only exist during activity

subject: science
statement: Momentum and force are the same thing.
why: Both terms are used interchangeably in everyday language to describe 'impact' or 'strength'.
fix: Momentum is a state of motion (mv), while force is the agent that changes that state (rate of change of momentum).

probe.question: If a truck has a lot of momentum, does it automatically mean a large force is acting on it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, high momentum means there is a high force inside the truck.

root_belief: A word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: A constant force produces a constant velocity.
why: Students fail to distinguish between velocity and acceleration, thinking a steady push results in a steady speed.
fix: A constant unbalanced force produces a constant acceleration, meaning the velocity increases at a steady rate.

probe.question: If you keep pushing a crate with a constant net force, what happens to its speed?
probe.wrong_answer: The speed will stay constant as long as the force is constant.

root_belief: One event has one single cause

subject: science
statement: In a collision between a truck and a car, the truck exerts a larger force on the car.
why: Students believe that the object with more mass or more 'strength' must exert more force.
fix: According to the Third Law, both objects exert equal and opposite forces on each other regardless of their mass.

probe.question: A massive truck hits a small parked car. Which one experiences the greater force?
probe.wrong_answer: The truck exerts a greater force because it is much heavier.

root_belief: Bigger or more means more effect

subject: science
statement: Action and reaction forces cancel each other out.
why: Students think that because the forces are equal and opposite, they must result in a net force of zero.
fix: Action and reaction forces never cancel because they act on two different objects.

probe.question: If the cart pulls back on the horse as hard as the horse pulls the cart, how can the horse move the cart?
probe.wrong_answer: They cancel out, so the horse must pull slightly harder to start moving.

root_belief: One event has one single target

subject: science
statement: Passive objects like floors or tables cannot exert a force.
why: Students believe only living things or 'active' machines can exert a push or pull.
fix: Any surface that is compressed or deformed exerts a normal force in response to an applied force.

probe.question: When you stand on the floor, does the floor push up on you?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the floor is just in the way; it doesn't actually push.

root_belief: Only living things can exert force

subject: science
statement: Momentum is not conserved if the objects stick together after a collision.
why: Students confuse the loss of kinetic energy (inelastic collision) with the loss of momentum.
fix: Total momentum is conserved in all isolated systems, even if the objects stick together or change shape.

probe.question: Two lumps of clay collide and stick together. Is the total momentum before equal to the total momentum after?
probe.wrong_answer: No, momentum is lost because they stopped moving relative to each other.

root_belief: Change of form means loss of property

subject: science
statement: Force is a property of an object that it carries and uses up.
why: Students confuse force with energy or 'oomph' that an object possesses.
fix: Force is an interaction between two objects, not something an object 'has' or 'carries'.

probe.question: When a bowler throws a cricket ball, does the ball carry the 'force' of the throw with it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the ball carries the force until it hits the bat and uses it up.

root_belief: Force is an internal property

subject: science
statement: The reaction force happens slightly after the action force.
why: The names 'action' and 'reaction' suggest a cause-and-effect sequence in time.
fix: Action and reaction forces are perfectly simultaneous; they are two parts of a single interaction.

probe.question: When you kick a ball, when does the ball exert a force on your foot?
probe.wrong_answer: A split second after you kick it, as a reaction.

root_belief: Events in a pair must be sequential

subject: science
concept: Force proportional to product of masses
statement: Gravity only exists between planets or very large celestial bodies.
why: Students only hear about gravity in the context of Earth, the Moon, or the Sun in textbooks.
fix: Every object in the universe with mass attracts every other object with mass, no matter how small.

probe.question: Does a pen on your desk exert a gravitational force on you?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the pen is too small to have gravity.

root_belief: only large things have significant properties

subject: science
concept: Force inversely proportional to square of distance
statement: Earth's gravity ends as soon as you leave the atmosphere.
why: Students see videos of 'weightless' astronauts and assume gravity has vanished.
fix: Gravity extends infinitely into space, though it gets weaker with distance; astronauts are actually in free fall.

probe.question: If a satellite is orbiting just above the atmosphere, is Earth's gravity acting on it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is in space where there is no gravity.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
concept: g is independent of falling object's mass
statement: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter objects in a vacuum.
why: Everyday experience with air resistance (feathers vs stones) creates a strong intuition.
fix: In the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration 'g' regardless of mass.

probe.question: If a 10kg iron ball and a 1kg iron ball are dropped together in a vacuum, which hits first?
probe.wrong_answer: The 10kg ball because it is heavier.

root_belief: more mass means more speed

subject: science
statement: Mass and weight are the same thing and can be used interchangeably.
why: In everyday language, people use 'weight' when they mean 'mass' (e.g., 'my weight is 60 kg').
fix: Mass is the quantity of matter and is scalar; weight is the force of gravity acting on that mass and is a vector.

probe.question: What is the SI unit of weight?
probe.wrong_answer: Kilogram (kg).

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
concept: Mass is constant across the universe
statement: Your mass would change if you went to the Moon.
why: Students confuse the feeling of being 'lighter' with having less 'stuff' in their body.
fix: Mass is a constant property of an object; only the gravitational pull (weight) changes on the Moon.

probe.question: If your mass is 50kg on Earth, what is your mass on the Moon?
probe.wrong_answer: It would be less than 50kg.

root_belief: properties change when the environment changes

subject: science
statement: A large flat board exerts more pressure on the ground than a small sharp nail if pushed with the same force.
why: Students associate 'larger size' with 'more pressure' because the object looks more imposing.
fix: Pressure is force divided by area; a smaller area results in much higher pressure for the same force.

probe.question: Why does a sharp needle pierce skin easily compared to a blunt rod?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the needle is smaller and has less resistance.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: science
concept: Buoyant force equals weight of displaced fluid
statement: The buoyant force on an object depends on the object's weight.
why: Students think heavy objects 'push back' harder against the water.
fix: Buoyant force depends only on the volume of the displaced fluid and the fluid's density, not the object's mass.

probe.question: Two balls of the same size, one lead and one plastic, are submerged. Which has more buoyant force?
probe.wrong_answer: The lead ball because it is heavier.

root_belief: the object is the sole cause of the force

subject: science
statement: Heavy objects always sink and light objects always float.
why: Observations of small stones sinking while large logs float are often misinterpreted by ignoring density.
fix: Sinking or floating depends on the density of the object relative to the fluid, not its total mass.

probe.question: Will a massive wooden log float or sink in a lake?
probe.wrong_answer: Sink, because it is very heavy.

root_belief: heaviness causes sinking

subject: science
statement: Objects lose mass when they are submerged in water.
why: Objects feel easier to lift in water, so students think the 'matter' has decreased.
fix: Objects only lose 'apparent weight' due to the upward buoyant force; their actual mass remains unchanged.

probe.question: If you weigh a stone in water, why does the scale show a lower reading?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the water dissolves some of its mass or makes it lighter.

root_belief: feelings represent physical changes in matter

subject: science
statement: There is no gravity in a vacuum.
why: Students confuse the absence of air with the absence of gravitational fields.
fix: Gravity is an interaction between masses and does not require a medium like air to act.

probe.question: If we pump all the air out of a room, will you float to the ceiling?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because there is no gravity in a vacuum.

root_belief: forces need a medium to travel

subject: science
concept: Force inversely proportional to square of distance
statement: The gravitational force between two objects doubles if the distance between them is halved.
why: Students assume a linear relationship rather than an inverse-square relationship.
fix: According to the inverse square law, if the distance is halved, the force becomes four times stronger.

probe.question: If the distance between two masses is reduced to half, what happens to the force?
probe.wrong_answer: The force doubles.

root_belief: relationships are always linear

subject: science
statement: Fluids only exert pressure in the downward direction.
why: Students associate pressure with weight, which they know acts downwards.
fix: Fluid pressure acts in all directions at any given point within the fluid.

probe.question: Does water in a bucket push against the side walls?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it only pushes on the bottom because of its weight.

root_belief: gravity only works downwards

subject: science
statement: If I push a heavy wall until I am exhausted, I have done a lot of work.
why: Students confuse biological effort and fatigue with the physics definition of work.
fix: In physics, work is only done when a force causes a displacement; if the wall doesn't move, work is zero.

probe.question: A student pushes a stationary truck for 1 hour but it doesn't budge. How much work is done?
probe.wrong_answer: A large amount of work because the student is tired.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
statement: A coolie carrying a suitcase on his head while walking horizontally is doing work on the suitcase.
why: Students see movement and force and assume work must be happening.
fix: Work is zero when the force (upward) is perpendicular to the displacement (horizontal).

probe.question: A person holds a 10kg box and walks 5m on a level floor. What is the work done by the lifting force?
probe.wrong_answer: 50 Joules

root_belief: effort equals work

subject: science
statement: If the speed of a car doubles, its kinetic energy also doubles.
why: Students often assume linear relationships between variables.
fix: Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of velocity, so doubling speed quadruples the energy.

probe.question: A car's speed increases from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. By what factor does its KE change?
probe.wrong_answer: It doubles.

root_belief: linear relationships apply to everything

subject: science
statement: Potential energy depends on the path taken to reach a certain height.
why: Students think a longer path (like a ramp) requires more energy to overcome.
fix: Gravitational potential energy depends only on the vertical height difference, not the path taken.

probe.question: Object A is lifted vertically 2m. Object B is pushed up a 5m ramp to the same 2m height. Which has more PE?
probe.wrong_answer: Object B because the path is longer.

root_belief: the process determines the final state

subject: science
statement: When a moving ball comes to a stop on the floor, its energy is destroyed.
why: Students cannot see the heat or sound energy, so they assume the energy vanished.
fix: Energy is never destroyed; it transforms into other forms like heat due to friction and sound.

probe.question: A rolling ball stops due to friction. Where did its kinetic energy go?
probe.wrong_answer: It was used up and now it is gone.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: A person who finishes a job faster has done more work than a slower person.
why: Students confuse the rate of doing work (power) with the total amount of work.
fix: Work depends only on force and displacement; time only affects the power.

probe.question: Anil climbs stairs in 10s. Sunil climbs the same stairs in 20s. Who did more work?

root_belief: faster means more

subject: science
statement: The kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a unit of power.
why: The presence of the word 'watt' leads students to associate it with power.
fix: kWh is a unit of energy (Power x Time), used for commercial electricity billing.

probe.question: Your electricity bill says you used 50 units (kWh). What physical quantity is this?

root_belief: similar names mean similar things

subject: science
statement: Only living things or machines have energy.
why: Students associate energy with the ability to move or 'life force'.
fix: All objects, living or non-living, can possess energy based on their motion or position.

probe.question: Does a non-living rock sitting on a cliff have energy?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is not alive and not moving.

root_belief: only active things have properties

subject: science
statement: An object on the ground has zero potential energy.
why: Students treat the ground as an absolute zero for energy.
fix: Potential energy is relative; an object on the ground still has PE relative to a basement or a pit.

probe.question: If we dig a hole next to a ball on the ground, does the ball's potential energy change relative to the hole?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is zero because it is on the ground.

root_belief: zero is an absolute floor

subject: science
statement: Work cannot be negative because it is not a vector.
why: Students confuse the scalar nature of work with the inability to have a negative value.
fix: Work is a scalar, but it can be negative if the force and displacement are in opposite directions.

probe.question: What is the sign of work done by friction on a sliding block?
probe.wrong_answer: Positive, because work is a scalar.

root_belief: scalars cannot be negative

subject: science
statement: Batteries and fuels create energy.
why: Language like 'generating power' or 'producing energy' suggests creation from nothing.
fix: Batteries and fuels only transform stored chemical energy into other forms like electrical or heat energy.

probe.question: Where does the energy in a battery come from?
probe.wrong_answer: The battery creates it when you turn it on.

root_belief: sources create things from nothing

subject: science
statement: A more powerful engine always does more work than a less powerful one.
why: Students equate 'power' with 'strength' or 'total capacity'.
fix: A more powerful engine does work faster, but a less powerful engine can do more total work if it runs for a longer time.

probe.question: Engine A (100W) runs for 1 hour. Engine B (500W) runs for 1 minute. Which did more work?
probe.wrong_answer: Engine B because it is more powerful.

root_belief: strength and power are the same

subject: science
statement: Air particles travel from the speaker's mouth to the listener's ear.
why: Students confuse the motion of the wave with the motion of the medium, similar to wind.
fix: Particles only vibrate back and forth about their mean position; it is the energy/disturbance that travels.

probe.question: If a bell rings in a room, do the air molecules near the bell eventually reach your ear?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they carry the sound to my ear.

root_belief: matter moves with the energy

subject: science
statement: Sound waves move up and down like waves on a string.
why: Textbooks represent sound using sine graphs, which students interpret as the physical shape of the wave.
fix: Sound is a longitudinal wave where particles move parallel to the direction of wave travel, not perpendicular.

probe.question: In which direction do air particles move relative to the direction of a sound wave?
probe.wrong_answer: They move up and down at right angles to the wave.

root_belief: visual representations are literal reality

subject: science
statement: Sound travels faster in air than in solids because solids are too dense to move through.
why: Students apply their experience of walking through air vs. water/solids to sound.
fix: Sound travels fastest in solids because the particles are closer together, allowing the disturbance to transfer more quickly.

probe.question: Will sound travel faster through a steel rod or through the air?
probe.wrong_answer: Through the air because it is thinner.

root_belief: less dense means less resistance to motion
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
statement: A high pitch sound is always louder than a low pitch sound.
why: Students use 'high' and 'low' interchangeably for both volume and frequency in everyday speech.
fix: Pitch depends on frequency, while loudness depends on amplitude; they are independent properties.

probe.question: If you whistle very softly but at a high note, is it necessarily louder than a deep drum beat?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because high notes are more powerful.

root_belief: different properties are actually the same

subject: science
statement: If you increase the frequency of a sound, its speed increases.
why: Students think 'vibrating faster' must mean 'moving forward faster'.
fix: The speed of sound is constant in a given medium; increasing frequency results in a shorter wavelength.

probe.question: If a singer hits a higher note, does that sound reach the back of the hall sooner than a lower note?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, higher frequencies travel faster.

root_belief: faster vibration means faster travel

subject: science
statement: Sound can travel through space if the explosion is big enough.
why: Science fiction movies often show loud explosions in space.
fix: Sound is a mechanical wave and requires a material medium to propagate; it cannot travel through a vacuum.

probe.question: Can astronauts on the moon hear a nearby rock crash without using radios?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if the crash is loud enough to cross the gap.

root_belief: more of one thing means more of another

subject: science
statement: A rarefaction is a region where there are no air particles at all.
why: Students interpret 'low pressure' or 'low density' as 'empty'.
fix: Rarefaction is a region where particles are spread further apart than average, but they are still present.

probe.question: What is inside a rarefaction in an air-borne sound wave?
probe.wrong_answer: A vacuum or empty space.

root_belief: low density means nothingness

subject: science
statement: Echoes only occur in large empty halls or mountains.
why: These are the only places where the time delay is long enough for humans to distinguish the echo.
fix: Sound reflects off almost all surfaces, but we only hear an 'echo' if the reflected sound reaches us after 0.1 seconds.

probe.question: Does sound reflect off the walls of a small furnished bedroom?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because there is no echo in a small room.

root_belief: phenomena only occur in extreme settings

subject: science
statement: Ultrasound is just very loud sound that can damage ears.
why: The prefix 'ultra' is associated with 'extreme' or 'extra' in common usage.
fix: Ultrasound refers to sound with a frequency higher than 20,000 Hz, which is beyond the human hearing range regardless of loudness.

probe.question: What makes a sound 'ultrasound'?
probe.wrong_answer: It is sound that is so loud it is dangerous.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: Humans can hear ultrasound if it is played at a very high volume.
why: Students believe the limit of hearing is based on intensity rather than biological frequency response.
fix: The human ear is biologically incapable of detecting frequencies above 20 kHz, no matter how loud they are.

probe.question: If we turn up the volume of a 30,000 Hz signal, will you eventually hear it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it will become audible once it is loud enough.

subject: science
statement: The speed of sound is a universal constant like the speed of light.
why: Students often memorize '344 m/s' as a fixed number without considering environmental factors.
fix: The speed of sound changes significantly with temperature, humidity, and the nature of the medium.

probe.question: Does sound travel at the same speed on a hot summer day and a cold winter night?

root_belief: physical properties are independent of environment

subject: science
statement: Loudness is determined by how fast the source is vibrating.
why: Confusion between the 'strength' of a vibration (amplitude) and the 'speed' of vibration (frequency).
fix: Loudness is determined by the amplitude of the vibration, while the speed of vibration determines the pitch.

probe.question: If you hit a drum harder, what property of the vibration are you primarily changing?

subject: science
statement: The image formed by a mirror is located on the surface of the mirror.
why: Students see the reflection 'on' the glass and do not perceive the depth of the virtual or real image.

probe.question: If you move closer to a plane mirror, where does your image move?

root_belief: what you see is where it is

subject: science
statement: Virtual images cannot be seen because they are not real.
why: The word 'virtual' in everyday language implies something that doesn't exist or is fake.
fix: Virtual images can be seen by the eye because the eye's lens converges the diverging rays onto the retina.

probe.question: Can you see your own reflection in a mirror? Is it real or virtual?

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: The object distance 'u' is always positive because the object is a real physical thing.
why: Students confuse physical existence with the mathematical sign convention.
fix: According to the Cartesian sign convention, the object is placed to the left of the mirror, making 'u' always negative.

probe.question: An object is 10cm from a mirror. What value of 'u' do you use in the formula?

root_belief: positive numbers represent real physical presence

subject: science
statement: A negative magnification means the image is smaller than the object.
why: In mathematics, negative numbers are smaller than positive numbers.

probe.question: If magnification is -2, is the image enlarged or diminished?

subject: science
statement: Light bends inside the second medium, not at the boundary.
why: Students often draw curved paths or delayed bending in ray diagrams.
fix: Refraction is the change in direction that occurs exactly at the interface of two media with different optical densities.

probe.question: Where does light change its path when entering water from air?

root_belief: processes happen over space not instantly

subject: science
statement: If you cover the top half of a lens, you will only see the bottom half of the image.
why: Students believe each part of the lens is responsible for a specific part of the object.
fix: Every part of the lens forms the whole image; covering half only reduces the brightness of the full image.

probe.question: What happens to the image of a tree if you block the upper half of the lens with black paper?
probe.wrong_answer: The top of the tree disappears from the image.

root_belief: parts of cause create parts of effect

subject: science
statement: Light rays stop at the point where the image is formed.
why: Ray diagrams usually end at the image point, leading to the belief that light is 'consumed'.
fix: Light rays continue to travel past the image point unless blocked by a screen.

probe.question: If you place your eye exactly at the image position of a real image, what do you see?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, because the light has stopped there.

subject: science
statement: A lens with a higher power has a longer focal length.
why: The word 'power' suggests 'bigger' or 'longer' dimensions.

probe.question: Which lens is more powerful: one with f=10cm or f=20cm?

subject: science
statement: The lens formula is exactly the same as the mirror formula.
why: The formulas look very similar and students fail to distinguish the sign between terms.
fix: The mirror formula uses addition (1/v + 1/u) while the lens formula uses subtraction (1/v - 1/u).

probe.question: Write the relationship between u, v, and f for a thin convex lens.

root_belief: a rule from one context works everywhere

subject: science
statement: Focal length is the distance from the object to the mirror's focus.
why: Students confuse the 'focus' as a point relative to the object rather than the mirror.
fix: Focal length is the fixed distance between the Pole of the mirror and its Principal Focus.

probe.question: If you move the object further away, what happens to the focal length of the mirror?

subject: science
statement: Light only refracts when it enters a liquid like water.
why: Common classroom examples often use water or glass blocks, and air is seen as 'nothing'.
fix: Refraction occurs whenever light passes between any two media of different optical densities, including air to glass or air to oil.

probe.question: Does light bend when it passes from air into a solid diamond?

root_belief: only specific materials have specific properties

subject: science
statement: Concave lenses can form real images if the object is placed very far away.

probe.question: Where should you place an object to get a real image from a concave lens?

root_belief: similar names imply similar functions

subject: science
statement: Convex mirrors are used in solar furnaces to concentrate sunlight.

fix: Concave mirrors are converging and used in solar furnaces; convex mirrors are diverging.

probe.question: Which mirror would you use to start a fire using sunlight?
probe.wrong_answer: A convex mirror because it is curved outwards.

root_belief: words that sound similar are interchangeable

subject: science
statement: Light slows down in glass because it has to weave through the atoms.
why: Students apply macroscopic mechanical intuition (like walking through a crowd) to light.
fix: Light slows down due to the interaction of the electromagnetic wave with the electrons of the medium, not by physical 'weaving'.

probe.question: Why is the speed of light less in glass than in vacuum?

topic: The human eye and the colourful world
subject: science
statement: The eye lens moves forward and backward to focus on objects at different distances.
why: Students overgeneralize from how mechanical camera lenses or magnifying glasses are used.

source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

topic: The human eye and the colourful world
subject: science
statement: A person with myopia cannot see distant objects at all.
why: Students use everyday language where 'cannot see' implies total blindness for those objects.

probe.question: What does a myopic person see when looking at a far-off mountain?

topic: The human eye and the colourful world
subject: science
statement: Hypermetropic eyes see distant objects perfectly without any muscular effort.

probe.question: Does a hypermetropic eye need to adjust its lens to see a distant star?

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

topic: The human eye and the colourful world
subject: science
statement: A glass prism adds colors to the white light passing through it.
why: Students observe colors appearing where there were none, assuming the prism is the source.
fix: White light already contains all colors; the prism only separates them by refracting different wavelengths at different angles.

probe.question: Where do the colors in a spectrum come from?

topic: The human eye and the colourful world
subject: science
statement: A rainbow is a physical object located at a specific spot in the sky.
why: Its distinct shape and appearance make it look like a solid arch.

probe.question: If you walk toward a rainbow, can you eventually reach its base?

root_belief: what you see is a physical object

topic: The human eye and the colourful world
subject: science
statement: Stars twinkle because their actual brightness keeps changing.
why: Students assume the observed change in the product (light) must be due to a change in the source.
fix: Twinkling is caused by the continuous changing of the Earth's atmospheric density, which refracts star light randomly.

probe.question: Why do stars twinkle but planets usually do not?

topic: The human eye and the colourful world
subject: science
statement: We see the sun at its actual physical position during sunrise.
why: The brain assumes light travels in perfectly straight lines from the source to the eye.

topic: The human eye and the colourful world
subject: science
statement: The sky is blue because it reflects the color of the ocean.

topic: The human eye and the colourful world
subject: science
statement: The sun turns red at sunset because it is cooling down as the day ends.
why: Intuitive reasoning that red color is associated with lower heat or embers of a fire.

probe.question: Why does the sun look white at noon but red at sunset?

topic: The human eye and the colourful world
subject: science
statement: Concave lenses are used to treat far-sightedness because they make things look bigger.
why: Confusion between the names of lenses and the names of the defects they correct.

probe.question: Which lens would you give to someone who cannot see distant objects clearly?

topic: The human eye and the colourful world
subject: science
statement: The eye lens becomes thinner and flatter to focus on nearby objects.
why: Students confuse the relationship between lens thickness and focal length.

probe.question: What happens to the shape of the eye lens when you read a book closely?

topic: The human eye and the colourful world
subject: science
statement: Light is only scattered by large particles like dust and smoke.

subject: science
concept: Current is rate of flow of charge
statement: The current coming out of a bulb is less than the current going into it.
why: Students think of electricity as a fuel that is consumed to produce light.

probe.question: In a simple circuit with one bulb, how does the current at the positive terminal compare to the negative terminal?

subject: science
concept: Potential difference is work per unit charge

subject: science

subject: science
statement: If you cut a wire in half, its resistivity also becomes half.

subject: science
statement: In a series circuit, the bulb closer to the positive terminal glows brighter because it gets the current first.

subject: science

subject: science

probe.question: If you could capture all the smoke and ash from a burnt log, how would its weight compare to the original log and oxygen used?
probe.wrong_answer: It would weigh much less because most of the wood disappeared.

root_belief: matter can be destroyed or disappear

subject: science
statement: Boiling water is a chemical change because bubbles are formed.
why: Students are taught that gas evolution (bubbles) is a sign of a chemical change.
fix: In boiling, the bubbles are just water vapor (the same substance in gas form), so it is a physical change of state.

probe.question: Are the bubbles in boiling water a new substance being formed?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the water is turning into a new gas chemical.

root_belief: one sign always indicates one specific process

subject: science
statement: Melting and freezing are chemical changes because the substance looks different.
why: Students focus on the dramatic change in appearance between a solid and a liquid.
fix: Melting and freezing are physical changes because the chemical identity of the substance (e.g., H2O) remains the same.

probe.question: When ice melts into water, has a new substance been formed?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because ice is hard and water is liquid; they are different things.

root_belief: change in appearance means change in identity

subject: science
statement: Crystallisation is a chemical change because a new solid is created.
why: The sudden appearance of solid crystals from a clear solution looks like a chemical reaction.
fix: Crystallisation is a physical change used to purify substances; the substance in the crystal is the same as the one that was dissolved.

probe.question: When copper sulphate crystals form from a solution, is it a chemical change?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because a new solid material was produced.

root_belief: appearance of solid means new substance

subject: science
statement: Stainless steel does not rust because it is painted with a special coating.
why: Students are familiar with painting iron to prevent rust and assume all rust-prevention is a surface coating.
fix: Stainless steel is an alloy made by mixing iron with chromium and nickel; it resists rusting because of its internal composition.

probe.question: If you scratch a stainless steel spoon, will the scratched part start to rust?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the protective paint layer is gone.

root_belief: internal properties are caused by external coatings

subject: science
statement: A change in color always proves a new substance has formed.
why: Color change is a primary indicator taught for chemical reactions.
fix: While color change often indicates a chemical change, it can also be physical, like mixing paints or food coloring in water.

probe.question: If you mix blue ink into water and the water turns blue, is that a chemical change?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the color changed from clear to blue.

root_belief: one indicator is sufficient for a conclusion

subject: science
statement: Rust is just a layer of dirt that sticks to the iron.
why: Rust looks like a brown, flaky coating similar to dried mud or dirt.
fix: Rust is a new chemical substance called iron oxide that forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water.

probe.question: Can you turn rust back into iron simply by washing it with soap and water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is just dirt on the surface.

root_belief: new substances are just dirty versions of old ones

subject: science
statement: A chemical change only happens if you see an explosion or fire.
why: Dramatic examples like burning magnesium or crackers are more memorable than slow changes.
fix: Many chemical changes are slow and quiet, such as the digestion of food or the rusting of an iron gate.

probe.question: Is the digestion of food in our stomach a chemical change?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because there is no heat or fire produced.

root_belief: chemical changes must be dramatic and visible

subject: science
statement: All acids are dangerous and corrosive chemicals.
why: Students associate the word 'acid' with media portrayals of burning or industrial hazards.
fix: Many acids are found in food, like citric acid in lemons or lactic acid in curd, and are safe to consume.

probe.question: Is Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) a dangerous chemical?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because all acids are dangerous.

root_belief: labels describe the whole object

subject: science
statement: Acids are always liquids.
why: Most classroom experiments use aqueous solutions of acids.
fix: Acids can exist as solids, like citric acid crystals or tartaric acid, before they are dissolved in water.

probe.question: Can a dry solid powder be an acid?

subject: science
statement: If litmus paper does not change color, the substance must be water.
why: Students assume a lack of reaction implies the most common neutral substance they know.
fix: A lack of color change only means the substance is not of the type the indicator detects; it could be neutral, or already the same color as the paper.

probe.question: If blue litmus stays blue, is the liquid definitely water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it didn't change.

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: science
statement: Neutralisation results in the total disappearance of the acid and base.
why: Students see two liquids mix and the 'acidic' properties vanish, assuming the matter is gone.
fix: The atoms are rearranged to form new substances: a salt and water.

probe.question: What happens to the matter when an acid and base react?
probe.wrong_answer: The matter is destroyed and disappears.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Neutralisation always results in a solution with a pH of exactly 7.
why: The term 'neutralisation' implies a perfectly neutral outcome to students.
fix: The pH depends on the strength of the acid and base; a strong acid and weak base will produce an acidic salt.

probe.question: If you mix a strong acid with a weak base, is the result pH 7?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, neutralisation always makes it 7.

root_belief: opposite things cancel out completely

subject: science
statement: Antacids are a type of acid used to help the stomach.
why: The name contains the word 'acid', leading to linguistic confusion.
fix: Antacids are actually bases that react with excess stomach acid to neutralise it.

probe.question: What is the chemical nature of an antacid?
probe.wrong_answer: It is a type of acid.

subject: science
statement: A higher pH number means a stronger acid.
why: Students usually associate higher numbers with 'more' of a property.

probe.question: Which is a stronger acid: pH 1 or pH 5?
probe.wrong_answer: pH 5 because the number is higher.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: science
statement: A strong acid is the same as a concentrated acid.
why: In everyday language, 'strong' coffee or 'strong' smell refers to concentration.
fix: Strength refers to how much an acid dissociates into ions, while concentration refers to how much acid is dissolved in water.

probe.question: If I add a lot of water to a strong acid, does it become a weak acid?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is now weak.

root_belief: intensity is the same as quantity

subject: science
concept: Salts can be acidic or basic
statement: The word 'salt' only refers to the common salt used in the kitchen.
why: Students use the word 'salt' exclusively for Sodium Chloride in daily life.
fix: In chemistry, a salt is a general term for any ionic compound formed from the neutralisation of an acid and a base.

probe.question: Is copper sulfate a salt?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only the white powder we eat is salt.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
concept: Salts can be acidic or basic
statement: All salts are neutral.
why: Students believe that because salts are products of neutralisation, they must be neutral.
fix: Salts can be acidic, basic, or neutral depending on the strength of the parent acid and base.

probe.question: What is the pH of a salt solution formed from a strong acid and weak base?
probe.wrong_answer: It must be 7 because it is a salt.

root_belief: a category name implies one property

subject: science
statement: Bases are not harmful because they feel soapy and are used in soap.
why: Students contrast them with 'scary' acids and associate them with cleaning products.

probe.question: Are all bases safe to touch because they feel soapy?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, bases are not corrosive like acids.

subject: science
statement: When phenolphthalein turns colorless, the substance has been destroyed.

probe.question: When phenolphthalein turns colorless in acid, where did the pink substance go?
probe.wrong_answer: The substance was destroyed.

root_belief: visible changes are the only changes

subject: science
concept: Empty containers are full of air
statement: An empty glass contains nothing at all.
why: Air is invisible and cannot be felt when it is still.

probe.question: If you push an empty glass upside down into a bucket of water, why doesn't water enter it immediately?

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Air has no weight because it floats.
why: Students associate weight only with heavy, solid objects that they can feel.
fix: Air is matter and has mass; a balloon filled with air weighs more than a deflated one.

probe.question: Which is heavier: a flat football or the same football pumped up with air?

root_belief: gases have no mass or weight

subject: science
statement: Soil is a solid block with no space for air.
why: Soil looks like a continuous solid mass to the naked eye.
fix: Soil contains tiny spaces between its particles that are filled with air, which escapes as bubbles when water is added.

probe.question: Why do bubbles come out when you pour water on a lump of dry soil?

subject: science
statement: Fish breathe the oxygen atoms that are part of the water molecules (H2O).
why: Students confuse the chemical composition of water with dissolved gases.

subject: science
statement: Air is mostly made of oxygen because we need it to survive.
why: Students assume the most important gas for life must be the most abundant.
fix: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air, while oxygen is only about 21%.

probe.question: Which gas is the most abundant in the air around us?
probe.wrong_answer: Oxygen

root_belief: human needs dictate physical reality

subject: science
statement: Oxygen itself catches fire and burns.
why: Students confuse 'supporting combustion' with 'being flammable'.
fix: Oxygen helps other things burn but does not burn itself.

probe.question: If you light a match in a room full of pure oxygen, what happens?

subject: science
statement: Carbon dioxide is only a waste product and has no use in nature.
why: Textbooks often focus on CO2 as a pollutant or a waste product of respiration.
fix: Carbon dioxide is essential for plants to make food through photosynthesis.

probe.question: Is carbon dioxide useful for anything in the atmosphere?

root_belief: waste products have no value

subject: science
statement: Water vapour only exists in the air when it is raining or humid.
why: Water vapour is invisible, so students only acknowledge it when it condenses into visible droplets.
fix: Water vapour is always present in the air, though the amount varies by location and weather.

probe.question: Where does the water on the outside of a cold glass come from on a dry day?
probe.wrong_answer: It leaks through the glass from the inside.

subject: science
statement: Plants breathe in carbon dioxide and breathe out oxygen, but they do not respire like animals.
why: Students confuse the gas exchange of photosynthesis with the process of respiration.

probe.question: What gas do plants take in during the night when there is no sunlight?

subject: science
statement: Plants produce oxygen specifically so that animals can breathe.
why: A teleological view of nature where everything exists for a human or animal purpose.
fix: Oxygen is a byproduct of the plant's food-making process; plants do not 'intend' to provide for animals.

probe.question: Why do plants release oxygen into the air?
probe.wrong_answer: To make sure animals don't die.

root_belief: natural processes have a human-centric purpose
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
concept: Empty containers are full of air
statement: Air only exists when the wind is blowing.
why: We only feel the physical force of air when it is in motion.
fix: Air is a substance that is present even when it is perfectly still and we cannot feel it.

probe.question: Is there air in a closed room where no fan is running and no wind is blowing?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the air is gone because there is no wind.

subject: science
statement: Smoke is a gas, just like oxygen or nitrogen.
why: Smoke floats and spreads like a gas, and its individual particles are too small to see clearly.
fix: Smoke is a mixture of gases and tiny solid particles (soot/ash).

probe.question: If you filter smoke through a fine cloth, why does it leave a black stain?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the gas turned into a solid on the cloth.

root_belief: if it floats and spreads it must be a gas

subject: science
statement: The atmosphere is a very thick layer that goes on forever into space.
why: The sky looks infinitely high to a child looking up.
fix: The atmosphere is a relatively thin layer of air surrounding the Earth, becoming thinner as we go higher.

probe.question: Does the amount of air stay the same as you climb a very high mountain?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, air is everywhere in space.

subject: science
statement: Nitrogen is 'useless' air because we don't use it for breathing.
why: Students often categorize things as 'useful' or 'useless' based solely on human respiration.
fix: Nitrogen is vital for plant growth and it also prevents fires from burning out of control by diluting oxygen.

subject: science
statement: Cotton is a synthetic fibre because it is processed in large machines in factories.
why: Students often equate 'industrial processing' with 'synthetic' or 'man-made'.
fix: Cotton is natural because the raw material is obtained directly from the cotton plant, regardless of how it is spun.

probe.question: If a factory spins cotton into a shirt, does the fibre become synthetic?

subject: science
statement: Synthetic fibres are made of chemicals, but natural fibres are chemical-free.
why: In everyday language, 'chemicals' is used as a synonym for 'artificial' or 'toxic'.
fix: All matter, including natural fibres like cotton (cellulose), is made of chemical substances.

probe.question: Is the cellulose in a cotton plant a chemical?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is natural, so it has no chemicals.

root_belief: natural things do not contain chemicals

subject: science
statement: Rayon is a fully natural fibre because it is made from wood pulp.
why: Students focus on the biological origin of the raw material and ignore the chemical treatment.
fix: Rayon is semi-synthetic; although it comes from wood pulp, it requires extensive chemical processing to become a fibre.

probe.question: Why is Rayon called 'artificial silk' if it comes from wood?
probe.wrong_answer: Because wood is natural, so the silk it makes is natural.

root_belief: origin of raw material determines final classification

subject: science
statement: Natural fibres like silk are always stronger than synthetic fibres like nylon.
why: There is an intuitive belief that nature's designs are superior in strength to man-made ones.
fix: A nylon thread is actually stronger than a steel wire of the same thickness.

probe.question: Which is stronger: a nylon thread or a cotton thread of the same thickness?
probe.wrong_answer: Cotton, because it is natural.

subject: science
statement: All plastics can be melted and reshaped multiple times.
why: Students generalize their experience with plastic bottles and bags to all plastic items.
fix: Only thermoplastics can be melted and reshaped; thermosetting plastics stay hard once set.

probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all plastic melts when heated.

subject: science
statement: Thermosetting plastics like Bakelite are actually metals because they are hard and don't melt.
why: Students associate hardness and heat resistance exclusively with metals.

probe.question: Why doesn't a pressure cooker handle melt on the stove?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it is made of a black metal.

subject: science
statement: If you bury plastic in the soil for many years, it will eventually turn into compost.

probe.question: What happens to a plastic bag buried in the ground for 100 years?

subject: science
statement: Burning plastic is a good way to get rid of it because it disappears.
why: Visible disappearance of the solid object is equated with the removal of the problem.
