probe.question: Is burning plastic better for the environment than burying it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because burning makes it go away completely.

subject: science
statement: A polymer is a single large atom.
why: Confusion between the scale of atoms, molecules, and macroscopic objects.

probe.question: What is a polymer made of?

subject: science
statement: Recycling is the only 'R' that matters for saving the environment from plastic.

subject: science
statement: Polyester is better for summer because it is thin and light.
why: Students confuse the weight of the fabric with its ability to absorb sweat and allow air circulation.
fix: Polyester absorbs very little water and traps heat, making it uncomfortable in hot, humid weather compared to cotton.

probe.question: Why do we prefer cotton clothes in summer over polyester?
probe.wrong_answer: We don't; polyester is lighter so it must be cooler.

root_belief: lighter weight means cooler temperature

subject: science
statement: Biodegradable materials like paper never cause any environmental pollution.
why: The term 'biodegradable' is often perceived as 'perfectly safe' in all contexts.

probe.question: Can throwing too much paper in a river be harmful?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because paper is biodegradable and will just disappear.

subject: science
concept: Metals are generally hard and solid

why: Students generalize from common metals like iron and copper used in construction.

subject: science
statement: Non-metals never conduct electricity.

subject: science

subject: science
statement: All metal oxides are basic in nature.

subject: science
statement: Rusting is just a layer of dirt or mud that sticks to the iron.

subject: science

subject: science

subject: science

subject: science

subject: science
statement: We don't need to conserve fossil fuels because new ones are being formed every day.
why: Students confuse the 'process' of formation with the 'rate' of formation.
fix: While formation is a continuous process, it takes millions of years, making the rate of formation negligible compared to our rate of consumption.

probe.question: Why is coal considered a non-renewable resource if it is still forming underground?
probe.wrong_answer: It is actually renewable because it never stops forming.

root_belief: continuous processes provide infinite supply

subject: science
statement: Coal tar is only used for surfacing roads.
why: This is the most visible and common everyday use students observe.
fix: Coal tar is a starting material for many products like synthetic dyes, drugs, perfumes, and even naphthalene balls.

probe.question: Where else might the chemicals from coal tar be found besides roads?
probe.wrong_answer: Nowhere else, it is only for road construction.

root_belief: an object has only its most visible use

subject: science
statement: All products obtained from petroleum are liquids.
why: Petroleum itself is a liquid, so students assume its 'parts' must be liquids too.
fix: Petroleum refining produces gases (LPG), liquids (Petrol, Diesel), and solids/semi-solids (Paraffin wax, Bitumen).

probe.question: Is bitumen, used for roads, a liquid like petrol?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all petroleum products must be liquid to flow through pipes.

root_belief: properties of the whole apply to all parts

subject: science
statement: Combustion is a physical change because the fuel just disappears.
why: Students observe the fuel vanishing and don't see the gaseous products formed.
fix: Combustion is a chemical change where fuel reacts with oxygen to form new substances like CO2 and water vapor.

probe.question: If you burn 1kg of wood, why does the remaining ash weigh much less?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the matter was destroyed or turned into nothing.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
source_hint: HBCSE diagnostic research on chemical changes

subject: science
statement: A substance with a high ignition temperature catches fire very easily.
why: Students confuse 'high' with 'high reactivity' or 'high speed'.
fix: Ignition temperature is the minimum temperature required; a lower ignition temperature means it catches fire more easily.

probe.question: Substance A has an ignition temperature of 40°C and B has 400°C. Which is more dangerous to store?
probe.wrong_answer: Substance B because it has a higher temperature.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: science
statement: Air is the fuel that burns in a fire.
why: Students see that blowing on a fire makes it grow, assuming air is the source of the fire.
fix: Air (oxygen) is only a supporter of combustion; the substance being consumed (like wood or wax) is the fuel.

probe.question: In a candle flame, what is actually being used up as the primary source of energy?
probe.wrong_answer: The surrounding air.

root_belief: the agent of change is the source

subject: science
statement: Water is the best way to put out an electrical fire.
why: Generalization that water puts out all fires from everyday experience with wood fires.
fix: Water conducts electricity and can give the person a shock; use CO2 or sand for electrical fires.

probe.question: Why shouldn't we use water on a fire caused by a short circuit?
probe.wrong_answer: Because water will make the fire spread faster like oil.

root_belief: a rule for one case works everywhere

subject: science
statement: The yellow part of a candle flame is the hottest zone.
why: Yellow and orange are intuitively associated with heat (like the sun or glowing iron).
fix: The outermost blue zone is the hottest because it has a continuous supply of oxygen for complete combustion.

probe.question: Which part of the flame should a goldsmith use to melt gold?
probe.wrong_answer: The yellow luminous zone.

root_belief: brightest or most colorful is most intense

subject: science
statement: Spontaneous combustion happens without any reason or heat.
why: The lack of an visible external spark makes it seem like magic or 'no cause'.
fix: It happens when a substance reaches its ignition temperature due to internal heating (like bacterial action or oxidation).

probe.question: How can a heap of hay catch fire on its own in a barn?
probe.wrong_answer: It just happens randomly without any temperature change.

root_belief: events without visible causes have no cause

subject: science
statement: A fuel with a higher calorific value is always the 'best' fuel.
why: Focusing on energy output while ignoring safety, cost, and pollution.
fix: An ideal fuel must have high calorific value AND be cheap, easy to store, and non-polluting.

probe.question: Is Hydrogen the best domestic fuel because it has the highest calorific value?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it gives the most heat.

root_belief: more of one good attribute makes the whole best

subject: science
statement: Fire is a form of matter, like a gas.
why: Fire occupies space and moves, leading students to categorize it as a substance.
fix: Fire is a process (a chemical reaction) and the flame is the region where gases glow; it is not a substance itself.

probe.question: If you put fire in a sealed jar, does the weight of the jar increase because of the fire?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because fire is a gas and gas has weight.

root_belief: processes are material objects
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's research on the nature of fire

subject: science
statement: Incomplete combustion only produces smoke, not any dangerous gases.
why: Smoke is visible, while Carbon Monoxide is invisible and its danger is not immediately apparent.
fix: Incomplete combustion produces Carbon Monoxide, a highly poisonous gas that can be fatal in closed rooms.

probe.question: Why is it dangerous to sleep in a closed room with a coal fire?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the smoke will make you cough and wake up.

root_belief: what you cannot see cannot hurt you

subject: science
statement: Metals are non-combustible and can never burn.
why: In daily life, metal utensils are used over fire without burning.
fix: Many metals like Magnesium or Sodium are highly combustible under the right conditions.

probe.question: What happens when a magnesium ribbon is heated over a burner?
probe.wrong_answer: It just melts because metals don't burn.

root_belief: everyday experience applies to all conditions

subject: science
statement: Blowing on a candle puts it out because you are removing the oxygen.
why: Students know fire needs oxygen and think their breath 'pushes' it away.
fix: Blowing puts out a candle primarily by cooling the vapors below their ignition temperature.

probe.question: Why does a small candle go out when you blow on it, but a bonfire gets bigger?
probe.wrong_answer: Because your breath has no oxygen for the candle but has oxygen for the bonfire.

root_belief: one action has only one possible mechanism

subject: science
statement: The wick of the candle is what burns to produce the flame.
why: The wick is where the flame is attached and it turns black/disappears.
fix: The wax vapors are the actual fuel; the wick just helps transport the liquid wax upwards.

probe.question: If you could remove the wax but keep the wick, would the candle burn for hours?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the wick is the fuel.

root_belief: the most central part is the source
source_hint: Faraday's Chemical History of a Candle (educational adaptations)

subject: science
concept: Matter is made of tiny particles
statement: Matter is continuous like a solid block and has no internal structure.
why: The macroscopic appearance of solids like wood or iron suggests a single continuous entity.
fix: Matter is particulate in nature, meaning it is made of millions of tiny, discrete particles with spaces between them.

probe.question: If you dissolve sugar in water, why does the water level not rise significantly?
probe.wrong_answer: Because sugar is a liquid or it disappears into the water's volume.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
source_hint: HBCSE research on particulate nature of matter

subject: science
statement: The space between particles is filled with air.
why: Students find it difficult to conceptualize a vacuum and assume air is everywhere.
fix: The space between particles of a substance is empty (vacuum); air is itself made of particles with space between them.

probe.question: What exists in the space between two water molecules?
probe.wrong_answer: Air or oxygen.

root_belief: empty space must be filled with air
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
statement: Particles in a solid do not move at all.
why: Since the solid object is stationary, students assume its internal components are also stationary.
fix: Particles in a solid are in continuous motion, but they only vibrate about their fixed positions.

probe.question: Do the particles in a block of ice move?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are frozen in place and cannot move.

root_belief: macro properties apply to micro particles

subject: science
statement: Individual particles expand or grow larger when heated.
why: Students observe the whole object expanding and attribute this change to the particles themselves.
fix: Particles do not change size; heating increases their kinetic energy, causing them to move further apart.

probe.question: When an iron rod is heated and expands, what happens to the size of each iron atom?
probe.wrong_answer: Each atom gets slightly bigger.

root_belief: properties of the whole belong to the parts

subject: science
statement: Gases can be compressed because the particles themselves are soft and squishy.
why: Students relate compressibility to the texture of everyday objects like sponges.
fix: Gases are compressible because there are large empty spaces between the particles, not because the particles change shape.

probe.question: Why can you push the piston of a syringe filled with air?
probe.wrong_answer: Because air particles are soft and can be flattened.

root_belief: material properties explain physical behavior

subject: science
statement: Temperature always increases when heat is supplied to a substance.
why: In everyday experience, heating usually results in a temperature rise.
fix: During a change of state, the temperature remains constant because the heat is used as latent heat to break forces of attraction.

probe.question: What happens to the temperature of boiling water as you continue to heat it?
probe.wrong_answer: The temperature keeps rising above 100 degrees Celsius.

root_belief: more input always means more output

subject: science
concept: Latent heat of fusion and vaporization
statement: Latent heat is 'hidden' because it is stored inside the particles as a substance.
why: The word 'latent' means hidden, leading to the idea of physical storage.
fix: Latent heat is the energy consumed to overcome the inter-particle forces of attraction during a phase change.

probe.question: Where does the energy go when ice melts at 0 degrees?
probe.wrong_answer: It is hidden inside the water molecules.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: Evaporation only occurs at the boiling point of a liquid.
why: Students confuse evaporation with boiling because both involve a liquid becoming a gas.
fix: Evaporation is a surface phenomenon that occurs at any temperature below the boiling point.

probe.question: How do wet clothes dry on a cold day?
probe.wrong_answer: The water must reach 100 degrees to turn into vapor.

root_belief: similar processes are identical

subject: science
statement: Bubbles in boiling water are made of air or heat.
why: Students see bubbles and associate them with the most common gas they know (air).
fix: The bubbles in boiling water consist of water vapor (water in gaseous state).

probe.question: What is inside the bubbles that rise when water boils?
probe.wrong_answer: Air that was trapped in the water.

root_belief: all gases are air

subject: science
statement: Humidity increases the rate of evaporation.
why: Students may think 'more water in the air' helps 'pull' more water out.
fix: High humidity decreases the rate of evaporation because the air already holds a lot of water vapor.

probe.question: Why do we sweat more and feel sticky on a rainy day?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the high humidity makes our sweat evaporate faster.

root_belief: more of a factor increases the process

subject: science
statement: Diffusion is a force that pulls particles together.
why: Students see substances mixing and assume an active force is driving the movement.
fix: Diffusion is the spontaneous intermixing of particles due to their own random kinetic motion.

probe.question: Why does the smell of perfume spread in a room?
probe.wrong_answer: The air pulls the perfume particles toward the corners.

root_belief: motion requires an active force

subject: science
concept: Matter is made of tiny particles
statement: Particles of a liquid are 'wet' or 'blue' if the liquid is blue.
why: Macro-scale properties like color or state are projected onto the microscopic particles.
fix: Individual particles do not have properties like 'wetness' or 'color'; these are collective properties of many particles.

probe.question: If you look at a single water molecule, is it wet?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because water is a liquid and all liquids are wet.

root_belief: properties of the whole belong to the parts

subject: science
statement: A substance is pure if it is natural and contains no harmful additives.
why: Students use the everyday marketing definition of 'pure' (like pure ghee or milk) instead of the chemical one.
fix: In chemistry, a pure substance consists of only one type of particle (atoms or molecules) with the same chemical nature.

probe.question: Is full-cream milk a pure substance in chemistry?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it comes directly from the cow without adding water.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's research on children's ideas

subject: science
statement: If a mixture looks uniform and clear to the naked eye, it must be a pure substance.
why: Students rely on macroscopic visual evidence to determine microscopic composition.
fix: Homogeneous mixtures like salt solutions look uniform but contain different types of particles that can be separated physically.

probe.question: You are given a clear, colorless liquid. Can you conclude it is a pure substance?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because I cannot see any different parts in it.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: A solute must always be a solid and a solvent must always be a liquid.
why: The most common examples taught (salt in water) become the prototype for all solutions.
fix: Solutions can exist in any state; for example, air is a gas-in-gas solution and brass is a solid-in-solid solution.

probe.question: In the alloy brass (zinc and copper), which one is the solvent?
probe.wrong_answer: Neither, because they are both solids and solutions must be liquid.

root_belief: a prototype represents the entire category

subject: science
statement: Colloids are homogeneous mixtures because they do not settle over time.
why: Students equate stability and lack of visible settling with homogeneity.
fix: Colloids are heterogeneous because the particle size is large enough to scatter light, even if they don't settle.

probe.question: Why is milk classified as a heterogeneous mixture even though it looks uniform?
probe.wrong_answer: It is actually homogeneous because the fat doesn't settle at the bottom.

root_belief: stability implies uniformity

subject: science
statement: Concentration is calculated by dividing the mass of solute by the mass of the solvent.
why: Students confuse the 'solvent' with the 'total solution' in the denominator.
fix: Mass percentage is (Mass of Solute / Mass of Solution) × 100, where solution mass is solute + solvent.

probe.question: If 10g of salt is added to 100g of water, what is the mass of the solution used in the denominator?

root_belief: the whole is the same as the largest part

subject: science
statement: A saturated solution is 'full' and cannot dissolve any other substance.
why: Students think 'saturated' means the solvent has no space left for any particles at all.
fix: A solution saturated with one solute can still dissolve a different solute.

probe.question: If a solution is saturated with salt, can it dissolve any sugar?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the solution is already saturated and full.

root_belief: a limit for one thing is a limit for all

subject: science
statement: When a solution evaporates, the solute also disappears or turns into gas.
why: Students often believe that when the liquid 'goes away', the whole mixture is gone.
fix: Evaporation only removes the volatile solvent; the non-volatile solute is left behind as a solid.

probe.question: What happens to the salt when a salt-water solution is heated to dryness?
probe.wrong_answer: The salt evaporates along with the water.

root_belief: matter disappears when it changes state
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

subject: science
statement: A compound has the same properties as the elements it is made from.
why: Students confuse the nature of mixtures (which retain properties) with compounds.
fix: A compound has entirely different properties from its constituent elements.

probe.question: Since Hydrogen and Oxygen are gases, why is water (H2O) a liquid at room temperature?
probe.wrong_answer: Water must actually be a gas that we see as liquid, or it must act like a gas.

root_belief: the whole is just the sum of its parts

subject: science
statement: Distillation and boiling are the same process.
why: Both involve heating a liquid to its boiling point, so students miss the condensation step.
fix: Boiling is just a phase change; distillation is a separation technique involving both evaporation and condensation.

probe.question: Can you perform distillation using only a heater and an open beaker?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because distillation is just boiling the liquid.

root_belief: one part of a process defines the whole

subject: science
statement: Compounds can be separated into their elements by physical methods like filtration or distillation.
why: Students do not distinguish between the physical bonds in a mixture and chemical bonds in a compound.
fix: Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical or electrochemical reactions.

probe.question: How can we separate Hydrogen gas from water?
probe.wrong_answer: By filtering the water through a very fine filter paper.

root_belief: all mixtures and compounds are separated the same way

subject: science
statement: The Tyndall effect is caused by the liquid itself reflecting light.
why: Students don't realize it is the suspended particles, not the medium, that scatter light.
fix: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of a beam of light by medium-sized colloidal particles.

probe.question: Why do we see the path of light in a forest on a misty morning?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the air itself is glowing.

root_belief: the medium and the object are the same

subject: science
statement: Mixtures have a fixed melting and boiling point just like pure substances.
why: Students overgeneralize the property of 'matter' having fixed points to all forms of matter.
fix: Mixtures do not have fixed melting/boiling points; they melt or boil over a range of temperatures depending on composition.

probe.question: Does salt water always boil at exactly 100 degrees Celsius?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because water is the main part and its boiling point is fixed.

root_belief: a rule for a part applies to the whole

subject: science
statement: Centrifugation works by making the heavier particles lighter so they can float.
why: Students observe separation but misinterpret the physics of density and force.
fix: Centrifugation uses rapid rotation to force denser particles to the bottom and lighter particles to the top.

probe.question: In a cream separator, why does the cream collect at the top?
probe.wrong_answer: The machine spins so fast that the cream becomes weightless and floats.

root_belief: motion changes the intrinsic properties of matter

subject: science
statement: Chromatography only works for separating colors.
why: The name 'chroma' (color) and the common ink experiment lead to this narrow view.
fix: Chromatography separates any solutes that dissolve in the same solvent but move at different speeds, even colorless ones.

probe.question: Can chromatography be used to separate different colorless drugs in a blood sample?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because chromatography only works if the substances have different colors.

root_belief: the name of a process limits its function

subject: science
statement: Alloys are compounds because they cannot be separated by simple filtration.
why: Students think if you can't filter it, it must be chemically bonded.
fix: Alloys are mixtures because they show the properties of their constituents and have variable composition, even if they require melting to separate.

probe.question: Why is brass considered a mixture and not a compound?
probe.wrong_answer: It is actually a compound because you cannot see the zinc and copper separately.

root_belief: difficulty of separation defines the type of matter

subject: science
statement: Mass is lost during a chemical reaction if a gas is produced.
why: Students do not perceive gas as having mass because it is often invisible and escapes.
fix: Mass is always conserved; if a gas is produced, its mass must be included in the total product mass.

probe.question: If 10g of calcium carbonate is heated in an open vessel and 4.4g of CO2 escapes, what is the mass of the remaining residue?

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
source_hint: HBCSE diagnostic studies on conservation of mass

subject: science
statement: The ratio of elements in a compound depends on how the compound was prepared.
why: Students think the process or source of a substance dictates its internal composition.
fix: A pure chemical compound always contains the same elements combined in the same proportion by mass, regardless of source.

probe.question: Will water from a river and water made in a lab have different mass ratios of Hydrogen to Oxygen?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, lab water is purer so the ratio is different.

root_belief: the process determines the product properties

subject: science
statement: Atoms expand or grow in size when a substance is heated.
why: Students apply the macroscopic observation of thermal expansion to the microscopic particles themselves.
fix: Atoms do not change size; heating only increases the space and vibration between them.

probe.question: What happens to the size of an individual iron atom when an iron rod is heated?
probe.wrong_answer: The atom gets larger.

root_belief: macro properties apply to micro particles
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
statement: The atomic mass of an element is the actual mass of one single atom in grams.
why: Students struggle with the scale of $10^{-24}$ grams and find relative units abstract.
fix: Atomic mass is a relative mass compared to 1/12th the mass of a Carbon-12 atom, expressed in 'u'.

probe.question: If the atomic mass of Oxygen is 16u, does one atom of Oxygen weigh 16 grams?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes

root_belief: a number must represent a familiar unit

subject: science
statement: Molecules only exist in compounds, not in elements.
why: Everyday language suggests a 'molecule' is a mixture or combination of different things.
fix: Molecules can be formed by atoms of the same element (e.g., O2) or different elements (e.g., H2O).

probe.question: Is O2 considered a molecule or just two atoms?
probe.wrong_answer: It is just two atoms, not a molecule.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: A positive ion (cation) is formed when an atom gains a proton.
why: Students associate the 'plus' sign with the mathematical operation of addition.
fix: Ions are formed only by the loss or gain of electrons; a cation is formed by losing electrons.

probe.question: How does a neutral Sodium atom become a Na+ ion?
probe.wrong_answer: By adding a proton to the nucleus.

root_belief: positive means adding something

subject: science
statement: In a chemical formula like H2O, the number 2 refers to the Oxygen atom.
why: Students may read left-to-right and associate the number with the symbol that follows it.
fix: The subscript in a chemical formula always refers to the atom immediately preceding it.

probe.question: In the formula MgCl2, how many Magnesium atoms are there?
probe.wrong_answer: Two

root_belief: spatial proximity determines relationship

subject: science
statement: One mole of a heavy substance contains more particles than one mole of a light substance.
why: Students confuse the 'amount of substance' (count) with the 'mass' of the substance.
fix: One mole of any substance always contains exactly $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ particles, regardless of its mass.

probe.question: Which contains more atoms: 1 mole of Gold or 1 mole of Helium?
probe.wrong_answer: 1 mole of Gold because Gold atoms are heavier.

root_belief: heavier or bigger means more quantity

subject: science
statement: Molar mass is the mass of one single molecule in grams.
why: Confusion between the mass of a single microscopic particle and the mass of a macroscopic collection (a mole).
fix: Molar mass is the mass of $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ particles in grams; it is numerically equal to atomic/molecular mass.

probe.question: What is the mass of one single water molecule?
probe.wrong_answer: 18 grams

root_belief: confusing the part with the whole

subject: science
statement: Valency and ionic charge are the same thing.
why: For many simple ions, the magnitude of the charge is equal to the valency, leading to overgeneralization.
fix: Valency is the combining capacity (a number), while charge is an electrical state (positive or negative).

probe.question: What is the valency of Chlorine in NaCl?

root_belief: related concepts are identical

subject: science
statement: Atoms are like tiny solid balls with no empty space inside.
why: The 'billiard ball' model used in early instruction is taken literally by students.
fix: Atoms consist of a tiny nucleus and a large amount of empty space where electrons are present.

probe.question: If you could look inside an atom, what would you see between the nucleus and electrons?
probe.wrong_answer: Solid matter or air.

root_belief: matter is continuous and solid
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
statement: To find the number of moles, you should multiply the given mass by the molar mass.
why: Students often guess the mathematical operation (multiplication vs division) without understanding the relationship.
fix: Number of moles is calculated by dividing the given mass by the molar mass.

probe.question: How many moles are in 36g of water (Molar mass = 18g/mol)?
probe.wrong_answer: 648 moles

root_belief: math in science is just picking an operation

subject: science
statement: Atoms are solid spheres like marbles.
why: Students apply macroscopic properties of small round objects to the microscopic level.
fix: Atoms are mostly empty space with a tiny nucleus and distant electrons.

probe.question: If you could zoom into an atom, what would you see between the nucleus and electrons?
probe.wrong_answer: Solid matter or a hard surface.

root_belief: macroscopic properties apply to microscopic

subject: science
statement: Electrons are stationary within the atom.
why: Static diagrams in textbooks make electrons look like they are stuck in place.
fix: Electrons are in constant motion within specific energy levels or orbits.

probe.question: In Thomson's model, do the electrons move around?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are fixed like seeds in a watermelon.

root_belief: static objects are simpler than moving

subject: science
statement: Alpha particles bounce off the electron cloud.
why: Students think the outer boundary of the atom is a solid wall.
fix: Alpha particles pass through the electron cloud easily and only deflect when hitting the dense nucleus.

probe.question: Why did most alpha particles pass straight through the gold foil?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they were small enough to fit between electrons.

root_belief: visible surface is the barrier

subject: science
statement: The empty space in an atom is filled with air.
why: In everyday life, 'empty' containers are usually filled with air.
fix: The space between the nucleus and electrons is a vacuum, containing no matter at all.

probe.question: What exists in the space between the nucleus and the electron shells?
probe.wrong_answer: Air or oxygen.

root_belief: empty space must contain a substance

subject: science
statement: Electrons move in random, chaotic paths like flies.
why: Students struggle with the idea of fixed orbits without physical tracks.
fix: Electrons move in specific, discrete orbits called energy levels.

probe.question: Can an electron move anywhere it wants inside the atom?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it flies around randomly in the empty space.

root_belief: lack of visible structure implies chaos

subject: science
statement: Neutrons have a positive charge because they are in the nucleus.
why: Students associate the nucleus only with positive charge and ignore neutrality.
fix: Neutrons are neutral particles; only protons provide the positive charge to the nucleus.

probe.question: What is the charge of a neutron found in the nucleus?
probe.wrong_answer: Positive.

root_belief: location determines property

subject: science
statement: Electron shells are physical containers or hard walls.
why: The word 'shell' implies a hard outer covering in everyday language.
fix: Shells are just regions of space representing specific energy levels.

probe.question: What are electron shells made of?
probe.wrong_answer: A thin plastic-like or solid material.

root_belief: abstract boundaries are physical objects

subject: science
statement: Valency is always equal to the number of valence electrons.
why: Students confuse the count of electrons in the outer shell with the combining capacity.
fix: Valency is the number of electrons gained, lost, or shared to complete an octet.

probe.question: If an atom has 7 valence electrons, what is its valency?

root_belief: similar words mean the same thing

subject: science
statement: Atoms with more valence electrons are always more reactive.
why: Students think 'more' of a subatomic particle leads to 'more' chemical activity.
fix: Reactivity depends on how easily an atom can achieve a stable octet, not just the count.

probe.question: Is an atom with 7 valence electrons more reactive than one with 1?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has more electrons to react with.

root_belief: more of a thing means more value

subject: science
statement: Isotopes of an element are different chemical elements.
why: Students think any change in the composition of an atom changes its identity.
fix: Identity is determined by the number of protons; isotopes are the same element with different neutron counts.

probe.question: Are Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 different elements?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they have different masses.

root_belief: any change in composition creates new identity

subject: science
statement: Mass number is the actual weight of one atom in grams.
why: Students confuse the dimensionless mass number with absolute mass.
fix: Mass number is the sum of protons and neutrons; it is a count, not a weight in grams.

probe.question: If the mass number of Carbon is 12, does one atom weigh 12 grams?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes.

root_belief: relative units are the same as absolute units

subject: science
statement: Electrons are larger than the nucleus because they take up more space.
why: Students equate the volume of the electron cloud with the size of the individual particles.
fix: The nucleus is much heavier and denser than electrons, though it occupies very little space.

probe.question: Which is heavier: the entire electron cloud or the tiny nucleus?
probe.wrong_answer: The electron cloud because it is bigger.

root_belief: bigger size means more mass

subject: science
statement: Protons and electrons have the same mass.
why: Students assume that because their charges are equal and opposite, their masses must be too.
fix: A proton is approximately 2000 times more massive than an electron.

probe.question: How does the mass of a proton compare to an electron?
probe.wrong_answer: They are equal because the atom is neutral.

root_belief: symmetry in one property implies symmetry in all

subject: science
statement: Positive charge in an atom is a fluid-like substance.
why: The 'plum pudding' analogy suggests a continuous medium rather than discrete particles.
fix: Positive charge is carried by discrete particles called protons located in the nucleus.

probe.question: In Thomson's model, what is the 'pudding' made of?
probe.wrong_answer: A positive liquid or jelly.

root_belief: matter is continuous rather than particulate

subject: science
statement: Atoms can be seen with a powerful light microscope.
why: Students believe that better technology just means 'more zoom' on visible light.
fix: Atoms are smaller than the wavelength of visible light and cannot be seen with optical microscopes.

probe.question: Can we see the structure of an atom using a school microscope?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if the lens is strong enough.

root_belief: what exists must be visible

subject: science
statement: I can change the subscripts in a chemical formula to balance an equation.
why: Students treat subscripts as flexible numbers similar to coefficients in math equations.
fix: Subscripts define the identity of a substance; changing them creates a different substance. Only coefficients can be changed.

probe.question: To balance H2 + O2 -> H2O, why can't we just write H2 + O2 -> H2O2?
probe.wrong_answer: Because H2O2 is easier to write but the teacher said no.

root_belief: a rule from one context works everywhere

subject: science
statement: The symbol (aq) means the substance is in a liquid state.
why: Students confuse 'aqueous' (dissolved in water) with the 'liquid' state of a pure substance.
fix: (aq) means a solid, liquid, or gas is dissolved in water, whereas (l) is for pure liquids like water or molten metals.

probe.question: If you dissolve salt in water, what state symbol do you use for salt?

subject: science
statement: When a gas is produced in a reaction, the total mass of the system decreases.
why: Students do not account for invisible gases as having mass.
fix: Mass is always conserved; if a gas escapes, the remaining solid/liquid weighs less, but the total mass (including gas) is unchanged.

probe.question: If 10g of calcium carbonate is heated in an open flask and 6g of solid remains, what happened to the mass?
probe.wrong_answer: The mass was destroyed by heat.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Decomposition is just a physical breaking of a substance into smaller pieces.
why: The everyday use of 'decompose' implies rotting or breaking apart physically.
fix: Decomposition is a chemical change where one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances with different properties.

probe.question: Is crushing a chalk stick into powder a decomposition reaction?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the chalk is breaking down.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: Any metal can displace any other metal from its salt solution.
why: Students ignore the specific hierarchy of the reactivity series.
fix: A displacement reaction only occurs if the standalone metal is more reactive than the metal in the compound.

probe.question: Will a copper wire react if placed in a zinc sulphate solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, copper will displace zinc.

root_belief: all members of a category are equal

subject: science
statement: Exothermic reactions require constant heating to keep going.
why: Confusion between the activation energy (initial spark) and the overall energy profile.
fix: Exothermic reactions release energy; once started, they often provide enough energy to sustain themselves.

probe.question: Does a candle need a match to keep burning for an hour?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it needs heat from the match the whole time.

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: science
statement: Oxidation can only happen if oxygen is present as a reactant.
why: The name 'oxidation' strongly implies oxygen is the only possible agent.
fix: Oxidation is also defined as the loss of hydrogen or the loss of electrons, even without oxygen.

probe.question: In the reaction H2S + Cl2 -> 2HCl + S, is H2S being oxidized?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because there is no oxygen involved.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: Rusting is the term used for the corrosion of all metals.
why: Rusting (iron) is the most common everyday example of corrosion students see.
fix: Rusting is specific to iron; corrosion is the general term for the deterioration of any metal due to environmental interaction.

probe.question: What do you call the green layer that forms on copper?
probe.wrong_answer: Green rust.

root_belief: one member represents the whole group

subject: science
statement: Balancing an equation means making the total number of molecules equal on both sides.
why: Students confuse the number of atoms (which must be equal) with the number of molecules.
fix: Balancing ensures the number of atoms of each element is the same; the number of molecules can change.

probe.question: In N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, is the equation balanced? Why?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because there are 4 molecules on the left and only 2 on the right.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: science
statement: A precipitate is a gas that forms and bubbles out of a solution.
why: Students associate 'new product forming in liquid' with bubbles (gas) rather than solids.
fix: A precipitate is an insoluble solid that emerges from a liquid solution during a chemical reaction.

probe.question: When you see a white cloudy solid forming in a clear liquid, what is it?
probe.wrong_answer: It is a gas trapped in the water.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Rancidity is caused by bacteria eating the food.
why: Students associate all food spoilage with biological 'germs' rather than chemical oxidation.
fix: Rancidity is specifically the chemical oxidation of fats and oils, which changes the smell and taste.

probe.question: Why do potato chip packets contain nitrogen gas?
probe.wrong_answer: To kill the bacteria inside the packet.

root_belief: biological causes for all natural changes

subject: science
statement: Endothermic reactions feel hot because they are 'taking in' heat.
why: Students confuse the 'presence' of heat with the 'direction' of heat flow.
fix: Endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings, making the surroundings (and the container) feel colder.

probe.question: If a reaction in a test tube is endothermic, what will your hand feel?
probe.wrong_answer: It will feel hot because heat is being used.

root_belief: more of a quality means more perception

subject: science
statement: Combination reactions always involve two elements forming one compound.
why: Introductory examples (like Mg + O2) usually feature elements, leading to overgeneralization.
fix: Combination reactions can involve two compounds (like CaO + H2O) or an element and a compound.

probe.question: Is NH3 + HCl -> NH4Cl a combination reaction?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because NH3 and HCl are already compounds.

root_belief: the simplest case is the only case

subject: science
statement: The coefficient in front of a formula only applies to the first element.
why: Students read chemical formulas like English text, applying the 'modifier' only to the immediate next 'word'.
fix: A coefficient multiplies every atom in the entire chemical formula that follows it.

probe.question: How many oxygen atoms are in 2Ca(OH)2?

root_belief: local effect instead of global

subject: science
statement: Covalent bonds are weaker than ionic bonds because sharing is less permanent than giving.
why: Students apply the social meaning of 'sharing' (temporary) versus 'giving' (permanent) to chemical bonds.
fix: Covalent bonds are strong chemical bonds formed by the mutual sharing of electron pairs between atoms to achieve stability.

probe.question: Which bond is inherently 'weak' because atoms can take back their shared electrons?
probe.wrong_answer: Covalent bond

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: Carbon can only form four single bonds.
why: Students interpret 'tetravalency' as exactly four separate lines or connections.
fix: Carbon has four valence electrons and can form four single bonds, or combinations of double and triple bonds to satisfy its valency.

probe.question: Can a carbon atom be part of a triple bond and still follow the tetravalency rule?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it can only have four single bonds.

root_belief: a rule has only one visual representation

subject: science
statement: Saturated hydrocarbons are more reactive because they are 'full' of energy.
why: The word 'saturated' is associated with being full or heavy in everyday contexts like fats or sponges.
fix: Saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes) are generally unreactive because all carbon valencies are satisfied by single bonds.

probe.question: Which is more reactive: an alkane or an alkene?
probe.wrong_answer: Alkane, because it is saturated.

root_belief: saturated means more of everything
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's studies on student ideas

subject: science
statement: The -OH group in alcohols makes the solution basic like NaOH.
why: Students see 'OH' and immediately associate it with the hydroxide ion (OH-) from inorganic bases.
fix: The -OH in alcohols is a covalently bonded functional group and does not ionize in water to release hydroxide ions.

probe.question: Will ethanol turn red litmus paper blue because of its -OH group?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it contains hydroxide.

root_belief: similar appearance implies identical behavior

subject: science
statement: Members of a homologous series have the same physical properties.
why: Students confuse 'similar chemical properties' with 'identical physical properties'.
fix: Members of a homologous series show a regular gradation in physical properties (like boiling point) as molecular mass increases.

probe.question: Do methane and butane have the same boiling point since they are both alkanes?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they are in the same series.

root_belief: similarity in one aspect means similarity in all

subject: science
statement: Addition reactions can occur in alkanes if you add enough reagent.
why: Students think 'addition' just means adding any chemical to another.
fix: Addition reactions only occur in unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkenes/alkynes) where a double or triple bond can open up.

probe.question: Can you add hydrogen to ethane to make it more saturated?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, by an addition reaction.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: The hydrophobic tail of a soap molecule attracts water.
why: Confusion between the prefixes 'hydro-' (water) and 'philic/phobic' (love/fear).
fix: The hydrophobic tail is 'water-fearing' and dissolves in oils, while the hydrophilic head is 'water-loving'.

probe.question: Which part of the soap molecule points towards the water in a micelle?
probe.wrong_answer: The hydrophobic tail.

root_belief: scientific terms are interchangeable

subject: science
statement: Scum is formed because soap evaporates in hard water.
why: Students observe the disappearance of lather and the appearance of a solid, assuming the liquid part 'left'.
fix: Scum is an insoluble precipitate formed when soap reacts with calcium and magnesium salts in hard water.

probe.question: What is the white curd-like substance formed when soap is used in hard water?
probe.wrong_answer: Dried soap left after evaporation.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Ethanoic acid is a strong acid because it is used in laboratories.
why: Students often believe all 'chemical' acids are strong, unlike 'natural' ones.
fix: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid because it does not ionize completely in water, unlike mineral acids like HCl.

probe.question: Is vinegar (dilute ethanoic acid) a strong acid?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a pure chemical.

root_belief: chemicals are inherently powerful or dangerous

subject: science
statement: In a dot structure, the shared electrons belong only to the atom that originally brought them.
why: Students struggle with the concept of 'collective ownership' of electrons in a bond.
fix: Shared electrons in a covalent bond belong to the valence shells of both participating atoms simultaneously.

probe.question: In H-H, does each electron still only belong to its original hydrogen atom?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they just sit next to each other.

root_belief: objects retain their original identity in a group

subject: science
statement: Catenation is unique to carbon and no other element can do it.
why: Textbooks emphasize carbon's catenation so much that students assume it is an exclusive property.
fix: While carbon shows catenation to the maximum extent, other elements like Silicon also show catenation, though to a much lesser degree.

probe.question: Can any element other than carbon form chains of its own atoms?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only carbon can.

root_belief: a highlighted property is an exclusive property

subject: science
statement: Micelles are flat circles of soap molecules on the surface of water.
why: Textbook diagrams are 2D, leading students to perceive 3D structures as flat shapes.
fix: Micelles are spherical clusters where the hydrophobic tails point inwards and hydrophilic heads point outwards in 3D space.

probe.question: What is the 3D shape of a soap micelle in water?
probe.wrong_answer: A flat ring or circle.

root_belief: 2D representations are literal 3D shapes

subject: science
statement: Water vapor only exists when water is boiling on a stove.
why: Students associate steam with high heat and visible bubbling.
fix: Water evaporates at all temperatures, even at room temperature, turning into invisible water vapor in the air.

probe.question: If a wet cloth dries in the sun, where does the water go?
probe.wrong_answer: It disappears because it didn't reach boiling point to become vapor.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: All freshwater on Earth is available for us to drink.
why: Students assume 'fresh' means 'ready to use' and ignore physical barriers.
fix: Most freshwater is locked in glaciers, ice caps, or deep underground and is not easily accessible.

probe.question: Why is there a water crisis if 0.6% of Earth's water is freshwater?
probe.wrong_answer: Because we are drinking all of it too fast, even the glaciers.

root_belief: ignoring inaccessible parts of a whole

subject: science
statement: Clouds are made of water vapor gas.
why: Students confuse the invisible gas state with the visible white clouds.
fix: Clouds are actually made of tiny liquid water droplets or ice crystals formed by condensation.

probe.question: What state of matter is a cloud?
probe.wrong_answer: Gas, because it floats in the air like steam.

root_belief: visible gas-like things are gases

subject: science
statement: Groundwater is stored in large empty underground swimming pools or rivers.
why: Students apply their knowledge of surface water bodies to the subsurface.
fix: Groundwater is stored in the tiny spaces between soil particles and cracks in rocks.

probe.question: If you dig a hole to find groundwater, what will you mostly find?
probe.wrong_answer: A large open cave filled with flowing water.

root_belief: underground structures mirror surface structures

subject: science
statement: The water table is a permanent line that never moves.
why: Students view geological features as static rather than dynamic.
fix: The water table rises with heavy rain and falls during droughts or heavy pumping.

probe.question: What happens to the water table level in a village during a very dry summer?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays at the same depth because the ground doesn't change.

root_belief: geological features are static

subject: science
statement: Soil is solid and does not allow water to pass through it.
why: Soil looks like a solid barrier when viewed from the surface.
fix: Water seeps through the pores in soil in a process called infiltration.

probe.question: How does rain water reach the aquifer deep underground?
probe.wrong_answer: It only goes through cracks or holes made by humans.

root_belief: solid-looking objects have no gaps

subject: science
statement: Water scarcity is only caused by people wasting water at home.
why: School campaigns focus heavily on individual actions like closing taps.
fix: Industrial use, large-scale agriculture, and deforestation are major causes of water depletion.

probe.question: Why is the groundwater level falling in many farming states of India?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the farmers are leaving their home taps running.

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: science
statement: Rainwater harvesting is only for storing water in tanks for immediate use.
why: Rooftop collection into tanks is the most visible form of harvesting.
fix: Rainwater harvesting also includes directing water into the ground to recharge aquifers.

probe.question: Can rainwater harvesting help a dried-up borewell?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because harvesting only fills plastic tanks on the roof.

root_belief: the most visible part is the whole

subject: science
statement: Sewage is just water with mud and trash in it.
why: Students only identify visible physical impurities.
fix: Sewage contains dissolved organic matter, nutrients, and dangerous disease-causing microbes.

probe.question: Why is it dangerous to touch sewage water even if it looks clear?
probe.wrong_answer: It is only dangerous if there is visible trash or mud.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Water from a treatment plant is 100% pure water with nothing else in it.
why: The word 'treatment' or 'purification' implies absolute purity to students.
fix: Treated water is safe for disposal or reuse but still contains dissolved salts and minerals.

probe.question: Is treated sewage water the same as distilled water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the treatment plant removes every single thing that isn't water.

root_belief: clean means perfectly pure

subject: science
statement: Plants only take in water; they do not release any water into the air.

probe.question: How do forests contribute to rainfall?

subject: science
statement: Snow and ice are different substances from water.
why: Different physical properties (hardness, temperature) lead to different classifications in everyday language.
fix: Snow and ice are simply the solid state of the chemical substance water.

probe.question: If you melt 1kg of snow, what do you get?
probe.wrong_answer: A different liquid that looks like water but is actually melted snow.

root_belief: different appearance means different substance

subject: science
statement: Vitamins provide energy to the body for playing and running.

subject: science
concept: Fats provide more energy than carbs

why: Everyday health warnings about obesity lead students to view fats as purely toxic substances.

subject: science
statement: Roughage is a nutrient that helps us grow taller.

subject: science
statement: A balanced diet means eating equal amounts of every nutrient.

probe.question: If you eat 100g of fats, 100g of vitamins, and 100g of proteins, is that a balanced diet?

subject: science
statement: Deficiency diseases like scurvy can spread from one person to another by coughing.

subject: science
statement: Washing vegetables after cutting them makes them cleaner and healthier.

subject: science

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science

probe.question: Will a solution of plain table sugar turn blue-black when iodine is added?

subject: science
statement: We only get water for our body when we drink it from a glass.

probe.question: If you eat a juicy watermelon, are you providing water to your body?

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
concept: Fats provide more energy than carbs
statement: If a food item does not leave an oily mark on paper, it contains no fats.
why: Reliance on the simplest physical test without considering hidden or bound fats.
fix: While the paper test is a good indicator, some foods have very small amounts of fat or 'hidden' fats that might not leave a visible oily patch easily.

probe.question: Can a food have fat even if it doesn't feel greasy to touch?

root_belief: physical properties are always immediately apparent

subject: science
statement: Only people who want to build big muscles need to eat protein.

probe.question: Does a child who doesn't exercise still need protein?

subject: science

probe.question: Why is a growing cloud not considered a living organism?

subject: science

subject: science
statement: Plants do not respond to stimuli because they don't have senses.
why: Plant responses are often slow or subtle compared to the quick reactions of animals.
fix: Plants respond to stimuli like light, gravity, and touch, such as a sunflower turning towards the sun.

subject: science
statement: Dry seeds are non-living objects until they are planted in soil.
why: Seeds in a packet show no visible signs of life like growth or movement.

subject: science
concept: Soil and Air as abiotic factors
statement: Abiotic factors like soil and air are just surroundings and not part of the habitat.
why: Students often focus only on the living residents when defining a 'home'.
fix: A habitat includes both biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components that interact to support life.

probe.question: What makes up a pond habitat?

subject: science
statement: Camels store liquid water in their humps to survive in the desert.
why: The hump is a prominent storage-like structure and camels go long periods without drinking.

probe.question: What is inside a camel's hump?

subject: science

subject: science
statement: Plants do not excrete waste because they don't have a digestive system.

probe.question: How do plants get rid of unwanted materials?

subject: science
statement: A piece of wood is an abiotic component because it is not moving or growing.

fix: Biotic components include living things and things that were once part of a living organism, like fallen leaves or wood.

probe.question: Is a fallen branch in a forest biotic or abiotic?

subject: science
statement: Fish breathe by swallowing water and turning it into air in their stomachs.
why: Students see fish opening and closing their mouths constantly.

probe.question: Why do fish constantly open their mouths?

subject: science
statement: Cactus spines are only for protection against animals.

probe.question: Why does a cactus have spines instead of broad leaves?

root_belief: structures have one obvious purpose

subject: science
statement: Any small plant with a green stem is a baby tree.

probe.question: If you see a small plant with a soft green stem, will it definitely grow into a tall tree?

root_belief: small things are just young versions of big things

subject: science
statement: The stem only carries water from the roots to the leaves.

subject: science
statement: Plants get their food from the soil through their roots.

probe.question: Where does a plant get the energy-rich food it needs to grow?

subject: science
statement: Transpiration is the plant 'sweating' to stay cool like humans.

fix: Transpiration is the loss of water vapor from leaves, which helps in pulling water up from the roots.

probe.question: Why do plants release water vapor from their leaves?

subject: science
statement: If a plant part is underground, it must be a root.
