probe.question: Is a potato a root because it grows under the ground?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, everything under the ground is a root.

root_belief: location defines the identity of an object

subject: science
statement: The green leaf-like parts at the base of a flower are just small leaves.
why: They look identical to leaves in color and texture.
fix: These are sepals, which are specific flower parts that protect the bud.

probe.question: What are the green leaf-like structures protecting a flower bud called?
probe.wrong_answer: They are just baby leaves of the plant.

root_belief: things that look alike are the same thing

subject: science
statement: All plants have one main thick root going deep into the soil.
why: The taproot is the 'prototypical' root taught first or seen in diagrams.
fix: Many plants, like grass and wheat, have fibrous roots where all roots look similar and spread out.

probe.question: Does a bunch of grass have one main central root?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, every plant has one main thick root.

root_belief: one example represents the whole category

subject: science
statement: Leaf venation is just a pattern and has no relation to other plant parts.
why: Students see patterns as decorative rather than functional or structural indicators.
fix: Leaf venation is directly linked to the type of root system the plant has.

probe.question: Can you guess the type of roots a plant has by looking at its leaves?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the leaf pattern has nothing to do with the roots.

root_belief: different parts of a system are independent

subject: science
statement: Only the colorful petals are part of the flower; the inner parts are something else.
why: Petals are the most visible and 'famous' part of the flower.
fix: A flower includes sepals, petals, stamens, and the pistil; all are essential parts.

probe.question: If you remove the petals, is the remaining center part still part of the flower?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the flower is gone once the petals are removed.

root_belief: the most prominent part is the whole object

subject: science
statement: Sunlight is a material that plants 'eat' to grow.
why: Confusion between energy sources and matter/food.
fix: Sunlight provides the energy for a chemical process; it is not a physical food item.

probe.question: Is sunlight a type of food for the plant?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is the main food that plants eat.

root_belief: energy and matter are the same thing

subject: science
statement: Shrubs are just herbs that have grown for a few years.
why: Difficulty distinguishing between growth stages and distinct biological categories.
fix: Shrubs are a distinct category with hard, woody stems branching near the base, unlike herbs.

probe.question: Will a coriander herb eventually become a rose shrub if we wait long enough?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it will grow a woody stem and become a shrub.

root_belief: all small plants are just early stages of larger ones

subject: science
statement: Roots only hold the plant in the ground; they don't do anything else.
why: Anchorage is the most physically obvious function when pulling a weed.
fix: Roots also absorb water and essential minerals from the soil for the plant.

probe.question: If we put a plant in water without soil, why does it need roots?
probe.wrong_answer: It doesn't; roots are only for sticking to the soil.

root_belief: an object has only its most obvious function

subject: science
statement: Bones are non-living structures like rocks.
why: Bones feel hard and dry, and students do not see them grow or bleed in everyday life.
fix: Bones are living tissues that grow, require nutrients from blood, and can repair themselves if broken.

probe.question: If a child breaks a bone, how does it eventually join back together?
probe.wrong_answer: The doctor glues it or it just stays stuck together like a broken toy.

root_belief: internal parts are not alive
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
statement: The backbone is one single, long, continuous bone.
why: It feels like a single rigid rod when running a finger down the center of the back.
fix: The backbone is made of 33 small bones called vertebrae that allow the body to bend and twist.

probe.question: If your backbone was one single long bone, would you be able to touch your toes?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because bones are flexible enough to bend like a stick.

root_belief: a single function implies a single part

subject: science
statement: All joints in the human body are designed to allow movement.
why: In everyday language, a 'joint' is where things move, like a door hinge.
fix: Some joints, like those in the skull, are fixed and do not allow any movement at all.

probe.question: Can you move the bones in the upper part of your head (skull)?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they must move slightly when I think or talk.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: A single muscle can both pull and push a bone.
why: Students observe their arm moving back and forth and assume one muscle does both actions.
fix: Muscles can only pull; they cannot push. They work in pairs where one contracts to pull and the other relaxes.

probe.question: When you straighten your arm after bending it, what is the bicep muscle doing?
probe.wrong_answer: The bicep is pushing the arm bone back down.

root_belief: actions are symmetric and reversible

subject: science
statement: Earthworms move using tiny legs that are too small to see.
why: Students believe that all animals must have legs to walk or move across the ground.
fix: Earthworms have no legs; they use muscles to shorten and lengthen their body and tiny bristles to grip the ground.

probe.question: How does an earthworm stay fixed to the ground while pulling its back part forward?
probe.wrong_answer: It uses its many tiny legs to hold onto the soil.

root_belief: movement requires specific visible appendages

subject: science
statement: Fish move forward by only flapping their tail fin left and right.
why: The tail is the most visible moving part of a fish.
fix: Fish move by forming curves with their whole body on alternate sides, creating a jerk that pushes them forward.

probe.question: If a fish's body was rigid and only its tail moved, how would it swim?
probe.wrong_answer: It would swim exactly the same way it does now.

root_belief: the most visible part does all work

subject: science
statement: Cartilage is just soft bone that will eventually turn into hard bone.
why: Students hear that babies have 'softer' skeletons and confuse development with tissue types.
fix: Cartilage is a distinct, flexible tissue found in parts like the ear and joints; it remains cartilage throughout life.

probe.question: Will the cartilage in your external ear eventually turn into hard bone as you get older?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all soft parts of the skeleton harden over time.

root_belief: different materials are just stages of one

subject: science
statement: The rib cage is a solid wall of bone protecting the chest.
why: Diagrams often show ribs close together, and 'cage' implies a continuous barrier.
fix: The rib cage consists of separate curved bones joined to the backbone and breastbone, allowing the chest to expand.

probe.question: What happens to your ribs when you take a very deep breath?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, because the rib cage is a solid structure that cannot change shape.

root_belief: protection requires a continuous surface

subject: science
statement: Birds can fly because they have no weight or are weightless.
why: Students equate 'lightweight' or 'hollow' with having no mass at all.
fix: Birds have weight, but their hollow bones and powerful flight muscles make them light enough to fly.

probe.question: If you put a living bird on a weighing scale, what would it show?
probe.wrong_answer: It would show zero because birds are weightless to help them fly.

root_belief: light things have no mass

subject: science
statement: Muscles are only found in 'strong' places like arms and legs.
why: Students only notice muscles when they bulge during exercise.
fix: Muscles are present throughout the body, including the face, chest, and even inside organs like the heart.

probe.question: Do you use muscles when you blink your eyes or smile?
probe.wrong_answer: No, those are just skin movements; muscles are for lifting heavy things.

root_belief: size determines existence
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

subject: science
statement: The knee joint is a ball and socket joint because it moves a lot.
why: Students confuse 'large range of motion' with 'circular motion'.
fix: The knee is a hinge joint that only moves back and forth; the shoulder is a ball and socket joint.

probe.question: Can you rotate your lower leg in a full circle at the knee like you can with your arm at the shoulder?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the knee joint allows movement in all directions.

root_belief: similar functions imply identical structures

subject: science
statement: Snakes move forward in a perfectly straight line.
why: Students imagine the snake's body as a simple sliding rope.
fix: Snakes move by forming many loops that push against the ground to propel them forward in a zig-zag manner.

probe.question: Can a snake move forward if it is placed on a completely smooth glass surface with no friction?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it just slides its body straight forward.

root_belief: the shortest path is the only path

subject: science
statement: The snail's shell is a tool it uses to push itself forward.
why: Students look for an external 'engine' or tool for movement.
fix: The shell is for protection and is carried; the snail moves using a large, flat muscular foot that produces slime.

probe.question: What part of the snail actually touches the ground to make it move?
probe.wrong_answer: The edge of the shell pushes against the ground.

root_belief: external features always aid primary function

subject: science
statement: The pivotal joint in the neck allows us to turn our head 360 degrees.
why: Students over-extrapolate the idea of 'rotation' mentioned in textbooks.
fix: The pivotal joint allows us to turn our head left and right and up and down, but only within a limited range.

probe.question: Can you turn your head to look directly at your own back without moving your shoulders?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the neck joint is a pivot so it can rotate fully.

root_belief: rotation has no physical limits

subject: science
statement: Cartilage is only found in the ears and nose.
why: These are the only places where students can easily feel 'flexible bone' from the outside.
fix: Cartilage is also found at the ends of bones at joints to reduce friction and in the rings of the windpipe.

probe.question: Is there any cartilage inside your knee or elbow joints?
probe.wrong_answer: No, joints only contain hard bones and empty space.

root_belief: one example defines the whole category

subject: science
statement: Plants get their food from the soil through their roots.
why: Students observe roots in soil and fertilizers being added, leading to an analogy with animals eating.
fix: Plants make their own food (glucose) using sunlight, CO2, and water; soil only provides minerals and water.

probe.question: If a plant is grown in a pot of soil, where does the bulk of its new weight come from?
probe.wrong_answer: From the soil particles absorbed by the roots.

root_belief: food must be taken in from outside

subject: science
statement: Leaves that are not green do not have chlorophyll and cannot do photosynthesis.
why: The green color of chlorophyll is masked by other pigments like red or brown.
fix: Large amounts of other pigments can hide the green color, but chlorophyll is still present for photosynthesis.

probe.question: Can a plant with dark red leaves perform photosynthesis?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it doesn't have the green color needed.

root_belief: visible traits define internal composition

subject: science
statement: Plants only take in carbon dioxide and never use oxygen.
why: Students confuse the net gas exchange of photosynthesis with the process of respiration.
fix: Plants use oxygen for respiration all the time (day and night), just like animals.

probe.question: Do plants use oxygen at night?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they only use carbon dioxide.

root_belief: opposite processes are mutually exclusive

subject: science
statement: Insectivorous plants eat insects because they cannot make their own food.
why: Students assume that if an organism eats something, it must be a heterotroph like an animal.
fix: These plants are green and do photosynthesis; they eat insects only to get nitrogen which is missing in their soil.

probe.question: Why does a pitcher plant trap an insect?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it cannot make glucose from sunlight.

root_belief: one trait excludes another

subject: science
statement: Fungi are a type of plant because they grow in the ground and don't move.
why: Superficial similarities in lifestyle lead to incorrect biological classification.
fix: Fungi have a different mode of nutrition (saprotrophic) and do not have chlorophyll, so they are not plants.

probe.question: Is a mushroom a plant?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it grows in the soil and stays in one place.

root_belief: immobile organisms are all plants

subject: science
statement: Sunlight is a material ingredient that turns into food.
why: Students struggle to distinguish between energy (light) and matter (CO2/water).
fix: Sunlight provides the energy to drive the chemical reaction; it does not have mass or turn into atoms of food.

probe.question: Is sunlight a substance that plants 'eat'?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a material that makes up the body of the plant.

root_belief: energy is a substance

subject: science
statement: Plants can take nitrogen directly from the air through their leaves.
why: Since CO2 is taken from the air, students assume the 78% nitrogen in air is also directly accessible.
fix: Gaseous nitrogen cannot be used by plants; it must be converted into soluble forms by bacteria in the soil.

probe.question: How does nitrogen enter a plant?
probe.wrong_answer: Through the stomata in the leaves from the atmosphere.

root_belief: gases enter through any opening

subject: science
statement: Saprotrophs eat dead matter by swallowing it.
why: Students apply the human model of 'eating' to all organisms.
fix: Saprotrophs secrete digestive juices onto the dead matter outside their bodies and then absorb the nutrients.

probe.question: How does a fungus get nutrients from a piece of bread?
probe.wrong_answer: It takes pieces of bread inside its body to digest them.

root_belief: digestion must happen inside a body

subject: science
statement: Parasitic plants like Cuscuta help the host plant by sharing nutrients.
why: A misunderstanding of biological interactions as always being cooperative.
fix: Parasites take valuable nutrients from the host plant, depriving it of food and potentially harming it.

probe.question: What happens to a tree when Cuscuta grows on it?
probe.wrong_answer: The tree grows better because they share food.

root_belief: biological interactions are always helpful

subject: science
statement: Stomata are only found on the upper surface of leaves to catch sunlight.
why: Students associate the top of the leaf with 'activity' because it faces the sun.
fix: Stomata are usually more numerous on the lower surface to reduce water loss while allowing gas exchange.

probe.question: Where are most of the tiny pores (stomata) located on a leaf?
probe.wrong_answer: Only on the top side where the sun hits.

root_belief: exposure to sun is necessary for all parts

subject: science
statement: Rhizobium bacteria are harmful pests for the plants they live on.
why: General belief that all 'bacteria' or 'germs' cause disease.
fix: Rhizobium has a symbiotic relationship where it provides nitrogen to the plant in exchange for food and shelter.

probe.question: Are the bacteria in the root nodules of a pea plant bad for the plant?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they are infecting the plant and making it sick.

root_belief: all bacteria are harmful

subject: science
statement: Plants produce food only for humans and animals.
why: An anthropocentric view of nature where plants exist to serve consumers.
fix: Plants produce food primarily for their own growth, survival, and reproduction.

probe.question: Why does a plant make starch?
probe.wrong_answer: So that humans have something to eat.

root_belief: nature exists to serve humans

subject: science
statement: Digestion only happens in the stomach.
why: The stomach is the most famous organ associated with food and hunger in everyday talk.
fix: Digestion begins in the mouth with saliva and continues in the small intestine where it is actually completed.

probe.question: Where does the chemical breakdown of food first begin?
probe.wrong_answer: In the stomach

root_belief: one organ does all the work

subject: science
statement: Saliva only makes food slippery so it can be swallowed easily.
why: Students only feel the physical lubrication of saliva and cannot see the chemical breakdown of starch.
fix: Saliva contains enzymes that chemically break down complex starch into simpler sugars.

probe.question: If you chew bread for a long time, it tastes sweet. Why?
probe.wrong_answer: Because saliva is naturally a sweet liquid

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Stomach acid is used to melt all the food we eat into a liquid.
why: Students equate 'acid' with 'corrosive liquid' that dissolves everything like in cartoons.
fix: Stomach acid primarily kills bacteria and creates an acidic environment for protein-digesting juices to work.

probe.question: What is the main purpose of hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
probe.wrong_answer: To melt the food into a liquid state

root_belief: substances act like universal solvents

subject: science
statement: The large intestine is where the most important nutrients are absorbed.
why: Students assume the 'large' intestine is more important or that absorption happens at the very end of the journey.
fix: Almost all nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine; the large intestine only absorbs water and some salts.

probe.question: In which part of the digestive tract are nutrients like proteins and fats absorbed?
probe.wrong_answer: Large intestine

root_belief: bigger means more important

subject: science
statement: Villi are tiny hairs that filter out waste from the food.
why: Students confuse the appearance of villi with eyelashes or air filters that 'trap' things.
fix: Villi are finger-like outgrowths that increase surface area to help absorb digested food into the blood.

probe.question: What is the function of the villi in the small intestine?
probe.wrong_answer: To filter out dirt and waste from food

root_belief: biological structures act like macroscopic tools

subject: science
statement: Humans could digest grass if we just chewed it as much as cows do.
why: Students think the difference is mechanical (chewing) rather than chemical (enzymes/bacteria).
fix: Humans lack the specific bacteria and stomach chambers required to break down cellulose found in grass.

probe.question: Why can't humans survive by eating only grass?
probe.wrong_answer: Because our teeth are not strong enough to chew it

root_belief: physical effort can overcome chemical limitations

subject: science
statement: Amoeba has a tiny mouth that is too small to see.
why: Students believe all living things must have the same basic organs as humans (anthropomorphism).
fix: Amoeba has no fixed mouth; it uses temporary finger-like extensions called pseudopodia to engulf food.

probe.question: How does an Amoeba take in its food?
probe.wrong_answer: Through a microscopic mouth opening

root_belief: all life must have human-like structures

subject: science
statement: Bile is produced by the stomach to digest all types of food.
why: Students associate all digestive juices with the stomach and don't distinguish between food types.
fix: Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder; it specifically helps in the digestion of fats.

probe.question: Which organ produces bile and what does it help digest?
probe.wrong_answer: The stomach digests proteins

root_belief: all digestive fluids are the same

subject: science
statement: Egestion and excretion are just two words for the same process.
why: Both involve removing waste from the body, and students don't distinguish between undigested food and cellular waste.
fix: Egestion is the removal of undigested food (faeces), while excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes like urine.

probe.question: Is the removal of undigested food called excretion?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is waste leaving the body

root_belief: similar outcomes imply identical processes

subject: science
statement: Food is converted into energy inside the stomach.
why: Students feel an immediate 'energy boost' after eating and link it to the first place food goes.
fix: Food is broken down into nutrients, absorbed into the blood, and then used by cells throughout the body to release energy.

probe.question: Where is the energy from food actually released for the body to use?
probe.wrong_answer: In the stomach during digestion

root_belief: the start of a process is where the result happens

subject: science
statement: Milk teeth have no roots and that is why they fall out.
why: Because they fall out easily, children assume they aren't 'anchored' like permanent teeth.
fix: Milk teeth do have roots; these roots are gradually dissolved by the permanent teeth growing underneath them.

probe.question: Why do milk teeth fall out?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they are just sitting on the gums without roots

root_belief: temporary things have no functional depth

subject: science
statement: Cows have four separate stomachs.
why: The term 'four-chambered stomach' is often misinterpreted as four independent organs.
fix: Ruminants have a single stomach divided into four distinct compartments or chambers.

probe.question: How many stomachs does a cow have?
probe.wrong_answer: Four stomachs

root_belief: chambers are the same as whole organs

subject: science
statement: Respiration is just another word for breathing.
why: In everyday conversation, people use 'respiration' to mean inhaling and exhaling.
fix: Breathing is the physical act of gas exchange, while respiration is the chemical process of breaking down food for energy inside cells.

probe.question: If a cell has oxygen but no glucose, can it perform respiration?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it can still breathe.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

subject: science
statement: Aerobic respiration is the process of 'making' oxygen for the body.
why: Confusion between 'using' and 'producing' in chemical cycles.
fix: Aerobic respiration consumes oxygen to release energy from food; it does not create oxygen.

probe.question: Does the amount of oxygen in a sealed jar increase if a mouse is respiring inside?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the mouse is respiring.

root_belief: inputs and outputs are interchangeable

subject: science
statement: Yeast only performs respiration when making bread rise.
why: Students only associate microbes with their industrial utility.
fix: Yeast respires to stay alive and grow; the CO2 that makes bread rise is just a byproduct of its survival process.

probe.question: Does yeast in a dry packet respire before you add it to dough?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it only starts when it needs to make bread.

root_belief: biological processes exist for human utility

subject: science
statement: Respiration only happens in the lungs of animals.
why: Lungs are the most visible organ associated with the word 'breathing'.
fix: Respiration occurs in every single living cell of an organism's body to provide energy for that cell.

probe.question: Does a cell in your big toe perform respiration?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only the lungs do that.

root_belief: a function only happens at its primary site

subject: science
statement: We inhale pure oxygen and exhale pure carbon dioxide.
why: Textbooks simplify gas exchange diagrams to show O2 going in and CO2 coming out.
fix: We inhale a mixture of gases (mostly nitrogen) and exhale a mixture that still contains significant oxygen but more CO2 than before.

probe.question: What is the most abundant gas in the air we breathe in?
probe.wrong_answer: Oxygen.

root_belief: only the functional component matters

subject: science
statement: Lactic acid is produced because the body stops respiring during heavy exercise.
why: Students think anaerobic means the normal process has failed or stopped.
fix: Anaerobic respiration is an additional pathway to provide energy quickly when oxygen supply is insufficient, not a replacement for all respiration.

probe.question: During a fast run, do your muscle cells stop using oxygen entirely?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they switch entirely to lactic acid.

root_belief: one process replaces another entirely

subject: science
statement: Breathing rate is a fixed number for every human.
why: Students often see a single 'average' value in textbooks and take it as a constant.
fix: Breathing rate varies significantly based on age, health, and physical activity levels.

probe.question: If your resting rate is 15, will it be 15 while you are sleeping?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it never changes.

root_belief: averages are absolute constants

subject: science
statement: Plants only respire at night when they are not doing photosynthesis.
why: Students think plants only need one gas exchange process at a time and photosynthesis is 'day breathing'.
fix: Respiration is a continuous process for all living cells to stay alive, occurring 24/7 in plants.

probe.question: Do plant cells need energy from glucose during the daytime?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they only make glucose then; they don't use it.

root_belief: mutually exclusive processes cannot happen simultaneously

subject: science
statement: Earthworms breathe through their mouths like humans do.
why: Students project human anatomy onto all animals.
fix: Earthworms exchange gases directly through their moist skin, not through a mouth or lungs.

probe.question: If an earthworm's skin dries out, can it still breathe through its mouth?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it will just use its mouth.

root_belief: all animals function like humans

subject: science
statement: Air entering the lungs causes the chest to expand.
why: It looks like a balloon being blown up where the air pressure creates the expansion.
fix: Muscle contraction (diaphragm and ribs) expands the chest cavity first, which then pulls air in.

probe.question: What happens first: the ribs move out or the air enters?
probe.wrong_answer: Air enters first and pushes the ribs.

root_belief: the visible result is the cause

subject: science
statement: Fish breathe by breaking down water molecules (H2O) to get oxygen.
why: Students know water contains oxygen atoms.
fix: Fish use gills to extract dissolved oxygen gas (O2) from the water, not the oxygen atoms inside water molecules.

probe.question: Can a fish breathe in distilled water that has no air bubbled into it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it gets oxygen from the H2O.

root_belief: substances are sums of their chemical parts
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

subject: science
statement: Roots do not need oxygen because they are buried in the soil.
why: Students assume oxygen is only available in the open air.
fix: Roots take up oxygen from the air spaces present between soil particles to perform respiration.

probe.question: Why does a plant die if the soil is waterlogged for a long time?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it gets too much water.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Stomata are only for letting out water (transpiration).
why: Students often learn transpiration first and don't link stomata to gas exchange.
fix: Stomata are the primary ports for the entry and exit of both oxygen and carbon dioxide.

probe.question: How does CO2 enter a leaf for photosynthesis?
probe.wrong_answer: Through the roots.

root_belief: one structure has only one function

subject: science
statement: Oxygen turns into carbon dioxide inside the lungs.
why: The proximity of the exchange makes it look like a direct conversion.
fix: Oxygen enters the blood to go to cells, while carbon dioxide produced by cells enters the lungs to be exhaled; they are different molecules.

probe.question: Is the carbon atom in exhaled CO2 the same atom that was in the inhaled oxygen?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes.

root_belief: matter changes identity through simple contact

subject: science
statement: Anaerobic respiration is just as efficient as aerobic respiration.
why: Students don't realize the difference in energy yield.
fix: Aerobic respiration releases much more energy per glucose molecule than anaerobic respiration.

probe.question: If a cell has no oxygen, will it get the same energy from one sugar molecule?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes.

root_belief: all similar processes have equal magnitude

subject: science
statement: Deoxygenated blood inside our veins is blue in color.
why: Veins appear blue through the skin and diagrams often use blue to represent deoxygenated blood.
fix: Human blood is always red; deoxygenated blood is just a darker shade of red. It looks blue through skin due to how light interacts with tissue.

probe.question: If you were to see blood inside a vein before it touches air, what color would it be?
probe.wrong_answer: Blue

root_belief: what you see is the only reality

subject: science
statement: All arteries carry oxygen-rich blood and all veins carry carbon dioxide-rich blood.
why: Students overgeneralize the primary function of the systemic circuit.
fix: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry it towards the heart. The pulmonary artery carries CO2-rich blood to the lungs, and the pulmonary vein carries O2-rich blood to the heart.

probe.question: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs?
probe.wrong_answer: Pulmonary vein

root_belief: rules have no exceptions

subject: science
statement: The heart is the organ where blood is actually created.
why: The heart is the central organ of the system, leading to the belief it is the source of the fluid itself.
fix: The heart only pumps blood; blood cells are actually produced in the bone marrow of certain bones.

probe.question: Where are new red blood cells made in the human body?
probe.wrong_answer: In the heart

root_belief: one organ does everything for a system

subject: science
statement: Pulse and heartbeat are two completely different and unrelated processes.
why: Students feel the pulse in the wrist and the heartbeat in the chest, perceiving them as separate events.
fix: The pulse is the direct result of the heartbeat; every time the heart pumps blood into the arteries, it creates a throb called a pulse.

probe.question: If your heart rate increases, what happens to your pulse rate?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays the same because they are different

root_belief: different locations mean different processes

subject: science
statement: Excretion and egestion are the same thing.
why: Both involve removing waste from the body, leading to linguistic and conceptual blurring.
fix: Excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes (like urea in urine) from the blood, while egestion is the removal of undigested food as faeces.

probe.question: Is passing stool (faeces) an example of excretion in the biological sense?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes

root_belief: all waste removal is the same process

subject: science
statement: Plants 'suck' water up through the xylem like a person using a straw.
why: Students apply human-centric mechanical actions to biological processes they cannot see.
fix: Water moves up due to transpiration pull, a physical force created by evaporation from leaves, and capillary action, not active sucking.

probe.question: What provides the main force to move water to the top of a tall tree?
probe.wrong_answer: The plant sucks it up using energy

root_belief: biological processes mimic human actions

subject: science
statement: Food in plants only moves downwards from the leaves to the roots.
why: Gravity and the fact that leaves are usually 'up' lead to the belief that transport is unidirectional.
fix: Phloem transports food in both upward and downward directions to reach all parts of the plant, including growing buds and storage organs.

probe.question: In spring, how does stored sugar move from roots to new growing buds?
probe.wrong_answer: It cannot move upwards in the phloem

root_belief: gravity dictates all movement

subject: science
statement: Transpiration is a waste of water and has no benefit to the plant.
why: Students see water loss as inherently negative for survival.
fix: Transpiration creates the suction pull needed to transport water and minerals and also helps in cooling the plant.

probe.question: What would happen to water transport if a plant stopped transpiring?
probe.wrong_answer: It would improve because water is saved

root_belief: loss is always bad

subject: science
statement: The kidneys produce urine directly from the food we eat in the stomach.
why: Students lack a clear understanding of the blood's role as an intermediary in transport.
fix: Kidneys filter waste from the blood; the food must first be digested and absorbed into the blood before wastes reach the kidneys.

probe.question: How does waste from your cells reach the kidneys?
probe.wrong_answer: Through the digestive pipe

root_belief: connected systems are one single pipe

subject: science
statement: The left and right sides of the heart are connected so blood can flow between them.
why: Students assume the heart is one big hollow bag rather than a partitioned pump.
fix: The heart has a wall called the septum that completely separates the left and right sides to prevent mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

probe.question: What prevents oxygen-rich blood from mixing with carbon dioxide-rich blood in the heart?
probe.wrong_answer: The blood knows which way to go

root_belief: an organ is a simple container

subject: science
statement: Roots 'search' for water in the soil and grow towards it intentionally.
why: Attributing human-like intentions and senses to plants.
fix: Roots grow in all directions; they simply grow more successfully and branch more in areas where they happen to encounter moisture.

probe.question: How do roots find water deep in the ground?
probe.wrong_answer: They sense where it is and turn towards it

root_belief: plants have intentions and desires

subject: science
statement: Blood is mostly made of red blood cells and contains very little liquid.
why: The name 'blood' and its red appearance make students focus on the cells rather than the medium.
fix: More than half of the blood (about 55%) is actually a straw-colored liquid called plasma.

probe.question: What is the largest component of human blood by volume?
probe.wrong_answer: Red blood cells

root_belief: the most visible part is the largest part

subject: science
statement: Plants can only grow from seeds.
why: Students primarily see seeds being planted in gardens or farms.
fix: Many plants can grow from vegetative parts like stems, roots, or leaves through asexual reproduction.

probe.question: If you plant a piece of a potato with an 'eye', will it grow into a plant?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because a potato is not a seed.

root_belief: only one way to do things

subject: science
statement: The 'bud' in yeast is the same as a flower bud.
why: The same word is used for two different biological structures.
fix: A yeast bud is a small outgrowth that becomes a new individual, while a flower bud is an undeveloped shoot that will open into a flower.

probe.question: Does a yeast bud eventually open up into petals?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a tiny flower waiting to bloom.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: Spores are just very tiny seeds.
why: Both are small particles that lead to new plant-like growth.
fix: Spores are single-celled asexual units, whereas seeds are multi-cellular structures containing an embryo and food, resulting from sexual reproduction.

probe.question: Are spores produced by the fusion of male and female cells?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, like seeds, they need two parents.

root_belief: different things that look similar are the same

subject: science
statement: Every flower has both male and female parts.
why: Common textbook diagrams often show bisexual flowers like Hibiscus.
fix: Some flowers, like corn or papaya, are unisexual and contain only stamens or only a pistil.

probe.question: Can a single flower have only stamens and no pistil?
probe.wrong_answer: No, a flower must have both to be a flower.

root_belief: all members of a group are identical

subject: science
statement: Pollination and fertilisation are the same thing.
why: Both processes are closely linked in the reproductive cycle.
fix: Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma, while fertilisation is the fusion of male and female gametes inside the ovary.

probe.question: Does fertilisation happen as soon as a bee touches a flower?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the bee fertilises the flower directly.

root_belief: sequential processes are a single event

subject: science
statement: Insects visit flowers because they want to help the plant reproduce.
why: Students attribute human intentions to animals (anthropomorphism).
fix: Insects visit flowers to collect nectar or pollen for food; pollination is an accidental byproduct of their movement.

probe.question: Why does a bee carry pollen from one flower to another?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it knows the plant needs to make seeds.

root_belief: living things have human-like intentions

subject: science
statement: Fertilisation occurs on the surface of the stigma.
why: The stigma is where the pollen lands and is visible.
fix: Fertilisation occurs deep inside the ovary after the pollen tube grows down the style.

probe.question: Where do the male and female cells actually meet?
probe.wrong_answer: On the sticky top of the flower.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Tomatoes and cucumbers are vegetables, not fruits.
why: Culinary definitions based on taste differ from botanical definitions.
fix: Botanically, any ripened ovary containing seeds is a fruit, including tomatoes, cucumbers, and ladyfingers.

probe.question: Is a cucumber a fruit or a vegetable in science?
probe.wrong_answer: A vegetable, because it is not sweet.

root_belief: everyday categories are scientific categories

subject: science
statement: Seeds are non-living objects because they don't move or breathe.
why: Seeds are dormant and show no visible signs of life.
fix: Seeds are living organisms in a state of dormancy; they respire slowly and contain a living embryo.

probe.question: Is a dry bean seed alive?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it only becomes alive when you water it.

root_belief: what is not moving is not alive

subject: science
statement: Pollen is the 'seed' of the flower.
why: Both are small grains involved in making new plants.
fix: Pollen contains male gametes; it must reach an egg to form a zygote, which then develops into a seed.

probe.question: If you plant pollen in the soil, will it grow into a plant?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because pollen is the plant's seed.

root_belief: different things that look similar are the same

subject: science
statement: If you cut a living thing into pieces, it always dies.
why: Generalisation from higher animals (like humans or pets) where injury is fatal.
fix: In fragmentation, organisms like Spirogyra can break into pieces, and each piece grows into a new individual.

probe.question: What happens if an alga filament breaks into three parts?
probe.wrong_answer: The alga dies because it is broken.

root_belief: breaking a whole destroys its life

subject: science
statement: All microorganisms are harmful germs that cause diseases.
why: Media and hygiene advertisements focus almost exclusively on 'killing germs' to stay healthy.
fix: Most microorganisms are harmless or beneficial; they are essential for making food, medicines, and cleaning the environment.

probe.question: If we could use a magic spray to kill every single microorganism on Earth, would humans be better off?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because there would be no more diseases or infections.

root_belief: what you cannot see is dangerous

subject: science
statement: Viruses are just a very small type of bacteria.
why: Both are microscopic and cause illness, leading students to group them into one category.
fix: Viruses are structurally different from bacteria and can only reproduce inside the cells of a host organism.

probe.question: Can a virus grow and multiply on its own on a piece of moist bread like bread mould does?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a microorganism and needs food to grow.

root_belief: all microscopic things are the same

subject: science
statement: Antibiotics are effective treatments for the common cold and flu.
why: People often take leftover antibiotics for any respiratory symptoms without understanding the cause.
fix: Antibiotics only kill bacteria; they have no effect on viruses, which are the cause of the common cold and flu.

probe.question: Why shouldn't a doctor prescribe penicillin for a patient with a viral flu?
probe.wrong_answer: Because penicillin is not a strong enough medicine for the flu.

root_belief: one medicine treats all similar illnesses

subject: science
statement: Vaccines are a cure given to people who are already suffering from a disease.
why: Vaccines are often administered via injections, which students associate with being sick and visiting a clinic.
fix: Vaccines are preventive; they are given to healthy people to train their immune system to recognize and fight future infections.

probe.question: When is the best time to receive a polio vaccine?
probe.wrong_answer: Immediately after the person shows symptoms of the polio disease.

root_belief: medicine is only for the sick

subject: science
statement: Mosquitoes and houseflies produce the diseases they carry inside their bodies.
why: The insect's bite or presence is the visible event that precedes the illness, so it is seen as the source.
fix: Insects like mosquitoes are only carriers (vectors) that transport pathogens like Plasmodium from one person to another.

probe.question: If a female Anopheles mosquito that does not carry the Plasmodium parasite bites you, will you get malaria?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the mosquito's saliva causes the malaria.

root_belief: the carrier is the source

subject: science
statement: Plants can directly absorb nitrogen gas from the atmosphere through their leaves.
why: Students know plants take in carbon dioxide from the air and assume they do the same for all nutrients.
fix: Plants cannot use atmospheric nitrogen; it must be converted into nitrates by bacteria like Rhizobium in the soil or root nodules.

probe.question: How does a leguminous plant like a pea plant get the nitrogen it needs to grow?
probe.wrong_answer: It breathes in nitrogen gas through the stomata in its leaves.

root_belief: organisms directly use all environmental resources
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's research on plant nutrition

subject: science
statement: Mushrooms and other fungi are a type of plant because they grow in the ground.
why: Fungi are stationary and often grow in soil, leading to a classification based on superficial appearance.
fix: Fungi are a separate kingdom; unlike plants, they do not have chlorophyll and cannot perform photosynthesis.

probe.question: Why is a mushroom not classified as a plant by scientists?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it is a plant that just doesn't have green leaves.

root_belief: stationary living things are plants
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

subject: science
statement: The bacteria in curd are 'bad' germs, but we eat them anyway.
why: The word 'bacteria' has a strong negative connotation in everyday language associated with filth.
fix: Lactobacillus is a 'friendly' bacterium that safely converts milk into curd without producing toxins.

probe.question: Is the presence of bacteria in a bowl of fresh curd a sign that the milk has spoiled?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, but it is a type of spoilage that humans have learned to like.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: Pasteurized milk is completely free of all microorganisms.
why: Students often believe that any heat treatment 'sterilizes' food perfectly and permanently.
fix: Pasteurization kills most harmful microbes but not all; it also doesn't prevent new microbes from entering if left open.

probe.question: If you buy a packet of pasteurized milk, can you leave it open on the kitchen counter for a week without it spoiling?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the heating process killed all the germs inside.

root_belief: treatment means total removal

subject: science
statement: When a dead leaf decomposes, its matter just disappears and turns into nothing.
why: The visible reduction in the size of the leaf as it rots suggests it is vanishing from existence.
fix: Decomposers break down organic matter into nutrients that return to the soil and gases like CO2 that enter the air.

probe.question: Where does the 'stuff' that makes up a fallen log go after it has completely rotted away?
probe.wrong_answer: It just vanishes and no longer exists anywhere.

root_belief: matter can vanish into nothing
source_hint: HBCSE Mumbai / Concept of matter conservation

subject: science
statement: Microorganisms cannot survive in extreme environments like boiling water or solid ice.
why: Students assume all life requires the same moderate temperature conditions that humans do.
fix: Some microorganisms, called extremophiles, are adapted to live in boiling hot springs and deep polar ice.

probe.question: Could any living thing survive in a hot sulfur spring where the water is near boiling?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the high heat would destroy the cells of any living thing.

root_belief: life only exists in human-comfortable conditions

subject: science
statement: Taking antibiotics makes my body's immune system stronger for the future.
why: Confusion between the medicine's direct action on germs and the body's own natural defense system.
fix: Antibiotics attack bacteria directly; they do not strengthen your immune system's natural ability to fight future infections.

probe.question: Does taking an antibiotic today help your body fight off a different bacterial infection next month?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the medicine has boosted my immunity.

root_belief: medicine changes the body's permanent nature

subject: science
statement: The nitrogen cycle only happens in the soil near the roots of plants.
why: Classroom focus is often on Rhizobium and root nodules, leading to a localized view of the cycle.
fix: The nitrogen cycle is a global process involving the atmosphere, soil, and all living organisms to recycle nitrogen.

probe.question: Does the nitrogen cycle involve the air we breathe in the atmosphere?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is a process that only happens underground in the soil.

root_belief: the part represents the whole

subject: science
statement: Cells are static like bricks in a wall.
why: Textbooks often use the 'bricks in a wall' analogy for cells, leading to a structural-only view.
fix: Cells are dynamic, living units that perform active metabolic processes, not just passive building blocks.

probe.question: If a cell is like a brick, what happens to it when the organism grows?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays exactly the same size and shape forever.

root_belief: analogies are literal representations of reality

subject: science
statement: Bigger organisms have bigger cells than smaller organisms.
why: Students intuitively believe that the size of the whole is determined by the size of the parts.
fix: The size of an organism depends on the number of cells, not the size of individual cells.

probe.question: Does an elephant have larger cells than a rat?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the elephant is much bigger.

root_belief: bigger whole means bigger parts

subject: science
statement: The cell membrane is a solid, impermeable skin.
why: Diagrams often show a thick line around the cell, suggesting a closed container.
fix: The cell membrane is selectively permeable, allowing specific substances to move in and out.

probe.question: How do nutrients get inside a cell if it has a membrane?
probe.wrong_answer: They wait for the membrane to break or disappear.

root_belief: boundaries are solid and impenetrable

subject: science
statement: The nucleus is the 'brain' of the cell and thinks for it.
why: The common 'brain' analogy leads students to believe the nucleus has consciousness or decision-making power.
fix: The nucleus contains genetic material and coordinates activities through chemical signals, not conscious thought.

probe.question: Does the nucleus 'decide' when to eat?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it thinks and tells the cell what to do.

root_belief: biological parts function like human organs

subject: science
statement: Only animal cells have mitochondria; plant cells have chloroplasts instead.
why: Students think organelles are mutually exclusive based on the primary energy source.
fix: Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria for cellular respiration; plants just have chloroplasts in addition.

probe.question: Where do plant cells get energy when there is no sunlight?
probe.wrong_answer: They don't need energy at night or they use chloroplasts.

root_belief: one function per organism type

subject: science
statement: All cells in a plant contain chloroplasts.
why: Students associate 'plant' with 'green' and 'photosynthesis' globally.
fix: Only green parts like leaves have chloroplasts; root cells or internal stem cells usually do not.

probe.question: Would you find chloroplasts in the root cells of an onion?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a plant.

root_belief: a part represents the whole

subject: science
statement: Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no DNA because they have no nucleus.
why: Students equate the absence of a container (nucleus) with the absence of the content (DNA).
fix: Prokaryotes have DNA, but it is not enclosed in a nuclear membrane; it lies in the cytoplasm as a nucleoid.

probe.question: How do bacteria pass on traits to their offspring without a nucleus?
probe.wrong_answer: They don't have traits or DNA.

root_belief: no container means no content

subject: science
statement: Vacuoles are just empty air bubbles inside the cell.
why: In diagrams, vacuoles are often drawn as empty white spaces.
fix: Vacuoles are fluid-filled sacs containing water, nutrients, or waste products.

probe.question: What is inside a large central vacuole of a plant cell?
probe.wrong_answer: Air or nothing.

root_belief: empty space contains nothing

subject: science
statement: Cells are made of atoms, but atoms are not inside cells.
why: Students struggle to bridge the gap between chemistry (atoms) and biology (cells).
fix: Cells are complex structures entirely made of molecules, which are made of atoms.

probe.question: If you zoom into a cell membrane, what would you eventually see?
probe.wrong_answer: Just more cell stuff, not atoms.

root_belief: different subjects describe different worlds

subject: science
statement: The cell wall and cell membrane are the same thing.
why: Both are outer boundaries, and students often use the terms interchangeably.
fix: The cell membrane is a flexible living layer in all cells; the cell wall is a rigid outer layer found only in plants, fungi, and bacteria.

probe.question: Do animal cells have a cell wall?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it's the same as the membrane.

root_belief: similar functions mean identical structures

subject: science
statement: Unicellular organisms are not 'alive' in the same way humans are.
why: Students often associate 'life' with complex organs like hearts or lungs.
fix: A single cell is a complete living organism that performs all essential life processes like respiration and reproduction.

probe.question: Does an Amoeba breathe or eat?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it's too small to have those functions.

root_belief: life requires complex visible organs

subject: science
statement: The nucleus is the only part of the cell that contains information.
why: Over-emphasis on the nucleus as the 'control center' ignores other organelles.
fix: While the nucleus holds most DNA, mitochondria and chloroplasts also have their own genetic material.

probe.question: Is DNA found anywhere else besides the nucleus?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only the nucleus has DNA.

root_belief: one location for one function

subject: science
statement: Reproduction is necessary for an individual animal to stay alive.
why: Students confuse the needs of a species with the physiological needs of an individual like breathing or eating.
fix: Reproduction is essential for the continuation of a species, but an individual can survive its full lifespan without reproducing.

probe.question: If a cat is unable to have kittens, will it die immediately?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because reproduction is a life process like digestion.

root_belief: all biological processes are for individual survival

subject: science
statement: Sperm and eggs are not actually cells because they are too small or liquid.
why: Students often associate 'cells' with the rectangular plant cells or skin cells they see in diagrams.
fix: Both sperm and eggs are single, specialized cells containing genetic material.

probe.question: Is a human sperm considered a cell?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is just a part of a fluid.

root_belief: cells must be box-shaped or visible

subject: science
statement: The zygote is a large multicellular structure that already looks like the parent.
why: Students struggle to conceptualize how a single microscopic cell can be the start of a complex organism.
fix: A zygote is the single cell formed by the fusion of a sperm and an egg.

probe.question: How many cells make up a zygote immediately after fertilisation?
probe.wrong_answer: Hundreds of cells.

root_belief: complex things must start large

subject: science
statement: External fertilisation is just a random accident and does not require both parents.
why: Because it happens in water, students think it is less 'organized' than internal fertilisation.
fix: External fertilisation is a coordinated process where both male and female release gametes at the same time and place.

probe.question: In frogs, does the male need to be present when the female lays eggs in water?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the eggs just find sperm later by chance.

root_belief: nature outside the body is random

subject: science
statement: A foetus and an embryo are exactly the same thing.
why: The terms are often used interchangeably in everyday conversation about pregnancy.
fix: An embryo is the early stage of development; it is called a foetus only when all body parts can be identified.

probe.question: When do we start calling a developing baby a foetus?
probe.wrong_answer: Right after the egg is fertilised.

root_belief: related terms mean the same thing

subject: science
statement: All animals that live in water are oviparous (lay eggs).
why: Students overgeneralize from fish and frogs to all aquatic life.
fix: While many aquatic animals lay eggs, some like whales and dolphins are viviparous and give birth to young ones.

probe.question: Do all animals in the ocean lay eggs?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they live in water.

root_belief: environment dictates all biological traits

subject: science
statement: Metamorphosis is just another word for an animal growing bigger.
why: Students often view all growth as a simple increase in size (linear growth).
fix: Metamorphosis involves a drastic change in form and structure from the larva to the adult stage.

probe.question: Is a caterpillar becoming a butterfly just 'growing up'?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is just getting bigger and older.

root_belief: growth is always linear

subject: science
statement: In binary fission, the parent Amoeba dies after the two daughters are born.
why: Students apply the human concept of 'parents' and 'children' where the parent is a separate, aging entity.
fix: In binary fission, the parent cell itself divides to become the two daughter cells; it doesn't die but becomes the offspring.

probe.question: What happens to the body of the parent Amoeba after it divides?
probe.wrong_answer: It dies and disappears.

root_belief: parents and offspring must be separate entities

subject: science
statement: Budding is a type of sexual reproduction because a 'baby' grows from the parent.
why: Students think any process that produces a small version of an organism must be sexual.
fix: Budding is asexual because it involves only one parent and no fusion of gametes.

probe.question: Does Hydra need a partner to produce a bud?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is making a baby.

root_belief: offspring implies sexual reproduction

subject: science
statement: Humans are the only animals that are viviparous.
why: Limited exposure to the diversity of the animal kingdom and mammal classification.
fix: Many animals, including most mammals like cows, dogs, and lions, are viviparous.

probe.question: Are dogs oviparous or viviparous?
probe.wrong_answer: Neither, only humans give birth like that.

root_belief: humans are biologically unique from all animals

subject: science
statement: Internal fertilisation only occurs in animals that live on land.
why: Students associate water with external fertilisation and land with internal fertilisation.
fix: Some aquatic animals, like sharks and whales, use internal fertilisation.

probe.question: Can internal fertilisation happen in the ocean?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it only happens on land so the sperm doesn't wash away.

root_belief: environment dictates all biological traits

subject: science
statement: The embryo gets all its food from the father's sperm.
why: Misunderstanding of the role of gametes; sometimes attributing 'strength' or 'food' to the male side.
fix: The egg usually provides the initial nutrients (yolk), and in many animals, the mother provides nourishment during development.

probe.question: Where does a developing chick inside an egg get its food?
probe.wrong_answer: From the sperm that fertilised it.

root_belief: one source provides everything

subject: science
statement: Any crop can grow in any season if we provide enough water.
why: Students often think water is the only limiting factor for plant growth.
fix: Crops like Kharif and Rabi depend on specific temperature, day length, and rainfall patterns, not just water quantity.

probe.question: If we provide plenty of irrigation, can we grow Paddy in the peak of a dry North Indian winter?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because paddy only needs lots of water to grow.

root_belief: one factor determines the outcome of a complex process

subject: science
statement: Ploughing is done only to kill weeds and has no effect on the soil itself.
why: The removal of weeds is a visible result, while soil aeration is invisible.
fix: Ploughing loosens the soil, allowing roots to breathe easily and penetrate deeper.

probe.question: Why do we turn the soil even if there are no weeds present?
probe.wrong_answer: It is just a traditional habit with no scientific benefit.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: science
statement: Seeds that float on water are healthy because they are light and easy to sprout.
why: Students may associate lightness with agility or ease of movement.
fix: Healthy seeds are heavy and sink; floating seeds are usually hollow or damaged by pests.

probe.question: You put seeds in a bucket of water and some float. Which ones will you sow?
probe.wrong_answer: The floating ones because they are light.

root_belief: lighter or smaller objects are more active

subject: science
statement: Fertilizers are the food that plants eat to grow.
why: Students use an analogy with human eating to understand plant nutrition.
fix: Plants make their own food through photosynthesis; fertilizers only provide mineral nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus.

probe.question: What is the primary purpose of adding urea to a field?
probe.wrong_answer: To provide food for the plant to eat.

root_belief: living things must eat external food to grow

subject: science
statement: Manure is harmful to plants because it is made from animal waste.
why: Everyday associations of 'waste' or 'dung' with germs and disease.
fix: Manure is organic matter that improves soil texture and adds humus, which is very beneficial.

probe.question: Is adding cow dung to soil safe for the crops we eat?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because waste contains toxins that will enter the fruit.

root_belief: waste products are always toxic and harmful

subject: science
statement: Drip irrigation is less effective because it doesn't soak the whole field.
why: Students believe that 'more water' or 'visible wetness' equals better growth.
fix: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the roots, minimizing wastage and preventing weed growth in empty spaces.

probe.question: Why might a farmer choose drip irrigation over flooding the whole field?
probe.wrong_answer: They wouldn't, because flooding ensures every part of the plant gets water.

root_belief: more of a good thing is always better

subject: science
statement: Weeds are harmless plants that just happen to grow in the wrong place.
why: Students don't see the invisible competition for resources happening underground.
fix: Weeds actively compete with crops for water, nutrients, space, and light, reducing crop yield.

probe.question: If a few wild grass plants grow among wheat, should the farmer worry?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are just extra plants and won't affect the wheat.

root_belief: resources in nature are infinite

subject: science
statement: Grains should be stored while they are slightly moist to keep them fresh.
why: In everyday life, 'fresh' vegetables are often moist or hydrated.
fix: Stored grains must be completely dry to prevent the growth of fungus and bacteria.

probe.question: Why do farmers sun-dry grains before packing them in gunny bags?
probe.wrong_answer: To make them lighter for transport.

root_belief: freshness is always associated with moisture

subject: science
statement: Paddy and Rice are two completely different species of plants.
why: The change in name after processing (removal of husk) confuses students.
fix: Paddy is the name of the crop in the field; rice is the grain obtained after removing the husk.

probe.question: What is the difference between a paddy field and a rice field?
probe.wrong_answer: They grow different types of grains used for different dishes.

root_belief: different names imply different biological entities

subject: science
statement: Earthworms are pests because they create holes in the soil.
why: Generalization that any 'worm' found in a farm is a pest that eats crops.
fix: Earthworms are 'friends of the farmer' because they help in loosening soil and adding humus.

probe.question: If you see many earthworms in your field, what should you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Apply pesticides to kill them before they eat the seeds.

root_belief: all small crawling animals are harmful pests

subject: science
statement: Soil is an inexhaustible source of minerals that never runs out.
why: Soil appears as a massive, permanent part of the earth that doesn't seem to change.
fix: Continuous cultivation of crops makes the soil poor in certain nutrients, requiring replenishment.

probe.question: Why can't we grow the same crop in the same field year after year without adding anything?
probe.wrong_answer: We can, the soil has infinite minerals for plants.

root_belief: large natural resources are infinite

subject: science
statement: Threshing and Winnowing are the same process.
why: Both involve separating parts of the harvested plant and are done close together in time.
fix: Threshing separates grains from the stalks, while winnowing separates grains from the lighter chaff using wind.

probe.question: Which process specifically requires the help of wind?
probe.wrong_answer: Threshing, because it blows the grain away.

root_belief: related steps in a sequence are identical

subject: science
statement: Plants only take in carbon dioxide and never release it.
why: Students think plants only perform photosynthesis and do not respire like animals.
fix: Plants respire all the time, taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide; they only consume more CO2 than they produce during daylight.

probe.question: Do plants release carbon dioxide at night?
probe.wrong_answer: No, plants only release oxygen and never release carbon dioxide.

subject: science
statement: Desertification means the soil physically turns into beach sand.
why: The word 'desert' triggers images of sand dunes rather than the loss of fertility.
fix: Desertification is the process where fertile land loses its nutrients and topsoil, becoming barren like a desert.

probe.question: What happens to the land during desertification?
probe.wrong_answer: The soil turns into sand from the ocean.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: science
statement: Endemic species are those that are found everywhere in the world.
why: Students confuse 'endemic' with 'epidemic' or common species.
fix: Endemic species are those found exclusively in a specific geographical area and nowhere else naturally.

probe.question: If a kangaroo is found naturally only in Australia, what is it called?
probe.wrong_answer: It is an endangered species because it is only in one place.
