root_belief: Wildlife policies date from the colonial era

subject: social
statement: Vulnerable species are those that are likely to be extinct within a few years.
why: Students treat the IUCN categories as interchangeable levels of 'in danger' and equate vulnerable with critically imminent extinction.
fix: Vulnerable species are likely to move into the endangered category in the near future if the factors threatening them continue. They are not yet endangered.

probe.question: What does the vulnerable category mean?
probe.wrong_answer: The species will become extinct in a few years.

root_belief: All threat categories mean imminent extinction

subject: social
statement: A species is extinct if it is no longer found in one particular area.
why: Students generalise local disappearance to global disappearance.
fix: Extinct species are those not found after searches of known or likely areas where they may occur. A species can vanish from one region yet survive elsewhere, which is not extinction.

probe.question: The Asiatic cheetah is no longer found in India. Is it therefore extinct everywhere?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if it is gone from India it is extinct.

root_belief: Local disappearance means global extinction

subject: social
statement: Community conservation works only when the government runs and funds it.
why: Students see conservation as an official job and overlook the role of local village groups.
fix: In places like Sariska and Alwar, villagers have protected forests themselves, even fighting mining, and Joint Forest Management involves local communities with the forest department.

probe.question: Who protected the forests in villages of Alwar, Rajasthan?
probe.wrong_answer: Only forest officials, since villagers cannot protect forests.

root_belief: Only government can conserve nature

subject: social
statement: Biodiversity loss is caused only by hunting and poaching of animals.
why: Media stories about poaching make it the most visible cause, so students ignore habitat and plant losses.
fix: Habitat destruction, deforestation, mining, overgrazing, large development projects, forest fires and the spread of invasive species also cause biodiversity loss, affecting plants as well as animals.

probe.question: Name the cause of the decline in forest biodiversity.
probe.wrong_answer: Only hunting and poaching of animals.

root_belief: One visible cause explains all loss

subject: social
concept: Scarcity is not just low rainfall
statement: Water scarcity is caused only by lack of rainfall.
why: Students equate scarcity with drought, ignoring human consumption patterns.
fix: Scarcity can occur even with sufficient rainfall due to over-exploitation, pollution, and unequal distribution.

probe.question: Can a region with high rainfall face water scarcity?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because rain provides enough water for everyone.

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: social
statement: Dams are always the best solution to prevent floods.
why: Students assume that if a structure is built to hold water, it must prevent all flooding.
fix: Dams often worsen floods during heavy releases or due to sedimentation, and they disrupt natural river flow.

probe.question: Do dams always stop floods?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they hold back all the extra water.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: social
statement: Rainwater harvesting is only for rural areas.
why: Students associate traditional systems with villages and ignore modern urban applications.
fix: Rainwater harvesting is highly effective in urban areas through rooftop collection to recharge groundwater.

probe.question: Can cities use rainwater harvesting?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is a traditional village practice.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: Water scarcity happens only in deserts and dry regions, never in places with big rivers.
why: Students link scarcity with visible dryness and ignore the problem of uneven availability and demand.
fix: Scarcity can occur even in areas with plenty of water, because of overuse, pollution and unequal access, as in Indian cities on large rivers.

probe.question: Can a city located beside a large river face a water shortage? Why or why not?
probe.wrong_answer: No, a city next to a big river always has enough water.

root_belief: Scarcity means physical dryness only

subject: social
statement: Industrial pollution of water does not cause water scarcity because the water is still there.
why: Students equate scarcity with the quantity of water and ignore quality.
fix: Polluted water is unfit for use, so it reduces the usable supply; NCERT lists pollution from industries and agriculture as a cause of scarcity.

probe.question: A river has plenty of water but is badly polluted by factories. Is there a water scarcity for people using it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, as long as the river has a lot of water there is no scarcity.

root_belief: Only the quantity of water matters, not quality

subject: social
statement: Population growth affects only the food supply, not the availability of water.
why: Students link population with food and housing but not with per-person water use.
fix: More people need more water for domestic use, irrigation and industry, so per capita availability falls and over-exploitation of water rises.

probe.question: How does a growing population affect water resources?
probe.wrong_answer: It only increases the demand for food and has no effect on water availability.

root_belief: Population pressure does not involve water demand

subject: social
statement: Irrigation and green revolution farming use very little water compared with households.
why: Students see daily household use but not the large water needs of crops and farms.
fix: Agriculture, especially irrigated crops like rice, wheat and sugarcane, is the biggest user of water and has led to falling groundwater levels.

probe.question: Which group uses the largest share of water: households or irrigated agriculture?
probe.wrong_answer: Households, because people use water every day and farms use only a little.

root_belief: Visible daily use equals the largest water use

subject: social
statement: Nehru called dams the temples of modern India because they are religious places built on rivers.
why: Students take the word temple literally and confuse the metaphor with worship.
fix: Nehru used 'temples of modern India' because dams bring industrial development, agricultural growth and jobs, not because they are religious.

probe.question: Why did Jawaharlal Nehru call dams the 'temples of modern India'?
probe.wrong_answer: Because temples were built near dams and people worship there.

root_belief: Metaphors in textbooks are literal statements

subject: social
statement: A multipurpose river project is built only to produce electricity.
why: Students identify dams such as Bhakra Nangal with hydroelectric power alone.
fix: Multipurpose projects serve several aims at once: irrigation, hydroelectricity, water supply, flood control, inland navigation and fish breeding.

probe.question: Why are dams like Hirakud called multipurpose projects?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they are used to generate electricity only.

root_belief: Dams exist for a single purpose

subject: social
statement: Dams have only benefits and cause no harm to rivers or the environment.
why: Textbook praise of development leads students to ignore ecological costs.
fix: Dams disturb the natural flow of rivers, cause sedimentation, harm aquatic life and vegetation, and can increase flood risk and conflicts, leading to protests like Narmada Bachao Andolan.

probe.question: Why did people protest against the Sardar Sarovar dam?
probe.wrong_answer: They had no real reason, as dams cause no damage to the environment.

root_belief: Development projects have no negative effects

subject: social
statement: People displaced by dams are always fully compensated and resettled, so they lose nothing.
why: Students assume government projects automatically give fair rehabilitation.
fix: Many displaced people, often tribals and the poor, lost land and livelihoods and were not adequately rehabilitated, which fuelled movements like Narmada Bachao Andolan.

probe.question: Why did displaced people oppose dams like Sardar Sarovar?
probe.wrong_answer: They did not oppose it because they were all given good land and homes.

root_belief: Official projects always treat affected people fairly

subject: social
statement: Traditional water harvesting methods like tankas and johads are outdated and useless today.
why: Students think modern technology like dams has replaced old methods.
fix: Tankas, johads, kuls and bamboo drip irrigation are low-cost, local and still used; Gendathur in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu's compulsory roof-top harvesting show their value.

probe.question: Are traditional methods like johads and tankas useful for water conservation today?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are old and only modern dams can conserve water.

root_belief: Old methods are always inferior to modern ones

subject: social
statement: Primitive farming is only practiced by tribal people in remote forests.
why: Students associate 'primitive' with 'tribal' due to media stereotypes.
fix: It is a method of cultivation based on natural environmental conditions and family labor, not defined by the ethnicity of the farmer.

probe.question: Can a farmer in a non-tribal village practice primitive subsistence farming?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because they are not tribal.

root_belief: Labels define the nature of an activity

subject: social
statement: Rabi crops are grown in summer because they need a lot of heat.
why: Students confuse the harvest time (summer) with the growing time.
fix: Rabi crops are sown in winter and harvested in summer; they require cool weather for germination and warm weather for maturation.

probe.question: When are wheat seeds sown?
probe.wrong_answer: In the summer, because it is a Rabi crop.

root_belief: Harvest time is the same as growing time

subject: social
statement: MSP is the price at which the government sells food to the poor.
why: Students confuse the procurement price (MSP) with the issue price (PDS).
fix: MSP is the price at which the government buys crops from farmers to ensure they get a fair return.

probe.question: Who receives the MSP payment?
probe.wrong_answer: The poor people buying ration.

root_belief: Government schemes always involve selling to the public

subject: social
concept: Use of HYV seeds and fertilizers
statement: Using more fertilizers always leads to higher crop yields indefinitely.
why: Students apply a linear 'more is better' logic without considering soil health.
fix: Excessive use of fertilizers degrades soil quality and reduces fertility over time, leading to lower yields in the long run.

probe.question: What happens if a farmer doubles the recommended fertilizer dose?
probe.wrong_answer: The crop will grow twice as fast and yield more.

root_belief: Bigger or more means more effect

subject: social
statement: Intensive subsistence farming means using lots of machines and big farms to grow crops for sale.
why: Students read 'intensive' as 'industrial' and link it with mechanisation and large scale.
fix: Intensive subsistence farming is done on small plots using lots of labour and farm inputs to get high output per unit of land, mainly to feed the farmer's family.

probe.question: A farmer in a crowded part of the Ganga plain works a tiny plot with family labour and grows rice for his family. Which type of farming is this?
probe.wrong_answer: Commercial farming, because the work is very intensive.

root_belief: Intensive means large-scale and machine-based

subject: social
statement: Commercial farming means farmers do not grow food crops like rice or wheat.
why: Students link commercial farming only with cash crops like tea and cotton.
fix: Commercial farming means crops are grown mainly for sale; the crop can be rice or wheat too, as in Punjab and Haryana, where the commercialisation level is high.

probe.question: Rice is grown for sale in Punjab and Haryana on a large scale. What type of farming is it?
probe.wrong_answer: Subsistence farming, because rice is a food crop.

root_belief: Crop type decides farming type, not purpose

subject: social
statement: Zaid crops are grown in the same season as Kharif crops, in the monsoon.
why: Students remember Zaid as a 'summer-ish' season and mix it with the rainy season.
fix: Zaid is a short season between Rabi and Kharif, in summer (March to June), with crops like watermelon, cucumber and fodder. Kharif starts with the monsoon in June–July.

probe.question: In which season are watermelon and cucumber mainly grown in India?
probe.wrong_answer: Kharif, because they need rain.

root_belief: Zaid is the same as Kharif

subject: social
statement: Food security just means that a country grows enough food in total.
why: Students focus on national production and ignore access and affordability.
fix: Food security means all people have availability, access and affordability of food at all times. Enough production does not help if poor people cannot buy it.

probe.question: India has big food grain stocks, yet some poor people still sleep hungry. Is India food secure?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because food is available in the country.

root_belief: Food security equals total food production
source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Economics / FAO definition studies

subject: social
statement: Slash and burn farming is done on the same plot every year.
why: Students picture a fixed field and do not see the shifting cycle.
fix: Farmers clear and burn a patch, grow crops for a few years, then abandon it when soil fertility falls and move to a new patch. This is also called shifting agriculture.

probe.question: After a few harvests on a burnt patch, what does the slash and burn farmer do?
probe.wrong_answer: Adds fertilizer and continues farming on the same patch.

root_belief: All farming uses permanent fixed fields

subject: social
statement: High population pressure on land is the reason farms in India are large.
why: Students think more people means more land taken up for farming.
fix: Land is limited, so more people means each family's plot gets divided into smaller holdings through inheritance. Small holdings lead to intensive farming.

probe.question: In densely populated areas, what happens to the size of farm holdings over generations?
probe.wrong_answer: They become larger because more people need more food.

root_belief: More people means bigger farms

subject: social
concept: Use of HYV seeds and fertilizers
statement: HYV seeds give high yields on their own without needing irrigation or other inputs.
why: The name 'high yielding' suggests the seed alone does everything.
fix: HYV seeds give high yields only with assured irrigation, fertilizers and pesticides. This package is why the Green Revolution worked best in Punjab, Haryana and western UP.

probe.question: A farmer sows HYV wheat in a dry field without irrigation or fertilizers. What happens to the yield?
probe.wrong_answer: It will still be very high because the seed is high yielding.

root_belief: Improved seeds alone guarantee high yield
source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Geography / Green Revolution case studies

subject: social
statement: Land reform acts took land from all farmers and gave it to the government.
why: Students mix land reform with land acquisition or collectivisation.
fix: Land reforms such as abolition of zamindari and land ceiling aimed to take surplus land from big landlords and give it to tenants and landless farmers, and to remove middlemen.

probe.question: Who received the surplus land taken from big landlords under land ceiling laws?
probe.wrong_answer: The government kept it all as state farms.

root_belief: Land reform means state takes all private land

subject: social
statement: All metallic minerals are ferrous.
why: Students often associate the word 'metal' with 'iron' due to its common usage.
fix: Ferrous minerals contain iron, while non-ferrous minerals like copper or gold do not contain iron.

probe.question: Is gold a ferrous mineral?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a metal.

root_belief: a category name implies all its members are identical

subject: social
statement: Mining is only done by digging deep vertical shafts.
why: Visuals of mining in media often focus on deep underground shafts.
fix: Mining can be open-cast (surface), shaft (deep underground), or drilling, depending on the depth of the mineral deposit.

probe.question: How is coal extracted if it is near the surface?
probe.wrong_answer: By digging a deep shaft.

root_belief: one specific example represents the entire process

subject: social
statement: Coal is a renewable resource because we keep finding more.
why: Confusing the rate of discovery with the rate of geological formation.
fix: Coal is a non-renewable resource because it takes millions of years to form and cannot be replaced once consumed.

probe.question: Will we run out of coal?
probe.wrong_answer: No, we keep finding new mines.

root_belief: human discovery equals natural replenishment

subject: social
statement: Non-conventional energy is always more efficient than conventional energy.
why: Marketing and media hype around 'green' energy often ignore efficiency and scale constraints.
fix: Non-conventional energy is sustainable, but its efficiency and reliability depend on technology and environmental conditions.

probe.question: Is solar energy always better than coal?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is non-conventional.

root_belief: new is always better than old

subject: social
statement: Metallic minerals are always hard and non-metallic minerals are always soft.
why: Students link 'metal' with strength and 'non-metal' with brittleness or softness, ignoring that diamond is non-metallic and very hard.
fix: Metallic minerals contain metals (iron, copper, bauxite); non-metallic ones (mica, limestone, diamond, coal) do not. Hardness is not what separates the groups.

probe.question: Diamond is the hardest natural substance. Is it a metallic or non-metallic mineral?
probe.wrong_answer: Metallic, because it is very hard.

root_belief: Hardness and strength define metallic minerals

subject: social
statement: Ferrous minerals are those that contain rust.
why: Students know iron rusts and mix up the word 'ferrous' with the rust that forms on iron.
fix: Ferrous minerals contain iron (iron ore, manganese, nickel, cobalt in steel-making); they are classified by iron content, not by rust. Non-ferrous minerals such as copper, bauxite and lead have no iron in them.

probe.question: Why is iron ore called a ferrous mineral?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it rusts when exposed to air and water.

root_belief: Classification names come from visible properties like rust

subject: social
statement: Open-cast mining is done only on the surface of the ground by simply picking up minerals, with no machines or blasting.
why: Students think 'open' means shallow and easy, and picture a small surface scraping.
fix: Open-cast mining removes minerals from shallow deposits by digging large open pits, often with blasting, drilling and heavy machines; it is cheaper and quicker than shaft mining, which is used for deep deposits.

probe.question: Which method needs heavy machinery and blasting, open-cast or shaft mining?
probe.wrong_answer: Only shaft mining; open-cast is just picking minerals from the surface.

root_belief: Open surface work means simple, small-scale activity

subject: social
statement: Mining methods are chosen by the type of mineral, not by how deep the deposit lies.
why: Students link a specific mineral with a specific method and miss the depth factor.
fix: The method depends mainly on the depth and position of the deposit: shallow deposits use open-cast, deep ones use shaft (underground) mining; quarrying is used for stones near the surface.

probe.question: A coal seam lies very close to the surface. Which mining method is likely used?
probe.wrong_answer: Shaft mining, because coal is always mined that way.

root_belief: Each mineral has one fixed mining method

subject: social
statement: Solar energy is renewable, so solar panels work equally well day and night and in all weather.
why: Students equate 'renewable and inexhaustible' with 'always available', ignoring that the Sun is not available at night or in cloud.
fix: Sunlight is a renewable resource, but the energy a panel gives depends on sunshine hours and weather, so storage (batteries) or other sources are needed at night and in cloudy periods.

probe.question: Can a solar panel alone power a village light all night?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because solar energy never runs out.

root_belief: Renewable means constantly available without limits
source_hint: studies on students' ideas about renewable energy

subject: social
statement: Coal is a fossil fuel because it is dug out of the ground like fossils.
why: Students take 'fossil' to mean anything dug from the earth, not its origin from ancient living matter.
fix: Coal is a fossil fuel because it formed over millions of years from plants buried and compressed under heat and pressure. Petroleum and natural gas form from marine organisms.

probe.question: Why is coal called a fossil fuel?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it is dug up from underground, like fossils.

root_belief: Fossil fuel means anything extracted from underground
source_hint: studies on students' ideas about fossil fuels

subject: social
statement: Conventional energy sources are the ones that are new and modern, while non-conventional ones are old.
why: Students read 'conventional' as 'advanced' rather than 'traditionally used'.
fix: Conventional sources (coal, petroleum, natural gas, firewood, hydel power) have been in common use for long and are mostly exhaustible; non-conventional sources (solar, wind, tidal, biogas, geothermal) are newer and largely renewable.

probe.question: Which is the conventional source: coal or wind energy?
probe.wrong_answer: Wind energy, because it is the modern technology.

root_belief: Conventional means modern or advanced

subject: social
statement: Conserving minerals means we should stop using them completely.
why: Students think saving a resource means not using it, instead of using it carefully.
fix: Sustainable use means using minerals and energy wisely: avoiding wastage, recycling metals, using substitutes and efficient technologies, and relying more on renewable sources so future generations also have them.

probe.question: What should we do to conserve mineral resources?
probe.wrong_answer: Stop mining and using them altogether.

root_belief: Conservation means total non-use
source_hint: research on students' conceptions of conservation

subject: social
statement: Industries are always located exactly where the raw material is found.
why: Students assume that proximity is the only factor in industrial location.
fix: Industries are located at the point where the cost of transporting raw materials and finished goods is minimized, considering labor, power, and market access.

probe.question: Why might a steel plant be located far from an iron ore mine?
probe.wrong_answer: It is impossible; steel plants must be at the mine site.

root_belief: one event has one single cause
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

subject: social
statement: Iron and steel is a consumer industry because we use steel utensils at home.
why: Students confuse the final product with the nature of the industry.
fix: Iron and steel is a basic or key industry because its products are used as raw materials for other manufacturing industries.

probe.question: Is the iron and steel industry a consumer or basic industry?
probe.wrong_answer: Consumer, because we buy steel plates.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: Industrial pollution only refers to smoke coming out of chimneys.
why: Visual bias towards air pollution as the most obvious form of industrial impact.
fix: Industrial pollution includes air, water, land, noise, and thermal pollution, which affects the environment in multiple ways.

probe.question: Which of these is an example of industrial pollution?
probe.wrong_answer: Only smoke from factory chimneys.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: social
statement: The IT industry does not cause any pollution because it does not have large factories.
why: The 'clean' appearance of software offices masks the environmental impact of hardware manufacturing and e-waste.
fix: The IT industry generates significant e-waste and consumes high amounts of electricity, contributing to environmental degradation.

probe.question: Does the IT industry impact the environment?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is a clean industry with no pollution.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: social
statement: Industries that use farm produce as raw material are called agro-based, so a sugar mill and a cotton mill are mineral-based industries.
why: Students mix up the source of raw material with where the industry is located or what it makes.
fix: Agro-based industries (cotton, jute, sugar, tea, rubber) use plant and animal products. Mineral-based industries (iron and steel, cement, aluminium) use minerals.

probe.question: Under which raw-material category does a sugar mill fall?
probe.wrong_answer: Mineral-based, because it makes a product used in factories.

root_belief: Industry type depends on product use, not raw material
source_hint: NCERT Class 8 Geography, school exam answer scripts

subject: social
statement: Public sector, private sector and joint sector industries are classified by the size of the factory.
why: Students link the word 'sector' and ownership with big or small scale.
fix: Ownership classifies industries as public (government), private (individuals or companies) or joint (government and private together). Size classifies them as small-scale or large-scale.

probe.question: Which kind of industry is Tata Steel, a privately owned company, classed as by ownership?
probe.wrong_answer: Large-scale industry, which is the same as the ownership class.

root_belief: Ownership and size are the same basis of classification

subject: social
statement: The only thing that decides where an industry is set up is the availability of cheap land.
why: Students pick one visible factor and ignore the others.
fix: Location depends on many factors together: raw material, power, labour, market, water, transport and government policy.

probe.question: Why was the cotton textile industry set up in Mumbai?
probe.wrong_answer: Because land was cheap there.

root_belief: One factor alone decides industrial location
source_hint: NCERT Class 8 and Class 10 geography; teacher observation

subject: social
statement: Cost minimization means the factory is always built where land and wages are lowest.
why: Students read cost as only land and labour.
fix: Industrialists look for the site with the least total cost, including transport of raw material and finished goods, power and labour. A cheap site with high transport cost may not be chosen.

probe.question: A factory finds cheap labour in a remote village with poor roads. Will it always be set up there?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, since cheap labour always gives the lowest cost.

root_belief: Lowest cost means lowest wages or land price
source_hint: Weber's least-cost theory as simplified in NCERT

subject: social
statement: The cotton textile industry needs to be near cotton fields, so it is found only in cotton-growing states.
why: Students extend the idea of raw-material pull without seeing that cotton is light and easy to move.
fix: Cotton is a pure raw material that loses little weight, so mills can be set up far from fields. Mills spread to places with a market, a port or power. Ahmedabad and Mumbai grew with these advantages.

probe.question: Why are there many cotton mills in Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra but also in places with little cotton?
probe.wrong_answer: There cannot be any mills outside cotton-growing areas.

root_belief: Industry must sit beside its raw material
source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Contemporary India II, Manufacturing Industries

subject: social
statement: Textile means only cotton cloth made in mills, so handloom and silk are not part of the textile industry.
why: Students think of the textile industry as one large factory type.
fix: The textile industry includes the organised mill sector and the decentralised handloom and powerloom sectors, and covers cotton, jute, silk, wool and synthetic fibres.

probe.question: Is a handloom weaver in a village part of the textile industry?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only big mills count as the textile industry.

root_belief: Only large factory production counts as industry

subject: social
statement: Iron and steel are the same thing, so a steel plant only melts iron ore and makes no alloys.
why: The words are used together and students miss the role of carbon and other elements.
fix: Steel is an alloy of iron with a small amount of carbon. Making steel needs iron ore, coking coal and limestone. The plant also needs manganese to make alloys.

probe.question: What is the difference between pig iron and steel?
probe.wrong_answer: There is no difference; both are just melted iron ore.

root_belief: Iron and steel are identical materials

subject: social
statement: Industrial pollution can be stopped fully by planting trees near the factory.
why: Students think one simple step, such as greenery, cancels all pollution.
fix: Mitigation needs several steps. These include treating effluents, fitting filters and scrubbers, recycling water, using cleaner fuel and following pollution laws. Trees help only a little.

probe.question: A factory discharges chemical waste into a river. Is planting trees enough to solve it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, trees around the factory remove all the pollution.

root_belief: One simple action fully solves pollution
source_hint: NCERT Class 8 and Class 10 geography, environmental education studies

subject: social
statement: The Golden Quadrilateral connects all major state capitals.
why: Students confuse the major metropolitan hubs with state capitals.
fix: It connects the four major metropolitan cities: Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, and Kolkata.

probe.question: Which city is NOT part of the Golden Quadrilateral?
probe.wrong_answer: Lucknow

root_belief: Important things are always administrative centers

subject: social
statement: Pipelines are only used to transport water.
why: Students associate pipes in daily life primarily with plumbing.
fix: Pipelines are a major mode of transport for crude oil, petroleum products, and natural gas.

probe.question: What is the primary use of the Hazira-Vijaipur-Jagdishpur pipeline?
probe.wrong_answer: Supplying drinking water

root_belief: A word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: A country is richer if it exports and imports the same amount.
why: Students confuse balance with equality in value.
fix: A favorable balance of trade occurs when the value of exports exceeds the value of imports.

probe.question: What is a favorable balance of trade?
probe.wrong_answer: When exports equal imports

root_belief: Equality is always the best state

subject: social
statement: All rivers in India are navigable for large ships.
why: Students assume all water bodies are deep enough for transport.
fix: Only specific stretches of rivers like the Ganga and Brahmaputra are navigable for large vessels.

probe.question: Are all Indian rivers used for inland waterways?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they are rivers

root_belief: Categories have uniform properties

subject: social
statement: Railways carry more passengers and goods in India than roadways do.
why: Students see the railway as the 'backbone' of Indian transport and assume it must carry the largest share.
fix: Roadways now carry the larger share of both passengers and goods in India, because they are cheaper for short distances and give door-to-door service. Railways are best for long distances and heavy goods.

probe.question: Which mode of transport carries the larger share of India's passengers and freight today?
probe.wrong_answer: Railways, because they are the main transport system.

root_belief: Most famous mode of transport is the most used
source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Contemporary India II, Ch. 7

subject: social
statement: The three railway gauges are broad, narrow and metre, and broad gauge is 1 metre wide.
why: Students link the name 'metre gauge' with 1 metre and mix up the widths of the other gauges.
fix: Broad gauge is 1.676 m, metre gauge is 1 m and narrow gauge is 0.762 m or 0.610 m wide.

probe.question: What is the width between the rails of a broad gauge line?
probe.wrong_answer: 1 metre.

root_belief: Gauge names directly state their measured width
source_hint: NCERT textbook text and class tests

subject: social
statement: Airways are the cheapest way to transport goods and are used for bulk cargo.
why: Students think the fastest mode must also be the most efficient and economical.
fix: Air transport is the fastest but also the costliest mode. It is used for valuable, light or perishable goods and for reaching remote areas, while bulk goods go by rail or water.

probe.question: Why is bulk coal not usually sent by air?
probe.wrong_answer: Air transport is cheap but cannot carry coal, so it is not used.

root_belief: Faster transport must also be cheaper

subject: social
statement: Inland waterways in India are used mainly for international trade with other countries.
why: Students confuse inland waterways with oceanic routes and sea ports.
fix: Inland waterways such as the Ganga (NW-1) and Brahmaputra (NW-2) carry goods and people within the country. International trade goes mostly by sea routes through ports.

probe.question: Which waterway would carry goods between India and Europe: National Waterway-1 or an ocean route?
probe.wrong_answer: National Waterway-1 on the Ganga.

root_belief: All waterways are the same kind of route

subject: social
statement: The Golden Quadrilateral is a railway network joining the four metropolitan cities.
why: The word 'quadrilateral' and the link to Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata make students think of a train network.
fix: The Golden Quadrilateral is a super-highway project of the National Highways Authority of India, a six-lane road network linking Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Mumbai.

probe.question: Which authority built the Golden Quadrilateral and what kind of route is it?
probe.wrong_answer: Indian Railways built it as a rail corridor.

root_belief: Linking big cities means a rail line

subject: social
statement: Pipelines are used to carry only liquids, never solids or gases.
why: Students link pipelines with water and oil and think gas and solids cannot flow through them.
fix: Pipelines carry crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas, and even solids in slurry form. They have a high initial cost but low running cost and cause no trans-shipment losses.

probe.question: Can natural gas be transported by pipeline, such as the Hazira-Vijaipur-Jagdishpur line?
probe.wrong_answer: No, pipelines only carry liquids like oil.

root_belief: Pipelines handle only liquids

subject: social
statement: Mass media like TV and radio is a two-way communication, so listeners reply directly.
why: Students mix mass communication with personal communication such as telephone and the internet.
fix: Radio, TV, newspapers and cinema reach a large audience at once, mainly one-way. Personal communication like the telephone, mobile and e-mail is two-way.

probe.question: Is a radio broadcast a personal or a mass communication medium?
probe.wrong_answer: Personal, because the listener can talk back to the broadcaster.

root_belief: All communication media are two-way

subject: social
statement: International trade is only done by sea and air routes, never by roads or rail.
why: Students link 'international' with distance and overseas ports, forgetting land borders.
fix: Trade can also go by land across borders using roads and railways, for example with Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh. The mode depends on cost, goods and geography.

probe.question: How does India send goods to neighbouring Nepal?
probe.wrong_answer: Only by ship or aeroplane since it is international.

root_belief: Foreign trade needs sea or air

subject: social
statement: People who speak different languages or wear different clothes are unequal.
why: Students often conflate 'difference' with 'hierarchy' based on social observation.
fix: Diversity means having different cultures, but everyone has equal value and rights.

probe.question: If two people speak different languages, who is more important?
probe.wrong_answer: The one who speaks the dominant language.

root_belief: Difference implies a ranking of value
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in social science

subject: social
statement: All members of a group share the same personality traits.
why: Cognitive tendency to simplify complex social information into categories.
fix: Individuals within any group are unique and have diverse personalities and interests.

probe.question: Are all people from a specific region lazy?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they are known to be lazy.

root_belief: Categorization defines the essence of individuals

subject: social
statement: Prejudice is just having a strong opinion about something.
why: Confusion between personal preference and social prejudice.
fix: Prejudice is judging others negatively without knowing the facts or having evidence.

probe.question: Is it prejudice to dislike a specific food?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, that is prejudice.

root_belief: A word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: The law automatically makes everyone equal in real life.
why: Students assume legal rules have immediate, perfect enforcement.
fix: The law provides the framework for equality, but social discrimination still persists in practice.

probe.question: Since the Constitution says everyone is equal, does discrimination exist anymore?
probe.wrong_answer: No, discrimination has ended because it is illegal.

root_belief: Rules are always perfectly followed

subject: social
statement: Diversity means people from different groups live separately and should not mix.
why: Students see visible differences and assume each group lives in its own space; they confuse variety with separation.
fix: Diversity means many different groups live together and share places, festivals and daily life. India's unity comes from this coexistence.

probe.question: In a diverse village, where would people of different religions and languages live and celebrate festivals?
probe.wrong_answer: Each group should live in its own area and celebrate only among themselves.

root_belief: Difference requires separation, not coexistence

subject: social
statement: Diversity in India means only differences of religion.
why: Religion is the most visible and discussed difference, so students narrow diversity to it.
fix: Diversity includes language, food, dress, festivals, region, religion and ways of life. Each is part of India's variety.

probe.question: List the kinds of diversity you can find in India.
probe.wrong_answer: Only different religions like Hindu, Muslim, Sikh and Christian.

root_belief: One familiar kind of difference stands for all diversity

subject: social
statement: A stereotype is always a bad or insulting thing said about a group.
why: Students link stereotypes only with abuse, ignoring that fixed 'positive' ideas also stereotype.
fix: A stereotype is a fixed, oversimplified idea about a group. Even a 'good' one, like 'all girls are good at cooking', is a stereotype and limits people.

probe.question: Is 'boys are naturally good at maths' a stereotype?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is a compliment, so it is not a stereotype.

root_belief: Only negative statements count as stereotypes

subject: social
statement: Stereotypes are true because they come from what many people say.
why: Students treat repeated or popular statements as evidence.
fix: Stereotypes are not based on facts about each person. Many people repeating an idea does not make it true; we must check by knowing individuals.

probe.question: Everyone in class says people from a certain region are lazy. Is it true?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, since so many people say it, it must be true.

root_belief: Popular belief is proof of truth

subject: social
statement: Prejudice is only about disliking people; it cannot be a favourable feeling.
why: The word is heard only in contexts of hatred, so students miss that pre-judging can be favourable too.
fix: Prejudice means forming a judgement about someone before knowing them. It can be negative or favourable, but it is still unfair because it ignores the person.

probe.question: A teacher assumes a new student from a rich family will be clever without knowing them. Is this prejudice?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the teacher likes the student, prejudice is only dislike.

root_belief: Prejudice means only hatred

subject: social
statement: Prejudice goes away once we meet a person from that group even once.
why: Students think one meeting fully corrects a view, ignoring how deeply held ideas persist.
fix: Prejudice reduces when we get to know many individuals and question our ideas over time. One meeting may not change an old belief.

probe.question: Rohan met one kind person from another community. Is his prejudice about that community now finished?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, meeting one person removes all prejudice.

root_belief: One experience fully removes deep-held prejudice

subject: social
statement: Caste-based discrimination ended long ago and no longer happens in India.
why: Students see caste in history chapters and assume it belongs only to the past (presentism-like gap).
fix: Though the Constitution forbids it, caste discrimination still occurs in some places today. Laws and everyday change both need effort.

probe.question: Does anyone in India today face discrimination because of caste?
probe.wrong_answer: No, caste discrimination ended in the past.

root_belief: Social evils end once they are outlawed

subject: social
statement: Ambedkar faced discrimination because he was uneducated or poor.
why: Students link unfair treatment with lack of schooling or money, missing the caste cause.
fix: Ambedkar was a brilliant student who studied widely, yet he was treated unfairly because of his caste. Discrimination was about birth, not ability.

probe.question: Why was young Ambedkar made to sit separately and denied water at school?
probe.wrong_answer: Because he was poor and not good at studies.

root_belief: Discrimination is caused by poverty or lack of ability

subject: social
statement: The village government is independent of the national government.
why: Students see the local office as the only one they interact with.
fix: All levels of government are connected; local bodies follow laws made at state and national levels.

probe.question: Can a village make a law that contradicts a national law?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is their village.

root_belief: Local events are isolated from larger systems

subject: social
statement: In a democracy, the government can do whatever the majority wants.
why: Confusion between majority rule and the protection of rights.
fix: Democracy protects the rights of minorities and follows a constitution, not just the majority's whim.

probe.question: If 90% of people want to ban a minority group's religion, can the government do it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because democracy means majority rule.

root_belief: Majority opinion is always the correct rule

subject: social
statement: Monarchs in history were always cruel dictators.
why: Pop culture and stories often portray kings as villains.
fix: Some monarchs were benevolent and worked for the welfare of their subjects.

probe.question: Was every king in history a bad person?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, kings only care about themselves.

root_belief: Roles are defined by fixed character traits

subject: social
statement: Universal adult franchise means everyone in the country can vote.
why: Students often ignore the word 'adult' and think it means 'all people'.
fix: Only citizens who have reached the age of 18 or older are eligible to vote.

probe.question: Can a 10-year-old child vote in an election?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is universal franchise.

root_belief: A word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: The Gram Panchayat is run by officials sent from the state capital, not chosen by villagers.
why: Students see government as officers appointed from above and do not know that villagers elect their own panchayat members.
fix: The Gram Panchayat is elected by the adults of the village (the Gram Sabha). The Sarpanch and ward members are chosen by voting.

probe.question: Who chooses the members of the Gram Panchayat?
probe.wrong_answer: The state government sends officers to run it.

root_belief: Local government is appointed from above, not elected

subject: social
statement: The Gram Panchayat only handles village festivals and has no real responsibilities.
why: Students see local government as ceremonial and only notice visible events in the village.
fix: The Gram Panchayat looks after village roads, drinking water, street lights, sanitation and schools, and collects local taxes.

probe.question: Name one job of the Gram Panchayat.
probe.wrong_answer: Organising the village fair; it does not do anything else.

root_belief: Local government has trivial, limited functions

subject: social
statement: The State Government makes the laws for the whole country.
why: Students mix up the State and the Centre because both are called government and both make laws.
fix: The State Government makes laws and decisions for its own state on subjects such as police, farming and local administration. Laws for the whole country are made by the Central Government.

probe.question: Who makes the laws that apply to all states of India?
probe.wrong_answer: The State Government of each state.

root_belief: State and national governments have the same reach

subject: social
statement: The Central Government only works in Delhi and looks after only Delhi.
why: Students link the Central Government to its location in the capital and think its work is limited there.
fix: The Central Government sits in Delhi but makes decisions for the whole country, such as defence, currency, railways and foreign affairs.

probe.question: Which area does the Central Government look after?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the city of Delhi.

root_belief: Government's work is limited to where its office is

subject: social
statement: People take part in government only by voting, and nothing else counts.
why: Voting is the most visible form of participation, so students think it is the only one.
fix: People also take part by attending Gram Sabha meetings, giving suggestions, paying taxes, and asking officials questions or raising problems.

probe.question: How can a villager take part in government between elections?
probe.wrong_answer: They cannot; they can only vote once in five years.

root_belief: Participation means only voting

subject: social
statement: A king could be punished or removed by the people if they disliked the decisions.
why: Students carry the idea of democratic accountability into monarchy.
fix: In a monarchy the king or queen holds power by birth, and the position passes down in the family. Ordinary people had no legal way to remove them.

probe.question: How was a monarch chosen and changed in a monarchy?
probe.wrong_answer: People voted to choose or replace the king.

root_belief: All rulers are accountable to voters

subject: social
statement: The right to vote depends on how much money or education a person has.
why: Students hear that rich or educated people are important and assume they alone get a say.
fix: Every adult citizen can vote regardless of wealth, education, religion, caste or gender. This is the equal right to vote.

probe.question: Can a poor villager who never went to school vote in India?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only educated or rich people can vote.

root_belief: Wealth or education decides political rights

subject: social
statement: A monarchy and a democracy are the same, since in both someone rules the country.
why: Students focus on 'someone rules' and ignore how the ruler comes to power.
fix: In a democracy the people elect their leaders for a fixed time. In a monarchy the ruler gets power by birth and often rules for life.

probe.question: What is the main difference between a monarchy and a democracy?
probe.wrong_answer: There is no difference; in both a leader rules the country.

root_belief: All governments work the same way

subject: social
statement: The Gram Sabha consists only of the elected members of the Panchayat.
why: Students confuse the executive body with the general assembly of voters.
fix: The Gram Sabha includes every person in the village who is 18 years or older and on the voters' list.

probe.question: Who attends the Gram Sabha meeting?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the Sarpanch and the Ward members.

root_belief: Only leaders participate in government decisions

subject: social
statement: The Sarpanch has absolute power to make all village decisions alone.
why: Students equate the Sarpanch with a monarch or a single boss.
fix: The Sarpanch works with the Gram Panchayat members and is accountable to the Gram Sabha.

probe.question: Can the Sarpanch decide to build a road without asking anyone?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because he is the head of the village.

root_belief: Leadership means having total authority

subject: social
statement: The Zila Parishad makes laws for the whole country.
why: Students overgeneralize the term 'Parishad' or 'Council' to national levels.
fix: The Zila Parishad operates at the district level and coordinates activities of the Panchayat Samitis.

probe.question: What is the scope of the Zila Parishad?
probe.wrong_answer: It is the highest law-making body in India.

root_belief: Bigger names imply national authority

subject: social
statement: Ward councillors are appointed by the government, not elected.
why: Students assume local urban officials are bureaucrats rather than representatives.
fix: Ward councillors are elected representatives chosen by the people living in that specific ward.

probe.question: How does a person become a ward councillor?
probe.wrong_answer: They are selected by the city mayor or government officials.

root_belief: Government officials are always appointed by superiors

subject: social
statement: The Gram Panchayat builds and runs the village's roads, school and hospital entirely by itself with no outside help.
why: Students see the Panchayat as the only local authority and ignore its links to higher bodies and government schemes.
fix: The Gram Panchayat looks after local work like drinking water, street lights, roads and sanitation, but it works with Panchayat Samiti, Zila Parishad and government grants.

probe.question: Who provides all the money and builds the village school and hospital?
probe.wrong_answer: The Gram Panchayat alone does everything without any help.

root_belief: Local body works alone, independent of other levels

subject: social
statement: The Panchayat Samiti is the body at the district level above the Zila Parishad.
why: Students mix up the order of the three tiers and think bigger names mean lower or higher levels wrongly.
fix: The three tiers are Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti (block) and Zila Parishad (district), the highest tier.

probe.question: Which is the highest body of the Panchayati Raj system: Panchayat Samiti or Zila Parishad?
probe.wrong_answer: Panchayat Samiti is at the top because it covers the district.

root_belief: Hierarchy order of tiers is arbitrary or reversed

subject: social
statement: A ward councillor looks after the whole city and not just one ward.
why: Students think the word councillor means a city head, not the representative of a small area.
fix: A ward councillor is elected by the people of one ward, a small part of the town or city, and speaks for the problems of that ward in the council.

probe.question: Whom should a family in Ward 5 meet about a broken drain in their lane?
probe.wrong_answer: The councillor of the whole city, since he looks after every area.

root_belief: Representatives cover entire area, not a constituency

subject: social
statement: Only men who own land in the village can attend and vote in the Gram Sabha.
why: Students carry over social stereotypes about who counts in village decisions.
fix: All adult men and women in the village who are on the voter list (18 years or older) are members of the Gram Sabha, whether or not they own land.

probe.question: Can a woman who owns no land and works as a labourer attend the Gram Sabha?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only landowning men can attend the Gram Sabha.

root_belief: Only property-owning men have a say in decisions

subject: social
statement: The Sarpanch is appointed by the district collector and not chosen by villagers.
why: Students confuse the Sarpanch with government officers like the collector or the village secretary.
fix: The Sarpanch is the head of the Gram Panchayat, chosen through election by the villagers (in the Panchayat's ward members' elections), not appointed by an officer.

probe.question: How does a person become Sarpanch of a village?
probe.wrong_answer: The collector selects and appoints him.

root_belief: Local leaders are appointed by government officials

subject: social
statement: Panchayat funds come only from the pocket money of the Sarpanch and members.
why: Students think of money as personal and do not know about taxes, grants and schemes.
fix: Panchayat funds come from local taxes and fees, and grants from the state and central governments, used for public works.

probe.question: Where does the Panchayat get money to repair the village well?
probe.wrong_answer: From the personal money of the Sarpanch.

root_belief: Public money equals leader's personal money

subject: social
statement: The Zila Parishad looks after the problems of a single village like a broken lane.
why: Students think the highest rural body handles all matters, including tiny local ones.
fix: The Zila Parishad works at the district level, planning and coordinating development across many blocks and villages; village matters are handled by the Gram Panchayat.

probe.question: Who should first handle a small drainage problem in one village?
probe.wrong_answer: The Zila Parishad, since it is the biggest body.

root_belief: Higher bodies handle every small local issue

subject: social
statement: Municipal Corporation and Municipal Council are the same, and both are found in villages.
why: Students treat similar-sounding words as synonyms and forget the rural-urban divide.
fix: Municipal Corporations govern big cities and Municipal Councils govern smaller towns; villages have Gram Panchayats instead.

probe.question: Which body governs a big city like Mumbai: Gram Panchayat or Municipal Corporation?
probe.wrong_answer: Both are the same and run villages.

root_belief: Similar-sounding institutions are interchangeable

subject: social
statement: All farmers in India own the land they cultivate.
why: Students often generalize from stories of wealthy landowners in media.
fix: Many rural workers are landless labourers who work on others' fields for daily wages.

probe.question: Who does a landless labourer work for?
probe.wrong_answer: They work on their own small plot of land.

root_belief: everyone has the same status

subject: social
statement: Farmers have work throughout the entire year.
why: Students assume work is a continuous process like school or office jobs.
fix: Farming is seasonal; labourers often face unemployment during the months between sowing and harvesting.

probe.question: What do farm labourers do during the off-season?
probe.wrong_answer: They continue working on the same farm every day.

root_belief: work is always a continuous activity
source_hint: Rosalind Driver children's ideas in social science

subject: social
statement: Street vendors are always poor because they are lazy.
why: Students confuse economic status with personal character traits.
fix: Street vendors work very hard but lack permanent shops and face daily uncertainty.

probe.question: Why do street vendors work on the sidewalk?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they do not want to work hard in a shop.

root_belief: poverty is a result of personal failure

subject: social
statement: All city jobs provide medical leave and pensions.
why: Students project the benefits of their parents' or teachers' jobs onto all urban work.
fix: Only permanent, formal jobs offer benefits; casual workers have no such security.

probe.question: Does a daily wage worker get paid sick leave?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all city workers get paid leave.

root_belief: my experience is the universal experience

subject: social
statement: Farm work is only done by men.
why: Students see men ploughing and selling in images and stories, and overlook women's daily field labour.
fix: Women and men both do farm work: sowing, transplanting, weeding and harvesting. Women do a large share of it, often without recognition or equal pay.

probe.question: Who does the work of transplanting paddy and harvesting in a village?
probe.wrong_answer: Only men do it; women stay at home.

root_belief: Gender roles strictly divide who does productive work

subject: social
statement: Everyone in a village works in farming.
why: Villages are strongly linked with fields and crops, so students assume no other work exists there.
fix: Villages also have non-farm work such as weaving, pottery, shopkeeping, teaching, carpentry, tailoring and running small shops.

probe.question: Name a person in a village who does not work on a farm. What do they do?
probe.wrong_answer: There is no such person; everyone in a village is a farmer.

root_belief: Rural means only agriculture
source_hint: research on children's conceptions of rural life

subject: social
statement: Street vendors do not need to work hard or buy anything because they sell for free on the road.
why: Students see vendors on open pavements with no shop, so they think there is no cost or effort.
fix: Street vendors buy goods from wholesale markets, carry or arrange them, stand for long hours and sell in all weather. They may also pay fees or face being moved away.

probe.question: Where does a fruit seller on the street get the fruit he sells?
probe.wrong_answer: He gets it free from nowhere, so he has no cost.

root_belief: No shop means no investment or effort

subject: social
statement: Formal jobs mean only government jobs.
why: Students link permanent salaried work only with government offices, police and schools.
fix: Formal jobs have fixed pay, fixed hours and written terms. They exist in government offices and also in many private companies and factories.

probe.question: Does a worker in a big private company with a fixed salary and contract have a formal job?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only government workers have formal jobs.

root_belief: Formal employment equals government service

subject: social
statement: Landless labourers are people who do not work.
why: The word 'landless' is read as having nothing to do, since they have no farm of their own.
fix: Landless labourers work on other people's fields for daily or seasonal wages. They do the hard farm work but do not own the land.

probe.question: What do landless labourers do for a living?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, because they have no land to farm.

root_belief: No ownership means no work

subject: social
statement: Farming work is the same amount in every month, so farmers earn the same all year.
why: Students do not link crop cycles like sowing and harvesting to periods of heavy and light work.
fix: Farm work is heavy during sowing and harvest and light in between. Many farm families earn mainly after harvest and look for other work in the slack months.

probe.question: Why do many farm families look for other work or migrate in some months?
probe.wrong_answer: Farming gives the same work every month, so they leave only for fun.

root_belief: Work and income are constant across seasons

subject: social
statement: Self-employed people in villages always have an employer who pays them a salary.
why: Students think everyone who works is paid a monthly wage by some boss.
fix: Self-employed people such as potters, tailors and shopkeepers run their own work. They buy materials, sell goods or services, and their earnings depend on customers.

probe.question: Who pays a village potter for the pots he makes and sells?
probe.wrong_answer: His employer pays him a fixed monthly salary.

root_belief: All workers are paid salaries by employers

subject: social
statement: Casual labourers in cities have a regular job with a fixed monthly salary.
why: Students think anyone doing city work, like construction, has the same steady pay as an office worker.
fix: Casual labourers, such as construction workers, are hired for a day or a short job and paid daily wages. They have no fixed pay, no long-term contract and may wait at labour chowks for work.

probe.question: How is a construction worker who stands at a labour chowk paid?
probe.wrong_answer: He gets a fixed monthly salary and is sure of work every day.

root_belief: All city work is steady salaried work

subject: social
statement: Rich people's votes count more than poor people's votes.
why: Students observe that wealth influences political outcomes in reality, confusing influence with the legal value of a vote.
fix: In a democracy, every citizen's vote has the exact same value regardless of their wealth, education, or social status.

probe.question: Whose vote counts more in an election: a billionaire or a daily wage worker?
probe.wrong_answer: The billionaire's vote counts more.

root_belief: Wealth determines power and value

subject: social
statement: Private shops can refuse entry to people based on their caste.
why: Students confuse private property rights with the constitutional mandate of equality in public spaces.
fix: The Constitution prohibits discrimination in all public places, including shops, hotels, and restaurants, regardless of ownership.

probe.question: Can a shopkeeper refuse to sell goods to someone because of their caste?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is their private shop.

root_belief: Private ownership overrides public laws

subject: social
statement: The mid-day meal is only to provide food to hungry children.
why: Students focus on the immediate physical outcome (food) rather than the social objective (equality).
fix: The mid-day meal aims to improve attendance and reduce social inequality by having children of all castes eat together.

probe.question: Why did the government start the mid-day meal scheme?
probe.wrong_answer: To stop children from being hungry.

root_belief: One event has one single cause

subject: social
statement: Dignity is something you earn through good behavior.
why: Students conflate the moral concept of 'respect' with the legal/human rights concept of 'dignity'.
fix: Dignity is an inherent right of every human being, not something that needs to be earned or deserved.

probe.question: Who deserves to be treated with dignity?
probe.wrong_answer: Only those who behave well and follow rules.

root_belief: Rights are rewards for good behavior

subject: social
statement: Only people who can read and write have the right to vote.
why: Students link voting with reading ballots and assume literacy is needed, as with old restricted franchises.
fix: In India every citizen aged 18 or above can vote, whether literate or not. Symbols on the ballot help those who cannot read.

probe.question: Can an 18-year-old citizen who has never been to school vote in India?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because voters must be able to read and write.

root_belief: Voting needs education or literacy

subject: social
statement: Only men from landowning families have the right to vote.
why: Students carry over history lessons about old kingdoms and colonial rule where only some people could vote.
fix: Under universal adult franchise every adult citizen, women and men, rich or poor, of any caste or religion, can vote.

probe.question: Can a woman from a poor, landless family vote in elections in India?
probe.wrong_answer: No, voting is only for men who own land.

root_belief: Voting is limited to property-owning men

subject: social
statement: A person gets more votes if they belong to more groups, like a caste and a village committee.
why: Students confuse membership in several groups with the number of votes an individual casts.
fix: Every adult has exactly one vote in an election, no matter how many groups they belong to.

probe.question: A man is a farmer, a village elder and a temple trustee. How many votes does he have in the Lok Sabha election?
probe.wrong_answer: Three votes, one for each role.

root_belief: Social roles add up to extra votes

subject: social
statement: Equality before law means all people must be given exactly the same punishment or benefits.
why: Students read equality as identical treatment, which ignores that law applies the same rules, not the same outcomes.
fix: Equality before law means everyone, including the highest officials, is subject to the same laws and no one is above the law. Punishment depends on the crime, not on who the person is.

probe.question: What does equality before law mean for a minister who breaks a law?
probe.wrong_answer: The minister gets exactly the same punishment as every other person for every crime, whatever the crime was.

root_belief: Equality means identical treatment for everyone

subject: social
statement: Government officers and ministers are above the law while in office.
why: Students see the power and security of officials and assume they cannot be taken to court.
fix: Equality before law applies to all, so ministers and officers can be tried in court like any other citizen.

probe.question: Can a police officer be taken to court if they break the law?
probe.wrong_answer: No, officers are above the law while they hold their post.

root_belief: Power gives immunity from the law

subject: social
statement: Article 15 bans discrimination only on the basis of caste.
why: Caste is the most discussed example in the chapter, so students take it as the only ground.
fix: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.

probe.question: Can a government school refuse a child admission because of her religion or because she is a girl, under Article 15?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, Article 15 only protects against caste discrimination.

root_belief: Anti-discrimination law covers only caste
source_hint: NCERT Class 7 Civics; Constitution of India

subject: social
statement: Public places like wells, temples and hotels can be kept separate for some castes if the community agrees.
why: Local customs and community pressure make students think social agreement can override the Constitution.
fix: Public places such as wells, roads, shops and hotels are open to all; no community can deny entry on grounds such as caste.

probe.question: If the whole village agrees, can a village well be reserved only for upper-caste families?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if everyone in the village agrees, the well can be reserved.

root_belief: Community custom overrides constitutional equality

subject: social
statement: Because children eat the mid-day meal, caste discrimination has ended in all schools.
why: Students overgeneralise the positive effect of shared meals into a complete solution.
fix: The mid-day meal helps children of different castes eat together and reduces bias, but discrimination can still occur and must be actively checked and stopped.

probe.question: If a school runs the mid-day meal, can caste discrimination still occur there?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the mid-day meal has already ended all caste discrimination.

root_belief: One scheme fully solves a social problem
source_hint: NCERT Class 7 Civics, Chapter 1 (Tamil Nadu cook example)

subject: social
statement: A constituency is the same as a district.
why: Students often conflate administrative boundaries with electoral boundaries.
fix: A constituency is an area specifically demarcated for electing a representative, which may not align with district borders.

probe.question: If a district has 5 lakh people, does it always have only one MLA?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because one district equals one constituency.

root_belief: Administrative units are identical to electoral units

subject: social
statement: Majority means getting the most votes among all candidates.
why: Students confuse 'majority' with 'plurality' (winning the most votes).
fix: Majority means having more than half the total number of seats in the assembly.

probe.question: If there are 100 seats, can a party with 30 seats form the government?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if 30 is the highest number of seats any party got.

root_belief: Winning means having more than others

subject: social
statement: The Chief Minister is elected directly by the people of the state.
why: Students project the direct voting for an MLA onto the CM position.
fix: The CM is appointed by the Governor, usually being the leader of the party that won the majority of seats.

probe.question: Who votes directly for the Chief Minister?
probe.wrong_answer: The citizens of the state during the election.

root_belief: All leaders are chosen by direct public vote

subject: social
statement: The Governor makes all the laws for the state.
why: Students see the Governor as the 'boss' and assume they have absolute power.
fix: The Legislative Assembly makes the laws; the Governor gives formal assent to bills passed by the assembly.

probe.question: Who has the power to pass a new law in the state?
probe.wrong_answer: The Governor, because they are the head of the state.

root_belief: One powerful person makes all decisions

subject: social
statement: An MLA is a member of the state's government who works only for the party that is in power.
why: Students see MLAs of the ruling party in the news and assume the government is made up of one party's MLAs only.
fix: Every elected person in the Legislative Assembly is an MLA. MLAs of the ruling party and of the opposition all represent their constituency and all take part in the Assembly.

probe.question: An MLA belongs to the opposition party. Is that person still an MLA of the constituency?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only MLAs of the ruling party are real MLAs.

root_belief: Only ruling party members count as representatives

subject: social
statement: An MLA is paid by the people of the constituency and must do whatever voters in the area ask.
why: Students think a representative is like a personal servant of the voters and has no duty to the whole state or to the law.
fix: An MLA represents the people of the constituency and raises their problems in the Assembly. The MLA also takes part in making laws for the whole state, and is paid by the state government.

probe.question: A voter asks the MLA to break a state rule for their family. What must the MLA do?
probe.wrong_answer: Do it, because the MLA must obey every voter.

root_belief: Representatives are servants who obey every voter

subject: social
statement: The Legislative Assembly is the building where the Chief Minister and ministers work in their offices.
why: Students mix up the place with the people and the work done there, and confuse it with the Secretariat.
fix: The Legislative Assembly is the body of all the MLAs of the state. It meets to discuss problems, debate and make laws. The ministers' offices are separate.

probe.question: Who are the members of the Legislative Assembly?
probe.wrong_answer: The Chief Minister and the ministers only.

root_belief: Assembly means the government's office building

subject: social
statement: Debate in the Assembly is just fighting and shouting, and it has no real use for the state.
why: Students see news clips of noisy walkouts and think debate is only arguing between parties.
fix: Debate lets MLAs of all parties question the government, discuss problems of the people and examine proposed laws before a decision is made.

probe.question: Why do MLAs debate a proposed law in the Assembly?
probe.wrong_answer: To fight with the other party and show who is stronger.

root_belief: Political discussion is only quarrelling

subject: social
statement: The Governor chooses anyone he likes as Chief Minister, even a person who has no support of the MLAs.
why: Students know the Governor appoints the CM but miss the condition about majority support in the Assembly.
fix: The Governor appoints as Chief Minister the leader of the party or group that has the support of a majority of MLAs in the Assembly.

probe.question: Whom does the Governor appoint as Chief Minister?
probe.wrong_answer: Any person the Governor prefers.

root_belief: Appointing power means free personal choice

subject: social
statement: The party that wins the most seats forms the government even if it is far short of half the MLAs.
why: Students link winning with being the largest party and forget that a government needs support of more than half the MLAs.
fix: A party or group needs the support of more than half the members of the Assembly to form the government. If no party has it, parties may join together.

probe.question: In an Assembly of 200 seats, a party wins 70 seats and others win less. Can it form the government alone?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has won the most seats.

root_belief: Largest party automatically governs

subject: social
statement: The Governor is elected by the people of the state and belongs to the ruling party.
why: Students assume all important state posts are filled by voting like MLAs.
fix: The Governor is appointed by the central government (the President) and acts as the head of the state, not as an elected leader.

probe.question: How does a person become the Governor of a state?
probe.wrong_answer: By winning a vote of the people of the state.

root_belief: Every high office holder is elected by voters

subject: social
statement: The Chief Minister has to leave office after five years even if the party still has a majority.
why: Students mix a fixed term with the MLAs' five-year term and think the CM is like a fixed-term post.
fix: The CM stays as long as he or she has the support of a majority of MLAs. After an election, a new Assembly is formed, and the leader with majority becomes CM, which can be the same person.

probe.question: A CM's party wins the next election with a majority. Can the same person be CM again?
probe.wrong_answer: No, one person cannot be CM for more than one term.

root_belief: Political posts have fixed one-term limits

subject: social
statement: If a news channel is independent, it must be telling the absolute truth.
why: Students conflate 'independent from government' with 'objective and unbiased'.
fix: Independent media is free from government control but can still be biased due to corporate interests or editorial choices.

probe.question: Can a private newspaper be biased?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only government-run media is biased.

root_belief: Independence equals total objectivity

subject: social
statement: Advertisements are only meant to inform us about new products.
why: Students focus on the explicit content of the ad rather than the underlying persuasive intent.
fix: Advertisements are designed to persuade consumers to buy products by creating a desire or associating the product with a lifestyle.

probe.question: Why do companies spend money on ads?
probe.wrong_answer: To tell people what products are available.

root_belief: Information is the only purpose of communication

subject: social
statement: The media tells us what is important, so we should believe everything they highlight.
why: Students assume that the frequency of news coverage equals the objective importance of an event.
fix: Media sets the agenda by choosing which stories to highlight, but this does not mean those are the only important issues.

probe.question: If the news talks about a celebrity all day, is it the most important event in the country?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the news says it is.

root_belief: Frequency equals importance

subject: social
statement: Expensive brands are always better quality than cheaper, unbranded goods.
why: Students internalize the messaging of advertisements that equate price with quality.
fix: Advertising creates a brand image that makes products seem superior, but the actual quality may be the same as unbranded items.

probe.question: Is a branded shirt always better than a local one?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the brand is famous.

root_belief: Higher price means higher quality

subject: social
statement: Newspapers and TV channels earn all their money from people buying them, not from advertisements.
why: Students see the copy price or cable bill and do not notice that ads pay most production costs.
fix: Media houses earn a large part of their income from advertisements. Sale price alone does not cover the cost, so ads fund media and keep it cheap.

probe.question: A newspaper costs only Rs 5 but is expensive to print. Where does most of the extra money come from?
probe.wrong_answer: From readers paying more money for each copy.

root_belief: Consumers alone pay for all media costs
source_hint: NCERT Class 7 Social Science textbook; classroom observation

subject: social
statement: Media is free for us, so it costs nothing to run a TV channel or newspaper.
why: Students watch TV or read free websites without paying and assume there are no costs.
fix: Running media needs money for reporters, equipment, printing, broadcasting and salaries. Someone, often advertisers, pays for these.

probe.question: Why does a free TV channel still need money?
probe.wrong_answer: It does not need money because viewers watch it free.

root_belief: Free to the viewer means free to produce

subject: social
statement: Technology only changed how media looks, not who can reach or use it.
why: Students see new gadgets as better screens and not as a change in access and speed.
fix: New technology such as printing, radio, TV and the internet changed how fast news spreads and how many people can share or receive it.

probe.question: How did the internet change media compared with early newspapers?
probe.wrong_answer: It only made pictures look better; nothing else changed.

root_belief: Technology changes only appearance, not reach

subject: social
statement: Mass media means only television and nothing else reaches millions.
why: TV is the most familiar medium at home, so students equate it with mass media.
fix: Mass media includes newspapers, radio, TV, films and the internet. All of them reach very large numbers of people.

probe.question: Which of these are mass media: newspaper, radio, TV, internet?
probe.wrong_answer: Only TV is mass media.

root_belief: Mass media equals television only

subject: social
statement: If I like a brand's advertisement, I should buy that brand because the ad proves it is the best.
