why: Students treat an appealing ad, jingle or celebrity as evidence of product quality.
fix: Ads aim to make people like and stay loyal to a brand, but they do not prove quality. We should compare price, quality and need before buying.

probe.question: A popular actor appears in a biscuit ad you love. What does this show about the biscuit?
probe.wrong_answer: It shows the biscuit must be the best quality.

root_belief: Likeable advertising proves product quality
source_hint: media literacy research on children and advertising

subject: social
statement: Advertisements affect only adults, so children are not influenced by them.
why: Students think buying decisions belong only to those who earn money.
fix: Ads target children too, and children influence what families buy, such as snacks, toys and clothes.

probe.question: Why do companies make colourful ads with cartoons during children's shows?
probe.wrong_answer: Children cannot be influenced, so it is only for decoration.

root_belief: Only earners are influenced by advertising
source_hint: research on children's awareness of advertising intent

subject: social
statement: Balanced reporting means giving equal time to every opinion, even a false one.
why: Students link balance with fairness in counting, not with checking facts.
fix: Balanced reporting presents different sides fairly and accurately, based on facts, and does not treat falsehood as equal to evidence.

probe.question: A channel gives the same airtime to a proven fact and a rumour. Is this balanced reporting?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, equal time to both makes it balanced.

root_belief: Balance means equal time regardless of facts

subject: social
statement: In a democracy, media should always support the government.
why: Students confuse respect for government with the media's duty to inform.
fix: In a democracy, media should report on government work, including its mistakes, so citizens can question and make informed choices.

probe.question: A newspaper reports a mistake in a government scheme. What should the media have done?
probe.wrong_answer: It should have stayed quiet and supported the government.

root_belief: Good media must agree with the government
source_hint: NCERT Class 7 Social Science textbook; civics teaching

subject: social
statement: Weekly markets are only for poor people.
why: Students associate the lack of permanent infrastructure with lower social status.
fix: Weekly markets are for everyone as they offer a wide variety of goods at competitive prices, often cheaper than permanent shops.

probe.question: Who shops at a weekly market?
probe.wrong_answer: Only people who cannot afford to go to malls.

root_belief: Appearance determines the quality and target audience

subject: social
statement: All items in a mall are of better quality than those in a local shop.
why: Students equate high price and fancy surroundings with superior product quality.
fix: Malls sell branded goods which may be expensive due to advertising and overheads, but the quality is not necessarily better than unbranded goods.

probe.question: Is a shirt from a mall always better than one from a local shop?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is sold in a mall.

root_belief: Higher price always means higher quality

subject: social
statement: Wholesale markets are where goods are made.
why: Students confuse the place of sale (wholesale) with the place of production (factory).
fix: Wholesale markets are where traders buy goods in bulk from factories to sell to retailers, not where production happens.

probe.question: Where does a wholesaler get their goods?
probe.wrong_answer: They make them in the wholesale market.

root_belief: A place is defined by its primary activity

subject: social
statement: The price of a product is the same everywhere in the chain.
why: Students ignore the costs added by transport, storage, and profit margins at each step.
fix: The price increases as a product moves from the factory to the wholesaler, then the retailer, because each person adds their profit and covers expenses.

probe.question: Why is a pen more expensive in a shop than at the factory?
probe.wrong_answer: The shopkeeper is just charging extra for no reason.

root_belief: One event has one single cause

subject: social
statement: A weekly market is held on the same fixed day in every town and village.
why: Students generalise from their own local market's day and assume the schedule is uniform everywhere.
fix: Each weekly market is held on a particular day of the week, and the day differs from place to place so traders can move between markets on different days.

probe.question: A trader sells in the weekly market of Village A on Monday. On which day will the weekly market of nearby Village B be held?
probe.wrong_answer: Also on Monday, because all weekly markets are held on the same day.

root_belief: Local arrangements are the same everywhere

subject: social
statement: Goods in a weekly market are costlier than in shops because there are no permanent shops.
why: Students link a shop's permanence and rent with lower prices, or assume temporary means expensive.
fix: Weekly markets have no fixed shops and so traders' costs are low; goods are often cheaper and bargaining is common.

probe.question: Why do people often find vegetables cheaper in the weekly market than in a shop?
probe.wrong_answer: They are not cheaper; weekly market goods are always costlier than in shops.

root_belief: Temporary sellers must charge higher prices

subject: social
statement: A shop and a mall are the same thing, only the name is different.
why: Both sell goods directly to buyers, so students treat them as one kind of market.
fix: Shops are usually single, smaller places selling a few kinds of goods; malls are large buildings housing many shops, often air-conditioned, under one roof.

probe.question: How is a mall different from a neighbourhood shop?
probe.wrong_answer: There is no difference; a mall is just another name for a shop.

root_belief: Similar-looking places are identical

subject: social
statement: Bargaining is possible in malls just as in weekly markets.
why: Students carry the habit of bargaining from weekly markets and street shops to all places.
fix: In malls, prices are fixed and printed on the items; bargaining is common in weekly markets and small shops.

probe.question: Meena wants a lower price for a shirt in a mall. What will she most likely be able to do?
probe.wrong_answer: Bargain with the salesperson, as people do in every market.

root_belief: All markets work like the one I know

subject: social
statement: Retailers sell goods only to wholesalers and not to ordinary customers.
why: Students reverse the direction of the chain or mix up the two terms.
fix: Retailers buy from wholesalers and sell small quantities directly to consumers; wholesalers sell in large quantities to retailers.

probe.question: To whom does a retailer sell goods?
probe.wrong_answer: To wholesalers, who then sell to the customers.

root_belief: Chain direction is reversible

subject: social
statement: Intermediaries in the market chain are unnecessary and only raise the price for no reason.
why: Students see that each middleman adds a margin and conclude they add no value.
fix: Traders in the chain collect, store, transport and distribute goods to buyers far away, though their margins add to the final price.

probe.question: Why do goods pass through wholesalers and traders before reaching the buyer?
probe.wrong_answer: They serve no purpose; they only make goods more expensive.

root_belief: Middlemen serve no useful function

subject: social
statement: Anyone buying a large quantity of goods for personal use is a wholesaler.
why: Students focus on the word bulk and ignore that wholesalers buy to resell.
fix: Wholesalers buy in bulk in order to sell to retailers; a family buying lots of rice for its own use is still a consumer.

probe.question: A family buys 50 kg of rice for its own use. What are they?
probe.wrong_answer: Wholesalers, because they bought a large quantity.

root_belief: Quantity alone defines the buyer type

subject: social
statement: Everyone can buy the same goods because anyone can walk into any market.
why: Students think that access to a market means equal ability to buy.
fix: What people can buy depends on their income and purchasing power; markets are open but poorer people can afford fewer things.

probe.question: Two families visit the same mall. Why might they buy very different things?
probe.wrong_answer: They will not; everyone in the same market can buy the same goods.

root_belief: Open access means equal ability to buy

subject: social
statement: The Constitution is a list of laws that the government imposes on the people.
why: Students often confuse the Constitution with the Penal Code or general government orders.
fix: The Constitution is a set of rules that defines the powers of the government and protects the rights of the citizens against the government.

probe.question: Who is the Constitution primarily meant to control?
probe.wrong_answer: The citizens

root_belief: Authority always flows top-down

subject: social
statement: Federalism means the Central government is the boss of the State government.
why: Students observe the central government having more visibility in national news.
fix: Federalism means power is shared between the central and state governments, with each having its own sphere of authority.

probe.question: Can a state government make its own laws on subjects in the State List?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it must ask the center first.

root_belief: Hierarchy is the only way to organize power

subject: social
statement: The Judiciary is a branch of the government that helps the Prime Minister make laws.
why: Students often see all government branches as a single team working together.
fix: The Judiciary is independent and acts as a check on the other branches, ensuring laws follow the Constitution.

probe.question: What is the role of the Judiciary?
probe.wrong_answer: To assist the government in implementing policies.

root_belief: All government parts have the same goal

subject: social
statement: Fundamental Rights mean I can do whatever I want at any time.
why: Students conflate 'rights' with 'absolute freedom' without considering social responsibility.
fix: Fundamental Rights are subject to 'reasonable restrictions' to ensure the rights of others and public order.

probe.question: Can you shout fire in a crowded theater just because you have freedom of speech?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is my right.

root_belief: A word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: In India the President actually runs the country and takes all the big decisions himself.
why: Students see the President as the head of state with the highest rank and assume formal power means real power.
fix: India has a parliamentary form: the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers, answerable to Parliament, hold real executive power, and the President acts on their advice.

probe.question: Who is really responsible for running the government day to day and answers to the Lok Sabha?
probe.wrong_answer: The President

root_belief: Highest rank means real decision-making power
source_hint: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life; teacher observation

subject: social
statement: Only people who are educated or own property can vote in India.
why: Students carry over ideas about older systems or assume voting needs a qualification.
fix: Universal Adult Franchise means every citizen aged 18 and above can vote, whatever their education, wealth, religion, caste or gender.

probe.question: Can a 40-year-old citizen who never went to school vote in a Lok Sabha election?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because she is not educated.

root_belief: Voting is a privilege earned by qualifications

subject: social
statement: Separation of powers means the legislature, executive and judiciary work separately and never interact with each other.
why: The word 'separation' is read as complete isolation rather than a division of functions.
fix: Each organ has its own role, but they check and balance one another, for example courts can strike down unconstitutional laws and Parliament passes the laws the executive carries out.

probe.question: Can the judiciary ever check what Parliament or the executive does?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are separate so they cannot interfere in each other's work.

root_belief: Separation means complete isolation, with no checks

subject: social
statement: The police and officials who implement laws are part of the legislature.
why: Students link anything to do with laws to the body that makes them.
fix: The legislature (Parliament, State Assemblies) makes laws; the executive, including the PM, ministers and civil servants such as police, implements them.

probe.question: Which organ of government does a District Collector belong to?
probe.wrong_answer: The legislature, because they work with laws.

root_belief: Anyone dealing with laws belongs to law-making body
source_hint: NCERT Class 8 Civics; common student confusion

subject: social
statement: Right to Equality means everyone must be treated exactly the same, so reservations and special help are unconstitutional.
why: Equality is understood as identical treatment, not as fairness for people who start from unequal positions.
fix: Right to Equality means equality before law and no discrimination on grounds like religion, caste, sex or birth; the Constitution also allows special provisions for disadvantaged groups to achieve real equality.

probe.question: Is a seat reserved for Scheduled Castes in Parliament against the Right to Equality?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because everyone must be treated exactly the same.

root_belief: Equality means identical treatment in every case
source_hint: research on student conceptions of equality in civics education

subject: social
statement: Fundamental Duties are laws, and a citizen who ignores them can be taken to court by the Constitution automatically.
why: Students treat everything in the Constitution as an enforceable punishment-backed rule.
fix: Fundamental Duties are moral obligations of citizens, like respecting the national flag and protecting public property, and are not directly enforceable in court, though other laws may apply to related acts.

probe.question: Will a person be jailed under the Fundamental Duties just for not valuing our composite culture?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the Constitution punishes anyone who breaks a duty.

root_belief: Every constitutional clause carries direct legal punishment

subject: social
concept: More than one level of government
statement: States have their own powers only because the Centre allows it, and these powers can be taken away whenever the Centre wants.
why: Students see the Centre as the bigger level and think State powers are lent.
fix: The Constitution divides powers between Union, State and Concurrent lists. State powers are given by the Constitution itself, not by the Centre's favour.

probe.question: Who decides what subjects a State government can make laws on?
probe.wrong_answer: The Central government decides this whenever it likes.

root_belief: Lower governments hold only borrowed power

subject: social
statement: Only ordinary citizens need to follow the Constitution; the Prime Minister and ministers are above it.
why: Students see leaders as powerful and assume rules bind only the weak.
fix: The Constitution binds everyone, including the PM, ministers and officials. It limits their power so they cannot misuse it, and courts can set aside their unlawful acts.

probe.question: If a minister breaks a constitutional rule, can a court declare the action invalid?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because ministers are above the Constitution.

root_belief: Powerful people are exempt from rules

subject: social
concept: Secularism means no religion in public
statement: Secularism means the government must ban all religious symbols and prayers in public spaces.
why: Students confuse the Western 'wall of separation' model with the Indian context.
fix: Indian secularism allows the state to maintain a principled distance, not a total ban on religious expression in public life.

probe.question: Should the government remove all religious statues from public offices?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because secularism requires the complete absence of religion in public.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: If the government gives money to a religious school, it is not secular.
why: Students assume secularism means zero interaction between state and religion.
fix: The state can support religious institutions if it does so without bias or discrimination among different religions.

probe.question: Is it unconstitutional for the state to provide grants to a religious school?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the state must have nothing to do with religion.

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: social
concept: State can ban harmful religious practices
statement: The government should never interfere in religious matters, even if they are harmful.
why: Students confuse secularism with total non-interference or religious freedom.
fix: The state can intervene to protect fundamental rights, such as banning untouchability or child marriage within religious groups.

probe.question: Can the state ban a religious practice that discriminates against women?
probe.wrong_answer: No, that would violate the religious freedom of the group.

root_belief: a rule from one context works everywhere

subject: social
statement: Secularism means the government is against religion or is atheist.
why: Students confuse 'no official state religion' with 'opposing religion', mixing secular with non-believer.
fix: A secular state does not oppose religion. It keeps itself neutral, has no official religion, and lets every person follow any religion or none.

probe.question: Is a secular government opposed to religion? Why or why not?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a secular government does not like religion and wants people to stop practising it.

root_belief: Secular means anti-religion or atheist
source_hint: studies of student conceptions of secularism in India

subject: social
statement: A secular country is one where only one religion is followed by everyone.
why: Students mix up 'secular' with 'uniform' or a single shared way of life.
fix: A secular country has people of many religions and none, and the state treats all of them equally.

probe.question: What kind of country is a secular country?
probe.wrong_answer: A country where everyone follows the same religion so there are no fights.

root_belief: Secularism means religious uniformity

subject: social
statement: If the majority community's festivals are celebrated more widely, the state is still fully secular.
why: Students think numbers justify favouring the largest group and do not see this as domination.
fix: Secularism prevents domination of one religious group over others, including a majority over minorities. The state must not favour any group.

probe.question: A government gives special privileges only to the largest religious group. Is it secular?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because most people follow that religion, so it is fair.

root_belief: Majority rule justifies religious favouritism

subject: social
statement: Religious domination only happens between different religions, never inside one religion.
why: Students see domination only as one community over another and miss caste or gender discrimination within a religion.
fix: Secularism also opposes domination within a religion, such as untouchability or discrimination against women, so the state can act on it.

probe.question: Can a secular state stop a religion from barring some of its own members from temples?
probe.wrong_answer: No, domination only means one religion dominating another, so this is not the state's business.

root_belief: Domination is only between different religions

subject: social
statement: Principled distance means the state keeps equal distance and never gets involved with any religion.
why: Students equate principled distance with the strict wall of separation, ignoring that involvement may be allowed on principle.
fix: Principled distance means the state may stay out or step in depending on the situation, guided by equality, liberty and non-domination.

probe.question: What does principled distance mean in Indian secularism?
probe.wrong_answer: The state always stays away from all religions and never takes part in anything religious.

root_belief: Principled distance equals strict non-involvement

subject: social
statement: Principled distance means the state helps whichever religion it likes best.
why: Students read 'principle' loosely and think the state may choose by preference, not by fairness.
fix: Principled distance means decisions follow constitutional principles applied equally to all religions, not the state's preference.

probe.question: Can a state using principled distance give help to only one religion it prefers?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, principled distance lets the state support the religion it thinks is best.

root_belief: Principled means state's own choice

subject: social
statement: Freedom of religion protects only the religion of the majority.
why: Students think rights go with numbers and majority religion needs the most protection.
fix: The Constitution protects the religious freedom of every individual and community, including minorities, to practise, profess and propagate.

probe.question: Whose religious freedom does the Indian Constitution protect?
probe.wrong_answer: Mainly the religion followed by most Indians, since minority religions are small.

root_belief: Rights follow majority numbers

subject: social
statement: If the state declares a holiday for a festival, it is promoting that religion over others.
why: Students see any state recognition of a festival as favouritism, forgetting holidays for many religions.
fix: The Indian state gives public holidays for festivals of many religions, which treats all equally and is consistent with secularism.

probe.question: India has holidays for Diwali, Eid, Christmas and Guru Nanak Jayanti. Is this against secularism?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the government is supporting religions, so it is not secular.

root_belief: Any state support of religion breaks secularism

subject: social
concept: State can ban harmful religious practices
statement: Banning a practice like untouchability or sati hurts secularism because it limits religious freedom.
why: Students treat every religious freedom as absolute and miss that harmful practices violate others' rights.
fix: Religious freedom is limited by others' rights. The state may ban practices like untouchability, sati and child marriage because they harm people's equality and dignity.

probe.question: Was it secular for India to ban untouchability even though some defended it as religious?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the state interfered with people's religion.

root_belief: Religious freedom is absolute and unlimited
source_hint: NCERT Social and Political Life and studies of student conceptions

topic: Parliament and the making of laws
subject: social
statement: The Rajya Sabha is more powerful than the Lok Sabha because it is the 'Upper House'.
why: Students equate the word 'upper' with higher authority or power in a hierarchy.
fix: The Lok Sabha is more powerful because its members are directly elected by the people, and it controls the executive.

probe.question: If the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha disagree on a money bill, who prevails?
probe.wrong_answer: The Rajya Sabha because it is the Upper House.

root_belief: Words have their literal everyday meaning

topic: Parliament and the making of laws
subject: social
statement: The Prime Minister is directly elected by the citizens of India.
why: Students confuse the election of local MPs with the direct election of the head of government.
fix: Citizens elect MPs to the Lok Sabha; the party with the majority then selects their leader to be the Prime Minister.

probe.question: Who do you vote for in a general election?
probe.wrong_answer: I vote for the Prime Minister.

root_belief: One event has one single cause

topic: Parliament and the making of laws
subject: social
statement: The President can reject any law passed by Parliament if they do not like it.
why: Students assume the President acts like a monarch or a supreme ruler with absolute veto power.
fix: The President is a constitutional head and must sign a bill once it is passed by both houses of Parliament.

probe.question: Can the President stop a bill from becoming law?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if they disagree with the law.

root_belief: Authority figures have absolute personal power

topic: Parliament and the making of laws
subject: social
statement: The role of the opposition is to stop all government work.
why: Students see opposition in media as mere fighting and assume the goal is obstructionism.
fix: The opposition highlights flaws in policies and ensures the government remains accountable to the public.

probe.question: What is the main job of the opposition party?
probe.wrong_answer: To block every law the government proposes.

root_belief: Conflict is inherently destructive

topic: Parliament and the making of laws
subject: social
statement: Laws are only changed when the government decides to change them.
why: Students ignore the role of civil society and public pressure in the legislative process.
fix: Citizens can influence the law-making process through protests, media campaigns, and public opinion.

probe.question: How can a law be changed if it is unpopular?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the government can decide to change it.

root_belief: Power flows only from the top down

topic: Parliament and the making of laws
subject: social
statement: All members of the Lok Sabha are chosen by the President.
why: Students confuse the nominated members of the Rajya Sabha with the Lok Sabha, and think top officials appoint the 'main' house.
fix: Lok Sabha members are elected directly by adult citizens (18+) from constituencies through general elections, usually every five years.

probe.question: How does a person become a Member of the Lok Sabha?
probe.wrong_answer: The President selects them.

root_belief: Top officials appoint legislators rather than voters electing them
source_hint: classroom discussion / NCERT Social and Political Life

topic: Parliament and the making of laws
subject: social
statement: Citizens vote directly to choose the members of the Rajya Sabha.
why: Students assume every house of Parliament is elected the same way as the Lok Sabha.
fix: Rajya Sabha members are elected indirectly by the elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (and a few are nominated by the President for their work in arts, science, etc.).

probe.question: Who votes to elect Rajya Sabha members?
probe.wrong_answer: All adult citizens vote for them in the general election.

root_belief: All legislative houses are elected the same way

topic: Parliament and the making of laws
subject: social
statement: Only the Prime Minister can introduce a bill in Parliament.
why: Students link lawmaking only with the most visible leader of the government.
fix: A bill can be introduced by a minister (government bill) or by any other member of Parliament (private member's bill), in either house (money bills only in the Lok Sabha).

probe.question: Who can bring a new bill before Parliament?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the Prime Minister.

root_belief: Only the top leader can start lawmaking

topic: Parliament and the making of laws
subject: social
statement: A bill becomes a law as soon as the Lok Sabha passes it.
why: Students treat the Lok Sabha as the whole Parliament because it is the more prominent house.
fix: An ordinary bill must be passed by both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha (in the same form) and then get the President's assent before it becomes law.

probe.question: A bill has just been passed by the Lok Sabha. Is it now a law?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the Lok Sabha passing it is enough to make it a law.

root_belief: One house alone is the whole Parliament

topic: Parliament and the making of laws
subject: social
statement: A bill is voted on immediately after it is introduced, without any discussion.
why: Students imagine lawmaking as a single vote instead of a series of stages.
fix: A bill goes through stages: introduction (first reading), detailed discussion and debate, often examination by a committee, amendments, and then voting.

probe.question: What happens right after a bill is introduced in the House?
probe.wrong_answer: Members vote on it straight away with no debate.

root_belief: Lawmaking is one quick vote

topic: Parliament and the making of laws
subject: social
statement: Public protests and media have no role in the making of laws in a democracy.
why: Students think only elected members and the government matter once elections are over.
fix: Citizens can express opinions through peaceful protests, petitions, the media and meetings with representatives; this public pressure can lead Parliament to debate, amend or make laws (e.g., the Right to Information Act).

probe.question: Can a citizens' campaign influence what law Parliament makes?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only MPs decide laws and the public cannot affect them.

root_belief: Citizens' voice ends after voting

topic: Parliament and the making of laws
subject: social
statement: A person from the party that gets the most votes in a constituency becomes the MP only if they get more than half of all votes.
why: Students carry over the idea of 'majority' as more than 50% to constituency results.
fix: In a constituency the candidate who gets the highest number of votes wins, even if that is less than half of the total votes cast.

probe.question: In a constituency, A gets 40 votes, B gets 35 and C gets 25. Who wins?
probe.wrong_answer: No one wins because nobody has more than 50 votes.

root_belief: Winning always requires more than half the votes

subject: social
statement: The Supreme Court can directly hear any case from a village.
why: Students assume the highest authority has total control over all levels.
fix: The Supreme Court usually hears cases that have already gone through lower courts or involve constitutional matters.

probe.question: Can you go to the Supreme Court for a minor land dispute in your village?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is the highest court.

root_belief: Higher authority has absolute power over everything

subject: social
concept: Judges are not controlled by politicians
statement: The President or Prime Minister can fire a judge if they dislike a verdict.
why: Students conflate executive power with judicial power.
fix: Judges have security of tenure and can only be removed through a complex impeachment process by Parliament.

probe.question: What happens if the government is unhappy with a Supreme Court verdict?
probe.wrong_answer: The government can dismiss the judges.

root_belief: The leader controls all government branches

subject: social
statement: Civil law is about punishing people for crimes like theft.
why: Students use the everyday meaning of 'civil' as 'polite' or 'non-violent'.
fix: Civil law deals with disputes over property, rent, or contracts, not crimes.

probe.question: Is theft a civil law case?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a dispute between two people.

root_belief: A word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: A PIL is a case filed by the government to help the poor.
why: Students assume the government is the only entity that can initiate public welfare.
fix: A PIL can be filed by any individual or organization on behalf of those whose rights are violated.

probe.question: Who can file a PIL?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the government or the police.

root_belief: One event has one single cause (government)

subject: social
statement: The High Court is a lower court that sits under the District Court in each district.
why: Students think 'High' and 'District' are ordered by local size, or read the court list in the wrong order.
fix: The order is Supreme Court at the top, then High Court at the state level, then District Court, then subordinate courts. High Courts are above District Courts.

probe.question: Which court is higher in the hierarchy, the High Court or the District Court?
probe.wrong_answer: The District Court, because the High Court works under it.

root_belief: Court rank follows local area size, not hierarchy
source_hint: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life, chapter on the judiciary

subject: social
statement: Once a District Court gives a judgment, nobody can challenge it.
why: Students treat a court verdict as the end of the matter, like a final exam result.
fix: A person who is not satisfied with a lower court's decision can appeal to a higher court. This is the appellate system.

probe.question: Rahim loses his case in the District Court and thinks the decision is wrong. What can he do?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, because the District Court's decision is final.

root_belief: Any court verdict is final and unchangeable
source_hint: NCERT Class 8 judiciary chapter, section on appeal

subject: social
statement: An appeal means filing the same case again in the same court.
why: Students confuse 'appeal' with 'refiling' or 'repeating' a case.
fix: An appeal is a petition to a higher court asking it to review and change the lower court's decision.

probe.question: What does it mean to file an appeal?
probe.wrong_answer: It means starting the same case again in the same court from the beginning.

root_belief: An appeal repeats the case at the same level
source_hint: Class 8 student interviews or classroom discussion

subject: social
statement: Judicial independence means judges can do whatever they like and nobody can question them.
why: Students mix up independence from the legislature and executive with having no rules or accountability.
fix: Independence means judges are not controlled by the government in giving decisions. They still follow the Constitution and the law, and their decisions can be reviewed by higher courts.

probe.question: Since the judiciary is independent, can a High Court judge's decision ever be reviewed?
probe.wrong_answer: No, independent judges cannot be questioned or reviewed by anyone.

root_belief: Independence means freedom from all rules
source_hint: Civics education research on separation of powers

subject: social
concept: Judges are not controlled by politicians
statement: Only the government can bring a case against a minister, because courts cannot try those in power.
why: Students assume that powerful officials are above the courts.
fix: The judiciary can hear cases against the government and its officials. Everyone, including ministers, is equal before the law and subject to the courts.

probe.question: A citizen believes a minister has broken the law. Can the court hear a case against the minister?
probe.wrong_answer: No, ministers are too powerful to be taken to court.

root_belief: Powerful officials are above the courts
source_hint: NCERT Class 8, rule of law and the courts

subject: social
statement: Civil and criminal cases are both tried by a police officer who decides who is guilty.
why: Students confuse the police role of investigation with the judge's role of deciding.
fix: In a criminal case the police investigate and file a charge sheet, but the court decides guilt after a fair trial. In a civil case, a person approaches the court directly with a petition.

probe.question: In a criminal case such as theft, who decides whether the accused is guilty?
probe.wrong_answer: The police officer decides guilt after the investigation.

root_belief: Police and courts perform the same function
source_hint: Research on children's understanding of legal institutions

subject: social
statement: A poor person cannot get justice because every case needs an expensive lawyer.
why: Students generalise from the cost of private lawyers and miss legal aid and the PIL route.
fix: The Constitution seeks equal access to justice. Legal aid supports the poor, and through PIL even a letter or postcard can start a case on behalf of others.

probe.question: Can a person with no money still approach a court for justice?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only people who can pay a lawyer can go to court.

root_belief: Justice access depends only on ability to pay
source_hint: NCERT Class 8 judiciary chapter on access to justice

subject: social
statement: A High Court can hear cases from anywhere in India.
why: Students blur the nationwide reach of the Supreme Court with the state-level reach of a High Court.
fix: A High Court has jurisdiction over its own state or group of states and hears appeals from the lower courts in that area. The Supreme Court is the court for the whole country.

probe.question: Can the Kerala High Court hear an appeal against a District Court judgment from Punjab?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a High Court can hear cases from every state in India.

root_belief: All higher courts cover the entire country

subject: social
concept: Social exclusion is based only on poverty
statement: Marginalisation happens only because people are poor.
why: Students often conflate economic status with social status.
fix: Marginalisation is a complex social process involving exclusion based on caste, language, religion, or customs, not just income.

probe.question: Can a wealthy person still be marginalised in society?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because they have money to buy respect.

root_belief: Economic status determines all social outcomes

subject: social
statement: Adivasis are people who live in jungles and wear traditional clothes.
why: Media stereotypes portray Adivasis as 'exotic' or 'primitive' subjects.
fix: Adivasis are modern citizens with diverse lifestyles; they have historically lived in forests but are not defined by primitive technology.

probe.question: Are all Adivasis living in forests today?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, that is where they belong.

root_belief: Culture is static and tied to specific geography
source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

subject: social
statement: Minority only refers to religious groups like Muslims or Christians.
why: The term is frequently used in political discourse specifically regarding religion.
fix: Minorities include both religious and linguistic groups that are numerically small in a specific region.

probe.question: Can a group be a minority based on language?
probe.wrong_answer: No, minority is only about religion.

root_belief: A word means its everyday media usage

subject: social
statement: Reservation is a form of charity or favor given to the poor.
why: Students often view equality as 'treating everyone the same' rather than 'equity'.
fix: Reservation is a constitutional mechanism to ensure representation and social justice for historically oppressed groups.

probe.question: Why does the government provide reservations?
probe.wrong_answer: To help poor people who cannot afford schools.

root_belief: Equality means identical treatment for everyone

subject: social
statement: Adivasis are a single tribe with one common language and culture.
why: Students see 'Adivasi' as one label and assume the people it names are uniform.
fix: Adivasis are many distinct communities, such as Gonds, Santhals, Bhils and Oraons. Each has its own language, customs and way of life, and they live in many regions.

probe.question: Do all Adivasis in India speak the same language and follow the same customs?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they all share one language and culture because they are all Adivasis.

root_belief: A group label means every member is the same
source_hint: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life, textbook analysis

subject: social
statement: Adivasis live only in forests and have never lived in cities or done modern jobs.
why: Images in media and textbooks show Adivasis only in forest settings.
fix: Many Adivasis live in villages, towns and cities and work as farmers, labourers, teachers and in mines and industry. Some Adivasi communities live in forests, but not all do.

probe.question: Can an Adivasi person be a doctor or live in a city like Mumbai?
probe.wrong_answer: No, Adivasis live only in forests and cannot have modern jobs.

root_belief: A social group is fixed in one place and lifestyle

subject: social
statement: Minorities are weak groups who get special treatment that the majority does not get.
why: Students see minority rights as favours that take away from others.
fix: The Constitution gives minorities rights, such as running their own educational institutions and protecting their language and culture, so that they are treated equally and not dominated by the majority.

probe.question: Why does the Constitution give minorities the right to set up their own schools?
probe.wrong_answer: To give them an unfair advantage over the majority.

root_belief: Protecting rights equals giving unfair privileges
source_hint: Textbook analysis and civic education research

subject: social
statement: A minority group is any group with less money, whatever its size.
why: Students mix up minority with being poor or powerless.
fix: A minority is a community that is small in numbers compared with the rest of the population, such as religious or linguistic groups. Being a minority is about numbers and also about the risk of being left out, not only about wealth.

probe.question: Is a rich community that is small in number a minority in the Indian sense?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only poor groups can be minorities.

root_belief: Minority means poor or powerless, not small in number

subject: social
statement: The Constitution has no special provisions for Dalits and Adivasis, it only says everyone is equal.
why: Students think that equality means identical treatment and that no special measures exist.
fix: The Constitution declares equality but also has special safeguards, such as the abolition of untouchability under Article 17 and reserved seats and jobs for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

probe.question: Which Article of the Constitution abolishes untouchability?
probe.wrong_answer: None, the Constitution only says everyone is equal and does not mention untouchability.

root_belief: Equality means no special protections are needed
source_hint: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life

subject: social
statement: Fundamental Rights protect only citizens who belong to marginalised groups.
why: Students link rights and safeguards only with the discussion of marginalised groups.
fix: Fundamental Rights, such as equality and freedom, apply to all citizens. Special safeguards are added to help marginalised groups get the same rights in practice.

probe.question: Who can use the Fundamental Right to equality before the law?
probe.wrong_answer: Only Dalits, Adivasis and minorities.

root_belief: Rights belong to specific groups only

subject: social
concept: Untouchability is a thing of the past
statement: Untouchability ended in 1950 and nobody faces caste discrimination today.
why: Students take the legal abolition as the end of the practice.
fix: Article 17 abolished untouchability and the 1989 SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act punishes caste atrocities, but discrimination still occurs, so laws must be enforced and attitudes must change.

probe.question: Since untouchability was abolished in 1950, does caste discrimination still exist?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the law ended it completely, so nobody faces it now.

root_belief: A law passed means the problem is solved
source_hint: NCERT Class 8 and education research on caste awareness

subject: social
concept: Forest Rights Act restores land rights
statement: The Forest Rights Act took forest land from Adivasis and gave it to the government.
why: Students confuse forest laws that restricted access with the 2006 Act that recognised rights.
fix: The Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognises the rights of forest-dwelling Adivasis and other forest dwellers over land and forest produce they have used for generations.

probe.question: What does the Forest Rights Act, 2006 do for forest dwellers?
probe.wrong_answer: It takes their land away and hands it over to the government.

root_belief: Forest laws always take rights away from forest people

subject: social
statement: Water is a commodity that should only be provided to those who can pay for it.
why: Students often equate public services with private market goods.
fix: Water is a fundamental right essential for life, and the government must ensure universal access regardless of ability to pay.

probe.question: Should the government provide free water to poor households?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because water costs money to process and distribute.

root_belief: Market rules apply to all human needs

subject: social
statement: Minimum wage laws are unnecessary because employers should pay whatever they want.
why: Students often view labor as a simple transaction without power imbalances.
fix: Minimum wages prevent the exploitation of workers who have little bargaining power against powerful employers.

probe.question: Why does the government set a minimum wage?
probe.wrong_answer: To stop companies from making too much profit.

root_belief: Free market is always fair

subject: social
statement: The Bhopal Gas Tragedy was just an accident caused by bad luck.
why: Students often ignore systemic negligence in favor of random chance.
fix: It was a result of corporate negligence and weak safety laws that prioritized profit over human lives.

probe.question: What was the main cause of the Bhopal disaster?
probe.wrong_answer: It was an unavoidable accident that could happen anywhere.

root_belief: Bad outcomes are just accidents

subject: social
statement: Providing clean water and sanitation is the job of individual households, not the government.
why: Students see families buying filters, tanks and tankers, and assume water supply is a private matter.
fix: Water supply and sanitation are public facilities that the government must provide to everyone. Private effort cannot replace a public system, and the poor cannot afford it.

probe.question: Who is mainly responsible for building water pipelines and sewage systems in a city?
probe.wrong_answer: Each household should arrange its own water and sewage.

root_belief: Public services are private responsibilities

subject: social
statement: If a city has a water supply, every neighbourhood in it gets enough water.
why: Students assume that the existence of a service means equal access to it.
fix: Water supply is often unequal. Rich colonies get plenty while poor settlements get little and pay more to private tankers. Governments must reduce this inequality.

probe.question: A city has a municipal water supply. Does every area get equal water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, once a city has water supply all areas get equal and enough water.

root_belief: Existence of service means equal access
source_hint: NCERT Social and Political Life textbook

subject: social
statement: Public transport like buses and trains is only for poor people who cannot buy vehicles.
why: Students link private cars with status and buses with poverty.
fix: Public transport is a public facility for everyone. It reduces traffic, pollution and cost, and serves people of all incomes.

probe.question: Who is public transport meant for?
probe.wrong_answer: Only poor people who cannot afford their own vehicle.

root_belief: Public facilities are only for the poor

subject: social
statement: Private vehicles are better than public transport for society because they carry people more conveniently.
why: Students judge by personal convenience rather than overall benefit to the community.
fix: Buses and trains carry many more people per road space and use less fuel per person. Many private cars cause jams and pollution.

probe.question: Which solves a city's traffic problem better, more private cars or more buses?
probe.wrong_answer: More private cars, since they are more convenient.

root_belief: Individual convenience equals social benefit

subject: social
statement: Labour laws protect only factory workers and not farm workers, domestic helpers or daily wage workers.
why: Students picture workers only as people in factories with uniforms.
fix: Labour laws aim to protect all workers, including those in the unorganised sector such as daily wage labourers, farm and domestic workers, though enforcement is weaker there.

probe.question: Does a construction labourer paid daily have rights under labour laws?
probe.wrong_answer: No, laws only cover factory workers.

root_belief: Laws cover only formal workplaces

subject: social
statement: The Bhopal Gas Tragedy happened at a government-run plant.
why: Students assume large factories and disasters are always linked to the government.
fix: The gas leak in December 1984 was from Union Carbide, a foreign-owned private company's pesticide plant. The government's duty was to enforce safety rules and help victims.

probe.question: Who ran the factory where the Bhopal gas leaked?
probe.wrong_answer: The Indian government.

root_belief: Big enterprises are government-owned
source_hint: NCERT Social and Political Life textbook

subject: social
statement: A fundamental right to water means water must be free for everyone and nobody can be charged anything.
why: Students confuse right to access with zero price.
fix: The Supreme Court held that the Right to Life under Article 21 includes safe water. The government must ensure everyone can access it, and charges must be affordable, with the poor protected.

probe.question: If water is a fundamental right, can the government charge any fee?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it must always be completely free.

root_belief: Right to access means free of cost
source_hint: NCERT Social and Political Life textbook

subject: social
statement: Worker safety is the worker's own responsibility, not the employer's.
why: Students think accidents occur because workers are careless.
fix: Employers must provide safe conditions, equipment and training, and the government must enforce safety laws. Workers' care alone cannot prevent disasters.

probe.question: A worker is injured by faulty machinery. Who is responsible for safety?
probe.wrong_answer: The worker should have been more careful.

root_belief: Blame lies with the individual, not the system

subject: social
statement: Once a company pays a small compensation, it has no further responsibility for harm it caused.
why: Students treat payment as settling everything, ignoring prevention and punishment.
fix: Companies must be accountable: pay adequate compensation, clean up damage, and follow safety laws. Courts and government must ensure justice, as the Bhopal victims' continuing struggle shows.

probe.question: A company pays some money after a gas leak. Is it now free of responsibility?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, paying compensation ends its responsibility.

root_belief: Payment cancels all responsibility

subject: social
statement: Any country with a parliament is a democracy.
why: Students confuse the existence of a building or institution with the actual practice of democratic power.
fix: A democracy requires that the final decision-making power rests with those elected by the people, not just the existence of a legislative body.

probe.question: If a country has a parliament but the military makes all the laws, is it a democracy?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has a parliament.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
concept: One person, one vote, one value
statement: Democracy means everyone gets exactly what they want.
why: Students equate democracy with the fulfillment of personal desires rather than a process of collective decision-making.
fix: Democracy is a system of government where people have a say in choosing their leaders and laws, but it does not guarantee that every individual's specific wish will be granted.

probe.question: If the government passes a law you dislike, is the country still a democracy?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because democracy means everyone gets what they want.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: Elections are free and fair if everyone is allowed to vote.
why: Students focus only on the act of voting and ignore the conditions required for a genuine choice.
fix: Free and fair elections require that the ruling party has a fair chance of losing and that there is a genuine choice between alternatives.

probe.question: If there is only one party on the ballot, is it a fair election?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because everyone is allowed to vote.

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: social
statement: In a democracy, the government can do whatever the majority wants.
why: Students confuse democracy with 'majority rule' without considering constitutional limits.
fix: Democracy requires the government to respect the rights of minorities and operate within the limits set by the constitution.

probe.question: Can a majority vote to take away the rights of a minority group in a democracy?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the majority decision is always democratic.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: social
statement: In a democracy, the people themselves make every decision directly.
why: Students equate democracy with its ancient direct form and miss that modern democracies work through representatives.
fix: In modern democracies people elect representatives, and these elected representatives take decisions on their behalf.

probe.question: Who takes the decisions about laws in India's democracy?
probe.wrong_answer: All citizens vote directly on every law and decision.

root_belief: Democracy means direct rule by all people

subject: social
statement: Army officers or unelected officials can hold the final power in a democracy if they are skilled.
why: Students value expertise and efficiency over accountability and think any capable ruler works.
fix: In a democracy the final decision-making power rests with elected representatives, not with unelected officers or the military.

probe.question: In a democracy, who should have the final say over the government's decisions: elected leaders or the army chief?
probe.wrong_answer: The army chief, since they are more experienced and trained.

root_belief: Competence matters more than being elected

subject: social
concept: One person, one vote, one value
statement: One person, one vote, one value means every voter gets the same result as the winner.
why: Students confuse equal value of votes with equal outcomes.
fix: It means each adult citizen has one vote and every vote counts equally, whatever the person's wealth, religion, caste or gender; it does not guarantee the voter's choice wins.

probe.question: What does 'one person, one vote, one value' mean?
probe.wrong_answer: Everyone who votes gets their chosen candidate to win.

root_belief: Equal vote means equal outcome

subject: social
statement: Political equality means all citizens must have equal wealth and property.
why: Students mix political equality with economic equality.
fix: Political equality means every citizen has equal right to vote and be elected; economic inequalities may still exist.

probe.question: A rich businessman and a poor labourer both have one vote. Is this political equality?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because they do not have equal money.

root_belief: Political equality equals economic equality

subject: social
statement: Regular competition for power is harmful because it only causes quarrels and instability.
why: Students see rival parties' fights and think a stable government needs no competition.
fix: Regular competition gives voters choice, keeps leaders answerable and lets them remove those who perform badly.

probe.question: Why do democracies hold regular elections with many parties competing?
probe.wrong_answer: It is wasteful and just creates quarrels; one party ruling would be better.

root_belief: Competition is conflict without benefit

subject: social
statement: Rule of law means the law applies to ordinary people but top leaders are above it.
why: Students observe powerful people escaping punishment and generalise this as how law works.
fix: In a democracy everyone, including the Prime Minister and ministers, is equally subject to the law and its rights.

probe.question: Can a Minister who breaks the law be tried in court like any citizen?
probe.wrong_answer: No, ministers are above the law because they are elected.

root_belief: Elected power exempts leaders from law

subject: social
statement: Elections in a democracy only need to be held once, after which leaders can rule as long as they like.
why: Students think elections are a one-time event for choosing rulers.
fix: Elections must be held regularly after a fixed term so the people can change their rulers.

probe.question: How often must elections be held in a democracy?
probe.wrong_answer: Once is enough; the elected leader can continue for life.

root_belief: Elections are one-time, not periodic

subject: social
concept: Democracy provides method to deal with differences
statement: Democracy removes all conflicts between people, so a country with disputes cannot be democratic.
why: Students think peaceful agreement is the sign of democracy and see conflicts as failure.
fix: Democracy gives a peaceful method to handle differences and conflicts through discussion and negotiation; it does not remove them.

probe.question: There are disputes over sharing river water between states in India. Does this show India is not a democracy?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a real democracy would have no disputes.

root_belief: Democracy means absence of conflict

subject: social
statement: Elections are only held to choose the most popular leader.
why: Students focus on the personality of candidates rather than the accountability mechanism.
fix: Elections allow voters to choose representatives who will make laws and hold the government accountable.

probe.question: Why do we have elections in a democracy?
probe.wrong_answer: To see who is the most famous person in the country.

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: social
statement: Reserved constituencies mean only people from that caste can vote there.
why: Confusion between the candidate's eligibility and the voter's right to vote.
fix: All voters in a reserved constituency vote, but only candidates from the reserved category can contest.

probe.question: Who can vote in a reserved constituency?
probe.wrong_answer: Only people belonging to the reserved caste.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: The Election Commission is part of the ruling government.
why: Students assume all government bodies work under the Prime Minister.
fix: The Election Commission is an independent body that functions separately from the executive government.

probe.question: Who controls the Election Commission?
probe.wrong_answer: The Prime Minister or the ruling party.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: social
statement: Constituencies are drawn based on the number of houses in an area.
why: Students equate geographical area with population density.
fix: Constituencies are demarcated based on population size to ensure equal representation.

probe.question: How are constituency boundaries decided?
probe.wrong_answer: By the size of the land area.

root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

subject: social
statement: Voting for a candidate means the voter is choosing the person who will personally rule the country.
why: Students merge the idea of a local representative with the head of government, so the vote seems to pick a ruler directly.
fix: In a Lok Sabha election voters choose their own constituency's representative (MP). The party or alliance with a majority of MPs forms the government, and the Prime Minister is chosen from among them.

probe.question: When you vote in a Lok Sabha election, whom are you directly choosing?
probe.wrong_answer: The Prime Minister of the country.

root_belief: Voters directly choose the head of government
source_hint: classroom questioning on parliamentary vs presidential systems

subject: social
statement: A voter can freely choose a candidate only if all parties are equally strong and have equal money.
why: Students think choice requires equality of resources, so they doubt whether real choice exists when parties differ in strength.
fix: Democratic choice means voters have more than one candidate or party to pick from and can vote freely and secretly. Parties and candidates are unequal in resources, but the choice is still real. Fair, free elections aim to make it meaningful.

probe.question: Rich party A and small party B contest an election. Is the voters' choice a democratic choice?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because choice is real only when both parties have equal money and strength.

root_belief: Real choice needs equal resources among competitors

subject: social
statement: Each constituency elects as many representatives as it likes, so a big constituency sends several MPs.
why: Students think a larger or more populous area should get more than one representative to be fairly represented.
fix: In Lok Sabha elections each constituency elects one representative (MP), and in Assembly elections one MLA. Total seats come from the number of constituencies, and the whole country is divided into many constituencies.

probe.question: A Lok Sabha constituency has a very large population. How many MPs does it elect?
probe.wrong_answer: Several MPs, more than one, because it is large.

root_belief: Bigger areas elect more representatives each

subject: social
statement: A voter can vote in any constituency in the country in which they happen to be on polling day.
why: Students think voting is tied to the person rather than to the place they live and are registered in, so being anywhere is enough.
fix: Each area is a constituency, and a voter votes only in the constituency where they live and are listed in the voters' list. A person has one vote, cast in their own area.

probe.question: Meena lives in Jaipur but is visiting Chennai on polling day. Where can she vote in the general election?
probe.wrong_answer: In Chennai, because she is in the country and can vote anywhere.

root_belief: Voting is not tied to residence-based constituency

subject: social
statement: Every citizen above 18 is automatically in the voters' list, so no one needs to register.
why: Students see the right to vote as automatic at 18 and overlook the need for the name to be on the list.
fix: The voters' list (electoral roll) is prepared before elections and people aged 18 and above must have their names on it to vote. A person whose name is missing cannot vote, so those not listed must apply to be added; the list is updated regularly.

probe.question: Ravi turned 19, but his name is not on the voters' list. Can he vote on polling day?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because he is above 18 and is automatically a voter.

root_belief: Age eligibility alone entitles voting without registration
source_hint: NCERT text on voters' list and Class 9 teacher observations

subject: social
statement: The EPIC voter ID card is the only document a person needs and replaces the voters' list.
why: Students treat the card as the thing that grants voting and miss that the roll is the main record of who may vote.
fix: The Election Photo Identity Card (EPIC) is given to voters to prevent fraud and is used for identification at the booth. The name must still be on the voters' list. The card is an identity aid, not a substitute for being on the list.

probe.question: Anil has an EPIC card but his name was removed from the voters' list. Can he vote?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the card alone is enough to vote.

root_belief: Identity card replaces the voters' list

subject: social
concept: Reservation ensures weaker sections have a voice
statement: Reserved constituencies are meant to give SC and ST candidates a guaranteed win in elections.
why: Students read reservation as a guarantee of success instead of a guarantee of candidacy, as with seat reservation in a bus.
fix: In reserved constituencies only SC (or ST) candidates can contest, but everyone in the area votes, and the winner is chosen by votes. Reservation ensures weaker sections get a voice and representation in the legislature, not a certain win for any one person.

probe.question: In a seat reserved for SC, five SC candidates contest. Who wins?
probe.wrong_answer: All of them or one is picked automatically without needing votes.

root_belief: Reservation means guaranteed victory, not guaranteed candidacy

subject: social
statement: The Model Code of Conduct is a law passed by Parliament that sends violators straight to jail.
why: Students assume any binding rule enforced by the Election Commission must be a statutory law with court punishments.
fix: The Model Code of Conduct is a set of guidelines agreed to by parties and candidates, which the Election Commission enforces during elections. For example, ministers cannot announce new schemes or use government resources for campaigning. The Commission can warn, censure or stop violators during the election period.

probe.question: What is the Model Code of Conduct and who made it a law?
probe.wrong_answer: A law passed by Parliament that sends violators to jail.

root_belief: Every enforced election rule is a statute

subject: social
statement: The Rajya Sabha is more powerful than the Lok Sabha because it is the Upper House.
why: Students confuse the term 'Upper' with 'higher authority' or 'greater power'.
fix: The Lok Sabha is more powerful because its members are directly elected and it controls the budget and the government's survival.

probe.question: If the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha disagree on a normal bill, whose decision prevails?
probe.wrong_answer: The Rajya Sabha's decision prevails.

root_belief: Hierarchy implies power

subject: social
statement: The Prime Minister is the head of the country.
why: Media focus on the PM as the face of the government leads to conflating the head of government with the head of state.
fix: The President is the head of state, while the Prime Minister is the head of government.

probe.question: Who is the official Head of State in India?
probe.wrong_answer: The Prime Minister.

root_belief: The most visible person is the most powerful

subject: social
statement: Civil servants make the final decisions on government policy.
why: Students see bureaucrats implementing laws and assume they are the ones who created them.
fix: Civil servants assist in policy implementation, but the final decision-making power rests with the elected political executive.

probe.question: Who takes the final decision on a policy proposal?
probe.wrong_answer: The civil servant or bureaucrat.

root_belief: Those who do the work have the authority
source_hint: Rosalind Driver children's ideas in social studies

subject: social
statement: The Supreme Court can change any law passed by Parliament at any time.
why: Students overgeneralize the concept of judicial review, ignoring the constitutional limitations.
fix: The Supreme Court can only declare a law invalid if it violates the basic structure or provisions of the Constitution.

probe.question: Can the Supreme Court strike down any law it dislikes?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it has the power to change any law.

root_belief: One institution has absolute power

subject: social
statement: Members of Parliament are chosen by the people for both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha in the same way.
why: Students know that Parliament is 'elected by the people' and assume both Houses are filled by the same direct voting.
fix: Lok Sabha members are directly elected by the people from constituencies. Rajya Sabha members are indirectly elected by the elected members (MLAs) of State Legislative Assemblies.

probe.question: Who elects the members of the Rajya Sabha?
probe.wrong_answer: All the voting citizens of India elect them directly, as they elect Lok Sabha members.

root_belief: Both Houses are filled by identical direct elections

subject: social
statement: The President is not a part of Parliament; Parliament means only the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
why: Students picture Parliament as the two Houses with seats and debates, and see the President as a separate ceremonial office.
fix: Parliament consists of the President and the two Houses, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. A bill becomes a law only after the President gives assent.

probe.question: Name the parts that together make up the Indian Parliament.
probe.wrong_answer: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha only.

root_belief: Parliament equals only the houses where debates happen

subject: social
statement: A bill passed by both Houses of Parliament becomes a law automatically.
why: Students focus on voting in Parliament as the end of the law-making process and ignore the final step.
fix: After both Houses pass a bill, it goes to the President. It becomes a law only when the President gives assent.

probe.question: What must happen after both Houses pass a bill before it becomes a law?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing more is needed; it becomes a law as soon as both Houses vote for it.

root_belief: Voting in the legislature alone completes law-making

subject: social
statement: The Rajya Sabha can reject a Money Bill passed by the Lok Sabha.
why: Students generalise that each House has an equal veto over bills, so the second House can stop any bill.
fix: A Money Bill is introduced only in the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha can only give recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may accept or ignore, and it cannot block the bill.

probe.question: If the Rajya Sabha disagrees with a Money Bill passed by the Lok Sabha, what can it do?
probe.wrong_answer: It can reject the bill and stop it from becoming a law.

root_belief: Both Houses have equal veto over every bill

subject: social
statement: Lok Sabha members are elected by the people, so the Lok Sabha can be dissolved but the Rajya Sabha can also be dissolved.
why: Students think every legislative body is dissolved and re-elected together after five years.
fix: The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and is never dissolved as a whole. One-third of its members retire every two years. The Lok Sabha is elected for five years and can be dissolved.

probe.question: What happens to the Rajya Sabha when a new Lok Sabha is elected after five years?
probe.wrong_answer: It is dissolved too and all its members are elected afresh.

root_belief: All legislative bodies share the same fixed term

subject: social
statement: The Prime Minister is appointed by the President by personal choice, so the President can pick anyone.
why: Students read 'the President appoints the Prime Minister' literally and miss the role of the Lok Sabha majority.
fix: The President appoints the leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha as Prime Minister. The President cannot choose freely.

probe.question: On what basis does the President appoint the Prime Minister?
probe.wrong_answer: The President selects whichever person they think is best.

root_belief: Formal appointment means free personal choice by appointer

subject: social
statement: Ministers are permanent executive and stay in office even after elections are lost.
why: Students see ministers and civil servants both running departments and assume both hold their posts for a fixed long period.
fix: Ministers are the political executive, elected for a term and removed when their party loses. Civil servants are the permanent executive, appointed on merit, and stay in office even when the government changes.

probe.question: Who continues to work in the ministry after a new party forms the government?
probe.wrong_answer: The old ministers, because ministers are the permanent executive.

root_belief: All people running government departments have equal tenure

subject: social
statement: Judges are appointed and can be removed by the government whenever it wants.
why: Students assume that those who appoint can also dismiss, and that the government controls all institutions.
fix: Judges are appointed by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice, and a judge can be removed only by an impeachment process in Parliament. This keeps the judiciary independent.

probe.question: If the government is unhappy with a judge's verdict, can it remove the judge?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the government can dismiss the judge at any time.

root_belief: Appointing authority has unlimited power to dismiss

subject: social
statement: Fundamental rights are absolute and can never be restricted.
why: Students confuse the concept of 'right' with 'unlimited power'.
fix: Rights are subject to reasonable restrictions by the state to maintain public order and security.

probe.question: Can the government stop a protest if it blocks an emergency hospital route?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because freedom of assembly is a fundamental right.

root_belief: a right is an absolute permission

subject: social
statement: Right to equality means everyone must be treated exactly the same regardless of circumstances.
why: Students interpret 'equality' as 'sameness' rather than 'equity'.
fix: Equality means equal opportunity and protection, but the state can make special provisions for disadvantaged groups.

probe.question: Is reservation for SC/ST/OBC a violation of the right to equality?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it treats people differently based on caste.

root_belief: equality means identical treatment
source_hint: HBCSE research on social science concepts

subject: social
statement: The NHRC can punish people who violate human rights.
why: Students assume any government body with 'Commission' in its name has judicial power.
fix: The NHRC is a recommendatory body; it can investigate and suggest action but cannot pass binding sentences.

probe.question: What can the NHRC do if it finds a police officer guilty of torture?
probe.wrong_answer: It can sentence the officer to jail.

root_belief: all government bodies have power to punish

subject: social
statement: Freedom of speech allows me to say anything I want, including inciting violence.
why: Students take 'freedom' to mean lack of any responsibility or consequence.
fix: Freedom of speech is protected, but it does not cover speech that incites violence or threatens national security.

probe.question: Can you be arrested for making a speech that calls for a riot?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because I have the fundamental right to freedom of speech.

root_belief: freedom means absence of all constraints

subject: social
statement: Fundamental rights are just promises written in the Constitution and a court cannot enforce them.
why: Students treat the Constitution as a statement of ideals, like a pledge or a list of aims, and do not see that rights can be enforced.
fix: Fundamental Rights are justiciable. If a right is violated, a citizen can go to the High Court or Supreme Court, and the court can order the government to protect it.

probe.question: A person's right to freedom is violated by an official. Can a court force the government to restore that right?
probe.wrong_answer: No, rights are only guidelines in the Constitution, so the court cannot force anything.

root_belief: Constitutional rights are ideals, not legally enforceable

subject: social
statement: A writ is a punishment given by a court to a person who breaks the law.
why: Students link court orders with punishment and fines, and have heard of 'writs' only in crime stories.
fix: A writ is a formal order from the High Court or Supreme Court to the government or an authority to protect a citizen's Fundamental Right, e.g. habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto.

probe.question: What is the purpose of a writ of habeas corpus?
probe.wrong_answer: It is the punishment given to a criminal after a trial.

root_belief: Court orders mean punishment for wrongdoers
source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Democratic Politics chapter text

subject: social
statement: Only the Supreme Court can be approached when a Fundamental Right is violated.
why: Students remember Dr Ambedkar's description of this right as the heart and soul of the Constitution and the Supreme Court as the main court, and forget the High Courts.
fix: Citizens can go directly to the Supreme Court or to the High Court of their state under the Right to Constitutional Remedies.

probe.question: Where can a villager file a petition if their Fundamental Right is violated?
probe.wrong_answer: Only in the Supreme Court in Delhi.

root_belief: Highest court is the only court for rights
source_hint: teacher observation or board exam answers

subject: social
statement: The NHRC is a court, so anyone dissatisfied with a court can appeal to it.
why: Students see 'Commission' as a court-like body with a judge and think it ranks with the judiciary.
fix: The NHRC is an independent commission set up by law in 1993. It is not a court. It investigates and recommends, and it has no power to decide cases or hear appeals from courts.

probe.question: A person loses a case in the High Court. Can they appeal to the NHRC?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the NHRC is a higher court and can change the High Court's decision.

root_belief: Commissions function as courts
source_hint: NCERT Class 9 chapter text and exercises

subject: social
statement: The NHRC only looks into violations of rights by private citizens and companies.
why: Students assume human rights violations are done by criminals, not by government, and don't realise the NHRC deals with state agencies.
fix: The NHRC mainly looks into violations by government officials and agencies, such as police custody abuses, and can take up a case on its own or on a complaint.

probe.question: Can the NHRC investigate a case of custodial torture by police?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the police are the government, and the NHRC deals only with private persons.

root_belief: Only private persons violate rights, not the state

subject: social
statement: The Right to Equality means all people must have the same income and property.
why: Students read 'equality' as economic equality, equal wealth, instead of legal and social equality.
fix: The Right to Equality means equality before law, no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, equal access to public places, equal opportunity in public employment, and abolition of untouchability. It does not mean equal wealth.

probe.question: Does the Right to Equality ensure that a rich and a poor person own the same amount of property?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, equality means everyone should have equal wealth.

root_belief: Equality means equal wealth

subject: social
statement: Right to Freedom means I can live in and settle in any country I choose.
why: Students stretch 'freedom of movement' and 'residence' to mean worldwide, ignoring the words 'throughout the territory of India'.
fix: Right to Freedom allows citizens to move freely and reside in any part of the territory of India, not abroad. Foreign travel depends on passports and visas of other countries.

probe.question: Does the Right to Freedom let an Indian citizen settle in any country without permission?
