probe.wrong_answer: Yes, freedom of movement means I can reside anywhere in the world.

root_belief: Freedom of movement has no territorial limit

subject: social
statement: The Right to Education means every child gets free education in school up to Class 12.
why: Students mix the RTE Act with the general idea of free schooling and remember 'school' without the age range.
fix: The Right to Education makes free and compulsory education a Fundamental Right for children aged 6 to 14, i.e. up to elementary level (Class 8). It is not a right up to Class 12.

probe.question: Up to which age or class does the Right to Education guarantee free and compulsory education?
probe.wrong_answer: Up to Class 12, for all children until they finish school.

root_belief: Right to Education covers all school classes
source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Democratic Politics and RTE Act text

subject: social
statement: Democracy means the majority community should decide everything for the country.
why: Students confuse the democratic principle of majority rule with the ethical requirement to protect minority rights.
fix: Democracy requires that the majority rules while respecting the identity and rights of minority groups to prevent tyranny.

probe.question: In a democracy, if 80% of people belong to one religion, should they make all laws?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because democracy is the rule of the majority.

root_belief: Majority rule is the only definition of democracy

subject: social
statement: Horizontal power sharing means the government is divided into different levels like central and state.
why: Students confuse the physical layout of government (levels) with the functional division of power (organs).
fix: Horizontal power sharing refers to the division of power among the legislature, executive, and judiciary at the same level.

probe.question: Which of these is an example of horizontal power sharing?
probe.wrong_answer: The division of power between the Central and State governments.

root_belief: All divisions of power are the same

subject: social
statement: The Central government can make laws on any subject it wants.
why: Students assume that because the Central government is 'higher', it has absolute authority over all subjects.
fix: The Constitution explicitly defines the Union, State, and Concurrent lists, limiting the Central government's power to specific subjects.

probe.question: Can the Central government make laws on subjects in the State list?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is the supreme authority in the country.

root_belief: Bigger or higher means more power

subject: social
statement: Decentralisation means the state government loses all power to the local government.
why: Students interpret 'transfer of power' as a zero-sum game where one loses what the other gains.
fix: Decentralisation is the transfer of power from central and state governments to local bodies, but the higher levels retain their constitutional authority.

probe.question: What happens to the State government's power after decentralisation?
probe.wrong_answer: It is abolished or becomes powerless.

root_belief: Power is a finite resource that must be lost to be shared

subject: social
concept: Case Studies: Belgium vs Sri Lanka
statement: Belgium solved its ethnic tensions by giving all power to the Dutch-speaking majority.
why: Students carry over the majoritarian idea from Sri Lanka and assume the larger group must rule in any country.
fix: Belgium accommodated differences by sharing power. Dutch and French speakers have equal representation in the Central government, and Brussels has a separate government in which both communities have equal representation.

probe.question: How did Belgium deal with the Dutch-French divide, and why did it avoid civil war?
probe.wrong_answer: The Dutch-speaking majority took control of the government and the French speakers accepted it.

root_belief: Stable countries are ruled by their largest group
source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.1; classroom error analysis

subject: social
statement: Power sharing is useful only because it reduces conflict, so it has no value beyond that.
why: Students remember the prudential reasons (avoiding conflict) best because the case studies stress them.
fix: There are two reasons. The prudential reason is that power sharing reduces conflict and brings stability. The moral reason is that power sharing is valuable in itself, because it is the spirit of democracy and lets people have a say in how they are governed.

probe.question: If a country has no social conflict at all, is power sharing still needed? Why?
probe.wrong_answer: No, power sharing is needed only to stop conflict, so without conflict it is not needed.

root_belief: Only practical benefits justify a political arrangement
source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.1; teacher observation

subject: social
statement: Horizontal power sharing means the government shares power with social groups such as religious or linguistic communities.
why: Students mix up the horizontal form with the community-based form and with political parties and pressure groups.
fix: Horizontal power sharing is among the organs of government at the same level: legislature, executive and judiciary. Sharing among social groups is a separate form, and sharing among parties, movements and pressure groups is another.

probe.question: Which form of power sharing is the separation of powers among the legislature, executive and judiciary?
probe.wrong_answer: It is power sharing among religious and linguistic communities.

root_belief: Horizontal means spread across social groups
source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.1; classroom error analysis

subject: social
statement: Vertical power sharing is the same as federalism, so any country with a central government and local governments is a federation.
why: Students treat the term federalism as just any division of power between levels.
fix: Vertical power sharing is the division of power among governments at different levels. Federalism is a system with two or more levels of government whose powers are constitutionally guaranteed. In a unitary system, the lower-level governments work under the central one and can be changed by it.

probe.question: A country has a central government and local governments, but the centre can dissolve the local bodies at will. Is it a federation?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has two levels of government sharing power.

root_belief: Any multi-level government counts as federal
source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.2

subject: social
statement: Education and forests are on the Union List because they are important for the whole country.
why: Students guess from how important a subject sounds and do not remember which list holds it.
fix: The Union List has national-level subjects such as defence, foreign affairs, banking and currency. The State List has subjects such as police, trade, commerce, agriculture and irrigation. The Concurrent List has subjects of common interest such as education, forests, trade unions, marriage, adoption and succession. Both the Union and State governments can make laws on it, and the Union law prevails in case of a conflict.

probe.question: Which list do education and forests belong to, and who can make laws on them?
probe.wrong_answer: The Union List, so only the Central government can make laws on them.

root_belief: Important subjects always belong to the Centre
source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.2

subject: social
statement: Decentralisation was introduced in India only in 1992 when local governments were created.
why: Students link decentralisation only with the 1992 amendment and ignore the earlier federal division of power.
fix: India's Constitution already provided for a two-tier system, the Union and the States, and later a third tier. Local governments existed earlier but had no constitutional status or regular elections. The 1992 amendment made them stronger by making elections regular and giving them constitutional status and reserved seats.

probe.question: What did the 1992 Constitutional amendment change about local government in India?
probe.wrong_answer: It created local government in India for the first time.

root_belief: A reform marks the start of the thing it reformed
source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.2

subject: social
statement: Residuary powers in India belong to the State governments because states are closer to the people.
why: Students assume the 'leftover' subjects go to the lower level, as in the example of local administration.
fix: Residuary subjects are those that were not on any list, such as computer software, which did not exist when the Constitution was made. In India these go to the Union government. In some other federations, such as the USA and Australia, they go to the states.

probe.question: Which government can make laws on a new subject, such as computer software, that is on none of the three lists?
probe.wrong_answer: The State governments, because they are closer to the people.

root_belief: Leftover power goes to the lower government
source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.2

subject: social
statement: A Panchayati Raj gram panchayat is chosen by the state government, which appoints its sarpanch.
why: Students see local bodies as administrative offices working under state officials and not as elected bodies.
fix: The gram panchayat is the local government in a village or group of villages. Its members are elected by all adult residents who are members of the gram sabha, and the sarpanch is its elected president. The gram sabha meets to approve the budget and review the work of the panchayat.

probe.question: Who chooses the members of the gram panchayat and the sarpanch?
probe.wrong_answer: The state government appoints them.

root_belief: Local bodies are appointed, not elected
source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Democratic Politics I, Ch.2; teacher observation

subject: social
statement: Political parties and the government are the same entity.
why: Students often see party leaders acting as ministers and fail to distinguish between the party organization and the state machinery.
fix: A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections, while the government is the body that exercises executive power.

probe.question: If a party loses an election, does the government cease to exist?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the party is the government.

root_belief: different labels refer to the same thing

subject: social
statement: A multi-party system is always better than a two-party system.
why: Students equate 'more' with 'better' in a democratic context without considering stability.
fix: No system is inherently better; multi-party systems offer more choice but can lead to instability, while two-party systems are more stable.

probe.question: Which system is the most democratic?
probe.wrong_answer: Multi-party system because it has more parties.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: social
statement: Any party that wins a few seats in a state is automatically a state party.
why: Students ignore the specific percentage and seat criteria set by the Election Commission.
fix: A party must secure at least 6% of the total votes in a legislative assembly election and win at least two seats to be recognized as a state party.

probe.question: If a party wins 1 seat in a state, is it a state party?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it represents the state.

root_belief: rules are flexible and based on intuition

subject: social
statement: Dynastic succession is only a problem in monarchies, not democracies.
why: Students associate 'dynasty' solely with historical kings and queens.
fix: Dynastic succession occurs in democracies when top positions are held by members of one family, limiting opportunities for ordinary workers.

probe.question: Can a democracy have a dynasty?
probe.wrong_answer: No, democracy means no dynasties.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: Opposition parties have no role in policy making because only the ruling party makes policies.
why: Students link policy making only with those in power and see opposition as merely criticising.
fix: Parties in opposition voice different views, criticise failures, mobilise opinion and force the government to modify policies; they also put forward alternative policies.

probe.question: Does a party that lost the election have any role in shaping policy?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only the winning party makes policy; the opposition just complains.

root_belief: Only the ruling group influences policy

subject: social
statement: The party that wins the most seats always forms the government, even without a majority.
why: Students mix 'largest party' with 'majority'.
fix: A party or alliance needs majority support (272 of 543 in Lok Sabha). If no party has it, parties form a coalition.

probe.question: A party wins 200 of 543 seats and no other party joins it. Can it form the government?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has the most seats.

root_belief: Largest party equals majority party

subject: social
statement: India has a two-party system because Congress and BJP are the only parties that matter.
why: Media focus on two big national parties hides the many regional parties in coalitions.
fix: India has a multi-party system: many parties compete and several win seats and join alliances; no single party usually wins alone.

probe.question: Which party system does India have?
probe.wrong_answer: A two-party system, with Congress and BJP.

root_belief: Biggest parties represent the entire system

subject: social
statement: A two-party system means only two parties are allowed to contest elections.
why: Students read the name literally as a legal limit.
fix: In a two-party system, many parties may contest but only two have a real chance of winning, as in the USA and UK.

probe.question: Can a third party contest elections in the USA?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only two parties are allowed by law.

root_belief: Party system is set by law

subject: social
statement: A party becomes a national party by contesting elections in many states.
why: Students think spread of candidates is enough, ignoring votes or seats.
fix: A party must win at least 6% votes in Lok Sabha or Assembly elections in four states and win at least four Lok Sabha seats, or win 2% seats from at least three states.

probe.question: A party contests in 15 states but wins few votes. Is it a national party?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it contests in many states.

root_belief: Contesting widely gives national status

subject: social
statement: The Election Commission gives state party status to any party that wins 6% of votes anywhere.
why: Students recall '6%' but forget the seat condition and the state in which it is earned.
fix: A state party must secure at least 6% of votes in an Assembly election in that state and also win at least two seats.

probe.question: A party gets 7% votes in a state but wins no seats. Is it a state party?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it crossed 6% of votes.

root_belief: One vote percentage alone decides status

subject: social
statement: Internal democracy is unnecessary because voters already choose leaders in elections.
why: Students think public elections make a party's own working democratic.
fix: Parties often lack open membership registers, regular organisational elections and independent decisions; leaders hold power, so reforms such as mandatory internal elections are recommended.

probe.question: Why should parties hold internal elections?
probe.wrong_answer: No need, since the public already elects them.

root_belief: Public elections make parties internally democratic

subject: social
statement: A one-party system is democratic as long as the single party wins elections.
why: Students equate winning elections with democracy.
fix: Democracy needs free choice and competition; in a one-party system, as in China, voters cannot choose among parties, so it is not a good democratic option.

probe.question: Is a country with only one party and regular elections democratic?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because elections are held and the party wins.

root_belief: Elections alone make a system democratic

topic: Gender, religion and caste in politics
subject: social
statement: The sexual division of labour is a natural biological necessity.
why: Students confuse social roles with biological traits.
fix: It is a social construct where domestic work is assigned to women and public work to men, not a biological requirement.

probe.question: Why do women do most of the housework?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they are naturally better at it.

root_belief: Social norms are natural laws

topic: Gender, religion and caste in politics
subject: social
statement: Women have 33% reservation in the Lok Sabha.
why: Students confuse local government reservation with national parliament reservation.
fix: Reservation for women exists in local bodies (Panchayats/Municipalities), but not yet in the Lok Sabha or State Assemblies.

probe.question: Is there reservation for women in the Indian Parliament?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, 33 percent.

root_belief: Rules apply uniformly across all levels

topic: Gender, religion and caste in politics
subject: social
statement: Communalism is simply being religious.
why: Students equate personal faith with political ideology.
fix: Communalism is the belief that followers of a particular religion must belong to one community and their interests are fundamentally opposed to others.

probe.question: What is communalism?
probe.wrong_answer: It means being very religious and following all rituals.

root_belief: A word means its everyday meaning

topic: Gender, religion and caste in politics
subject: social
statement: A secular state must be anti-religious.
why: Students confuse the Western model of separation with the Indian model of equal respect.
fix: The Indian secular state does not separate religion and state entirely but ensures equal distance and respect for all religions.

probe.question: Does a secular state ban religious symbols?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it must be neutral by removing all religion.

root_belief: Neutrality requires total absence

topic: Gender, religion and caste in politics
subject: social
statement: Caste in politics always leads to negative outcomes.
why: Students over-focus on caste-based violence and ignore political representation.
fix: Caste in politics can also give marginalized groups a voice and power, leading to more inclusive decision-making.

probe.question: Is caste in politics always bad?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it only causes division and conflict.

root_belief: One event has one single cause

topic: Gender, religion and caste in politics
subject: social
statement: Women's representation in politics is high in India because women vote in large numbers.
why: Students equate high voter turnout with holding office, so they conflate participation as voters with representation as elected members.
fix: Women's turnout is now close to men's, but women are still few among elected members: about 14% of Lok Sabha members and under 5% in many state assemblies.

probe.question: Women vote in large numbers in India. Does this mean women are well represented in the Lok Sabha?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because many women vote, they are well represented in Parliament.

root_belief: Voting participation equals representation in elected bodies
source_hint: NCERT Democratic Politics II, Ch. 4 and classroom assessment

topic: Gender, religion and caste in politics
subject: social
statement: Gender division means only that boys and girls are biologically different.
why: Students use 'gender' and 'sex' interchangeably and miss that gender division is a social hierarchy of roles and status.
fix: Gender division is a social arrangement based on stereotyped roles, not biology. It shows up in unequal literacy, wages and sex ratio, and in the belief that public life is for men.

probe.question: What does gender division mean?
probe.wrong_answer: It means the natural physical differences between men and women.

root_belief: Gender is the same as biological sex
source_hint: Research on students' gender-sex concept confusion; NCERT Ch. 4

topic: Gender, religion and caste in politics
subject: social
statement: Panchayats and municipalities have no reservation for women; reservation exists only in Parliament.
why: Students know reservation as a debated Parliament issue and miss that local bodies already have it.
fix: Since 1992-93 amendments, one-third of seats in rural panchayats and urban municipalities are reserved for women. Reservation for Parliament and state assemblies was a pending demand then.

probe.question: Where in India are one-third of seats reserved for women in elected bodies?
probe.wrong_answer: Only in the Lok Sabha; local bodies have none.

root_belief: Reservation applies only at the national level

topic: Gender, religion and caste in politics
subject: social
statement: Communalism is a problem only of the majority religious community.
why: Students link communalism with riots by the majority and miss that any community can follow communal politics.
fix: Communalism is the idea that religion is the basis of social community and political interests. Any religious group, majority or minority, can practise it.

probe.question: Can a minority community's leaders also practise communal politics?
probe.wrong_answer: No, communalism is only done by the majority community.

root_belief: Communalism belongs to one kind of group
source_hint: NCERT Ch. 4 on communalism in various forms

topic: Gender, religion and caste in politics
subject: social
statement: A secular state has an official religion chosen by the majority.
why: Students mix democracy as majority rule with secularism and assume the majority religion becomes the state religion.
fix: India has no official religion. The Constitution gives no special status to any religion and protects freedom to profess, practise and propagate any faith.

probe.question: Which religion is the official religion of India since most people follow it?
probe.wrong_answer: Hinduism, because the majority follows it, is the state religion.

root_belief: Majority rule means majority religion governs the state

topic: Gender, religion and caste in politics
subject: social
statement: The caste system has disappeared from India because it is now illegal.
why: Students think that laws and urbanisation have ended caste in practice.
fix: Caste discrimination is banned and economic change has weakened some old practices. But caste identity still shapes marriage, jobs and politics, and inequalities remain.

probe.question: Does caste still matter in India after laws banned caste discrimination?
probe.wrong_answer: No, caste has completely vanished because the law made it illegal.

root_belief: A law banning a practice ends it
source_hint: NCERT Ch. 4 on caste inequalities today

topic: Gender, religion and caste in politics
subject: social
statement: Elections in India are decided only by caste and a candidate wins if their caste has most voters.
why: Students see caste mentioned in electoral politics and turn it into the only cause of results.
fix: Parties consider caste composition, but voters also weigh party, performance, leaders and issues. Voters of one caste are not all united, and sitting governments often lose.

probe.question: Why does a party win in a constituency where one caste has the most voters?
probe.wrong_answer: Only because that caste has the most voters, so its candidate always wins.

root_belief: One social factor alone decides election outcomes

topic: Factors of production: the story of a village
subject: social
statement: Land can be increased by clearing more forests for farming indefinitely.
why: Students confuse local land expansion with the economic concept of fixed land supply.
fix: Land is a fixed natural resource; while we can convert forest to farm, the total land area available for cultivation is limited.

probe.question: If a village needs more food, can they just keep adding more land forever?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they can always clear more forest or reclaim land.

root_belief: resources are infinite

topic: Factors of production: the story of a village
subject: social
statement: Money used to buy seeds is fixed capital because it stays in the business.
why: Students confuse the 'permanence' of the business with the 'nature' of the asset.
fix: Fixed capital (like machines) is used over many years, while working capital (like seeds/money) is consumed in one production cycle.

probe.question: Is the money spent on raw materials considered fixed capital?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is invested in the farm.

root_belief: all business investment is the same

topic: Factors of production: the story of a village
subject: social
statement: The Green Revolution only helped farmers by increasing the total land area.
why: Students associate 'revolution' with physical expansion rather than technological intensification.
fix: The Green Revolution increased productivity per hectare using HYV seeds, fertilizers, and irrigation, not by increasing land area.

probe.question: How did the Green Revolution primarily increase production?
probe.wrong_answer: By acquiring more land for the village.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

topic: Factors of production: the story of a village
subject: social
statement: Human capital is just the number of people working in a field.
why: Students confuse 'labour' (quantity) with 'human capital' (quality/skill).
fix: Human capital refers to the knowledge, skills, and health of the people, which makes them more productive.

probe.question: What is human capital?
probe.wrong_answer: The total number of laborers available in the village.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

topic: Factors of production: the story of a village
subject: social
statement: Labour means only skilled or educated workers, so farm labourers who do manual work are not labour.
why: Students link 'labour' with trained jobs and overlook that every person who works in production counts.
fix: Labour is the effort of workers, skilled or unskilled, educated or not. Farm labourers, farmers and family members who work are all labour.

probe.question: Is a landless farm labourer who weeds fields for daily wages part of labour as a factor of production?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because he has no skills or education, so he is not counted as labour.

root_belief: Labour means only skilled, trained workers
source_hint: classroom error analysis of NCERT Class 9 Economics responses

topic: Factors of production: the story of a village
subject: social
statement: Land is a fixed resource, so its output cannot be increased at all.
why: Students mix up fixed area with fixed production and ignore multiple cropping and better methods.
fix: The area of land is fixed, but production from the same land can rise through multiple cropping, irrigation and modern farming methods.

probe.question: Can a farmer with 1 hectare of land get more produce from it over the years?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because land is fixed, so the produce from it also stays the same.

root_belief: Fixed land area means fixed production
source_hint: teacher reports and NCERT chapter exercises

topic: Factors of production: the story of a village
subject: social
statement: Tools and machines are working capital because farmers use them every day.
why: Students think frequent use means the item is used up, confusing use with being consumed in one production cycle.
fix: Tools, machines and buildings last many production cycles, so they are fixed capital. Working capital (raw materials, cash) is used up in production.

probe.question: Is a tractor fixed capital or working capital for a farmer who uses it daily?
probe.wrong_answer: Working capital, because it is used every single day in the farm.

root_belief: Daily use makes capital working capital
source_hint: classroom error analysis of NCERT Class 9 Economics responses

topic: Factors of production: the story of a village
subject: social
statement: Capital means only money, so tools and machines are not capital.
why: The everyday word 'capital' suggests cash, hiding that physical items are also capital.
fix: Physical capital includes tools, machines, buildings, and raw materials plus money in hand. Capital is what is needed to produce goods.

probe.question: Is the pumpset a farmer buys for irrigation a part of capital?
probe.wrong_answer: No, a pumpset is a machine, not money, so it is not capital.

root_belief: Capital means only money in hand
source_hint: economics education research on everyday vs technical meanings of capital

topic: Factors of production: the story of a village
subject: social
statement: Multiple cropping means growing many different crops together on the same field at the same time.
why: The word 'multiple' is read as mixed crops rather than successive crops across the year.
fix: Multiple cropping means growing more than one crop on the same land in a year, one after another, such as potato after jowar and bajra.

probe.question: What is multiple cropping?
probe.wrong_answer: Growing several crops mixed together in the field in the same season.

root_belief: Multiple means mixed together, not successive in year
source_hint: teacher reports from NCERT Class 9 classroom discussions

topic: Factors of production: the story of a village
subject: social
statement: Green Revolution seeds work well with no extra water or inputs, so farmers need no extra capital.
why: Students hear 'high yielding' and assume the seed alone does the work.
fix: HYV seeds need plenty of water, chemical fertilisers and pesticides to give high yields, so farmers need more working capital.

probe.question: Why did small farmers struggle to use HYV seeds during the Green Revolution?
probe.wrong_answer: They did not struggle, because HYV seeds grow on their own without extra inputs.

root_belief: Improved seeds alone raise yield without inputs
source_hint: NCERT chapter text and classroom discussion

topic: Factors of production: the story of a village
subject: social
statement: Human capital is gained only by going to school, not by health or training.
why: Students link knowledge only with formal schooling and ignore health and skills.
fix: Human capital is the stock of skill and good health of people. Education, training and healthcare all build it up.

probe.question: How can a farm worker add to his human capital?
probe.wrong_answer: Only by attending a formal school and getting a degree.

root_belief: Human capital comes only from formal schooling
source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Economics exercises and teacher reports

topic: Factors of production: the story of a village
subject: social
statement: Small scale manufacturing in a village is done in big factories with many hired workers.
why: Students picture manufacturing as large industry and overlook household production.
fix: Village manufacturing is on a small scale, using simple methods, mostly with family labour at home or in the fields, with few hired workers.

probe.question: Where is manufacturing like making baskets or sweets typically done in a village?
probe.wrong_answer: In big factories with many hired workers and large machines.

root_belief: Manufacturing always happens in big factories
source_hint: classroom error analysis of NCERT Class 9 Economics responses

subject: social
statement: Spending on education is an expense, not an investment.
why: Students confuse personal household spending with economic capital formation.
fix: Investment in education yields future returns through higher productivity and earnings, similar to investing in machinery.

probe.question: Why is education considered an investment?
probe.wrong_answer: It is just a cost parents pay for school fees.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: Disguised unemployment means people are hiding from work.
why: The word 'disguised' is interpreted literally as 'hidden' or 'secret'.
fix: It refers to a situation where more people are working than required, so removing some would not reduce total output.

probe.question: What is disguised unemployment?
probe.wrong_answer: When people pretend to be unemployed to get government benefits.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: Primary sector only includes farming and crop production.
why: Textbooks often use farming as the primary example, leading to overgeneralization.
fix: The primary sector includes all extraction of natural resources, such as fishing, mining, and forestry, not just farming.

probe.question: Which of these is a primary activity?
probe.wrong_answer: Only farming.

root_belief: one example represents the whole category

subject: social
statement: Any work done at home is a non-market activity.
why: Students assume all domestic work is non-market, ignoring that some home-based work produces goods for sale.
fix: Non-market activities are those for self-consumption; if goods produced at home are sold in the market, they are market activities.

probe.question: Is weaving baskets at home for sale a market activity?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is done at home.

root_belief: location defines the nature of the activity

subject: social
statement: Health care only means going to a doctor when you are ill, so it does not affect a person's work or the country's growth.
why: Students link health only with treatment of disease and not with the ability to work and contribute to the economy.
fix: A healthy person is more efficient and can work longer and better. Good health, along with education, adds to a country's human capital and growth.

probe.question: Why does a government spend money on hospitals and public health in a country's economic development?
probe.wrong_answer: Only to cure sick people; it has nothing to do with the economy or production.

root_belief: Health matters only for individual illness, not economic output

subject: social
statement: Education increases only the educated person's own salary and does not benefit society.
why: Students see schooling as a personal route to a job and ignore its wider social effects.
fix: Education raises productivity and also gives social benefits such as better awareness, innovation, and growth of the whole economy, along with the individual's income.

probe.question: Who benefits when a country has a larger number of educated people?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the educated people themselves, through higher pay; society gains nothing.

root_belief: Benefits of education are purely private

subject: social
statement: The secondary sector is the sector that comes second in importance, not the one that processes raw materials.
why: Students read 'secondary' as ranking importance rather than the order of production.
fix: The secondary sector (manufacturing) turns raw materials from the primary sector into finished goods, e.g. cotton into cloth. Primary, secondary and tertiary show the stage of production, not importance.

probe.question: Why is the cloth-making factory called part of the secondary sector?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it is the second most important sector after agriculture.

root_belief: Sector names show importance rank

subject: social
statement: Tertiary sector workers like teachers, doctors and bankers do not produce anything, so they are not part of economic activity.
why: Students think only physical goods count as production.
fix: Tertiary sector activities provide services that help the primary and secondary sectors and are economic activities because they add value and earn income.

probe.question: Is a bank clerk's work an economic activity?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because a clerk does not make any goods.

root_belief: Only goods production counts as economic activity

subject: social
statement: Market activities are only those done in a market place where goods are bought and sold.
why: Students take 'market' literally as a physical place.
fix: Market activities are any activities done for pay or profit, including salaried jobs in offices, schools, hospitals or factories, not only shop-based trading.

probe.question: Is a teacher in a private school doing a market activity?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because a school is not a market place.

root_belief: Market activity means a physical market place

subject: social
statement: A housewife's work is non-market so it has no economic value at all.
why: Students equate lack of pay with lack of value or of being an economic activity.
fix: Non-market activities are done for self-consumption and not for pay; they are still valuable work, though not counted as market output. Housework is not paid but still has worth.

probe.question: Does the cooking and cleaning done by a homemaker have value to the family?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because she is not paid, so it is of no value.

root_belief: Unpaid work has no value

subject: social
statement: Seasonal unemployment happens only in farming because of bad weather like drought.
why: Students link 'seasonal' with weather and with farmers only.
fix: Seasonal unemployment is when people cannot find work in some months of the year because the work is not available then; it is common in agriculture but also in industries like ice-cream, umbrella or tourism work.

probe.question: An ice-cream factory worker has no job in winter months. What kind of unemployment is it?
probe.wrong_answer: Not seasonal, since seasonal unemployment is only for farmers.

root_belief: Seasonal unemployment is only for farmers

subject: social
statement: In disguised unemployment all the people in the family are without any work and earn nothing.
why: Students confuse partial or surplus work with complete joblessness.
fix: In disguised unemployment more people are working than needed, so some appear employed but add nothing to output; removing them does not reduce production.

probe.question: Five members work on a farm needing three. If two leave, what happens to output?
probe.wrong_answer: Output falls a lot, since all five were needed and busy.

root_belief: Visible work means productive contribution

subject: social
concept: Poverty Line is a fixed monetary value
statement: The poverty line is the same amount of money for every person in India.
why: Students ignore that the poverty line varies by rural/urban areas and states due to cost of living.
fix: The poverty line is a minimum threshold that varies based on regional price differences and rural-urban consumption needs.

probe.question: If the poverty line is Rs 816 in rural areas, is it the same in urban areas?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a national fixed standard.

root_belief: a single rule applies to all contexts

subject: social
concept: Poverty is only lack of money
statement: Poverty is only about not having enough money to buy food.
why: Students equate poverty with physical hunger, ignoring social exclusion and illiteracy.
fix: Poverty includes social exclusion, lack of access to healthcare, clean water, and education, not just income.

probe.question: Can a person with money still be considered poor?
probe.wrong_answer: No, if they have money they are not poor.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
source_hint: HBCSE research on social science concepts

subject: social
concept: Poverty is solely due to laziness
statement: People are poor because they do not work hard enough.
why: Students overemphasize individual agency while ignoring structural barriers like caste and historical exploitation.
fix: Poverty is often the result of structural factors like lack of land, low job opportunities, and historical social discrimination.

probe.question: Why are some communities consistently poorer than others?
probe.wrong_answer: They lack the motivation to work hard.

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: social
statement: MGNREGA guarantees a permanent job for everyone for their whole life.
why: Students confuse the 'right to work' with permanent employment.
fix: MGNREGA provides 100 days of guaranteed wage employment to rural households, not permanent jobs.

probe.question: Does MGNREGA provide a permanent government job?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a permanent job scheme.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: Poverty is measured only by income, so literacy, health and nutrition do not count as indicators.
why: Students equate poverty with low earnings and overlook the social indicators in the syllabus.
fix: Poverty indicators include income and consumption, but also illiteracy, malnutrition, poor health, lack of job opportunities, and lack of access to safe drinking water and sanitation.

probe.question: Which of these is used as an indicator of poverty: a child's malnutrition level, or only the family's monthly income?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the family's monthly income, because malnutrition is a health matter and not poverty.

root_belief: Poverty means income alone, not wider deprivation
source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Economics, Poverty as a Challenge

subject: social
statement: The poverty line is set by each village or family according to what they feel they need.
why: Students think the line is a personal or local opinion rather than an official estimate.
fix: The poverty line is estimated by the government (Planning Commission, now NITI Aayog, using NSSO survey data) from the money needed for a minimum calorie intake and other basic needs, with separate lines for rural and urban areas.

probe.question: Who estimates the poverty line in India?
probe.wrong_answer: Each village decides it for itself based on what its families feel they need.

root_belief: Poverty line is decided locally or personally
source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Economics, Poverty as a Challenge

subject: social
statement: The poverty line is based on a 2400 calorie requirement in both villages and cities.
why: Students memorise one calorie figure and apply it everywhere, overlooking that needs differ.
fix: The accepted norm is 2400 calories per person per day in rural areas and 2100 in urban areas, because rural people do more physical work.

probe.question: What daily calorie requirement is used for the urban poverty line?
probe.wrong_answer: 2400 calories, the same as the rural line.

root_belief: One calorie norm applies to all areas
source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Economics, Poverty as a Challenge

subject: social
statement: Poverty in India began only after independence because of government failure.
why: Students think of poverty as a recent political problem, ignoring colonial history.
fix: Widespread poverty has historical roots in British colonial rule, which decayed handicrafts and textiles, and in low growth rates and high population growth in the decades after.

probe.question: Which period's policies contributed to the historical roots of India's poverty?
probe.wrong_answer: Poverty began only after 1947 as a result of independent India's governments.

root_belief: Poverty is a recent problem with no colonial roots
source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Economics, Poverty as a Challenge

subject: social
statement: Rapid population growth is the only reason India has poverty.
why: Students pick up the 'too many people' explanation and treat it as the sole cause.
fix: Poverty has many causes: unequal land and income distribution, unemployment, low agricultural productivity, social customs and expensive ceremonies, illiteracy, and indebtedness, besides population growth.

probe.question: Why do many families in India remain poor?
probe.wrong_answer: Only because the population is too large.

root_belief: One cause alone explains poverty
source_hint: Research on student single-cause reasoning in social science; NCERT

subject: social
statement: Poverty affects all castes and households equally.
why: Students overgeneralise and ignore differences in who is more likely to be poor.
fix: Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe households, casual labourers in urban areas and agricultural labourers in rural areas are the most vulnerable; women, children and the elderly also suffer more within poor families.

probe.question: Which group is more likely to be poor: agricultural labourer households or all groups equally?
probe.wrong_answer: All groups are equally likely to be poor.

root_belief: Poverty hits every social group equally
source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Economics, Poverty as a Challenge

subject: social
statement: Poverty exists only in rural India, and cities have no poor people.
why: Students picture poverty as village landlessness and imagine cities as prosperous.
fix: Poverty exists in both rural and urban India; urban poor include casual labourers and slum dwellers, and the poverty line is estimated for both.

probe.question: Do poor people live in Indian cities too?
probe.wrong_answer: No, poverty is found only in villages.

root_belief: Poverty is a village-only phenomenon
source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Economics, Poverty as a Challenge

subject: social
statement: The Public Distribution System gives free food to everyone in India.
why: Students mix up PDS and free-meal schemes, and ignore the subsidised pricing and targeting.
fix: PDS supplies foodgrains and other items at subsidised prices through ration shops, with the poor targeted through ration cards; it is not free for all.

probe.question: How do families get food under the PDS?
probe.wrong_answer: Everyone receives it completely free from ration shops.

root_belief: Government schemes give everything free to all
source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Economics, Poverty as a Challenge

subject: social
statement: Food security means that every village must produce all the food it consumes.
why: Students confuse local self-sufficiency with national food security.
fix: Food security is achieved when food is available through production, imports, and efficient distribution, not just local production.

probe.question: If a region grows only cotton, is it food insecure?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it does not grow its own food.

root_belief: local production is the only source of supply

subject: social
statement: If food is available in the market, everyone is food secure.
why: Students equate market availability with individual access.
fix: Access requires the ability to purchase food; even if food is available, the poor may lack the money to buy it.

probe.question: Why do people starve when shops are full of grain?
probe.wrong_answer: Because there is no food available in the country.

root_belief: availability equals access

subject: social
statement: Buffer stocks are kept to make profit by selling grain when prices rise.
why: Students apply commercial business logic to government welfare functions.
fix: Buffer stocks are maintained by the FCI to ensure food availability during shortages and to stabilize prices for the poor.

probe.question: Why does the government store grain?
probe.wrong_answer: To sell it at high prices later for profit.

root_belief: all economic activity aims for profit

subject: social
statement: Ration shops provide free food to everyone in the country.
why: Students conflate the existence of a system with universal free access.
fix: Ration shops provide food at subsidized prices, and they are targeted primarily at families below the poverty line.

probe.question: Who can buy from a ration shop?
probe.wrong_answer: Anyone who wants free food.

root_belief: government services are always free for all

subject: social
statement: If India produces record foodgrains, no one in the country can be food insecure.
why: Students equate total production with food security and ignore distribution and purchasing power.
fix: Food security needs availability, access and affordability together; even with high production, poor households may not be able to buy enough food.

probe.question: India has record wheat and rice production this year. Can some people still go hungry? Explain.
probe.wrong_answer: No, because when production is high everyone gets enough food.

root_belief: Total production alone guarantees food security
source_hint: Class 9 NCERT Economics, Ch. 4 and teacher observation

subject: social
statement: India depends mainly on imported food grains to feed its people.
why: Students link food shortage and food security with imports, and recall past episodes like the 1960s wheat imports.
fix: India is self-sufficient in foodgrains after the Green Revolution, mainly wheat and rice; it feeds its people from its own production and holds buffer stocks.

probe.question: Where does most of the grain for India's ration shops come from?
probe.wrong_answer: It is mostly imported from other countries.

root_belief: India still relies on foreign grain

subject: social
statement: The poor are food insecure only because there is not enough food in the country.
why: Students think hunger comes from scarcity and overlook lack of income and employment.
fix: Poor people go hungry mainly because they lack the money to buy food (low purchasing power), even when food is available.

probe.question: Why can a poor landless labourer be hungry even when godowns are full?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the country does not have enough food.

root_belief: Hunger always comes from food scarcity
source_hint: Amartya Sen entitlement approach in NCERT discussion

subject: social
statement: The Food Corporation of India sells ration to people directly in the villages.
why: Students confuse FCI with ration shops, since both are connected to PDS.
fix: FCI buys wheat and rice from farmers at minimum support price and stores it; ration shops (fair price shops) sell to consumers.

probe.question: Who buys wheat from farmers at MSP and who sells it to card-holders?
probe.wrong_answer: FCI does both, buying from farmers and selling to consumers at its shops.

root_belief: FCI and ration shops are the same body

subject: social
statement: The government fixes minimum support price after the harvest, so it can lower it when there is a surplus.
why: Students mix up MSP with market price and think it changes with supply.
fix: MSP is announced by the government before the sowing season to encourage farmers to grow crops and ensure them a fair price.

probe.question: When is the minimum support price announced and why?
probe.wrong_answer: After harvest, to match the market price when there is a surplus.

root_belief: MSP is the same as market price

subject: social
statement: Every household with a ration card gets food at the same price.
why: Students think the PDS is uniform and overlook the categories of cards.
fix: Under targeted PDS, cards are issued as Antyodaya, BPL and APL, and each category gets a different quantity at a different price; poorer families pay less.

probe.question: Does a BPL family pay the same price for ration as an APL family?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all card-holders pay the same price at the ration shop.

root_belief: All ration cards carry identical benefits

subject: social
statement: A famine means many people have died of starvation, so deaths are needed to call it a famine.
why: Students see starvation deaths as the definition of famine, though deaths are a result.
fix: Famine is widespread hunger because of a lack of food or purchasing power, shown by rising food prices and people migrating; deaths are the extreme result, not the definition.

probe.question: Can a region be called famine-hit before anyone has died of starvation?
probe.wrong_answer: No, a famine only exists once many people have died.

root_belief: Famine is defined by deaths
source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Economics Ch. 4; Bengal famine 1943 discussion

subject: social
statement: A famine is caused only by drought or crop failure.
why: Students link famine with a natural disaster, forgetting that the Bengal famine of 1943 happened without a major fall in food availability.
fix: Famines also arise from lack of access: when people lose income or prices rise sharply, they cannot buy food even when stocks exist.

probe.question: Name the only cause of a famine such as the Bengal famine.
probe.wrong_answer: A drought that destroyed the crops.

root_belief: Natural disaster is the only cause of famine
source_hint: Amartya Sen's work on the Bengal famine; NCERT Class 9

subject: social
statement: A higher per capita income means everyone in the country is equally rich.
why: Students confuse the mathematical average with an equal distribution of wealth.
fix: Per capita income is an average; it does not show how income is distributed among the rich and the poor.

probe.question: If Country A has a higher average income than Country B, is every citizen in A richer than in B?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the average is higher.

root_belief: Averages represent the status of every individual

subject: social
statement: Development is only about earning more money.
why: Students equate economic growth with the broader concept of human development.
fix: Development includes non-material goals like freedom, security, equal treatment, and a clean environment.

probe.question: Which is a better measure of development: salary or freedom and health?
probe.wrong_answer: Salary, because money buys everything.

root_belief: Money is the sole indicator of success

subject: social
statement: Sustainability means we should stop using all natural resources.
why: Students interpret 'sustainability' as 'total preservation' rather than 'judicious use'.
fix: Sustainability means using resources in a way that meets current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

probe.question: Is sustainable development about stopping all mining?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, we must stop using resources to save them.

root_belief: Conservation means zero consumption

subject: social
statement: Literacy rate is the percentage of people who can write their name.
why: Students confuse basic literacy with functional literacy.
fix: Literacy rate measures the proportion of the 7-year-old and above population that can read and write with understanding in any language.

probe.question: Who is counted as literate?
probe.wrong_answer: Anyone who can sign their name.

root_belief: A word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: Per capita income is the total income earned by the whole country.
why: Students confuse 'per capita' with the national total and ignore that it is divided by population.
fix: Per capita income is the country's total income divided by its total population, so it is the average income per person.

probe.question: A country earns a total of Rs 10,00,000 crore and has 100 crore people. What is its per capita income?
probe.wrong_answer: Rs 10,00,000 crore, because per capita income is the total income of the country.

root_belief: per capita means total, not average per person

subject: social
statement: A country with a larger population always has a higher per capita income.
why: Students link a big population with a big economy and forget that population is the divisor.
fix: For the same total income, a larger population gives a lower per capita income because the income is shared among more people.

probe.question: Two countries have the same total income, but country A has twice the population of country B. Which has the higher per capita income?
probe.wrong_answer: Country A, because more people means more income per person.

root_belief: more people always means more income per person

subject: social
statement: HDI is calculated only from a country's income and wealth.
why: Students carry over the idea of income as the only measure of development and ignore the other HDI components.
fix: HDI combines three parts: health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and standard of living (per capita income).

probe.question: Name the components used to calculate the Human Development Index.
probe.wrong_answer: Only GDP and per capita income, since HDI measures how rich a country is.

root_belief: HDI is just another income measure

subject: social
statement: The HDI rank is given by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), and the World Bank prepares it.
why: Students mix up the UNDP, which publishes the Human Development Report, with the World Bank, which classifies countries by income.
fix: The UNDP publishes the Human Development Report and HDI rankings. The World Bank classifies countries by income as rich or low-income.

probe.question: Which organisation publishes the Human Development Report with HDI rankings?
probe.wrong_answer: The World Bank publishes the Human Development Report.

root_belief: all international development bodies do the same work

subject: social
statement: Groundwater and fossil fuels are renewable resources that will never run out.
why: Students see water and fuel as always available and mix up renewable and non-renewable resources.
fix: Groundwater is used faster than it is replenished in many places, and fossil fuels take millions of years to form, so overuse depletes them.

probe.question: Why do experts warn about falling groundwater levels in Punjab and Haryana?
probe.wrong_answer: They need not worry, because groundwater is renewable and always refills itself however much is used.

root_belief: renewable means unlimited whatever the rate of use

subject: social
statement: A country with a high per capita income must also have good health and education.
why: Students assume income automatically buys good health and schooling for everyone.
fix: Income does not buy everything. Kerala has a lower per capita income than Haryana but a better literacy rate and a lower infant mortality rate. Public facilities like schools and health centres matter.

probe.question: Haryana has a higher per capita income than Kerala. Which state has the better literacy rate and lower IMR?
probe.wrong_answer: Haryana, since its higher income gives better schools and hospitals.

root_belief: money alone guarantees health and education

subject: social
statement: If the average income of a country is high, then every person in it earns near that average.
why: Students read an average as a typical value and miss that a few very rich people can pull it up.
fix: An average hides differences. Some people may earn far more and others far less than the average, so look at the distribution too.

probe.question: Five people earn Rs 1,000 each and one earns Rs 25,000. The average is Rs 5,000. Is it a good picture of what most of them earn?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, most people in the group earn about Rs 5,000.

root_belief: an average represents each individual's value

subject: social
statement: Infant Mortality Rate is the number of infants who die out of every 100 people in the country.
why: Students mix up the base for IMR with percentages of the whole population.
fix: IMR is the number of children who die before the age of one year, per 1000 live births in that year.

probe.question: What does an IMR of 30 mean?
probe.wrong_answer: Thirty out of every hundred people in the country die in infancy.

root_belief: rates are always per hundred of the whole population

subject: social
statement: The primary sector is only about farming.
why: Students associate primary sector exclusively with agriculture due to common textbook examples.
fix: The primary sector includes all activities that use natural resources, such as mining, fishing, and forestry, not just agriculture.

probe.question: Is mining a primary sector activity?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is industrial.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: GDP is the sum of all goods produced in a country.
why: Students ignore the 'final' qualifier and double-count intermediate goods.
fix: GDP only counts the value of final goods and services to avoid double-counting the value of intermediate goods already included.

probe.question: If a farmer sells wheat to a miller for 10 rupees and the miller sells flour for 15, what is added to GDP?
probe.wrong_answer: 25 rupees

root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

subject: social
statement: Public sector industries are always loss-making.
why: Students confuse the motive of social welfare with financial incompetence.
fix: The public sector aims for social welfare and public interest, which may not always prioritize profit, but it does not mean they are inherently loss-making.

probe.question: Why does the government run the railway sector?
probe.wrong_answer: Because private companies cannot make a profit.

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: social
statement: MGNREGA provides employment to everyone in the city.
why: Students overgeneralize the scope of rural employment schemes.
fix: MGNREGA is specifically designed for rural areas to provide 100 days of guaranteed wage employment to households whose members volunteer to do unskilled manual work.

probe.question: Does MGNREGA apply to a software engineer in Delhi?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a government job guarantee.

root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

subject: social
statement: Any activity that uses machines is secondary sector, even if it only provides a service.
why: Students link the secondary sector with machines and factories, not with the transformation of natural products into other goods.
fix: The secondary sector converts natural products into other goods through manufacturing. Services such as transport, banking and teaching belong to the tertiary sector even if machines are used.

probe.question: A bank uses computers and ATMs to serve customers. Which sector does banking belong to?
probe.wrong_answer: Secondary sector, because it uses machines.

root_belief: Using machines defines the secondary sector

subject: social
statement: The tertiary sector does not produce anything, so it adds nothing to GDP.
why: Students think only visible goods count as production and that services are not real output.
fix: The tertiary sector produces services, which have value and are counted in GDP. It supports the primary and secondary sectors and is now the largest contributor to India's GDP.

probe.question: Does the value of a teacher's or doctor's services get counted in GDP?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because they do not produce goods.

root_belief: Only physical goods count as production

subject: social
statement: To find GDP we should add the value of every good at each stage, including intermediate goods.
why: Students think more counting means a more accurate total, so they add flour, bread and wheat separately.
fix: Only the value of final goods and services is counted. Intermediate goods are already included in the final good's value, so adding them would double count.

probe.question: A farmer sells wheat for Rs 20 to a mill, the mill sells flour for Rs 30 to a baker, and the baker sells bread for Rs 50. What value is added to GDP?
probe.wrong_answer: Rs 100, by adding 20, 30 and 50.

root_belief: Counting every transaction gives accurate total

subject: social
statement: All unorganised sector workers are poor and all organised sector workers are rich.
why: Students equate sector type with income level rather than with registration and the terms of employment.
fix: Organised sector enterprises are registered and follow government rules, with regular work and benefits. Unorganised sector jobs are irregular and low-paid with no security. The distinction is about the terms of employment, not simply about how much someone earns.

probe.question: Is a skilled, well-paid private plumber who runs his own small shop part of the organised sector?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because he earns a lot of money.

root_belief: Sector type is decided by income level

subject: social
statement: Workers in the organised sector can never be removed from their jobs.
why: Students hear about job security and take it to mean permanent, unconditional employment.
fix: Organised sector workers have security of employment, meaning they cannot be fired without a valid reason and following rules. They can still be removed for valid cause or retrenched by following the law.

probe.question: Can a company in the organised sector ever remove a worker from the job?
probe.wrong_answer: No, organised sector jobs are permanent for life.

root_belief: Job security means employment can never end

subject: social
statement: The private sector is owned by the government but run by companies.
why: Students mix up who owns assets with who operates them.
fix: In the public sector the government owns most assets and provides services, such as Indian Railways. In the private sector ownership of assets and delivery of services is in the hands of private individuals or companies, such as Tata Steel.

probe.question: Who owns the assets of a private company like Tata Steel?
probe.wrong_answer: The government owns them and the company only runs them.

root_belief: Ownership and operation are the same thing

subject: social
statement: Under MGNREGA the government gives a job only if the worker has farm land.
why: Students link the scheme to rural farming and assume land is needed to join.
fix: Under MGNREGA 2005, any adult in a rural household who is willing to do unskilled manual work can ask for work and get up to 100 days of employment a year in rural areas. No land is required. If work is not given, an unemployment allowance is due.

probe.question: A landless rural labourer asks for work under MGNREGA. Is he eligible?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only people who own farm land can get work.

root_belief: Rural schemes serve only landowning farmers

subject: social
statement: The public sector exists mainly to earn profit for the government.
why: Students assume every enterprise is run to make profit, as private firms do.
fix: The government undertakes activities that private firms may not, such as roads, railways, irrigation, health and education, and provides basic facilities. Its main motive is public welfare and development, not profit.

probe.question: Why does the government run railways and hospitals at low prices in rural areas?
probe.wrong_answer: To earn as much profit as it can.

root_belief: All enterprises exist to make profit

subject: social
statement: Barter is efficient if you have enough goods to trade.
why: Students assume that having more goods automatically solves the problem of finding a buyer.
fix: Barter requires both parties to want exactly what the other has, which is rare and difficult to coordinate.

probe.question: Why is barter difficult even if you have many goods?
probe.wrong_answer: Because you just need to find someone who wants your goods.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: social
statement: Modern paper money has intrinsic value like gold or silver.
why: Students confuse the physical material of money with its legal status as a medium of exchange.
fix: Modern money has no intrinsic value; it is accepted because the government authorizes it as a medium of exchange.

probe.question: Why is a 500 rupee note valuable?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the paper is special or it represents gold in the bank.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: social
statement: Collateral is a fee paid to the bank for taking a loan.
why: Students confuse collateral with interest or processing charges.
fix: Collateral is an asset owned by the borrower that serves as a guarantee to the lender until the loan is repaid.

probe.question: What happens to collateral after the loan is repaid?
probe.wrong_answer: The bank keeps it as a service fee.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: social
statement: The RBI directly gives loans to small farmers and businesses.
why: Students conflate the regulatory role of the central bank with the retail role of commercial banks.
fix: The RBI supervises banks to ensure they follow rules, but it does not lend money to the public.

probe.question: Who should a farmer approach for a loan?
probe.wrong_answer: The Reserve Bank of India.

root_belief: one central authority does everything

subject: social
statement: Money is valuable only because it can be saved, not because people accept it in exchange.
why: Students focus on the visible act of keeping money and overlook its role as a medium of exchange.
fix: Money is valuable because everyone accepts it in payment for goods and services; this removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.

probe.question: Why do shopkeepers accept currency notes in return for goods?
probe.wrong_answer: Because notes can be saved in a purse or bank for a long time.

root_belief: Money's worth comes from storage, not acceptance

subject: social
statement: Any currency note or coin can be legally refused by a seller, since only the government accepts it.
why: Students confuse everyday willingness to accept money with its legal status.
fix: In India the Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes, and the law makes them legal tender, so no one can refuse payment in rupees for settling a transaction.

probe.question: Can a person legally refuse to accept rupees as payment for a debt in India?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, only the government is bound to accept rupee notes.

root_belief: Legal tender is just custom, not law

subject: social
statement: Cheques are money in the same way that currency notes are.
why: Students see cheques being used to pay for things and treat them as currency itself.
fix: A cheque is only an instruction to the bank to pay from a deposit; the money is the balance in the account, and a cheque payment is not legal tender.

probe.question: When you pay by cheque, what is actually being transferred?
probe.wrong_answer: The cheque itself is the money being handed over.

root_belief: Anything used for payment is itself money
source_hint: economics education research on money concepts

subject: social
statement: The bank keeps all deposited money in its vault until depositors withdraw it.
why: Students imagine a bank as a safe, not as a lender.
fix: Banks keep only a small part of deposits as cash for daily withdrawals and lend out most of it, earning more interest on loans than they pay on deposits.

probe.question: What do banks do with the money people deposit?
probe.wrong_answer: They store all of it safely until people take it back.

root_belief: Banks only store money, never lend it
source_hint: studies of student understanding of banking

subject: social
statement: Interest on a deposit and interest on a loan are the same rate, so the bank earns nothing.
why: Students think of interest as one fixed number rather than two different rates.
fix: Banks charge a higher interest rate on loans than they pay on deposits, and the difference is their main source of income.

probe.question: How do banks make a profit from deposits and loans?
probe.wrong_answer: They cannot make a profit as both rates are equal; they only charge service fees.

root_belief: Interest rates are single and uniform

subject: social
statement: The terms of credit are fixed by law, so every borrower gets the same interest rate and conditions.
why: Students assume formal rules make credit uniform for everyone.
fix: Terms of credit such as interest rate, collateral, documentation and repayment mode vary between lenders and borrowers; they are agreed, not identical for all.

probe.question: Two farmers borrow from different lenders. Will their interest rate and repayment terms be the same?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the law fixes one interest rate and repayment rule for everyone.

root_belief: Credit terms are uniform and fixed

subject: social
statement: Collateral is taken only from poor borrowers, and the lender keeps it even after the loan is repaid.
why: Students link collateral with suspicion of the borrower and with a penalty.
fix: Collateral, such as land or a house, is security the lender holds against non-payment; it is returned when the loan is fully repaid and sold only if the borrower defaults.

probe.question: A farmer repays his loan fully. What happens to the land papers he gave as collateral?
probe.wrong_answer: The bank keeps them because collateral belongs to the bank.

root_belief: Collateral is ownership transferred to the lender

subject: social
statement: Self Help Groups give loans only from outside funds, with no savings needed from members.
why: Students think of SHGs as charity or a government scheme, not a savings group.
fix: SHG members, usually women, pool small regular savings, and the group gives loans from this pool at reasonable interest, often later linked to banks.

probe.question: Where does the money for loans in a Self Help Group first come from?
probe.wrong_answer: From government grants, not from members' savings.

root_belief: SHG is a charity, not member savings

subject: social
statement: MNCs only produce goods in their home country.
why: Students assume a company's identity is tied strictly to its country of origin.
fix: MNCs set up production units in countries where labor is cheap and resources are available to maximize profit.

probe.question: Where does a US-based MNC produce its goods?
probe.wrong_answer: Only in the USA

root_belief: A brand's origin dictates its entire operational geography

subject: social
statement: Removing trade barriers always helps every local producer.
why: Students equate 'free trade' with 'fair trade' for everyone.
fix: Removing barriers allows cheaper imports, which can force small, less efficient local producers out of business.

probe.question: What happens to small toy makers when trade barriers are removed?
probe.wrong_answer: They sell more because of global competition

root_belief: Competition is always beneficial for all participants

subject: social
statement: The WTO is a democratic body where all countries have equal power.
why: Students assume international organizations function like national parliaments.
fix: The WTO is dominated by developed countries that often force developing nations to follow rules that favor the rich.

probe.question: Does the WTO treat all member countries equally?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a democratic global parliament

root_belief: International organizations are inherently neutral and fair

subject: social
statement: Globalisation is a natural process that cannot be changed by government policy.
why: Students view globalisation as a technological inevitability rather than a political choice.
fix: Globalisation is shaped by government policies; fair globalisation can be achieved through better labor laws and support for small producers.

probe.question: Can the government make globalisation fairer?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is a global market force beyond control

root_belief: Economic forces are laws of nature

subject: social
statement: An MNC owns and runs all its factories itself in every country.
why: Students see big brand names and assume direct ownership everywhere, missing partnerships and contracts.
fix: MNCs often set up production by buying local companies, partnering with them, or placing orders with small local producers who supply goods at low prices.

probe.question: A large foreign brand gets its garments made in India by small local factories under orders. Who owns those factories?
probe.wrong_answer: The MNC owns them.

root_belief: Companies must own everything they sell
source_hint: NCERT Class 10 Economics Ch.4 text and classroom discussion

subject: social
statement: MNCs set up factories in a country mainly to help that country's people get jobs.
why: Students link foreign investment with job creation and ignore the company's own profit motive.
fix: MNCs set up production where costs of labour and other inputs are low and markets are close, so as to earn more profit; jobs are a side effect.

probe.question: Why does an MNC choose to set up a factory in a particular region of India?
probe.wrong_answer: To provide employment to the people there.

root_belief: Companies invest mainly to help the host country

subject: social
statement: Production across countries means a product is made completely in one place and then shipped abroad.
why: Students think of trade as only exchange of finished goods and not of production spread in stages.
fix: Production is split into parts made in different countries, where each stage is done at the place with the lowest cost, and then assembled.

probe.question: A phone's design is in one country, parts in another and assembly in a third. What is this called?
probe.wrong_answer: Ordinary export of a finished good.

root_belief: Goods are produced wholly in one place

subject: social
statement: Foreign trade only means exporting goods from a country to other countries.
why: Students notice exports in news and forget imports are also part of trade.
fix: Foreign trade includes both exports and imports; it links markets of different countries and gives buyers more choice of goods.

probe.question: When Indian shops sell imported Chinese toys, does this show integration with foreign markets?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because trade means only selling Indian goods abroad.

root_belief: Trade means selling abroad only

subject: social
statement: Foreign trade gives benefits only to the producers, not to consumers.
why: Students think of trade as business activity and overlook what buyers gain.
fix: Foreign trade gives consumers more choice and often lower prices, while producers get a wider market to sell in.

probe.question: After imports of goods began, what changed for Indian consumers?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing changed for consumers; only producers gained.

root_belief: Trade only benefits sellers

subject: social
statement: Trade barriers like import tax were removed in India because the WTO forced the country to do so in 1947.
why: Students mix the dates and the agents of reform, joining WTO and liberalisation together.
fix: India removed many trade barriers from 1991 as part of its own liberalisation policy; a tax on imports is a trade barrier and quotas also limit imports.

probe.question: When did India begin removing many trade barriers like import tax and quotas?
probe.wrong_answer: In 1947, at the WTO's order.

root_belief: Trade reforms came from outside at independence

subject: social
statement: After liberalisation, Indian small producers all became bigger and richer through competition.
why: Students take the word competition as always leading to growth and ignore weaker firms.
fix: Competition has helped some Indian companies grow, but many small producers, such as in batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys and vegetable oil, had to shut down or lose jobs.

probe.question: What happened to many small Indian toy makers when cheap imports came in?
probe.wrong_answer: They all grew bigger and earned more.

root_belief: Competition benefits all producers equally

subject: social
statement: Fair globalisation means every country should open its markets the same amount.
why: Students equate fairness with identical treatment and ignore differences in the capacity of rich and poor countries.
fix: Fair globalisation creates opportunities for all and ensures benefits are shared better; rules should protect the weak, and developed countries should also cut their own trade barriers.

probe.question: What would make globalisation fair for developing countries?
probe.wrong_answer: Every country, rich or poor, opening its markets equally.

root_belief: Fairness means identical rules for all
