statement: A cylinder has no edges because it is round.
why: Students link edges only with straight lines.
fix: A cylinder has two curved edges where its flat circular faces meet the curved surface.

probe.question: How many edges does a cylinder have?

root_belief: an edge must be straight like a polygon's

subject: maths
concept: Net of a cube has six connected squares
statement: Any six squares joined together fold into a cube.
why: Students only check the count of squares.
fix: Only certain arrangements of six squares fold into a cube; there are 11 such nets. Some arrangements overlap.

probe.question: Six squares are in a 2 by 3 block. Will it fold into a cube?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes

root_belief: having the right parts means it works
source_hint: studies on students' spatial visualisation when folding nets of cubes

subject: maths
concept: A solid can have more than one net
statement: A cube has only one net, the cross-shaped one.
why: The textbook shows one standard net.
fix: A cube has 11 different nets.

probe.question: How many different nets can a cube have?

root_belief: the first example shown is the only one
source_hint: research on prototype thinking in geometry

subject: maths
concept: Net of a cylinder has two circles and a rectangle
statement: The net of a cylinder is two circles and a rectangle whose length can be any size.
why: Students do not link the rectangle to the circle.
fix: The rectangle's length must equal the circumference of the circle so the sides meet when rolled.

probe.question: A cylinder has circles of radius 7 cm. Can a rectangle 10 cm long be its curved surface?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, any length works

root_belief: parts of a figure are independent

subject: maths
concept: A net is a flat pattern that folds into a solid
statement: A net is the picture of the solid drawn in perspective.
why: Students confuse net with drawing of the solid.
fix: A net is a flat 2D pattern of all faces joined, which can be folded to make the solid.

probe.question: Is a drawing of a cube with three visible faces its net?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: maths
concept: Top, front and side views depend on viewing direction
statement: The front view, top view and side view of a solid always look the same.
why: Cube examples have identical views.
fix: Different directions can give different views; only symmetric solids like a cube give identical ones.

probe.question: A cuboid has dimensions 2, 3, 4. Are its top and front views identical?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, always

root_belief: a special case holds for all cases
source_hint: studies of students' orthographic projection difficulties

subject: maths
concept: Top, front and side views depend on viewing direction
statement: The top view of a cone is a triangle, as its side view is.
why: Students use the familiar side-on picture.
fix: A cone's top view is a circle with a centre point; only its side and front views are triangles.

probe.question: What is the top view of a cone?
probe.wrong_answer: A triangle

root_belief: an object looks the same from every side

subject: maths
concept: Hidden cubes are not shown but still counted in a solid
statement: A view of stacked cubes shows how many cubes there are in total.
why: Students count squares in a view as cubes.
fix: A view shows only one side; hidden cubes behind or below must be inferred, so the count of squares can differ from the cubes in the solid.

probe.question: The front view of a block structure shows 4 squares. How many cubes does it have?

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
source_hint: research on students' interpretation of isometric and orthogonal drawings of cube buildings

subject: maths
concept: A slice or shadow shows a 2D shape of a solid
statement: A vertical slice of a cylinder always gives a circle.
why: Students picture the circular top.
fix: A slice parallel to the base is a circle, but a vertical slice through the axis is a rectangle.

probe.question: A cylinder is cut straight down along its axis. What shape is the cut face?
probe.wrong_answer: Circle

root_belief: one familiar view stands for all views
source_hint: research on student understanding of cross-sections of solids

subject: maths
concept: A slice or shadow shows a 2D shape of a solid
statement: The shadow of a solid is the same shape as the solid.
why: Students think shadows copy objects.
fix: A shadow is a 2D shape that depends on the light direction; a cube can cast a square or a hexagon.

probe.question: A ball is lit from above. What shape is its shadow?
probe.wrong_answer: A sphere

root_belief: a copy looks exactly like the original

subject: maths
statement: Euler's formula is F + V + E = 2.
why: Students misremember the sign of E.
fix: Euler's formula is F + V - E = 2.

probe.question: A cube has 6 faces, 8 vertices, 12 edges. Check Euler's formula.
probe.wrong_answer: 6 + 8 + 12 = 26, so it does not hold

root_belief: all quantities in a formula add

subject: maths
statement: To find edges using Euler's formula, E = F + V + 2.
why: Students rearrange the formula without changing signs.
fix: From F + V - E = 2 we get E = F + V - 2.

probe.question: A solid has 5 faces and 6 vertices. How many edges?

root_belief: moving a term across keeps its sign
source_hint: research on student errors in transposing terms in equations

subject: maths
concept: Euler's formula holds only for polyhedra
statement: Euler's formula works for every solid, including a cylinder or cone.
why: Students apply the rule to everything.
fix: Euler's formula is for polyhedra with flat faces and straight edges only.

probe.question: A cone has 2 faces, 1 vertex, 1 edge. Does F + V - E = 2?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, 2 + 1 - 1 = 2, so it holds for all solids

root_belief: a rule works everywhere once learned

subject: maths
concept: A polyhedron has only flat polygon faces
statement: A cylinder is a polyhedron since it has flat circular faces.
why: Flat faces are noticed without the polygon requirement.
fix: A polyhedron needs all faces to be flat polygons; a cylinder has a curved surface so it is not one.

probe.question: Is a cylinder a polyhedron?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes

root_belief: one matching feature means the same category

subject: maths
concept: A prism has two identical parallel bases
statement: Any solid with a rectangular face is a prism.
why: Prisms are remembered by their rectangular sides.
fix: A prism has two identical parallel bases joined by rectangular faces; a pyramid can have rectangular base without being a prism.

probe.question: A rectangular-based pyramid has a rectangle face. Is it a prism?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes

root_belief: one matching feature means the same category

subject: maths
concept: Increase alone does not imply proportion
statement: If two quantities both increase, they are in direct proportion.
why: Students notice the common direction and ignore whether the ratio stays fixed.
fix: Direct proportion needs the ratio to stay the same. Both can increase without being proportional, like age and height.

probe.question: Rahul is 10 years old and 140 cm tall. At 20 years, will he be 280 cm tall because age and height both increase?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, 280 cm, since both increase so they are proportional.

root_belief: same direction of change means a fixed relationship
source_hint: research on students' proportional reasoning and illusion of linearity

subject: maths
concept: Increase alone does not imply proportion
statement: If the difference between values is constant, the quantities are in direct proportion.
why: Students use additive thinking from whole number work instead of multiplicative thinking.
fix: Direct proportion means the values are multiplied by the same factor, not that the same amount is added.

probe.question: A pencil costs 5 rupees; 2 pencils cost 10 rupees. If 3 more pencils are added, 5 pencils cost how much if we add 3 to the cost?
probe.wrong_answer: 13 rupees, because 3 more pencils means 3 more rupees.

root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere
source_hint: research on additive versus multiplicative reasoning in proportion problems

subject: maths
concept: Ratio x/y stays same in direct variation
statement: In direct proportion, the difference x - y stays the same.
why: Students confuse constant ratio with constant difference.
fix: In direct proportion, the ratio x/y stays the same; the difference changes as the values change.

probe.question: x = 4 when y = 6. If x becomes 8, what is y if x - y stays the same?
probe.wrong_answer: 10, because the difference of 2 must stay the same.

root_belief: constant relationship means constant difference
source_hint: research on additive strategies in ratio problems

subject: maths
statement: In direct proportion, if one quantity becomes 3 times, the other adds 3.
why: Students mix up multiplying with adding the multiplier.
fix: If one quantity becomes 3 times, the other also becomes 3 times, so it is multiplied, not added.

probe.question: 4 kg of apples cost 200 rupees. What do 12 kg cost?
probe.wrong_answer: 203 rupees, since 12 is 3 times 4 so add 3.

root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

subject: maths
concept: Both quantities increase together in direct variation
statement: If one quantity increases and the other also increases, the relationship must be direct proportion and the ratio need not be checked.
why: Textbook examples are mostly clear direct cases, so students skip verification.
fix: Always check that the ratio of corresponding values is the same before calling it direct proportion.

probe.question: Is the table x: 1, 2, 3 and y: 2, 3, 4 direct proportion?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both increase.

root_belief: looking similar is enough to confirm a rule

subject: maths
concept: One goes up, other goes down in inverse variation
statement: Inverse proportion means one quantity is negative of the other.
why: Students link the word inverse with opposite sign or additive inverse.
fix: Inverse proportion means when one quantity increases, the other decreases so that their product stays the same. No negative numbers are involved.

probe.question: If x = 5 and y is inversely proportional to x, could y be -5?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, inverse means y = -x.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: maths
concept: Inverse is not simply any decrease
statement: If one quantity decreases when the other increases, they must be in inverse proportion.
why: Students remember only the opposite-direction part of the definition.
fix: Inverse proportion also needs the product to stay fixed. Some quantities fall as another rises without a constant product.

probe.question: Rohit gets 10 gifts in 1 year, 8 in 2 years, 7 in 3 years. Is this inverse proportion since gifts decrease as years increase?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, as years go up gifts go down.

root_belief: same direction of change means a fixed relationship
source_hint: research on students' confusion of inverse proportion with any decreasing relation

subject: maths
concept: Product xy stays same in inverse variation
statement: In inverse proportion, the sum x + y stays the same.
why: Students think a fall in one must be balanced by an equal rise in the other.
fix: In inverse proportion, the product xy stays the same, not the sum.

probe.question: x = 6 and y = 4 are inversely proportional. If x becomes 8, what is y?
probe.wrong_answer: 2, because the sum 10 stays the same.

root_belief: balancing means equal amount lost and gained
source_hint: research on additive reasoning in inverse proportion tasks

subject: maths
concept: Product xy stays same in inverse variation
statement: In inverse proportion, the ratio x/y stays the same.
why: Students apply the direct proportion rule everywhere.
fix: In inverse proportion, x multiplied by y is constant. A constant ratio is for direct proportion.

probe.question: x = 10 and y = 5 are inversely proportional. If x = 20, what is y?
probe.wrong_answer: 10, because x/y = 2 stays the same.

root_belief: one familiar rule works for every situation
source_hint: research on students applying the direct proportion method to inverse problems

subject: maths
statement: In inverse proportion, if one quantity doubles, the other decreases by 2.
why: Students replace halving with subtracting the same number.
fix: If one quantity doubles, the other becomes half, so it is divided by 2, not reduced by 2.

probe.question: 4 workers finish a job in 12 days. How many days will 8 workers take?
probe.wrong_answer: 10 days, since workers doubled so days go down by 2.

root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

subject: maths
concept: Find value of one unit first
statement: The unitary method always means dividing the given value by the given number.
why: Students memorise one step from direct problems.
fix: In direct problems we divide to find one unit; in inverse problems we first multiply to find the total, then divide.

probe.question: 3 pipes fill a tank in 20 hours. How long will 5 pipes take?
probe.wrong_answer: 20 ÷ 3 = 6.67 per pipe, then ×5 = 33.3 hours.

root_belief: a memorised procedure fits every problem
source_hint: research on misapplication of unitary method in inverse problems

subject: maths
concept: Inverse unitary: find total work or amount first
statement: For inverse problems, divide the given time by the new number of workers.
why: Students pick the division step without finding the total work.
fix: First find total work as workers × days, then divide by the new number of workers.

probe.question: 6 men build a wall in 10 days. How many days will 12 men take?
probe.wrong_answer: 10 ÷ 12 days, about 0.83 days.

root_belief: a memorised procedure fits every problem

subject: maths
statement: In the direct proportion equation, the ratio can be set up with the quantities mixed, like x1/y2 = x2/y1.
why: Students do not track which values correspond.
fix: Pair values of the same quantity or matching situation: x1/x2 = y1/y2, or x1/y1 = x2/y2.

probe.question: 2 kg costs 30 rupees. What does 5 kg cost?
probe.wrong_answer: Using 2/30 = 5/y... gives y = 75 but with 2/y = 5/30 gives 12, treating either as fine.

root_belief: order of terms in a ratio does not matter

subject: maths
statement: For inverse proportion we use the equation x1/y1 = x2/y2.
why: Students use the direct formula by default.
fix: For inverse proportion use x1y1 = x2y2, or equivalently x1/x2 = y2/y1.

probe.question: 5 pipes fill a tank in 12 hours. How long will 6 pipes take?

root_belief: one familiar rule works for every situation
source_hint: research on students' default use of direct proportion method

subject: maths
statement: Units need not match in proportion problems, so we can mix minutes and hours directly.
why: Students focus on the numbers rather than the quantities.
fix: Convert both values to the same unit before forming the ratio or product.

probe.question: A car goes 60 km in 1 hour. How far in 30 minutes?

root_belief: numbers matter but units do not
source_hint: research on neglect of units in ratio and rate problems

subject: maths
concept: Time, speed, workers, and pipes as inverse; cost, weight, distance at fixed speed as direct
statement: More workers always means more of everything, so days taken increase with workers.
why: Students think more people means more of every quantity.
fix: More workers finish the same job in fewer days, so days and workers are inversely proportional.

probe.question: If 5 workers take 8 days, how many days do 10 workers take?
probe.wrong_answer: 16 days, since more workers means more days.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
source_hint: research on students' misclassification of inverse situations as direct

subject: maths
concept: Time, speed, workers, and pipes as inverse; cost, weight, distance at fixed speed as direct
statement: Speed and time for a fixed distance are directly proportional.
why: Students link speed and time as both related to travel without thinking of trade-off.
fix: For a fixed distance, higher speed means less time, so they are inversely proportional.

probe.question: A bus at 40 km/h takes 6 hours. How long at 80 km/h?
probe.wrong_answer: 12 hours, since speed doubles so time doubles.

root_belief: related quantities move in the same direction
source_hint: research on speed-time misconceptions in proportional reasoning

subject: maths
statement: Every word problem with two quantities and a numeric relation is a proportion problem.
why: Students expect every school problem to follow the topic just taught.
fix: Proportion applies only when quantities change by a fixed ratio or product; check with a few values first.

probe.question: A girl is 120 cm at age 8. How tall at age 16?
probe.wrong_answer: 240 cm, using proportion.

root_belief: the lesson's rule applies to every problem
source_hint: research on the illusion of linearity in word problems

subject: maths
statement: In direct proportion, a quantity of zero for one variable can still have a nonzero value of the other.
why: Students do not link proportion with starting at zero.
fix: In direct proportion, if one quantity is zero the other is zero too, because the ratio is constant.

probe.question: Cost of pens is directly proportional to number of pens. What is the cost when the number of pens is 0?
probe.wrong_answer: A fixed amount like 10 rupees.

root_belief: a starting value can be anything

subject: maths
statement: Bars in a bar graph can have different widths because only the bar's area matters.
why: Students treat bars like drawings rather than measurement marks, and see width as decoration.
fix: In a bar graph the height (length) shows the value, and all bars should have equal width and equal gaps so they compare fairly.

probe.question: A bar for Mon is wide and the bar for Tue is narrow, both reach 40. Which shows more?
probe.wrong_answer: Mon, because its bar is bigger

root_belief: bigger looking means bigger value

subject: maths
concept: Choosing a scale for an axis
statement: Each square on a graph paper axis must always stand for 1 unit.
why: Students are used to rulers and number lines where each division is one.
fix: We choose a scale to suit the data, such as 1 square = 10 units, and keep it the same along the whole axis.

probe.question: Data values are 200, 400, 800. How many squares tall is the bar for 800 if 1 square = 1 unit?
probe.wrong_answer: It must be drawn 800 squares tall, so the graph cannot be drawn

root_belief: a scale always counts in ones
source_hint: research on students' interpretation of scales and axes in graphs

subject: maths
concept: Choosing a scale for an axis
statement: The numbers on an axis can be spaced unevenly if the data points are unevenly spread.
why: Students place labels only where data exists rather than at equal intervals.
fix: The scale on an axis must have equal gaps between equal steps, even where there is no data.

probe.question: Data are at 2, 3 and 10. An axis is labelled 2, 3, 10 at equal spacing. Is this correct?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, labels only need to be where there is data

root_belief: only what is present needs to be shown
source_hint: research on graph construction errors in school students

subject: maths
concept: Pie chart sectors show fractions of a whole
statement: A bigger sector in a pie chart always means a bigger number, regardless of the total of each pie chart.
why: Students compare sector sizes across two pies without noticing each pie stands for a different total.
fix: A sector shows a fraction of its own pie's total, so two equal sectors in pies with different totals stand for different amounts.

probe.question: Pie A (total 200 students) has a half sector for cricket; pie B (total 1000) has a quarter sector for cricket. Which has more cricket fans?
probe.wrong_answer: Pie A, since its sector is bigger

root_belief: bigger share always means bigger amount
source_hint: research on proportional reasoning and part-whole misreading of pie charts

subject: maths
concept: Pie chart sectors show fractions of a whole
statement: The angles of the sectors in a pie chart add up to 100.
why: Students mix up percentages, which total 100, with degrees.
fix: The sectors of a full circle have angles adding up to 360 degrees; their percentages add up to 100.

probe.question: Sectors are 30%, 20% and 50%. What do the central angles add up to?
probe.wrong_answer: 100 degrees

root_belief: similar-looking totals mean the same quantity

subject: maths
concept: Reading values from a line graph
statement: To read a value on a line graph you read the number on the axis closest to the line, whatever the point is.
why: Students read off the nearest labelled gridline instead of following the point across to the axis.
fix: Follow a straight line from the point to the axis; if it falls between two labels, estimate using the scale of the small divisions.

probe.question: A point lies midway between the labels 20 and 30 on the y-axis. What is its value?

root_belief: nearest label gives the exact value
source_hint: research on graph-reading errors (interpolation) among students

subject: maths
statement: If the line on a graph goes up and then down, the thing shown is actually going up and down in height or distance like a hill.
why: Students read the graph as a picture of the journey instead of as a relationship between two variables.
fix: A graph shows how one quantity changes with another; a falling line in a distance-time graph means getting back toward the start, not going downhill.

probe.question: On a distance-time graph the line rises, then is flat, then falls. What does the flat part mean?
probe.wrong_answer: The person is walking on level ground

root_belief: a graph is a picture of the real thing
source_hint: research on graph-as-picture misconception in kinematics graphs

subject: maths
statement: A steeper line on a graph always means a higher value, not a faster change.
why: Students attend to height of the line rather than how quickly it climbs.
fix: The steepness (slope) shows how fast the quantity changes; a line can be high but flat, meaning no change.

probe.question: Line A is high but flat; line B starts low but climbs quickly. Which one changes faster?
probe.wrong_answer: Line A, because it is higher

root_belief: larger value means faster change
source_hint: research on slope–height confusion in graph interpretation

subject: maths
concept: Choosing the right type of graph
statement: A line graph can be used to show any data, such as marks of different students in one test.
why: Students think joining points always makes a graph look better.
fix: A line graph is for data that changes continuously with time or another ordered variable; separate categories like students need a bar graph.

probe.question: Which graph suits the marks of five students, bar or line?
probe.wrong_answer: Line graph, join the marks of each student

root_belief: one method works for every case
source_hint: research on students' choice of graph type for categorical data

subject: maths
concept: Choosing the right type of graph
statement: A pie chart can show how a quantity changes over many days.
why: Students think a pie chart is a general-purpose picture for any data.
fix: A pie chart shows parts of one total at a single time; change over time is shown with a line graph.

probe.question: Which graph best shows daily temperature for a week?
probe.wrong_answer: A pie chart with one sector for each day

root_belief: one method works for every case

subject: maths
statement: The origin is the point where the x-axis and y-axis end, at the bottom left corner of the page.
why: Students see only first-quadrant graphs in earlier work, so the origin is always at the corner.
fix: The origin is where the axes cross, with coordinates (0,0); the axes extend into negative values too.

probe.question: Where is the origin on a graph with both axes extending to negative numbers?
probe.wrong_answer: At the bottom left corner of the grid

root_belief: the usual picture is the only picture
source_hint: research on coordinate-system understanding in school students

subject: maths
statement: All points with a negative coordinate lie in the same quadrant.
why: Students merge the idea of negative with 'left or below' and do not track both signs together.
fix: The quadrant depends on both signs: (-,+) is the second, (-,-) the third, and (+,-) the fourth quadrant.

probe.question: In which quadrant is (-3, -2)?
probe.wrong_answer: The second quadrant, since a negative number puts it to the left

root_belief: one feature decides a thing completely

subject: maths
statement: Quadrants are numbered clockwise starting from the top right.
why: Students associate clockwise with the clock and ignore the anticlockwise convention.
fix: Quadrants are numbered anticlockwise, starting with the top right as quadrant I, then top left, bottom left, bottom right.

probe.question: Which quadrant is the point (-4, 5) in?
probe.wrong_answer: Fourth quadrant

root_belief: turning direction is always clockwise

subject: maths
concept: x-coordinate (abscissa) is distance along the x-axis, written first
statement: The point (3, 5) and the point (5, 3) are the same point.
why: Students treat the pair like a set of numbers where order does not matter.
fix: Coordinates are an ordered pair; the x-value comes first and the y-value second, so (3,5) and (5,3) are different points.

probe.question: Are (2, 7) and (7, 2) the same point?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both have the numbers 2 and 7

root_belief: order of items does not matter
source_hint: research on order and coordinate-reversal errors in plotting

subject: maths
concept: x-coordinate (abscissa) is distance along the x-axis, written first
statement: The first number in a coordinate pair tells how far up the point is.
why: Students link first with vertical because many measurement scenes begin with height.
fix: The first number (x) tells the distance along the horizontal axis; the second (y) tells how far up or down.

probe.question: Where is (4, 1) relative to the origin?
probe.wrong_answer: 4 units up and 1 unit across

root_belief: first means the vertical thing
source_hint: research on coordinate-reversal errors in plotting

subject: maths
concept: Points on the axes have a zero coordinate
statement: A point on the y-axis has y-coordinate equal to 0.
why: Students mix up 'on the axis' with 'the value of that axis'.
fix: A point on the y-axis has x-coordinate 0, like (0,4); a point on the x-axis has y-coordinate 0, like (4,0).

probe.question: What are the coordinates of a point 4 units up the y-axis?

root_belief: the name of a thing tells its value
source_hint: research on plotting points on axes in school coordinate geometry

subject: maths
concept: Plotting means going across then up/down
statement: To plot (-2, 3) you count 2 units to the right because 2 is just a number and the minus sign can be ignored.
why: Students carry whole-number thinking and drop negative signs on the number line.
fix: A negative x-value means moving left of the origin and a negative y-value means moving down.

probe.question: Describe how to plot (-2, 3).
probe.wrong_answer: Go 2 to the right and 3 up

root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

subject: maths
concept: Plotting means going across then up/down
statement: To plot a point, count the grid lines starting from where you put the pencil, not from the origin.
why: Students treat each point as a fresh start instead of a position from the origin.
fix: Each point is always located by starting at the origin and moving x units horizontally, then y units vertically.

probe.question: After plotting (2,3), how do you plot (4,1)?
probe.wrong_answer: From (2,3) move 4 right and 1 up

root_belief: each step starts from the last position

subject: maths
statement: In a table of values, the x variable and y variable can be swapped without changing the graph.
why: Students see the table as a pair of columns of numbers and not as input-output.
fix: Swapping x and y reflects the points and changes the graph; the independent variable goes on the horizontal axis.

probe.question: For distance = 2 × time, which variable is plotted on the horizontal axis?
probe.wrong_answer: Distance, either one is fine

root_belief: order of items does not matter
source_hint: research on variable placement on axes in graphing tasks

subject: maths
concept: Joining points with a ruler and extending the line
statement: A line graph of a linear relation should stop at the first and last plotted points.
why: Students think a graph only exists where they have computed points.
fix: The straight line can be extended on both sides because the relation holds for other values too (within the context).

probe.question: You plotted y = 2x for x = 1, 2, 3. Does the line pass through (5, 10)?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the graph only goes up to x = 3

root_belief: only what is shown exists

subject: maths
concept: Joining points with a ruler and extending the line
statement: Points on a straight-line graph can be joined freehand and any wavy curve through the points is fine.
why: Students see joining as connecting dots, not as drawing a straight line through them.
fix: For a linear relation the points lie on one straight line, which is drawn with a ruler; if they do not line up, one point is probably wrong.

probe.question: Three points of y = x + 1 don't look aligned. What should you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Join them with a curve through all three

root_belief: connect the dots however they fall

subject: maths
concept: Every point on the line satisfies the relation
statement: Only the points you plotted lie on the graph of the relation; other points of the line do not satisfy the equation.
why: Students see the line as drawn dots, not as every solution.
fix: Every point on the line satisfies the relation, and every solution gives a point on the line.

probe.question: The line y = x + 2 is plotted from points (1,3), (2,4). Does (10,12) satisfy it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it was not plotted

root_belief: only what is shown exists
source_hint: research on understanding graphs as sets of solutions

subject: maths
concept: Distance-time graph as a linear graph
statement: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the object is moving at constant speed.
why: Students link a level line with steady or constant motion.
fix: A horizontal line means distance does not change with time, so the object is at rest; constant speed is a slanted straight line.

probe.question: What does a horizontal line on a distance-time graph show?
probe.wrong_answer: The object moves at constant speed

root_belief: a graph is a picture of the real thing
source_hint: research on misinterpretation of kinematics graphs

subject: maths
concept: Distance-time graph as a linear graph
statement: A steeper straight line on a distance-time graph means a slower object.
why: Students think that rising more means more time taken.
fix: The steeper the line, the more distance covered in the same time, so the faster the object.

probe.question: Two lines on one distance-time graph; line A is steeper. Which object is faster?
probe.wrong_answer: The one with the less steep line

root_belief: more change in the picture means more time

subject: maths
concept: A rational number has form p/q with q not zero
statement: A number is rational only if its numerator and denominator are both whole numbers that already appear as a fraction like 3/4, so 0.5 is not rational.
why: Students link 'rational' with the look of a written fraction rather than the possibility of writing one.
fix: A number is rational if it CAN be written as p/q with integers p and q, q not 0. So 0.5 = 1/2 is rational.

probe.question: How many solutions does x = 3 have as an equation in two variables?
probe.wrong_answer: Only one, x = 3.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
source_hint: classroom studies on equations with a missing variable

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
statement: In ax + by + c = 0, the constant c is on the right side and must be positive.
why: Students are used to writing equations as ax + by = c.
fix: The standard form has everything on the left equal to zero; a, b, c can be positive, negative or zero (a and b not both zero).

probe.question: Write 2x + 3y = 5 in the form ax + by + c = 0. What is c?

root_belief: the form seen first is the only form

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: Two points are enough to draw a line
statement: A line needs at least three points to be drawn, and two points can give a wrong line.
why: Students rely on plotting many points or distrust two points.
fix: Two points determine a line; a third point is only a check for arithmetic mistakes.

probe.question: Why do we plot a third point after two points on a line?
probe.wrong_answer: Because two points cannot decide the line.

root_belief: more steps are always needed for certainty

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: Plotting the graph of a line
statement: The graph of a linear equation is just the plotted points, not a line extended in both directions.
why: Students stop at the segment between points they plotted.
fix: The graph is a straight line extending endlessly in both directions, and every point on it is a solution.

probe.question: Is (10, -5) on the graph of x + y = 5 if the drawn segment ends near x = 4?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is outside the drawn part.

root_belief: what is drawn is all that exists
source_hint: research on students' graph interpretation as point plots vs. continuous objects

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
statement: A point near the line but not on it still counts as a solution.
why: Students judge by eye instead of substituting.
fix: Only points exactly on the line satisfy the equation; check by substituting.

probe.question: The point (2, 4) lies just above the line x + y = 5. Is it a solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is close enough to the line.

root_belief: looks close means is the same

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: Every solution lies on the line and every point on the line is a solution
statement: Points on the line are solutions only if the coordinates are whole numbers.
why: Only grid intersections are easily read from graph paper.
fix: Every point on the line, including those with fractional coordinates, is a solution.

probe.question: Is (1.5, 3.5) on the line x + y = 5 a solution?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is not on a grid crossing.

root_belief: only easily visible values count

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: Graph of y = k is horizontal and x = k is vertical
statement: The graph of x = 3 is a horizontal line.
why: Students link the letter y with vertical and x with horizontal, or mix up axes.
fix: x = 3 is the vertical line through all points whose x-coordinate is 3; y = 3 is horizontal.

probe.question: What is the direction of the graph of x = 3?
probe.wrong_answer: Horizontal, parallel to the x-axis.

root_belief: a symbol name tells the direction directly
source_hint: research on errors in graphing x = a and y = b

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: Graphs of a pair of equations
statement: Two lines drawn always meet at a point, so every pair has a solution.
why: Students picture two lines as crossing, as in most examples.
fix: Two lines may cross, be parallel, or coincide; parallel lines never meet and give no solution.

probe.question: Does x + y = 2 and x + y = 5 have a common solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the lines will meet somewhere.

root_belief: the usual example is the only case
source_hint: studies of systems of equations and graphical representations

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: Intersection point of two lines is the common solution
statement: The solution of a pair is the point where a line meets the x-axis.
why: Students recall x-intercepts from earlier graph work.
fix: The solution is where the two lines meet each other, not where they meet an axis.

probe.question: Lines x + y = 4 and x - y = 2 meet at (3, 1) and cross the x-axis at (4, 0) and (2, 0). What is the solution?
probe.wrong_answer: x = 4 and x = 2.

root_belief: a familiar graph feature is the answer

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: Substitute the expression for a variable in brackets into the other equation
statement: When substituting y = 5 - x into 2x + y = 7, you can write 2x + 5 - x without brackets even if the expression has a minus sign in a longer case.
why: Students treat the expression as a single number and drop brackets.
fix: Substitute the whole expression in brackets, then expand, because the sign applies to every term inside.

probe.question: Substitute x = 4 - y into 3x - 2x... use 3 - x with x = 4 - y; what is 3 - x?

root_belief: a minus sign affects only the next symbol
source_hint: research on algebraic sign and bracket errors

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: Multiply whole equation (both sides) to equalise coefficients
statement: To make coefficients equal, multiply only the term with the variable, not the whole equation.
why: Students focus on the coefficient they want to change.
fix: Multiply every term on both sides so the equation stays true.

probe.question: Multiply x + 2y = 3 by 2.

root_belief: only the part I care about needs changing
source_hint: research on algebraic manipulation errors in equation solving

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: Subtract equations term by term with signs
statement: When subtracting one equation from another, you only need to change the sign of the first term.
why: Students apply a shortcut sign change partially.
fix: Subtracting an equation means subtracting every term of it, so all the signs of the second equation reverse.

probe.question: Subtract (x - 2y = 1) from (x + 3y = 6).
probe.wrong_answer: 5y = 5... they write 2x + 3y... or 0x + y = 5

root_belief: a minus sign affects only the next symbol
source_hint: studies of sign errors when subtracting expressions

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: Subtract equations term by term with signs
statement: If the coefficients of a variable are equal, you must add the equations to eliminate it.
why: Students memorise add or subtract without checking the signs.
fix: Add when the coefficients are opposite in sign and subtract when they are equal, so the variable cancels.

probe.question: To eliminate x from x + y = 5 and x - y = 1, what do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Subtract them, as both have x.

root_belief: a rule works without checking its conditions

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: After finding one variable, substitute back to find the other
statement: Once x is found, the problem is solved and y is not needed.
why: Students think finding one number ends the question.
fix: The solution is the pair (x, y), so the second variable must also be found and stated.

probe.question: Solve x + y = 7 and x - y = 3.

root_belief: the first answer found is the final answer
source_hint: research on systems of equations solution strategies

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
statement: If the result after elimination is 0 = 0, the pair has no solution.
why: Students think a zero result means nothing is left.
fix: 0 = 0 is always true, so the lines coincide and there are infinitely many solutions; a false result like 0 = 4 means no solution.

probe.question: Solving x + y = 2 and 2x + 2y = 4 gives 0 = 0. What does it mean?
probe.wrong_answer: There is no solution.

root_belief: zero means nothing exists
source_hint: research on interpreting degenerate outcomes in systems of equations

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
statement: Parallel lines mean the equations are identical or the pair has infinitely many solutions.
why: Students mix up parallel with coincident.
fix: Parallel distinct lines never meet, so there is no solution; only coincident lines give infinitely many.

probe.question: x + y = 3 and 2x + 2y = 9 are parallel. How many solutions?
probe.wrong_answer: Infinitely many.

root_belief: similar sounding ideas mean the same

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: Types of pairs: consistent and inconsistent
statement: An inconsistent pair is one that is hard to solve or has mistakes in it.
why: The everyday meaning of inconsistent is unreliable.
fix: In maths, inconsistent means the pair has no solution; consistent means it has at least one.

probe.question: What does inconsistent mean for a pair of equations?
probe.wrong_answer: The equations have errors.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
source_hint: research on everyday versus mathematical meanings of terms

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: a1/a2 ≠ b1/b2 gives a unique solution
statement: If a1/a2 = b1/b2, the pair has a unique solution because the ratios are equal.
why: Students remember equal ratios as good without checking c.
fix: Unique solution needs a1/a2 not equal to b1/b2; equal a and b ratios mean parallel or coincident, depending on c.

probe.question: For x + 2y = 3 and 2x + 4y = 7, what kind of solution is there?
probe.wrong_answer: Unique, as 1/2 = 2/4.

root_belief: equal ratios always mean a good match

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: Coincident lines mean infinitely many solutions
statement: Coincident lines mean the two equations must look exactly the same.
why: Students look at the written form not at equivalence.
fix: Equations that are multiples of each other, like x + y = 2 and 3x + 3y = 6, give the same line.

probe.question: Do x + y = 2 and 3x + 3y = 6 give the same line?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the equations are different.

root_belief: different looking means different thing
source_hint: research on equivalence of equations in algebra

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
statement: In 'a pen costs 5 more than a pencil', write p = 5 + q as q = 5 + p.
why: Students write terms in the order the words appear.
fix: The pen costs more, so pen = pencil + 5; the larger quantity gets the added amount on the other side.

probe.question: A pen costs 5 more than a pencil; pen is x, pencil is y. Write the equation.
probe.wrong_answer: y = x + 5

root_belief: word order gives the order of symbols
source_hint: research on the student-professor and reversal errors in translating words

topic: Linear equations in two variables and pairs of equations
subject: maths
concept: Solution must make both equations true and fit the context
statement: If the answer to a word problem is negative or a fraction, it is still acceptable for number of persons.
why: Students trust algebra over the context.
fix: The solution must make sense in the situation; counts of people or items must be non-negative whole numbers.

probe.question: Solving a problem on number of children gives x = 2.5. Is this valid?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it satisfies the equations.

root_belief: the calculation matters more than the context
source_hint: research on sense-making in mathematical word problems

subject: maths
statement: Every axiom must be proved from other statements before it can be used.
why: Students are used to every maths result being proved or derived in class.
fix: Axioms are basic statements accepted as true without proof; all proofs start from them.

probe.question: Can Euclid's axiom 'things equal to the same thing are equal to one another' be used without proving it first?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it must be proved first.

root_belief: everything accepted in a subject has been proved

subject: maths
concept: A theorem is proved by logical reasoning
statement: Measuring angles in a few drawn triangles with a protractor proves a theorem.
why: Earlier classes verified properties by measuring or paper folding.
fix: A theorem is proved by logical steps from axioms and earlier theorems; measuring a few cases only checks them and cannot prove it for all cases.

probe.question: You measure the angle sum in five triangles and get 180 each time. Has the angle sum property been proved?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, five triangles prove it.

root_belief: seeing examples work proves a rule always works
source_hint: education research on students' proof schemes (empirical vs deductive proof)

subject: maths
concept: Equals added to or taken from equals stay equal
statement: The rule 'equals added to equals are equal' works only for numbers, not for lengths or angles.
why: Students link the word 'equal' only with numerical equations.
fix: The axiom applies to any quantities that can be compared, including lengths, angles and areas.

probe.question: AB = CD. Is AB + BC equal to CD + BC?
probe.wrong_answer: Cannot say, because these are lengths and not numbers.

root_belief: a rule from numbers does not apply to other quantities

subject: maths
concept: A line segment can be extended without end
statement: A straight line has two end points, just like a line segment.
why: Everyday and early-class drawings of a line are always finite with ends.
fix: A line extends endlessly in both directions; only a line segment has two end points.

probe.question: A line has two end points. True or false?
probe.wrong_answer: True.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
source_hint: studies of students' concept images of line, ray and segment

subject: maths
concept: Exactly one line passes through two points
statement: Many different straight lines can be drawn through two given points.
why: Through one point many lines pass, and students carry this over to two points.
fix: Through two distinct points exactly one straight line can be drawn.

probe.question: How many straight lines pass through both points A and B?
probe.wrong_answer: Many lines pass through both.

root_belief: what holds for one case holds for the next

subject: maths
concept: Fifth postulate: interior angles less than 180 make lines meet
statement: Two lines meet on the side where the interior angles add up to more than 180 degrees.
why: Students remember '180' from the postulate but not which side the lines meet.
fix: The lines meet on the side where the two interior angles add up to less than 180 degrees.

probe.question: A transversal makes interior angles of 100 and 95 degrees on one side. Do the lines meet on that side?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they meet there because the sum is more than 180.

root_belief: remembering a number means remembering the whole rule

subject: maths
concept: A linear pair adds to 180 degrees
statement: Any two adjacent angles form a linear pair.
why: Students remember only that a linear pair is adjacent and ignore the straight-line condition.
fix: A linear pair is two adjacent angles whose non-common arms form a straight line, so they add to 180 degrees.

probe.question: Angles of 50 and 60 degrees share an arm. Do they form a linear pair adding to 180?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they are adjacent so they form a linear pair.

root_belief: a partial condition is the full definition

subject: maths
concept: A linear pair adds to 180 degrees
statement: The two angles of a linear pair are always equal, each 90 degrees.
why: The standard picture shows a perpendicular line on a straight line.
fix: The angles of a linear pair are equal only when the line is perpendicular; in general they just add to 180 degrees.

probe.question: One angle of a linear pair is 120 degrees. What is the other?
probe.wrong_answer: 120 degrees, because they are equal.

root_belief: the usual picture is the only case
source_hint: research on prototype images in geometry

subject: maths
statement: Complementary angles add up to 180 degrees.
why: The words complementary and supplementary sound alike and are mixed up.
fix: Complementary angles add to 90 degrees; supplementary angles add to 180 degrees.

probe.question: What is the complement of 70 degrees?
probe.wrong_answer: 110 degrees.

root_belief: similar-sounding terms mean the same thing
source_hint: common error analyses in school geometry

subject: maths
statement: Complementary or supplementary angles must be next to each other.
why: Textbook diagrams always show these pairs as adjacent angles.
fix: The angles can be anywhere; only their sum (90 or 180 degrees) matters.

probe.question: Two separate angles are 30 and 60 degrees in different figures. Are they complementary?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are not adjacent.

root_belief: the usual picture is the only case

subject: maths
statement: Vertically opposite angles add up to 180 degrees.
why: They are confused with a linear pair, since both appear where two lines cross.
fix: Vertically opposite angles are equal; it is the neighbouring angles (linear pair) that add to 180 degrees.

probe.question: Two lines cross and one angle is 40 degrees. What is the angle opposite to it?
probe.wrong_answer: 140 degrees.

root_belief: similar-looking cases follow the same rule
source_hint: misconception studies on angle relations at intersecting lines

subject: maths
statement: Vertically opposite angles are equal only when the two lines are perpendicular.
why: Students see equal angles mainly in the symmetric picture of crossing at 90 degrees.
fix: Vertically opposite angles are equal for any two intersecting lines, whatever the angle between them.

probe.question: Two lines cross at 60 degrees. Are the opposite 60-degree angles equal?
probe.wrong_answer: Not necessarily, they are equal only if the lines are perpendicular.

root_belief: a special case is the general rule

subject: maths
concept: Corresponding angles are equal when lines are parallel
statement: Corresponding angles are equal for any two lines cut by a transversal.
why: Students forget the condition that the lines must be parallel.
fix: Corresponding angles are equal only if the two lines are parallel.

probe.question: Two non-parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Are the corresponding angles equal?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, corresponding angles are always equal.

root_belief: a rule works without its conditions
source_hint: research on students ignoring conditions in geometry theorems

subject: maths
concept: Alternate interior angles are equal when lines are parallel
statement: Alternate interior angles are the two angles between the lines on the same side of the transversal.
why: The names alternate and co-interior (same side) interior angles are mixed up.
fix: Alternate interior angles lie between the lines on opposite sides of the transversal.

probe.question: Lines are parallel. Two interior angles on the same side of the transversal are called alternate angles, so they are equal. Right?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they are alternate angles and equal.

root_belief: angle names can be used loosely

subject: maths
concept: Co-interior angles add to 180 when lines are parallel
statement: Co-interior angles on parallel lines are equal.
why: Students extend the equal-angle rule of corresponding and alternate angles to all pairs.
fix: Co-interior angles on parallel lines are supplementary; they add to 180 degrees.

probe.question: Parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One co-interior angle is 70 degrees. What is the other?
probe.wrong_answer: 70 degrees.

root_belief: one pattern applies to all similar cases
source_hint: error analyses of angle problems with parallel lines

subject: maths
statement: Parallel lines are always horizontal, so a tilted pair of lines cannot be parallel.
why: Textbook and board diagrams usually show parallel lines as horizontal.
fix: Lines in any direction are parallel if they never meet, i.e. stay the same distance apart.

probe.question: Two slanted lines both rise at the same slope. Are they parallel?
probe.wrong_answer: No, parallel lines must be horizontal.

root_belief: the usual picture is the only case
source_hint: research on prototype and orientation effects in geometry concepts

subject: maths
concept: Equal corresponding or alternate angles make lines parallel
statement: If two lines look parallel in a figure, they are parallel and no angle check is needed.
why: Students trust the diagram and do not check conditions.
fix: Lines are shown parallel only if given or if corresponding, alternate or co-interior angles satisfy the conditions; a figure may not be to scale.

probe.question: Alternate angles are 65 and 70 degrees but the lines look parallel. Are they parallel?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they look parallel.

root_belief: what looks true in a picture is true
source_hint: research on reliance on diagrams in geometric reasoning

subject: maths
concept: The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees
statement: A bigger triangle has a larger angle sum than a small triangle.
why: Students think greater size means greater quantity.
fix: The angle sum of every triangle is 180 degrees, whatever its size.

probe.question: A huge triangle and a tiny triangle: which has the bigger angle sum?
probe.wrong_answer: The huge triangle.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
source_hint: studies of students confusing side length with angle size

subject: maths
concept: The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees
statement: The angle sum of an obtuse-angled triangle is more than 180 degrees.
why: One large angle seems to push the total above 180.
fix: Every triangle, acute, right or obtuse, has angle sum 180 degrees.

probe.question: A triangle has angles 120, 30 and 30 degrees. What is its angle sum?
probe.wrong_answer: It has more than 180 because one angle is obtuse.

root_belief: a special case is the general rule

subject: maths
concept: Exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles
statement: An exterior angle equals the sum of its adjacent interior angle and one other interior angle.
why: Students mix up which interior angles are 'opposite' and which is adjacent.
fix: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles, not including the adjacent interior angle.

probe.question: Triangle angles are 50, 60, 70. The exterior angle at the 70 angle equals?
probe.wrong_answer: 130, adding the adjacent 70 and 60.

root_belief: similar-sounding terms mean the same thing
source_hint: error analyses of triangle exterior angle problems

subject: maths
statement: An angle with longer arms is a bigger angle.
why: Students judge the angle by how long the drawn arms look.
fix: The size of an angle is the amount of turn between the arms and does not depend on how long they are drawn.

probe.question: Two angles are both 40 degrees but one has arms 10 cm long and the other 3 cm. Which is bigger?
probe.wrong_answer: The one with 10 cm arms.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
source_hint: research on children's conceptions of angle size

subject: maths
concept: Lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other
statement: Two lines that are each parallel to a third line can meet each other.
why: Students do not accept that parallelism passes from one line to another.
fix: If two lines are parallel to the same line, they are parallel to each other and never meet.

probe.question: Lines l and m are both parallel to line n. Can l and m intersect?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they can meet if they are tilted differently.

root_belief: a relation does not carry over to a third thing

subject: maths
statement: The longest chord can be any chord passing near the middle of the circle.
why: Students see 'middle' chords as roughly the same length and do not link longest chord to the diameter.
fix: The diameter, which passes through the centre, is the longest chord. Any chord not through the centre is shorter than the diameter.

probe.question: Chord AB passes very close to but not through the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. Can AB be 10 cm long?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is almost the diameter so it can be 10 cm.

root_belief: nearly the same means exactly the same

subject: maths
concept: Equal chords subtend equal angles at centre
statement: Equal angles at the centre means nothing about chord lengths, since longer arcs always give longer chords.
why: Students rely on arc length intuition and ignore the congruent triangle link between angle and chord.
fix: Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre, and the converse is also true. Chord length depends on the angle at the centre in the same circle.

probe.question: Chords PQ and RS of the same circle subtend 60 degrees each at the centre. Compare PQ and RS.
probe.wrong_answer: Cannot say; they may differ in length.

root_belief: a rule works only in one direction

subject: maths
statement: The line from the centre to a chord always bisects the chord.
why: Students remember 'bisects' but forget the line must be perpendicular.
fix: Only the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord. A slanting line from the centre to a chord does not hit its midpoint.

probe.question: O is the centre and OM meets chord AB at M with angle OMA = 70 degrees. Is AM = MB?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a line from the centre bisects the chord.

subject: maths
concept: Angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees
statement: The angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees only when the triangle is isosceles.
why: Students see the textbook figure with the third point at the top middle and take that symmetric picture as the rule.
fix: For any point on the circle, the angle subtended by a diameter is 90 degrees. Its position on the semicircle does not matter.

probe.question: AB is a diameter and C is a point on the circle close to A, so AC is much shorter than BC. What is angle ACB?
probe.wrong_answer: It is not 90 degrees because the triangle is not isosceles.

root_belief: Theorem holds only for the typical symmetric diagram
source_hint: classroom observation of textbook diagram effects

subject: maths
concept: Opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180
statement: Any two opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are equal.
why: Students mix this with the property of parallelograms, where opposite angles are equal.
fix: In a cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles add up to 180 degrees. They are equal only when each is 90 degrees, as in a rectangle.

probe.question: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, angle A = 70 degrees. Find angle C.
probe.wrong_answer: Angle C = 70 degrees.

root_belief: Opposite angles in quadrilaterals are always equal
source_hint: geometry misconception studies on quadrilateral properties

subject: maths
concept: Exterior angle equals interior opposite angle
statement: The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the adjacent interior angle.
why: Students pick the wrong interior angle because they do not link 'opposite' to the vertex across the quadrilateral.
fix: The exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle. It is supplementary to the adjacent interior angle.

probe.question: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, side AB is extended to E and angle ABC = 100 degrees. What is the exterior angle CBE?
probe.wrong_answer: 100 degrees, the same as the adjacent angle ABC.

root_belief: Exterior angle equals the angle next to it

subject: maths
concept: Angles in same segment are equal
statement: Angles in the same segment are equal even when they stand on different chords.
why: Students remember only 'angles in the same segment are equal' and forget the same chord or arc condition.
fix: Angles are equal only if they stand on the same chord or arc and lie in the same segment.

probe.question: P and Q lie on the major arc. Angle APB stands on chord AB and angle CQD stands on chord CD, where CD is longer than AB. Are the two angles equal?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both angles are in the same segment so they are equal.

root_belief: Theorems apply without checking their conditions

subject: maths
concept: Angle at centre is double angle at remaining circle
statement: The angle at the centre is double the angle at the circle for any two angles on the same chord.
why: Students apply the double rule without checking that the circle angle lies on the major arc and the centre angle is the one on the same arc.
fix: The angle at the centre is double the angle at the circle only when both stand on the same arc. A point on the minor arc sees the reflex angle at the centre.

probe.question: Chord AB subtends an angle of 80 degrees at the centre O. What is the angle at a point P on the minor arc AB?
probe.wrong_answer: 40 degrees.

root_belief: Double rule works regardless of which arc
source_hint: research on circle theorem application errors

subject: maths
concept: Tangent is perpendicular to radius at contact point
statement: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at any point where it touches or crosses the circle.
why: Students treat the perpendicularity as a property of every line near the radius and forget the contact point condition.
fix: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to its point of contact only. A secant cuts the circle at two points and is not perpendicular to the radius.

probe.question: A line cuts the circle at A and B. Is it perpendicular to radius OA?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a line touching the circle at A is always perpendicular to OA.

root_belief: Words tangent and secant are interchangeable

subject: maths
concept: Tangent lengths from external point are equal
statement: Two tangents from an external point are equal only if the point is at the same distance as the centre of the circle from each point of contact.
why: Students think the two lengths depend on the angle between tangents and not on the right-angled triangles formed with the radius.
fix: Tangents from an external point are always equal, because the two right triangles share the hypotenuse OP and have equal radii.

probe.question: PA and PB are tangents from P to a circle with centre O. If PA = 7 cm and angle APB is 40 degrees, what is PB?
probe.wrong_answer: It cannot be found because the angle is not 60 degrees.

root_belief: Equality needs a special angle or symmetric picture

subject: maths
concept: Tangents from a point on or inside circle
statement: Two tangents can be drawn from a point inside a circle.
why: Students carry the rule 'two tangents from a point' from the external case to every position of the point.
fix: From an external point there are two tangents, from a point on the circle exactly one, and from an interior point none.

probe.question: How many tangents can be drawn to a circle from a point inside it?
probe.wrong_answer: Two.

root_belief: A rule for one case holds for all cases

subject: maths
concept: All four vertices must lie on one circle
statement: Any four points that form a quadrilateral always lie on one circle.
why: Students see circles as always available and do not realise that three points fix a circle, so the fourth must be checked.
fix: A circle passes through any three non-collinear points, but a fourth point lies on it only if the opposite angles add to 180 degrees.

probe.question: In quadrilateral ABCD angle A = 80 degrees and angle C = 70 degrees. Is ABCD cyclic?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, every quadrilateral can be inscribed in a circle.

root_belief: Every figure can be inscribed in a circle

subject: maths
concept: Area = half base times corresponding height
statement: The area of a triangle is base times height, with no half.
why: Students blend the rectangle rule with the triangle rule.

subject: maths
statement: Heron's formula is s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c), with the square root applied only to s.

concept: Take the square root at the end

subject: maths

subject: maths
concept: A diagonal splits a quadrilateral into two triangles

subject: maths
concept: Rhombus area is half product of diagonals

root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

subject: maths
concept: Parallelogram area is base times height, not slant side

probe.question: A parallelogram has sides 10 cm and 6 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm on the 10 cm base. Find its area.

subject: maths
statement: Quadrilaterals with the same perimeter have the same area.
why: Students link perimeter and area as one measure.

subject: maths
statement: Heron's formula needs the height, so it cannot be used before finding it.

subject: maths
statement: Total surface area is the same as curved surface area.

subject: maths
statement: The surface area of a cube is a³.

subject: maths
concept: Curved surface of cylinder is a rectangle 2πr × h

subject: maths
statement: The total surface area of a cylinder is 2πrh + πr².

statement: The slant height of a cone is the same as its vertical height.

concept: Constant difference, not ratio, defines an AP

probe.question: Are triangles with sides 3,4,5 and 5,6,7 similar?
