subject: general
statement: All germs are harmful and should be killed.
why: Advertisements show germs as enemies everywhere.
fix: Most microbes are harmless or useful, like those that make curd or help digestion. Only a few cause disease.

probe.question: Are the bacteria that turn milk into curd harmful?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all bacteria are harmful.

root_belief: a whole group is bad because some members are
source_hint: research on student ideas about microorganisms

subject: general
concept: Germs are too small to see with the eye
statement: If hands look clean, they have no germs.
why: Students trust what they can see.
fix: Germs are far too small to see, so clean-looking hands can carry many. Washing with soap is still needed.

probe.question: Hands look spotless. Do they need washing before eating?
probe.wrong_answer: No, there is no dirt so no germs.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
source_hint: studies on children's reasoning about invisible microbes

subject: general
concept: Germs spread by touch and surfaces
statement: Germs spread only through dirty or smelly things.
why: Dirt and bad smell are linked with disease in everyday talk.
fix: Germs can be on clean-looking things such as door handles, phones and hands. Touching them then your face or food spreads germs.

probe.question: Can a shiny, clean-looking door handle spread germs?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only dirty things have germs.

root_belief: appearance shows whether something is safe

subject: general
statement: Germs spread only when a sick person touches you.
why: Contact is the most obvious route to students.
fix: Some germs travel in tiny droplets from coughs, sneezes and talking, so you can catch them without touching.

probe.question: A sick classmate sneezes 1 metre away without touching you. Can you get infected?
probe.wrong_answer: No, there was no touch.

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: general
statement: You catch a cold from being out in cold weather or getting wet.
why: The word 'cold' and common advice from elders link weather with illness.
fix: Colds are caused by viruses spread from infected people. Cold weather itself does not cause them.

probe.question: What causes a common cold?
probe.wrong_answer: Cold air and getting wet in rain.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
source_hint: studies of lay beliefs about colds and flu

subject: general
concept: Germs spread through water, food and vectors
statement: Diseases like malaria and dengue spread from sick people by touch or air.
why: Students assume all diseases spread person to person directly.
fix: Malaria and dengue spread through mosquito bites, which carry the germ from one person to another.

probe.question: How does malaria spread?
probe.wrong_answer: By touching or breathing near a malaria patient.

root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere

subject: general
concept: Soap lifts and removes germs, mainly not killing instantly
statement: Soap works by killing all germs on the skin immediately.
why: Soap advertisements say 'kills 99.9% germs'.
fix: Soap mainly loosens germs and dirt from skin so water washes them off. Rubbing and rinsing do most of the work.

probe.question: Why must you rinse hands after soaping?
probe.wrong_answer: No need; soap already killed everything.

root_belief: products work by magic instantly

subject: general
concept: Soap lifts and removes germs, mainly not killing instantly
statement: Only antibacterial or liquid soap works; plain soap does not.
why: Marketing suggests special soaps are stronger.
fix: Plain soap and water remove germs well when used properly. Special antibacterial soaps are not needed for daily handwashing.

probe.question: Is plain bar soap enough to clean hands properly?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only antibacterial soap works.

root_belief: costlier or special product works better

subject: general
concept: Water alone does not remove oily dirt and germs well
statement: Rinsing hands with water alone is as good as using soap.
why: Wet hands look clean and feel clean.
fix: Water alone cannot lift greasy dirt and germs well. Soap breaks the grip of grease so germs wash away.

probe.question: Is a quick rinse under a tap enough before lunch?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, water washes germs away just as well.

root_belief: what looks clean is clean

subject: general
concept: Wash at least 20 seconds with soap
statement: Wetting hands and a quick soap rub of 5 seconds is enough.
why: Students think the soap itself acts instantly.
fix: Rub with soap for at least 20 seconds so germs are loosened and removed.

probe.question: How long should you scrub hands with soap?
probe.wrong_answer: About 5 seconds.

root_belief: a small amount gives the full effect

subject: general
concept: Clean palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs, nails
statement: Washing only the palms is enough to clean hands.
why: Palms are what students see touching things most.
fix: Germs hide on backs of hands, between fingers, under nails and around thumbs. All these must be scrubbed.

probe.question: Which parts of the hand need scrubbing?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the palms.

root_belief: the obvious part is the whole thing

subject: general
concept: Key times to wash: before eating, after toilet
statement: Hands need washing only when they look dirty.
why: Washing is linked to visible mess.
fix: Wash before eating or cooking and after using the toilet, coughing or touching animals, even when hands look clean.

probe.question: After using the toilet, hands look clean. Should you wash?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are clean.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: general
concept: Cough or sneeze into elbow or tissue
statement: Coughing into your bare palm is fine if you wipe it later.
why: Palm is the natural reflex to cover the mouth.
fix: Cough into your bent elbow or a tissue, because germs on palms spread to everything you touch.

probe.question: Best way to cover a sneeze?
probe.wrong_answer: Cover with the palm of the hand.

root_belief: covering anything is enough

subject: general
concept: Cough or sneeze into elbow or tissue
statement: Wearing a mask or covering the mouth is only for sick people.
why: Masks are linked to patients.
fix: Sick people should cover coughs, and masks can also protect healthy people in crowded or risky places.

probe.question: Can a healthy person benefit from a mask near a coughing patient?
probe.wrong_answer: No, masks are only for the sick.

root_belief: a rule for one group applies to only that group

subject: general
statement: Boiling water for a few seconds as it warms makes it safe.
why: Students think any heating kills germs.
fix: Water should reach a rolling boil and continue for about a minute. Then let it cool in a covered container.

probe.question: How long should drinking water boil?
probe.wrong_answer: Until bubbles first appear.

root_belief: a small amount gives the full effect

subject: general
concept: Clear water is not always safe
statement: If water looks clear and has no smell, it is safe to drink.
why: Clear water is associated with purity.
fix: Germs and some chemicals are invisible, so clear water may be unsafe. Boil, filter or chlorinate it if source is uncertain.

probe.question: Is clear river water safe to drink directly?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is clear so it is clean.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
source_hint: studies of children's ideas about water purity

subject: general
concept: Clear water is not always safe
statement: A filter or cloth removes all germs from water.
why: Filtering seems to remove everything unwanted.
fix: A cloth removes only large particles. Boiling or chlorination is needed to kill germs, unless a proper purifier is used.

probe.question: Does straining water through cloth make it safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all germs are removed.

root_belief: separation works for all sizes

subject: general
statement: Antibiotics cure colds and flu.
why: Antibiotics are called the medicine for infections.
fix: Colds and flu are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work only against bacteria. Use them only when a doctor prescribes.

probe.question: A child has flu. Will antibiotics cure it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, antibiotics kill the flu germs.

root_belief: one medicine treats all related things
source_hint: surveys of public understanding of antibiotics

subject: general
statement: Stop antibiotics once you feel better.
why: Symptoms vanish before all germs are gone.
fix: Finish the full course the doctor prescribed. Stopping early can leave bacteria alive and help them become resistant.

probe.question: Fever is gone on day 2 of a 5-day course. What should you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Stop taking the medicine.

root_belief: feeling better means problem is gone
source_hint: public health surveys on antibiotic use

subject: general
statement: Vaccines give you the disease so they are unsafe.
why: Students hear that a vaccine contains the germ.
fix: Vaccines use weakened, killed or partial germs, so the body learns to defend without getting the disease.

probe.question: Does a vaccine give you the disease?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it injects the disease into you.

root_belief: the cause itself is what is given

subject: general
statement: Sleep is just the body switching off to rest, and nothing useful happens.
why: The sleeping person is still and unresponsive, so it looks like nothing is happening.
fix: During sleep the body repairs itself, releases hormones, fights germs and the brain organises memories.

probe.question: What useful work does your body do while you sleep?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, it just rests like a switched-off machine.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not happen

subject: general
statement: The brain completely switches off when we sleep.
why: People are unaware of their surroundings, so students assume the brain stops.
fix: The brain stays very active in sleep, and in dream sleep it is nearly as active as when awake.

probe.question: Is the brain active during sleep?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it switches off until morning.

subject: general
statement: Everyone of every age needs exactly 8 hours of sleep.
why: The '8 hours' rule is repeated everywhere, so students treat it as one number for all ages.
fix: Sleep needs depend on age. Children aged 6-12 need about 9-12 hours and teenagers about 8-10 hours, while adults need about 7-9 hours.

probe.question: A 7-year-old and a 40-year-old both sleep exactly 8 hours. Are both getting the right amount?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because everyone needs exactly 8 hours.

root_belief: One sleep duration fits all ages
source_hint: WHO or national health guidelines on sleep duration

subject: general
statement: Teenagers sleep late only because they use phones and are not disciplined.
why: Students and adults blame the late bedtime on habits alone and ignore the body's own timing change.
fix: During puberty the body clock shifts later, so teens feel sleepy later at night. Phones can make it worse, but they are not the only cause.

probe.question: Why does a teenager often not feel sleepy until 11 pm or later?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they use phones and lack discipline, nothing else.

root_belief: Behaviour alone explains teen sleep timing

subject: general
statement: Missing sleep only makes you feel tired and has no other effect on the body.
why: Students link sleep loss only with the feeling of tiredness.
fix: Too little sleep also lowers attention and memory, affects mood, weakens the body's defence against infection and can slow growth in children.

probe.question: A student sleeps 4 hours daily for a week. Apart from tiredness, what changes?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing else changes, only tiredness.

root_belief: Sleep loss only causes tiredness
source_hint: school health textbook or public health sleep guidance

subject: general
statement: The body clock works only on how tired we are, and light does not affect it.
why: Students think sleepiness comes only from effort and activity during the day.
fix: The body clock is set mainly by light. Bright light in the morning keeps it on time, and light at night delays it.

probe.question: Does sitting in a brightly lit room at night change when you feel sleepy?
probe.wrong_answer: No, sleepiness depends only on how much work you did.

root_belief: Sleepiness comes only from tiredness

subject: general
statement: Watching TV or a phone in bed helps you relax and fall asleep faster.
why: Screens feel relaxing, so students assume they help sleep.
fix: Screen light delays melatonin, and exciting content keeps the mind alert, so screens before bed usually make it harder to fall asleep.

probe.question: Will watching videos in bed for an hour help you sleep sooner?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it relaxes you so you fall asleep faster.

root_belief: Relaxing activities always help sleep
source_hint: studies on adolescent bedtime screen use

subject: general
statement: Sleeping very long on Sunday fully makes up for sleeping little all week.
why: Students think sleep is like a bank balance that can be repaid in one go.
fix: Weekend sleep gives some relief, but it cannot fully repay weekday sleep debt, and it can upset the body clock. Regular sleep is better.

probe.question: You slept 5 hours on weekdays and 12 hours on Sunday. Is the damage fully repaired?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the extra hours cancel the lost sleep completely.

root_belief: Lost sleep can be repaid fully later

subject: general
statement: A cup of tea or cola at night does not affect sleep because it is a cold or sweet drink.
why: Students link caffeine only with hot coffee and ignore it in other drinks.
fix: Tea, cola and energy drinks contain caffeine, which keeps you alert for hours and can delay and disturb sleep if taken late.

probe.question: Does a cola at 9 pm affect sleep?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only hot coffee affects sleep.

root_belief: Only coffee contains caffeine
source_hint: health guidance on caffeine in drinks

subject: general
statement: Studying hard through the night before an exam is better than sleeping.
why: Students believe more hours of study always means more marks.
fix: Sleep helps the brain store what was studied and keeps attention sharp for the exam. Good sleep after studying helps more than extra hours awake.

probe.question: Is it better to stay up all night studying or sleep 8 hours before the exam?
probe.wrong_answer: Stay up, because more study time gives more marks.

root_belief: More waking study always beats sleep
source_hint: research on sleep and learning in students

subject: general
statement: We dream throughout the night in the same way, and sleep is one single steady state.
why: Students picture sleep as one flat stretch with no stages.
fix: Sleep moves in cycles of light, deep and dream (REM) sleep, repeated several times each night, and the brain behaves differently in each.

probe.question: Is the brain doing the same thing in the first hour and the fourth hour of sleep?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, sleep is the same all night.

root_belief: Sleep is uniform all night
source_hint: NCERT or standard biology sources on sleep stages

subject: general
statement: Children grow taller during the day while awake and sleep has nothing to do with growth.
why: Students link growth only with food and exercise.
fix: Growth hormone is released mostly in deep sleep, so sleep helps children's growth along with food and activity.

probe.question: Does sleep help a child grow taller?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only food and exercise help growth.

root_belief: Growth depends only on food and exercise

subject: general
statement: Feeling sad, angry or scared is bad, and good people only feel happy.
why: Children are often praised for being cheerful and scolded for showing anger or sadness.
fix: All emotions, including sadness, anger and fear, are natural and everyone feels them. What matters is how we handle them.

probe.question: Riya feels very sad after losing a match. Is something wrong with her for feeling this way?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a good person should not feel sad.

root_belief: some natural feelings are bad and must not exist

subject: general
statement: Boys should not cry or show feelings because it is a sign of weakness.
why: Social messages like 'be a man' teach children that showing emotion is shameful.
fix: Crying and showing feelings are normal human reactions for everyone. Letting feelings out is healthy, not weak.

probe.question: Arjun cries when he fails a test. What does this say about him?
probe.wrong_answer: That he is weak.

root_belief: gender decides how a person may feel
source_hint: studies on gender stereotypes and emotional expression in adolescents

subject: general
statement: The best way to deal with a worry is to keep it inside and not think about it.
why: Ignoring a problem gives short relief, so it seems to work.
fix: Bottled-up feelings usually grow stronger. Talking, writing or drawing about them helps them settle.

probe.question: Meena is upset about a fight with a friend. What is the best way to deal with it?
probe.wrong_answer: Keep quiet and forget about it.

root_belief: hiding a problem makes it go away
source_hint: research on emotional suppression and avoidance coping

subject: general
concept: Stress is the body's response to demands
statement: All stress is harmful and should be completely avoided.
why: The word 'stress' is mostly used in a negative way in daily talk.
fix: A small amount of stress can help us stay alert and prepare, such as before a race. It becomes a problem when it is too much or lasts too long.

probe.question: Is a little nervous energy before a school performance always bad?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all stress is bad.

root_belief: a thing is either wholly good or wholly bad

subject: general
concept: Healthy ways to cope with stress
statement: Sleeping less and studying all night is the best way to do well in exams.
why: Students think more hours of study always means more marks.
fix: The brain needs sleep to remember and think clearly. Regular sleep, breaks and exercise help performance and lower stress.

probe.question: Before an exam, Ravi studies the whole night without sleep. Is this a good plan?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, more study hours always give better marks.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
source_hint: sleep research on memory and adolescent exam performance

subject: general
statement: Feeling anxious or nervous means a person has a mental illness.
why: Students take one common feeling as proof of a disease.
fix: Everyone feels anxious sometimes. It becomes an anxiety problem only when it is very strong, lasts long and disturbs daily life.

probe.question: Sana feels nervous before an exam. Does she have an anxiety disorder?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, being nervous means she has a mental illness.

root_belief: one sign means the whole condition

subject: general
statement: Anxiety is just silliness, and a person can stop it by trying harder.
why: Anxiety cannot be seen, so people think it is only a matter of attitude.
fix: Anxiety is a real condition linked to the brain and body, and strong willpower alone cannot switch it off. Support and sometimes treatment help.

probe.question: A friend has constant strong anxiety. What should they do to stop it?
probe.wrong_answer: Just try harder and stop being silly.

root_belief: feelings can be switched off by will alone
source_hint: mental health literacy surveys on stigma toward anxiety

subject: general
statement: Anxiety is only in the mind and never causes body symptoms.
why: Students separate the mind and the body completely.
fix: Anxiety can cause a fast heartbeat, sweating, stomach ache, headache and trouble sleeping.

probe.question: Before a test Kabir gets a stomach ache and a racing heart. Can anxiety cause this?
probe.wrong_answer: No, anxiety only affects thoughts.

root_belief: mind and body are separate
source_hint: research on somatic symptoms in child and adolescent anxiety

subject: general
concept: Marks do not decide a person's worth
statement: Your marks show how valuable you are as a person.
why: Praise and comparison at home and school focus mainly on marks.
fix: Marks show how you did in one test. They do not measure your worth, kindness, talents or future.

probe.question: Neha got low marks in maths. Does it mean she is not a valuable person?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, low marks mean she is worth less.

root_belief: one number measures a whole person
source_hint: studies on academic contingent self-worth in Indian adolescents

subject: general
statement: The more pressure we feel before exams, the better we will perform.
why: Some pressure does push students to work, so they assume more is always better.
fix: Moderate pressure can motivate, but too much pressure causes panic and blocks memory and thinking.

probe.question: Will extreme pressure from everyone before the exam improve a student's score?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, more pressure gives better marks.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
source_hint: research on arousal and performance in test anxiety

subject: general
statement: Failing one exam ruins your whole life.
why: Adults and peers often talk about one board exam as the only chance.
fix: One exam is a single step. There are many chances and paths to try again and succeed.

probe.question: A student fails a unit test. Is their future finished?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, one failure ruins everything.

root_belief: one event decides everything forever

subject: general
concept: Planning, rest and breaks for exams
statement: Taking breaks or playing during exam days is wasting time.
why: Students link only continuous study with seriousness.
fix: Short breaks, play and rest refresh the brain and improve learning. A simple timetable with breaks reduces stress.

probe.question: Is a 20 minute walk during study time a waste?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it wastes study time.

root_belief: continuous effort always beats rest

subject: general
statement: Mental health and mental illness mean the same thing.
why: Both phrases contain 'mental' and are often used together.
fix: Mental health is our state of emotional and thinking well-being, which everyone has. Mental illness is a condition that affects it and can be treated.

probe.question: A student says 'I am working on my mental health.' Does this mean they are mentally ill?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, mental health means illness.

root_belief: related words mean the same thing
source_hint: mental health literacy research on terminology confusion

subject: general
statement: Mental health matters only for people who are already ill.
why: People talk about physical health only when someone falls sick.
fix: Like physical health, mental health needs care for everyone every day, through sleep, friends, activity and talking.

probe.question: Does a healthy, happy student need to care for their mental health?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only ill people need it.

root_belief: health matters only when sick

subject: general
statement: Having a mental illness is a sign of weakness or a character flaw.
why: Society treats strength as never struggling.
fix: Mental illness is a health condition, not a weakness. It can happen to anyone, just like diabetes or asthma.

probe.question: Why does a person get depression?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they are weak-minded.

root_belief: strength means never struggling
source_hint: WHO and surveys of stigma toward mental illness

subject: general
statement: People with mental illness are dangerous or 'mad'.
why: Films and news often show them as violent.
fix: Most people with mental illness are not dangerous. They are more likely to be hurt or left out than to hurt others.

probe.question: Should we stay away from a classmate who has anxiety?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they may be dangerous.

root_belief: what looks different is a threat
source_hint: media portrayal studies of mental illness

subject: general
statement: Mental illness never gets better, so treatment is useless.
why: Students think a long-lasting problem is permanent.
fix: Most mental health problems can be treated with talk therapy, medicines or both, and many people recover and lead full lives.

probe.question: Can a person with depression get better?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it never goes away.

root_belief: a long-lasting problem is permanent
source_hint: WHO mental health fact sheets on treatability

subject: general
statement: Positive thinking alone can cure any mental illness, so no treatment is needed.
why: Motivational messages say a good attitude fixes everything.
fix: Being positive helps, but real conditions often need support from counsellors or doctors, just like a fever needs care.

probe.question: A friend has severe depression. Is positive thinking alone enough?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, just think positive.

root_belief: positive thinking alone fixes any problem

subject: general
concept: Causes are not magic or punishment
statement: Mental illness is caused by black magic, evil spirits or punishment for bad deeds.
why: Traditional beliefs explain unseen problems with unseen forces.
fix: Mental illness comes from a mix of brain chemistry, genes, life events and stress, not from magic or punishment. Doctors can help.

probe.question: A man hears voices and feels very low. What is the likely cause?
probe.wrong_answer: An evil spirit or a curse.

root_belief: unseen causes explain what we cannot see
source_hint: studies of supernatural beliefs about mental illness in India

subject: general
concept: Talking to a trusted adult helps
statement: Talking about my problems will only make them worse or burden others.
why: Students fear being judged or being a nuisance.
fix: Sharing with a trusted adult usually brings relief and ideas for solving the problem. Most adults want to help.

probe.question: Tara is worried about bullying. Should she tell her teacher?
probe.wrong_answer: No, talking will make it worse.

root_belief: speaking about a problem makes it bigger

subject: general
concept: Who can be a trusted adult
statement: Only parents can be trusted adults.
why: Children think of help as coming only from home.
fix: A trusted adult can be a parent, relative, teacher, school counsellor or any adult who listens and keeps you safe.

probe.question: If a student cannot talk to parents, who else can they go to?
probe.wrong_answer: No one, only parents can help.

root_belief: only one kind of person can help

subject: general
statement: Only people who are 'mad' or in extreme crisis go to a counsellor or doctor.
why: Seeking help is linked with shame in many communities.
fix: Anyone can meet a counsellor for stress, worry or sadness. Going early is a wise step, like seeing a doctor for a fever.

probe.question: Aman feels very stressed but not in crisis. Should he see a counsellor?
probe.wrong_answer: No, counsellors are only for very serious cases.

root_belief: seek help only when it is extreme
source_hint: surveys on help-seeking barriers among Indian adolescents

subject: general
statement: Mental health helplines are only for adults and cost money.
why: Students assume services are meant for others and are paid.
fix: Free helplines such as Tele-MANAS (14416) run by the Government of India offer support round the clock, and young people can call too.

probe.question: Can a Class 9 student call Tele-MANAS 14416 for support?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is for adults and is paid.

root_belief: services are meant for others, not me

subject: general
concept: Helping a friend who is struggling
statement: If a friend shares their sadness, I must keep it a secret even if they might be in danger.
why: Loyalty is understood as never telling anyone.
fix: If a friend seems to be in danger or may hurt themselves, tell a trusted adult. This is caring, not betrayal.

probe.question: A friend says they feel hopeless and want to hurt themselves, but asks you to keep quiet. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Keep the secret and tell no one.

root_belief: loyalty means never telling anyone

subject: general
concept: Helping a friend who is struggling
statement: Asking a friend if they feel very low or hopeless will put harmful ideas in their head.
why: People fear that naming a danger creates it.
fix: Asking kindly and listening does not cause harm and often brings relief. Then help them reach a trusted adult.

probe.question: Should you ask a withdrawn friend, 'Are you okay?'
probe.wrong_answer: No, asking may make things worse.

root_belief: naming a danger creates the danger
source_hint: WHO guidance and studies on asking about suicidal thoughts

subject: general
statement: Tying a tight rope above a bleeding wound is the best way to stop bleeding.
why: Films and old stories show tourniquets as the standard answer to any bleeding.
fix: Pressing firmly on the wound with a clean cloth is the first step. A tight band can damage the limb and is only for trained people in life-threatening bleeding.

probe.question: A boy's arm is bleeding from a cut. What should you do first?
probe.wrong_answer: Tie a tight rope above the cut.

root_belief: stronger, more extreme action works better

subject: general
statement: If a cloth soaks through with blood, you should remove it and put on a fresh one.
why: Students think the soaked cloth is now useless and must be replaced.
fix: Do not remove the soaked cloth because it disturbs the clot. Add more cloth on top and keep pressing.

probe.question: The cloth on a wound is full of blood. What next?
probe.wrong_answer: Remove it and put a new cloth directly on the wound.

root_belief: used things must be replaced to work

subject: general
concept: Wash a minor cut with clean running water
statement: Pouring turmeric, ash or toothpaste on a cut heals it and prevents infection.
why: Home remedies are passed down in families as natural antiseptics.
fix: These can bring in germs and cause infection. Wash the cut with clean running water and cover it with a clean dressing.

probe.question: What should you put on a fresh cut to keep germs away?
probe.wrong_answer: Turmeric powder or ash.

root_belief: natural or traditional means safe and effective

subject: general
concept: Wash a minor cut with clean running water
statement: A cut must be rubbed or scrubbed hard to get it properly clean.
why: Students link cleaning with scrubbing as with dirty clothes or utensils.
fix: Rinse gently under clean running water and pat dry around it. Hard scrubbing hurts the tissue and can restart bleeding.

probe.question: How should you clean a scraped knee?
probe.wrong_answer: Scrub it hard with a cloth until no dirt is visible.

root_belief: a rule from one situation works everywhere

subject: general
concept: Nosebleed: sit up, lean forward, pinch soft nose
statement: For a nosebleed you should tilt your head back so the blood does not come out.
why: It seems that lifting the head will stop blood from flowing out.
fix: Sit up, lean slightly forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for about 10 minutes. Tilting back lets blood run down the throat.

probe.question: A girl has a nosebleed. How should she hold her head?
probe.wrong_answer: Tilt it backwards.

root_belief: hiding a problem is the same as solving it

subject: general
concept: Cool a burn under running water for 10-20 minutes
statement: Ice or ice-cold water is the best thing to put on a burn.
why: Students think the colder the cooling, the faster the relief.
fix: Use cool running tap water for 10 to 20 minutes. Ice can further damage burnt skin.

probe.question: What should you put on a hot-water burn on the hand?
probe.wrong_answer: Ice cubes.

subject: general
concept: Antivenom from hospital is the only treatment
statement: Sucking out the venom or using a herbal paste from a local healer is enough to treat a snake bite.
why: Stories and local practices suggest that removing venom from the bite or using herbs neutralises it, so hospital care seems optional.
fix: Only antivenom given in a hospital neutralises snake venom. Sucking or herbal remedies do not work and waste precious time. Go to hospital at once.

probe.question: A farmer is bitten by a snake. A villager offers a herbal paste that he says cures snake bites. What should the family do?
probe.wrong_answer: Apply the herbal paste and wait a day; go to hospital only if the swelling gets worse.

root_belief: Traditional home remedies can replace medical treatment
source_hint: WHO snakebite guidance; Government of India national snakebite management protocol

subject: general
concept: Keep the bitten limb still and get to hospital fast
statement: After a snake bite the person should run or walk quickly to the hospital.
why: Students think speed means moving fast on foot, but they forget that movement pumps venom faster through the body.
fix: Keep the person calm and the bitten limb still, and carry or transport them to hospital by vehicle. Walking and running spread the venom faster.

probe.question: A girl is bitten on the leg by a snake and the hospital is 1 km away. How should she get there?
probe.wrong_answer: She should run to the hospital as fast as she can so she gets there sooner.

root_belief: Faster own movement always means faster help
source_hint: WHO snakebite guidance; Government of India national snakebite management protocol

subject: general
concept: Do not give food or water until fully awake
statement: A person who has fainted should be given water or sprinkled with water on the face and made to drink it right away.
why: Films show people being splashed and given water to revive them, so students believe drinking helps wake them up.
fix: Lay the person down and raise their legs. Give nothing to eat or drink until fully awake, as they could choke.

probe.question: A classmate faints in assembly and starts to open their eyes. What do you do first?
probe.wrong_answer: Pour water into their mouth so they drink and recover quickly.

root_belief: Giving drinks revives anyone who feels weak
source_hint: Indian Red Cross / St John first aid manuals

subject: general
concept: Lay the person down and raise the legs
statement: A person who feels faint should be kept sitting or standing upright, with the head held high.
why: Students think upright is the normal healthy position, and lying down looks like giving up.
fix: Fainting happens when blood flow to the brain drops. Lying flat with legs raised helps blood reach the brain.

probe.question: A girl turns pale and says she feels faint. How should she be positioned?
probe.wrong_answer: Make her stand up straight, or hold her upright, and fan her.

root_belief: Upright posture keeps a person alert
source_hint: Indian Red Cross / St John first aid manuals

subject: general
concept: CPR keeps blood moving until help arrives; it does not restart the heart by itself
statement: CPR is done to make the heart start beating again, and it works like a restart button.
why: TV scenes show the person waking up right after compressions, so students think CPR restarts the heart.
fix: CPR only keeps blood and oxygen moving to the brain and organs until help arrives. A defibrillator and medical care are needed to restart a normal heartbeat.

probe.question: After 5 minutes of CPR the person has not woken up. What does this mean?
probe.wrong_answer: CPR has failed, so you should stop because it did not restart the heart.

root_belief: First aid fully cures the problem itself
source_hint: WHO / Indian Resuscitation Council CPR guidance

subject: general
concept: 112 is the single national emergency number
statement: In an emergency you must call 100 for police, 102 for ambulance and 101 for fire, and there is no single number.
why: Older separate numbers are widely known, so students think each service needs its own number.
fix: 112 is India's single national emergency number for police, fire and ambulance. Separate numbers like 108 also work in many states.

probe.question: A house is on fire and people are injured. Which number can you dial that reaches all services?
probe.wrong_answer: There is none; you must dial 101 for fire, then 102 for ambulance separately.

root_belief: Each emergency service has only its own number
source_hint: Government of India ERSS 112 official information

subject: general
concept: Cereals, pulses, vegetables, fruits, milk and oils are different groups
statement: Pulses and vegetables are the same food group.
why: Dal is cooked like a sabzi and both are eaten with roti, so they seem alike.
fix: Pulses (dals, beans) are rich in protein and belong with protein foods, while vegetables mainly give vitamins, minerals and fibre.

probe.question: Which group gives more protein: dal or lauki?
probe.wrong_answer: Both are the same group so they give the same protein.

root_belief: things used together belong to the same category

subject: general
concept: Cereals, pulses, vegetables, fruits, milk and oils are different groups
statement: Potato is a vegetable that counts the same as green leafy vegetables.
why: Potato is sold and cooked as a vegetable.
fix: Potato is mostly starch and acts like a cereal for energy, while green leafy vegetables give iron, vitamins and fibre.

probe.question: Is aloo sabzi enough for the vegetable part of the plate?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, potato is a vegetable so it fully covers it.

root_belief: a common name decides what something is

subject: general
concept: Variety within and across groups is needed
statement: If I eat plenty of one very healthy food, I do not need other foods.
why: Advertisements and 'superfoods' promote single foods as complete.
fix: No single food gives all nutrients, so we need a variety of foods from different groups each day.

probe.question: Is eating only milk and bananas daily enough for a child?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both are very healthy so nothing else is needed.

subject: general
concept: Carbohydrates give most of our energy
statement: Carbohydrates like rice and roti are only for fattening, so athletes and growing children should avoid them.
why: Diet-culture messages and low-carb trends make students see carbohydrates as a weight-gain nutrient rather than the body's main fuel.
fix: Carbohydrates are the body's main source of energy, and the brain and muscles depend on them. Government of India dietary guidelines (ICMR-NIN) say cereals and millets should supply a large share of daily energy. Weight gain comes from eating more energy than you use, not from carbohydrates alone.

probe.question: A cricketer plays for 3 hours daily. Should he cut out rice and roti to stay fit?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, rice and roti only make you fat, so he should stop eating them.

root_belief: Carbohydrates are inherently fattening and unhealthy

subject: general
concept: Fats are needed in small amounts for energy and vitamin absorption
statement: Eating any fat or oil makes you fat, so the healthiest diet has no fat at all.
why: The word 'fat' is confused with body fat, and advertisements for fat-free products reinforce this idea.
fix: The body needs a small amount of fat for energy, for absorbing vitamins A, D, E and K, and for cell health. WHO advises that fat should be limited and unsaturated fats preferred, not removed completely.

probe.question: If a child eats food cooked with no oil at all for a year, will they be healthier?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because fat is what makes people fat, so no oil is the healthiest.

root_belief: Dietary fat equals body fat, so avoid completely

subject: general
concept: Vitamins and minerals protect and regulate the body
statement: Vitamins and minerals give us energy, so a vitamin tablet can replace a meal.
why: Tonics and supplements are advertised as 'energy boosters', so students treat vitamins as fuel.
fix: Vitamins and minerals do not provide energy; they help the body work and protect it from disease. Energy comes from carbohydrates, fats and proteins. Supplements cannot replace food, which also gives energy, protein and fibre.

probe.question: A student skips lunch and takes a multivitamin tablet instead. Will they get the energy they need?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, vitamins give energy, so the tablet is as good as a meal.

root_belief: Vitamins and supplements are sources of energy

subject: general
concept: Fibre helps digestion and has no energy use
statement: Fibre is useless because the body cannot digest it, so peeled and refined foods are better.
why: Students hear that fibre is 'not digested' and conclude that it is waste with no function.
fix: Fibre gives no energy but keeps the gut moving, prevents constipation and helps control blood sugar. WHO recommends eating whole grains, vegetables, fruits and pulses to get enough fibre.

probe.question: Is it better to peel all vegetables and fruits and throw away the roughage?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, roughage is not digested so it is of no use and should be removed.

root_belief: Indigestible means useless to the body
source_hint: NCERT Science textbook; WHO healthy diet fact sheet

subject: general
concept: Pulses plus cereals give good quality protein for vegetarians
statement: Vegetarians cannot get enough protein without eating eggs or meat.
why: Eggs and meat are shown as the main protein foods, so students believe plant foods have little or poor protein.
fix: Pulses, dals, soya, nuts and milk products provide protein. Eating dal with roti or rice together gives a good mix of amino acids, so a vegetarian diet can meet protein needs. This is an established point in Indian dietary guidelines.

probe.question: Can a vegetarian child who eats dal, roti, rice and curd get enough protein?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only eggs and meat give enough protein, so they will be short of protein.

root_belief: Only animal foods can supply enough protein

subject: general
concept: Whole grains keep bran and germ; polishing removes nutrients
statement: White polished rice and maida are healthier than brown rice and whole wheat atta because they are cleaner and finer.
why: Students link whiteness and fine texture with purity and quality, and refined foods look more attractive.
fix: Polishing and refining remove the bran and germ, which hold fibre, B vitamins and minerals. Whole grains keep these nutrients. Government dietary guidelines recommend whole grains over refined ones.

probe.question: Which gives more nutrients: whole wheat atta or maida?
probe.wrong_answer: Maida, because it is finer and cleaner, so it is more nutritious.

root_belief: Refined or processed foods are purer, hence healthier

subject: general
concept: Eating more than the body needs is stored as fat
statement: Only eating fatty or oily food makes you gain weight; eating extra rice, roti or sweets does not.
why: Students connect the word 'fat' with fatty foods only and forget that extra carbohydrate energy is also stored.
fix: Any food eaten in excess of the body's energy needs, whether carbohydrate, fat or protein, is stored as body fat. WHO says weight gain comes from an energy imbalance: more energy taken in than used.

probe.question: A boy eats no oily food but takes extra helpings of rice and sweets every day and does little activity. Will he gain weight?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because he is not eating fat, so nothing can be stored as fat.

root_belief: Only fatty food causes body fat gain
source_hint: WHO obesity and overweight fact sheet

subject: general
concept: Balanced diet depends on age, activity and sex
statement: A balanced diet is the same amount and type of food for everyone, whatever their age or work.
why: Students see one food plate chart in books and assume it gives a single fixed diet for all people.
fix: The amount of food needed depends on age, sex, body size and activity. A growing teenager, a pregnant woman and a farm labourer need more energy and certain nutrients than an inactive adult. The food groups stay the same but quantities change.

probe.question: Should a child who plays sports daily and an office worker who sits all day eat exactly the same quantity of food?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a balanced diet is the same for everybody.

root_belief: One diet fits all people

subject: general
concept: Millets are rich in fibre, iron and calcium
statement: Millets are poor people's grains and have less nutrition than rice and wheat.
why: Millets were historically seen as low-status food and replaced by polished rice and wheat, so students assume they are lower quality.
fix: Millets like ragi, jowar and bajra are rich in fibre, iron, calcium and other minerals, and often have more of these than polished rice. The Government of India promoted millets as 'Shree Anna' and the UN declared 2023 the International Year of Millets.

probe.question: Which has more calcium: ragi or polished white rice?
probe.wrong_answer: White rice, because millets are only a poor man's food with little nutrition.

root_belief: Traditional low-status foods are nutritionally inferior
source_hint: Government of India Shree Anna / ICMR-NIN

subject: general
statement: Cold drinks are mostly flavoured water, so they have very little sugar.
why: Drinks look like clear liquid and do not feel like solid sweets.
fix: A typical 300 ml cold drink has about 30 g sugar, roughly 7 to 8 teaspoons.

probe.question: A 300 ml cold drink bottle has about how much sugar?
probe.wrong_answer: Hardly any, 1 or 2 grams, since it is mostly water.

root_belief: what is liquid or invisible has little content

subject: general
concept: Sugar hides in sauces and 'healthy' foods
statement: Only sweet-tasting foods contain sugar.
why: Students link sugar with taste alone.
fix: Tomato ketchup, sauces, flavoured yoghurt and biscuits have added sugar even if not very sweet.

probe.question: Does tomato ketchup contain added sugar?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it tastes sour and spicy, so no sugar.

subject: general
statement: Fruit juice is just as healthy as eating the whole fruit.
why: Students see juice as 'made from fruit' and assume the nutrition is identical, ignoring what is lost when fruit is squeezed.
fix: Juice has most of the fibre removed and its sugar becomes 'free sugar' that is absorbed quickly. Whole fruit is more filling and healthier; WHO advises limiting juice.

probe.question: Is a glass of orange juice as healthy as eating an orange?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both are the same because juice is made from the orange.

root_belief: Processing a natural food does not change its nutrition
source_hint: WHO sugar guideline; ICMR-NIN dietary guidelines

subject: general
statement: Energy drinks give real energy and can replace food or water after sports.
why: The name 'energy drink' and sports advertising suggest it fuels the body better than meals or water.
fix: Energy drinks mostly contain sugar and caffeine. They give a short boost, do not replace meals or water, and are not recommended for children.

probe.question: After a football match, what is best to drink to refill your body?
probe.wrong_answer: An energy drink, because it gives more energy than water.

root_belief: Product names and advertisements describe true benefits

subject: general
concept: Energy drinks have caffeine and sugar
statement: Energy drinks are safe for children because they are sold in shops like other drinks.
why: Students assume anything freely sold is safe for all ages.
fix: Energy drinks contain high caffeine and sugar, which can cause sleeplessness, fast heartbeat and anxiety in children. FSSAI requires warning labels and advises against use by children.

probe.question: Can a 12-year-old safely drink an energy drink every day?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is sold openly so it is safe for everyone.

root_belief: If a product is sold freely, it is safe

subject: general
concept: Too much salt raises blood pressure
statement: Salt only affects people who are old.
why: Students link blood pressure problems with old age and think children need not worry about salt.
fix: Eating too much salt raises blood pressure at any age, and food habits formed in childhood continue later. WHO advises less than 5 g of salt a day for adults, and less for children.

probe.question: Does a 13-year-old need to worry about eating very salty chips daily?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only old people get problems from salt.

root_belief: Diet-related diseases only concern older people

subject: general
concept: Salt is in processed food, not only added at table
statement: If I do not add salt at the table, I am not eating much salt.
why: Students think of salt only as what they sprinkle themselves.
fix: Most salt comes from processed and packaged foods like chips, pickles, bread, instant noodles and sauces, not just salt added at the table.

probe.question: A boy never uses the salt shaker but eats instant noodles and chips daily. Is his salt intake low?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because he never adds salt himself.

root_belief: Only visibly added ingredients count toward intake

subject: general
statement: Sodium and salt are two different things, so low-sodium means a food has no salt at all.
why: Labels list sodium, and students do not know that salt is sodium chloride.
fix: Salt is sodium chloride; sodium is the part in it that affects blood pressure. Salt in grams is about 2.5 times sodium in grams.

probe.question: A packet says 'sodium 400 mg'. Does it contain no salt?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, sodium is different from salt so it has no salt.

root_belief: Different names mean different substances
source_hint: WHO sodium and salt conversion; food label guides

subject: general
statement: Fried food made in vegetable oil is healthy because oil comes from plants.
why: Students link 'vegetable' with healthy and ignore calories in oil.
fix: All oils are high in fat and calories, and food absorbs oil during frying. Reused oil can also form harmful trans fats. Fried snacks should be eaten only occasionally.

probe.question: Is a samosa fried in vegetable oil a healthy daily snack?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, vegetable oil is from plants so it is healthy.

root_belief: Plant-based means automatically healthy
source_hint: WHO healthy diet fact sheet; FSSAI Eat Right India

subject: general
concept: Thin people can also have unhealthy diets
statement: Only fat people need to worry about eating junk food.
why: Students judge health by body size and assume a thin body means a healthy diet.
fix: Thin people can also have high sugar, salt and fat intakes, which can harm the heart and raise diabetes risk. Body size does not show diet quality.

probe.question: A thin boy eats chips and cold drinks daily. Is his diet healthy?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, he is thin so junk food cannot hurt him.

root_belief: Body weight shows how healthy someone is
source_hint: WHO obesity and malnutrition fact sheets

subject: general
concept: Diabetes is not caused by sugar alone or catching it
statement: Diabetes spreads from one person to another like a cold.
why: Students treat all illnesses as infections that pass through touch or sharing food.
fix: Diabetes is not infectious. It develops from the body's problem in controlling blood sugar, linked to genes, diet, weight and activity.

probe.question: Can you get diabetes by sitting next to a diabetic classmate?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it can spread through close contact.

root_belief: All diseases are infectious and catching

subject: general
concept: Sugar has other names on labels
statement: If the label says 'no added sugar' or lists only 'glucose syrup' or 'jaggery', the food has no sugar worth counting.
why: Students look only for the word 'sugar' and trust natural-sounding names.
fix: Sugar appears as glucose syrup, fructose, dextrose, maltose, honey and jaggery; these all count as free sugars. Check total sugar on the nutrition label.

probe.question: A biscuit lists glucose syrup and honey but not 'sugar'. Is it sugar-free?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the word sugar is not in the ingredients.

root_belief: Only the exact word counts, not other names
source_hint: FSSAI labelling guidance; WHO free sugar definition

subject: general
concept: Free sugar should be under about 10% of energy
statement: Sugar limits mean a person may eat a lot of sugar as long as it is not in tea.
why: Students think the limit only applies to spoon sugar they add.
fix: The limit covers all free sugars in food and drinks, including sweets, biscuits, juices and sauces. WHO advises under 10% of energy, about 6 to 12 teaspoons a day.

probe.question: A girl takes no sugar in tea but eats sweets, biscuits and a cold drink daily. Is she within the limit?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, she does not add sugar to her tea.

root_belief: Only visibly spooned sugar counts toward limits

subject: general
concept: Iron is a mineral needed in small amounts
statement: Iron in the body is the same metal as iron nails and tools.
why: The same word 'iron' is used for the metal and the nutrient.
fix: The body needs iron only as a tiny amount of a mineral in food; eating iron metal or rust is harmful and not a source.

probe.question: Will sucking on an iron nail or cooking rusty iron pieces help cure anaemia?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because iron is iron

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: general
concept: Iron is a mineral needed in small amounts
statement: The more iron we eat, the healthier we become, so large amounts are always good.
why: Students think a nutrient that is good must be good in any quantity.
fix: The body needs only a small, fixed amount of iron; too much iron from tablets can be poisonous.

probe.question: A girl takes many iron tablets daily without advice. Is this safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, more iron is always better

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: general
concept: Haemoglobin carries oxygen from lungs to body
statement: Haemoglobin carries food to the body cells.
why: Blood is known as the transport fluid, so students assume it carries everything the same way.
fix: Haemoglobin in red blood cells carries oxygen; digested food is carried mainly in the plasma.

probe.question: What does haemoglobin carry?
probe.wrong_answer: Digested food and energy to the cells

root_belief: one carrier does every transport job
source_hint: studies of student ideas about blood and circulation

subject: general
concept: Haemoglobin carries oxygen from lungs to body
statement: Haemoglobin makes the body produce energy by itself.
why: Students link oxygen and energy and skip the role of food and cells.
fix: Haemoglobin only carries oxygen; cells use oxygen to release energy from food.

probe.question: Where does the energy come from when haemoglobin delivers oxygen?
probe.wrong_answer: Haemoglobin itself makes the energy

root_belief: one thing alone produces the whole effect

subject: general
concept: Haemoglobin gives blood its red colour
statement: Blood is red because it has lots of red food colour or iron rust in it.
why: Students link redness with rust and everyday colouring.
fix: Blood is red because of haemoglobin, a protein containing iron, inside red blood cells.

probe.question: Why is blood red?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it contains rust-like iron particles

root_belief: colour comes from a visible coloured substance

subject: general
concept: Anaemia is low haemoglobin or red cells in blood
statement: Anaemia means a person has too little blood.
why: 'Lack of blood' is the common way anaemia is described in daily speech.
fix: Anaemia means the blood has too little haemoglobin or too few healthy red cells, not too little blood volume.

probe.question: What is anaemia?
probe.wrong_answer: Having less quantity of blood in the body

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
source_hint: teacher-reported and diagnostic-test studies on blood and health concepts

subject: general
concept: Anaemia is low haemoglobin or red cells in blood
statement: Anaemia means the blood has no white blood cells.
why: Students mix up red and white cells.
fix: Anaemia is about haemoglobin and red blood cells; white cells fight germs.

probe.question: Which blood part is low in anaemia?
probe.wrong_answer: White blood cells

root_belief: similar-sounding parts have the same job

subject: general
concept: Anaemia is not an infection and does not spread
statement: Anaemia spreads from one person to another like a cold.
why: Students treat every illness as caused by germs.
fix: Anaemia is a deficiency problem, not an infection, so it cannot spread by touch, air or sharing food.

probe.question: Can sitting next to an anaemic friend give you anaemia?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it spreads by contact

root_belief: all diseases are caused by germs
source_hint: research on children's ideas about disease causation (germ theory overgeneralised)

subject: general
concept: Tiredness, weakness, pale skin or inner eyelids
statement: Anaemia can be recognised only when a person is very sick and in bed.
why: Students expect diseases to look dramatic.
fix: Mild anaemia can show as slight tiredness, pale skin or nails; a blood test for haemoglobin confirms it.

probe.question: A girl is often tired and pale but goes to school. Can she be anaemic?
probe.wrong_answer: No, she would be in bed if anaemic

root_belief: a real problem is always obvious

subject: general
concept: Tiredness, weakness, pale skin or inner eyelids
statement: Anyone who looks pale or is tired must have anaemia.
why: Students treat a symptom as proof of one cause.
fix: Tiredness and paleness can have many causes; anaemia is confirmed by a haemoglobin blood test.

probe.question: A boy is tired after a late night and looks pale. Is it surely anaemia?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, these are signs of anaemia

root_belief: one sign means one single cause

subject: general
statement: Feeling breathless during a run means the lungs are damaged, never a blood problem.
why: Breathing is linked only to lungs.
fix: If blood has less haemoglobin, it carries less oxygen, so the person feels breathless and tires quickly even with healthy lungs.

probe.question: A girl with healthy lungs gets breathless climbing stairs. Which part may be the problem?
probe.wrong_answer: Only her lungs

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: general
concept: Adolescent girls lose iron in menstrual blood
statement: Anaemia in girls is caused by menstruation being a disease.
why: Menstruation is misunderstood as illness.
fix: Menstruation is normal; blood loss only raises the body's need for iron, so girls need iron-rich food.

probe.question: Why are adolescent girls more at risk of anaemia?
probe.wrong_answer: Because menstruation is a sickness

root_belief: natural changes are illnesses

subject: general
concept: Growth spurt raises iron needs in all adolescents
statement: Only girls can get anaemia; boys never need extra iron.
why: Anaemia messages are aimed mostly at girls and women.
fix: Boys also grow fast in adolescence and can be anaemic, though girls are at higher risk.

probe.question: Can a 14-year-old boy have anaemia?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only girls get it

root_belief: a risk group is the only group affected

subject: general
concept: Worm infections and poor diet also cause anaemia
statement: Anaemia is caused only by not eating enough iron.
why: Textbooks stress diet, so students think nothing else matters.
fix: Hookworm infection, blood loss, malaria and poor absorption can also cause anaemia.

probe.question: A child eats well but has hookworms. Can she be anaemic?
probe.wrong_answer: No, she gets enough iron from food

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: general
concept: Green leafy vegetables, jaggery, pulses, millets are iron sources
statement: Only meat and eggs have iron, so vegetarians cannot get enough.
why: Animal foods are widely advertised as 'strong' foods.
fix: Green leafy vegetables, jaggery, pulses, ragi and other millets give iron; eating them with vitamin C foods helps.

probe.question: Name an iron-rich food a vegetarian can eat.
probe.wrong_answer: None; only meat has iron

root_belief: only animal foods give strength

subject: general
concept: Green leafy vegetables, jaggery, pulses, millets are iron sources
statement: Spinach contains so much iron that eating it once instantly cures anaemia.
why: Popeye-type media stories exaggerate spinach.
fix: Iron-rich foods must be eaten regularly over weeks to months to restore haemoglobin; one meal cannot cure anaemia.

probe.question: How soon will one plate of spinach cure anaemia?
probe.wrong_answer: Immediately, in one day

root_belief: one big dose gives instant result

subject: general
concept: Milk is a poor source of iron
statement: Milk is the best food for preventing anaemia because it is a complete food.
why: Milk is called a complete or perfect food.
fix: Milk has very little iron; relying only on milk can cause anaemia in children, so iron-rich foods are needed too.

probe.question: A girl drinks lots of milk but eats few greens or pulses. Is she safe from anaemia?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, milk gives all nutrients including iron

root_belief: a complete food contains everything in plenty
source_hint: public health nutrition guidance on iron deficiency in children with milk-heavy diets

subject: general
concept: Vitamin C helps absorb iron from plant foods
statement: Vitamin C itself contains the iron that builds haemoglobin.
why: Students merge the two nutrients mentioned together.
fix: Vitamin C does not contain iron; it helps the body absorb more iron from plant foods eaten with it.

probe.question: Why add lemon juice to a spinach meal?
probe.wrong_answer: Lemon gives extra iron

root_belief: things named together do the same job

subject: general
concept: Vitamin C helps absorb iron from plant foods
statement: If iron is in the food, all of it automatically enters the blood.
why: Students assume eating equals absorbing.
fix: Only part of the iron in food is absorbed, and how much depends on the food combination, such as vitamin C present or tea.

probe.question: Two meals have the same iron. Will the body get the same iron from both?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all iron is absorbed equally

root_belief: what goes in is fully used

subject: general
concept: Tea and coffee with meals reduce iron absorption
statement: Drinking tea or coffee with meals gives extra iron and strength.
why: Tea is considered an energising everyday drink.
fix: Tannins and similar substances in tea and coffee reduce iron absorption, so it is better to drink them between meals, not with meals.

probe.question: Is tea with lunch good for anaemia?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it adds iron

root_belief: a common habit must be healthy

subject: general
concept: Tea and coffee with meals reduce iron absorption
statement: Tea blocks iron only if it is very strong or has no milk.
why: Students think only the dark colour matters.
fix: Tea reduces iron absorption in any strength, so keep a gap of an hour or two from meals.

probe.question: Is weak tea with a meal harmless for iron absorption?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, only strong tea blocks iron

root_belief: only a large amount has any effect

subject: general
concept: Iron-folic acid tablets are given weekly under government programme
statement: Iron-folic acid tablets are medicine only for sick people and are unsafe for healthy girls.
why: Tablets are mostly linked to treating illness.
fix: Government programmes give weekly iron-folic acid tablets to adolescents to prevent anaemia, and they are safe when taken as advised.

probe.question: Should a healthy schoolgirl take the weekly IFA tablet given at school?
probe.wrong_answer: No, tablets are only for sick people

root_belief: medicine is only for the sick

subject: general
concept: Iron-folic acid tablets are given weekly under government programme
statement: Taking iron tablets means we no longer need to eat iron-rich foods.
why: Tablets seem a complete replacement for food.
fix: Tablets support but do not replace a balanced diet that includes iron-rich foods.

probe.question: After taking IFA tablets, can a girl skip greens and pulses?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the tablet is enough

root_belief: a supplement can replace a whole diet

subject: general
concept: Ingredients are listed from most to least by weight
statement: The first ingredient on the label is the smallest amount.
why: Students think lists start with small things or read the list as an unordered mix.
fix: Ingredients are listed in descending order of weight, so the first one is present in the largest amount.

probe.question: A biscuit lists: wheat flour, sugar, palm oil, salt. Which is present in the largest amount?
probe.wrong_answer: Salt

root_belief: lists start with the least important item

subject: general
concept: Ingredients are listed from most to least by weight
statement: The order of ingredients on a label is random or alphabetical.
why: Students rarely notice that label lists follow a rule and assume any list is arbitrary.
fix: The order follows a rule: the ingredient with the most weight comes first and the least comes last.

probe.question: Why is sugar listed before salt in a juice label?
probe.wrong_answer: Because s comes before... it is just in any order

root_belief: a list has no hidden rule behind its order

subject: general
concept: Splitting one ingredient into several names pushes it down the list
statement: If sugar is not the first ingredient, the food has little sugar.
why: Students look only at the first item and ignore that sugar may be split into many names.
fix: A product can list sugar, glucose syrup and maltose separately, so each sits lower but together they may be the largest part.
