probe.wrong_answer: Endlessly with no change

root_belief: a cycle diagram means perfect endless repeat

subject: general
concept: Plastic must be sorted and cleaned, and quality drops on recycling
statement: Dirty mixed plastic can be thrown together into a recycling bin and recycled.
why: Students think the recycling plant sorts and cleans everything.
fix: Food-soiled and mixed plastics spoil a batch, so plastics should be rinsed and separated by type for good recycling.

probe.question: Should a greasy plastic wrapper go with clean bottles for recycling?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all plastic can go together

root_belief: the machine will fix any mistake

subject: general
concept: Burning plastic releases toxic gases and leaves residue
statement: Burning plastic gets rid of it completely, leaving nothing behind.
why: Fire seems to make things vanish into ash or smoke.
fix: Burning turns plastic into toxic gases like dioxins and carbon monoxide and ash that harm health and air. The atoms are not destroyed.

probe.question: What happens to plastic when it is burnt in the open?
probe.wrong_answer: It disappears and the problem is solved

root_belief: burning destroys matter completely
source_hint: research on students' ideas of combustion and conservation of matter

subject: general
concept: Burning plastic releases toxic gases and leaves residue
statement: Burning plastic is harmless because the smoke is just like smoke from wood.
why: All smoke looks similar.
fix: Burning plastic, especially PVC, releases poisonous gases such as dioxins that can cause breathing problems and cancer. Wood smoke is different in what it contains.

probe.question: Is it safe to burn plastic waste near houses?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is just smoke like from wood

root_belief: things that look alike behave alike

subject: general
concept: Burying plastic in landfill only stores it
statement: Burying plastic in the ground solves the plastic problem because it is hidden.
why: Out of sight is treated as out of the way.
fix: Buried plastic stays for hundreds of years and may leak chemicals into soil and groundwater. Burying only stores it.

probe.question: Is burying plastic a permanent solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, once buried it is gone

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

subject: general
concept: Reduce and reuse come before recycling
statement: If plastic can be recycled, it is fine to use as much as we like.
why: Recycling is seen as cancelling the harm of use.
fix: Recycling is the last of the three Rs. Reducing and reusing save more resources, and much plastic is never actually recycled.

probe.question: Which is better for the environment: recycling many bottles or using fewer bottles?
probe.wrong_answer: Recycling many, as it is all the same

root_belief: one fix cancels the whole problem

subject: general
concept: Plastic waste clogs drains and causes flooding
statement: Plastic litter on the road is only an ugly sight and does not affect anything else.
why: Litter is seen as a looks problem.
fix: Plastic blocks drains and can cause waterlogging and floods, and can breed mosquitoes in stagnant water.

probe.question: How can plastic in drains cause trouble in the monsoon?
probe.wrong_answer: It cannot, it only looks dirty

root_belief: a problem has only one kind of effect

subject: general
statement: PM2.5 means 2.5 percent of the air is pollution.
why: Students read the number as a percentage or amount because of the word 'PM' and the figure.
fix: PM2.5 means particles up to 2.5 micrometres across, not a percentage. PM10 means particles up to 10 micrometres across.

probe.question: What does the 2.5 in PM2.5 tell us?
probe.wrong_answer: That 2.5 percent of the air is pollution.

root_belief: a number in a name is an amount

subject: general
statement: PM10 particles are smaller than PM2.5 particles because 10 is a bigger number.
why: Students think a bigger number means a finer or stronger thing.
fix: PM10 includes particles up to 10 micrometres, which are larger than PM2.5 (up to 2.5 micrometres). PM2.5 is the finer dust.

probe.question: Which is finer, PM2.5 or PM10?
probe.wrong_answer: PM10, because 10 is more than 2.5.

root_belief: bigger number means smaller or finer thing

subject: general
concept: Particle size and entry into the body
statement: The larger particles, PM10, are more dangerous because they are bigger.
why: Students feel bigger or more visible particles must do more harm.
fix: Smaller PM2.5 particles go deeper into the lungs and can enter the blood, so they are usually more harmful to health. Larger particles mostly get caught in the nose and throat.

probe.question: Which particles go deeper into the lungs, PM2.5 or PM10?
probe.wrong_answer: PM10, because they are bigger and heavier.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

subject: general
statement: PM2.5 and PM10 are just dust from the ground.
why: Everyday word 'dust' is used for anything floating in dirty air.
fix: Particulate matter includes soot, smoke, ash, liquid droplets and particles formed from gases, as well as soil dust.

probe.question: Name what PM can be made of.
probe.wrong_answer: Only dust and sand from the soil.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: general
concept: Pollutant gases can be invisible and odourless
statement: If the air looks clear and has no smell, it is clean and safe to breathe.
why: Students rely on what they can see and smell.
fix: Many harmful pollutants, such as carbon monoxide and very fine particles, are invisible or odourless. Air quality is checked with instruments and the AQI, not by looking.

probe.question: The sky is blue and there is no smell. Is the air definitely clean?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, we can see it is clean.

subject: general
statement: If the AQI is 100, the air is 100 percent polluted.
why: Students read the AQI number as a percentage, like marks out of 100, instead of an index on a scale.
fix: AQI is an index, not a percentage. In India's scale, 0-50 is Good, 51-100 Satisfactory, 101-200 Moderate, 201-300 Poor, 301-400 Very Poor and 401-500 Severe. A bigger number means worse air.

probe.question: A city's AQI is 100. What does this number tell you?
probe.wrong_answer: The air is completely (100 percent) polluted.

root_belief: Index numbers are percentages

subject: general
statement: The AQI is the average of all pollutant values.
why: Students think a combined index must be a mean of everything measured, like an average of marks.
fix: For each pollutant a sub-index is calculated. The AQI is the highest sub-index, so the worst pollutant decides the AQI and the category.

probe.question: PM2.5 has a sub-index of 350 and all other pollutants are below 50. What is the AQI?
probe.wrong_answer: About 100, the average of all the pollutants.

root_belief: Combined indices are averages of parts

subject: general
concept: AQI is for a place and a time, not a fixed value
statement: A city has one fixed AQI that stays the same all day and everywhere in it.
why: Students hear a city's AQI quoted as a single number in the news and think it is a permanent property of the city.
fix: AQI changes with place, time of day, weather, wind and sources. Monitoring stations in the same city can show different values, and it is usually reported as a 24-hour average or live reading.

probe.question: The AQI at one station in Delhi is 380 in the morning. Will the AQI be 380 at another station in the evening?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a city has one AQI, so it stays 380 everywhere all day.

root_belief: Air quality is a fixed city property

subject: general
statement: Winter smog in North India is caused only by stubble burning.
why: News headlines each year highlight stubble burning, so students treat it as the single cause.
fix: Stubble burning adds a lot of smoke in October-November, but vehicles, industry, dust, construction and burning of waste also add pollution. Cold weather, low wind and temperature inversion trap the pollutants near the ground.

probe.question: If all stubble burning stopped, would Delhi's winter air become completely clean?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, stubble burning is the only cause of winter smog.

root_belief: One cause explains a complex problem
source_hint: Government of India / CAQM / news explainers

subject: general
statement: Air pollution from Diwali firecrackers disappears by the next morning.
why: Students see the smoke and noise end after the celebration and assume the pollution ends too.
fix: Fine particles and gases from crackers stay in the air for many hours to days, especially in cold, still weather, and can make AQI Severe or Very Poor for a long time.

probe.question: How long does the pollution from firecrackers burst on Diwali night stay in the air?
probe.wrong_answer: Only during the night; it is gone by morning.

root_belief: Pollution vanishes when visible source stops

subject: general
concept: Indoor air can be worse than outdoor
statement: Staying inside a closed house always keeps you safe from air pollution.
why: Students assume walls and doors keep all pollution outside and see indoors as safe.
fix: Outdoor particles seep in through gaps, and indoor sources like chulha smoke, incense, mosquito coils and cooking fumes add pollution. With poor ventilation, indoor air can be as bad or worse than outdoor air. WHO says household air pollution causes millions of deaths a year.

probe.question: A family cooks on a wood chulha in a small closed room. Is the air inside safe because it is indoors?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, being inside a closed room always protects from pollution.

root_belief: Indoors is always safe from pollution
source_hint: WHO household air pollution fact sheet

subject: general
concept: Cloth and surgical masks vs N95
statement: A cloth mask or a surgical mask protects as well as an N95 against PM2.5.
why: Students think any mask covering nose and mouth works the same against all dust and smoke.
fix: Cloth and ordinary surgical masks filter few fine particles and have gaps at the sides. A well-fitted N95 filters at least 95 percent of fine particles, including PM2.5.

probe.question: Which mask gives better protection from PM2.5 smoke: a cloth mask, or a well-fitted N95?
probe.wrong_answer: Both give the same protection.

root_belief: All masks filter equally
source_hint: WHO / MoHFW mask guidance; filtration studies

subject: general
concept: Plants and trees do not fully clean air
statement: Planting a few trees or keeping a few indoor plants will fully clean polluted city air.
why: Students learn that plants give oxygen and absorb carbon dioxide, and extend this to removing all pollution.
fix: Trees trap some dust and gases, but their effect is small compared with the amount of pollution released. A few plants cannot clean heavily polluted air. Cutting pollution at the source is essential, and trees are helpful as a addition.

probe.question: Can keeping many indoor plants in a room replace the need to reduce smoke from the chulha?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, plants will clean all the smoke from the air.

root_belief: Plants remove all air pollution
source_hint: Research on indoor plants and air cleaning; CPCB / MoEFCC

subject: general
statement: Any mask that covers the nose and mouth protects fully, even if it is loose.
why: Students focus on the mask material and ignore air leaking around the edges.
fix: Air takes the easiest path, so gaps at the nose, cheeks or chin let unfiltered air in. A mask protects well only when it seals snugly on the face.

probe.question: An N95 mask is loose and has gaps at the sides. Does it still filter 95 percent of particles you breathe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the filter material works the same however it fits.

root_belief: Mask material alone determines protection

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
statement: There is plenty of water on Earth, so we can never run out of usable water.
why: Students see that most of Earth is covered by water and assume all of it is usable.
fix: Most of Earth's water is salty sea water; only about 3% is fresh and much of that is frozen or deep underground, so usable water is limited.

probe.question: Earth is mostly water. Can people ever face a shortage of usable water?
probe.wrong_answer: No, there is so much water that it can never run short.

root_belief: big total means everything is available for use
source_hint: studies of children's ideas about the water cycle and water resources

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Only about 3% of Earth's water is fresh
statement: About half of the water on Earth is fresh water that we can drink.
why: Students guess a large share because water looks abundant everywhere.
fix: About 97% of Earth's water is salty and only about 3% is fresh, and most of that is not easily reachable.

probe.question: Roughly what share of Earth's water is fresh?
probe.wrong_answer: About half of it.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Most fresh water is frozen or underground, not in rivers
statement: Rivers and lakes hold most of the fresh water on Earth.
why: Rivers and lakes are the water students see, so they assume it is the main store.
fix: Most fresh water is locked in glaciers and ice caps or lies underground; rivers and lakes hold only a tiny part.

probe.question: Where is most of the Earth's fresh water stored?
probe.wrong_answer: In rivers and lakes.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
source_hint: research on students' ideas of where water is found on Earth

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Sea water cannot be drunk or used for crops directly
statement: Sea water can be used for drinking and irrigation if we have a lot of it.
why: Students think quantity makes up for quality.
fix: Salt in sea water harms the body and crops, so it must be desalinated first, which is costly.

probe.question: A village near the sea has no fresh water. Can it simply drink and irrigate with sea water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, sea water is water and can be used directly.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
statement: Rain refills all our water, so there is no need to save water.
why: Students see rain every year and think supply is automatically restored.
fix: Rain is uneven and much runs off or evaporates; our use, especially of groundwater, can exceed what rain refills, so saving is needed.

probe.question: Since it rains every monsoon, do we still need to save water?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the rain will refill everything again.

root_belief: nature always restores what we use
source_hint: studies of children's ideas on renewable resources

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Rain is uneven across place and season
statement: Every part of India gets about the same amount of rain.
why: Students generalise from the rain in their own area.
fix: Rainfall differs widely: Meghalaya gets very heavy rain while western Rajasthan gets very little.

probe.question: Does Jaisalmer get as much rain as Cherrapunji?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all parts of India get similar rain.

root_belief: my local experience applies everywhere

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Rainfall does not automatically become usable water
statement: All the rain that falls on the ground becomes drinking water.
why: Students link rain directly to water supply without thinking about losses.
fix: Much rain flows away in drains and rivers to the sea, evaporates, or gets polluted, so only part becomes usable unless it is collected or soaks in.

probe.question: In a city with paved roads, does all rain become usable water?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all of it turns into drinking water.

root_belief: one step is the whole process

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Groundwater is stored in soil and rock pores, not in underground lakes
statement: Groundwater is a big underground lake or river.
why: Pictures and the word underground water suggest a pool of water beneath the ground.
fix: Groundwater fills tiny gaps in soil, sand and rock, like water in a wet sponge.

probe.question: What does groundwater look like under the ground?
probe.wrong_answer: A large lake or river flowing underground.

root_belief: unseen things look like familiar visible things
source_hint: studies of students' conceptions of groundwater

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Water table is the upper level of groundwater
statement: The water table is a fixed level that never changes.
why: Students picture the water table as a permanent line in the diagram.
fix: The water table rises after rain and recharge and falls when much water is pumped out or when it is dry.

probe.question: Can the water table go up or down?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it always stays at the same depth.

root_belief: diagrams show things that never change

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
statement: Groundwater refills as fast as we pump it, so it can never run out.
why: Students assume nature restores resources at the rate they are used.
fix: Recharge through soil is slow, taking years, so heavy pumping can drain groundwater faster than it refills.

probe.question: If farmers pump many borewells, will the groundwater refill at once?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it refills as fast as we take it.

root_belief: nature always restores what we use
source_hint: studies of misconceptions about renewable resources and groundwater

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Falling water table dries wells and borewells
statement: If a borewell is dry, there is no more water anywhere below that area.
why: Students think a dry well shows the groundwater is totally gone, or the opposite, that a deeper well always fixes it.
fix: A dry borewell shows the water table has fallen below its depth; digging deeper may reach water for a while but it speeds up depletion.

probe.question: A borewell goes dry. What is the best long-term solution?
probe.wrong_answer: Dig a much deeper borewell; water will always be found.

root_belief: digging deeper always solves the problem

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Rooftop harvesting collects rain for use or storage
statement: Rainwater harvesting is only useful in places that get very heavy rain.
why: Students think collecting water only makes sense where there is plenty.
fix: Harvesting helps even in dry areas, because it stores scarce rain that would otherwise be lost, as in Rajasthan's johads and tankas.

probe.question: Is rainwater harvesting useful in a low-rainfall area?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only heavy-rain places need it.

root_belief: more resource means more need to manage it

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Recharge pits and percolation let rain refill groundwater
statement: Harvested rainwater is useful only for storing in tanks, not for refilling groundwater.
why: Students picture harvesting as only roof tanks.
fix: Recharge pits, trenches and percolation tanks let rain soak into the ground and raise the water table.

probe.question: How can rain collected in a pit help wells nearby?
probe.wrong_answer: It can't, because harvested water just stays in tanks.

root_belief: one thing has only one purpose

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
statement: My water footprint is only the water I drink and use for bathing.
why: Students count only the water they directly see being used.
fix: Water footprint includes direct use plus the water used to produce food, clothes and other things we use.

probe.question: Does the water used to grow your rice count in your water footprint?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only water from my taps counts.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
source_hint: studies on students' understanding of hidden/virtual water and resource footprints

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Water footprint includes hidden (virtual) water in food and goods
statement: Making a cotton T-shirt or a kilogram of rice uses only a few litres of water.
why: Students think only of the water visible in the final product.
fix: Producing cotton, rice and many goods takes thousands of litres of water, mostly for growing the crops.

probe.question: About how much water is needed to produce one T-shirt?
probe.wrong_answer: A few litres, about a bucketful.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: A dripping tap wastes many litres over a day
statement: A slowly dripping tap wastes so little water that it does not matter.
why: Each drop looks tiny, so students ignore it adding up over time.
fix: A dripping tap can waste dozens of litres a day and thousands of litres in a year.

probe.question: A tap drips 1 drop every second, with each drop about 0.05 mL. Is the waste important?
probe.wrong_answer: No, drops are tiny, so it makes no real difference.

root_belief: small things do not add up
source_hint: studies of children's reasoning about small repeated quantities and resource waste

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Closing tap while brushing saves water
statement: Leaving the tap running while brushing teeth does not waste water since the water goes down the drain and returns to nature.
why: Students think used water just goes back to the water cycle for free.
fix: Running water wastes treated, clean water which cost energy and effort to supply; closing the tap saves many litres each time.

probe.question: Does it matter if you keep the tap on while brushing?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the water just goes back to nature anyway.

root_belief: nature always restores what we use

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
statement: Saving water is the job of adults and the government, not students.
why: Students think large systems decide water use.
fix: Small daily habits in homes and schools add up to large savings, so everyone's actions count.

probe.question: Can a student's habits change how much water a school uses?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only adults and the government can.

root_belief: my small action has no effect

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
statement: Water used for washing clothes or vegetables is useless and must be thrown away.
why: Students think used water is dirty and has no further use.
fix: Such greywater can often be reused for mopping, flushing or watering plants, though not for drinking.

probe.question: What can we do with the water left after washing vegetables?
probe.wrong_answer: Throw it away because it can't be used again.

root_belief: used means finished

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Drip irrigation delivers water at the roots
statement: Drip irrigation gives plants more water than flooding the field.
why: Students think better watering means more water.
fix: Drip irrigation gives smaller, targeted amounts at the roots, saving water and often giving equal or better yields.

probe.question: Does drip irrigation use more water than flooding a field?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it gives plants much more water.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Drip irrigation reduces evaporation and runoff loss
statement: Water that runs off or evaporates from a field is not really lost, since it goes back to the water cycle.
why: Students see the water cycle as instant and local.
fix: Evaporated or runoff water leaves the farm and is no longer available to the crop or local wells; it may fall elsewhere later.

probe.question: Is water lost by evaporation from a flooded field a real loss for the farmer?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it returns to the cycle so nothing is lost.

root_belief: nature always restores what we use
source_hint: studies of children's ideas on the water cycle

topic: Saving water at home and school
subject: general
concept: Crop choice and timing of watering affect water use
statement: Watering plants at noon in strong sun is best because the sun helps them drink.
why: Students link sun with plant growth and so with watering.
fix: Watering in early morning or evening loses less water to evaporation, so more reaches the roots.

probe.question: When is the best time to water plants?
probe.wrong_answer: At noon, when the sun is strongest.

root_belief: more of a helpful thing is always better

subject: general
concept: Internet network of many networks, no single owner
statement: One company or government owns and controls the whole internet.
why: Students see a few big brands like Google and Jio and assume they run everything.
fix: The internet is thousands of separate networks run by companies, governments and universities that agree to connect using common rules. No one owner controls all of it.

probe.question: Who owns the internet?
probe.wrong_answer: Google (or the government) owns it.

root_belief: big visible things have one owner in charge

subject: general
concept: Internet network of many networks, no single owner
statement: The internet is a single giant computer somewhere.
why: People talk about 'the net' as one place or thing.
fix: The internet is a huge number of computers and devices joined by cables and radio links. There is no single central computer.

probe.question: Where is the internet located?
probe.wrong_answer: In one huge central computer.

root_belief: one name means one single object
source_hint: studies of students' mental models of the internet in computing education research

subject: general
statement: A router makes the internet; without it the internet does not exist.
why: Home internet stops when the router is off, so it seems to create the internet.
fix: A router only passes data between your devices and other networks. The internet itself is the worldwide set of connected networks.

probe.question: A router is the source of internet. True or false?
probe.wrong_answer: True, the router produces the internet.

root_belief: the device I touch is the source of everything

subject: general
concept: Wi-Fi only links device to router
statement: Wi-Fi and the internet are the same thing.
why: Phones show 'Wi-Fi' as the way to get online, so the words are used interchangeably.
fix: Wi-Fi is a radio link between your device and a router. A Wi-Fi network can exist with no internet connection at all.

probe.question: Your Wi-Fi is connected but no website opens. What is wrong?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, Wi-Fi connected means the internet is working.

root_belief: two related terms mean the same thing
source_hint: computing education research on learners confusing Wi-Fi, web and internet

subject: general
concept: ISP sells access to the internet
statement: Internet data is free because it just exists in the air; ISPs only fix wires.
why: Students never see the infrastructure cost behind the connection.
fix: An ISP owns or rents cables and equipment that connect you to the wider internet, and charges for that access.

probe.question: Why do we pay an ISP every month?
probe.wrong_answer: For nothing real, the internet is already in the air.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not cost anything

subject: general
concept: Web is a service that runs on the internet
statement: The World Wide Web and the internet are the same thing.
why: Everyday speech uses 'net' and 'web' interchangeably.
fix: The internet is the network of connected devices; the web is one service on it, made of web pages. Email and video calls also use the internet without being the web.

probe.question: Is email part of the web or the internet?
probe.wrong_answer: Email is the web, because the web is the internet.

root_belief: two related terms mean the same thing
source_hint: research on school students' conceptions of internet versus web

subject: general
concept: Every connected device has an IP address
statement: Only computers and phones have IP addresses; a smart TV or CCTV camera does not.
why: Students link addresses with obvious computing devices.
fix: Any device that connects to a network, such as a TV, camera or smartwatch, gets an IP address to be found.

probe.question: Does a Wi-Fi CCTV camera need an IP address?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only computers do.

root_belief: a rule applies only to the typical example

subject: general
concept: IP address is not a physical street location
statement: An IP address tells exactly which house a person lives in.
why: The word 'address' suggests a home address, and crime shows reinforce it.
fix: An IP address identifies a connection on a network and can change; it usually shows only a rough area of the provider, not a house.

probe.question: If you know someone's IP address, can you find their exact flat?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it gives the exact house location.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
source_hint: studies of misconceptions about IP addresses and online privacy

subject: general
concept: DNS turns names into IP addresses
statement: You must type the numbers of an IP address to reach a website; names like google.com are the real address.
why: Students only ever see names, so names seem to be the actual address.
fix: Computers find websites using IP numbers. DNS works like a phone book that looks up the number for the name you type.

probe.question: What does DNS do when you type a website name?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing; the name itself directly points to the website.

root_belief: what I see is all that is happening

subject: general
concept: Files are split into small packets
statement: A video or photo travels over the internet as one single block.
why: A file looks like one object on screen, so students assume it moves whole.
fix: Files are cut into many small packets, each with the destination address, and sent separately.

probe.question: How does a large photo get sent to a friend?
probe.wrong_answer: The whole photo moves as one piece along one path.

root_belief: things move the way they look
source_hint: research on learners' mental models of data transmission

subject: general
concept: Packets may take different routes and are reassembled
statement: All packets of a message follow the same path and arrive in order.
why: Students imagine one fixed road like a pipe or a train line.
fix: Each packet may take a different route and arrive out of order; the receiving device puts them back in order.

probe.question: Two packets of one message take different routes. What happens?
probe.wrong_answer: This cannot happen; all must use the same path.

root_belief: one fixed path connects start and end
source_hint: studies of students' pipe or direct-line models of the internet

subject: general
concept: Most international data travels by undersea fibre cables
statement: Most internet data between countries goes through satellites.
why: Satellites are famous in news and space lessons, while cables are hidden under the sea.
fix: About 95 percent or more of international data travels through undersea fibre-optic cables; satellites carry only a small share.

probe.question: How does a video call from India to the USA mostly travel?
probe.wrong_answer: Through satellites in space.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
source_hint: surveys of public and student beliefs about internet infrastructure

subject: general
concept: Fibre cables carry data as light pulses
statement: Undersea cables carry data as electricity in copper wires or as radio waves.
why: Students know wires from electricity lessons and assume all cables carry current.
fix: Undersea internet cables use hair-thin glass fibres that carry data as pulses of light.

probe.question: What carries data inside an undersea internet cable?
probe.wrong_answer: Electric current in copper wire.

root_belief: a familiar rule from one topic works everywhere

subject: general
concept: A mobile tower links phone to the wired network
statement: Mobile phones connect to the internet directly through satellites, with no towers needed.
why: Phone signals feel wireless and 'from the sky'.
fix: A phone sends radio signals to a nearby mobile tower, which is joined to the wired network by cables.

probe.question: What does your phone connect to when you open a website on mobile data?
probe.wrong_answer: A satellite directly above.

root_belief: wireless means nothing physical is involved
source_hint: research on students' ideas of wireless communication

subject: general
statement: Wireless internet needs no wires anywhere; the whole path is through the air.
why: The word 'wireless' is taken to apply to the whole journey.
fix: Wireless covers only the last hop from device to tower or router. After that, data travels through wires and fibre cables.

probe.question: Is any wire used when you browse on mobile data?
probe.wrong_answer: No wires at all, everything is in the air.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
source_hint: computing education studies on learners' mental models of wireless networks

subject: general
concept: A server is a computer that serves data on request
statement: A server is a special kind of machine different from ordinary computers.
why: The word 'server' sounds like exotic technology.
fix: A server is a computer running software that answers requests; it is usually more powerful and runs all the time.

probe.question: Can an ordinary laptop work as a server?
probe.wrong_answer: No, servers are a completely different kind of machine.

root_belief: special names mean special kinds of thing

subject: general
concept: Website data is stored on servers, not in the air
statement: A website's pages are stored on your own phone or are just floating in the internet.
why: Pages appear instantly, so they seem to be already here or everywhere.
fix: A website's files are stored on a server. Your browser requests them and shows a copy.

probe.question: Where is a website stored?
probe.wrong_answer: In the internet itself, or on my phone.

root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
source_hint: studies on learners' beliefs about where web content lives

subject: general
concept: The cloud is other people's computers in data centres
statement: The cloud is data floating in the sky or a magical space with no physical place.
why: The word 'cloud' and its icon suggest something in the air.
fix: The cloud means computers owned by other companies in large buildings called data centres, which you use over the internet.

probe.question: Where are your cloud photos really kept?
probe.wrong_answer: Up in the air in a cloud.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
source_hint: research on public and student understanding of cloud storage

subject: general
concept: The cloud is other people's computers in data centres
statement: Photos saved in the cloud can never be lost or deleted.
why: Cloud seems permanent and unlimited.
fix: Cloud data can be lost if an account is closed, deleted by mistake or hacked, so important files need backups.

probe.question: Do you need another copy of an important file saved in the cloud?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the cloud always keeps it safe forever.

root_belief: unseen things are perfectly safe and permanent

subject: general
statement: Faster internet always means the website's server is nearby.
why: Students think speed depends only on distance.
fix: Speed depends on many things: your connection, network traffic and server load, not only distance.

probe.question: A site loads slowly even though the server is in your city. Why?
probe.wrong_answer: Impossible; nearby servers are always fast.

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: general
statement: Sending data over the internet uses up the data like fuel, so it disappears from my device.
why: Mobile 'data packs' are described as being used up.
fix: Sending a file only copies it; the original stays with you. A data pack counts how much data is transferred.

probe.question: After you email a photo, is it still on your phone?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it has moved and is gone.

root_belief: sending something means you no longer have it

subject: general
concept: Length and variety make passwords strong
statement: A short password is fine if it has one capital letter and one number.
why: Students think a few special characters are what make a password strong, and ignore length.
fix: Length matters most. A long password or passphrase with many characters is much harder to guess than a short one with a few tricks.

probe.question: Which is stronger: 'Ravi@1' or 'blue-train-eats-seven-mangoes'?
probe.wrong_answer: Ravi@1, because it has capital letter, number and symbol.

root_belief: one visible feature decides the whole quality
source_hint: studies of user perceptions of password strength and security behaviour

subject: general
concept: Length and variety make passwords strong
statement: Replacing letters with similar numbers, like p@ssw0rd, makes a password very strong.
why: The change looks clever and complicated to the student.
fix: Attackers know common swaps like a to @ and o to 0. A common word with swaps is still easy to guess.

probe.question: Is 'p@ssw0rd' a strong password?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it uses symbols and numbers.

root_belief: looking complicated means being secure

subject: general
statement: A password made from my pet's name and birthday is safe because only I know it.
why: Students feel personal means secret, forgetting others can learn or guess this information.
fix: Names, birthdays and phone numbers can be found from posts or guessed by people who know you. Avoid personal details in passwords.

probe.question: Is 'Moti2010' (pet name and birth year) a good password?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because only I know my pet's name and year.

root_belief: what is personal to me is secret from others
source_hint: research on user password choices and personal information

subject: general
concept: Use a different password for each account
statement: Using one strong password for all my accounts is the safest and easiest way.
why: Students think a strong password is strong everywhere and find remembering many hard.
fix: If one site leaks the password, attackers try it on your other accounts. Use a different password for each important account.

probe.question: Aman uses one strong password for email, games and bank. Is that safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a strong password protects every account.

root_belief: one strong protection covers everything
source_hint: password reuse studies in security behaviour research

subject: general
concept: Never share passwords, even with friends
statement: It is fine to share my password with a close friend because friends are trustworthy.
why: Students link sharing with friendship and trust, and sharing games or streaming accounts is common.
fix: Passwords should stay private. A friend might leave it somewhere unsafe, use it by mistake, or fall out with you later.

probe.question: Your best friend asks for your email password to check something. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Give it, since a best friend can be trusted.

root_belief: trusting a person makes sharing secrets risk-free

subject: general
statement: Closing the browser window logs me out of my account on a shared computer.
why: Students think closing a window ends everything, like closing a book.
fix: Many sites keep you logged in after the window closes. Always click log out, especially on school, cyber cafe or shared devices.

probe.question: After checking email in a cyber cafe, you close the browser tab. Is your account safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, closing the tab logs me out.

root_belief: closing something means ending it

subject: general
concept: Never share an OTP with anyone
statement: It is safe to tell an OTP to a bank or company caller who knows my name.
why: Students think someone who knows their name and details must be genuine.
fix: Real banks and companies never ask for your OTP. Anyone asking for it, even with your name, may be a fraudster.

probe.question: A caller says he is from your bank, knows your name and asks for the OTP. Do you tell him?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, he knows my name so he is from the bank.

root_belief: knowing some details proves someone is genuine

subject: general
concept: Never share an OTP with anyone
statement: An OTP is only dangerous to share if it is a very long number.
why: Students think only a password-like secret needs protection and a short code seems harmless.
fix: An OTP is a key for one action, such as a payment or login, and it can be used within minutes. Sharing it lets someone else do that action.

probe.question: A stranger asks for the 6-digit OTP you got. Is it harmless since it is short and expires soon?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is just a small number and expires, so it is harmless.

root_belief: small or short-lived things cannot cause big harm

subject: general
concept: Banks and officials never ask for OTP, PIN or CVV
statement: I must give my OTP or PIN to the bank caller, or my account will be blocked.
why: Fear and urgency in the call make students obey authority figures quickly.
fix: Banks never ask for OTP, PIN or CVV on call or message. Cut the call and contact the bank using its official number.

probe.question: A caller says your account will be blocked in 10 minutes unless you tell your PIN. What now?
probe.wrong_answer: Tell the PIN quickly to save the account.

root_belief: authority and urgency must be obeyed

subject: general
statement: A link is safe if the message looks neat and has the company's logo.
why: Students judge trust by how professional the message looks.
fix: Fraudsters copy logos and designs easily. Check the full web address and avoid clicking links in unexpected messages.

probe.question: An SMS with a bank logo has a link to 'bank-kyc-update.xyz'. Is it safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it has the bank's logo so it is real.

root_belief: looks professional means it is genuine
source_hint: studies of how users judge phishing emails and websites

subject: general
statement: Only strangers send phishing links, so a link from a contact is always safe.
why: Students assume danger comes only from unknown people.
fix: A hacked account or a forwarded message can send a harmful link from a friend. Be careful with unexpected links even from known people.

probe.question: Your cousin's WhatsApp sends 'Click to win free recharge'. Is the link safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it came from my cousin.

root_belief: danger comes only from strangers

subject: general
concept: Fake prizes, offers and urgent threats
statement: If a message says I won a prize or lottery, it must be real because they have my number.
why: Students think a message reaching them personally means they were truly selected.
fix: Scammers send the same message to thousands of numbers. A prize you never entered for is almost always a scam.

probe.question: You get an SMS saying you won Rs 10 lakh and must pay a small fee. What is true?
probe.wrong_answer: It is real because they sent it to my number.

root_belief: being contacted personally means it is meant for me

subject: general
concept: Fake prizes, offers and urgent threats
statement: Scams are only about money, so a request that does not ask for money is harmless.
why: Students link fraud only with payments.
fix: Fraudsters also steal passwords, personal details and photos, which can lead to account theft or blackmail later.

probe.question: A form asks only for your Instagram password to give free followers. Is it harmless since no money is asked?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they are not asking for money.

root_belief: harm only means one familiar kind of loss

subject: general
concept: Use privacy settings to control who sees posts
statement: Once I set my profile to private, nothing I post can be seen or shared by anyone else.
why: Students think private means fully hidden from everyone.
fix: Private settings limit who can see posts, but followers can still screenshot or share them. Accept only people you know.

probe.question: Meena has a private account. Can her post still spread beyond her friends?
probe.wrong_answer: No, private means nobody else can ever see it.

root_belief: a label guarantees complete protection

subject: general
concept: Posts and photos can stay online permanently
statement: If I delete a post, it is gone from the internet forever.
why: On screen a deleted post vanishes, so students think it is erased everywhere.
fix: Others may have already saved, screenshotted or shared it. Information posted online can stay around, so think before posting.

probe.question: You post a photo and delete it after an hour. Can others still have it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, deleting removes it from everywhere.

root_belief: what I cannot see no longer exists
source_hint: studies of adolescents' understanding of digital footprints and online permanence

subject: general
concept: Incognito only stops saving history on the device
statement: Incognito mode makes me anonymous, so websites and my internet provider cannot see what I do.
why: The name and the spy-like icon suggest total invisibility.
fix: Incognito only stops the browser saving history and cookies on your device. Websites, your school or network, and your internet provider can still see activity.

probe.question: Using incognito at school Wi-Fi, can the school see which sites you visit?
probe.wrong_answer: No, incognito hides everything from everyone.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
source_hint: studies of user understanding of private browsing mode

subject: general
concept: Incognito only stops saving history on the device
statement: Incognito mode protects me from viruses and fake websites.
why: Students mix up being private with being protected.
fix: Incognito does not scan for harmful files or phishing. You can still get a virus or be tricked in incognito.

probe.question: Is it safe to download a strange file in incognito mode?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, incognito blocks viruses.

root_belief: private and safe mean the same thing

subject: general
concept: Secure sites use HTTPS but this does not prove trust
statement: A website with a padlock or https is definitely trustworthy and genuine.
why: The padlock is often taught as a safety sign without explaining its limit.
fix: HTTPS only means the connection is encrypted. Fake sites can also use HTTPS, so check the web address too.

probe.question: A fake bank site shows a padlock. Is it safe to enter your details?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the padlock means it is safe.

root_belief: one sign alone proves everything is fine
source_hint: research on users' interpretation of browser security indicators

subject: general
statement: Cyberbullying is only teasing and not serious since no one is physically hurt.
why: Students see only physical harm as real harm and treat online jokes as fun.
fix: Online bullying can cause fear, sadness and stress, and it can spread widely and be hard to remove. It is a serious harm.

probe.question: Classmates post mean memes of a girl. Is it just a joke?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, nobody is hurt physically so it is harmless.

root_belief: harm only counts if it is physical
source_hint: research on adolescent perceptions of cyberbullying and online harassment

subject: general
statement: People who bully online using fake names can never be traced.
why: Students believe hiding a name means complete anonymity.
fix: Phones, apps and networks keep records, and police cyber cells can trace many offenders. Cyberbullying can be reported and punished.

probe.question: A user with a fake name keeps threatening a student. Can anything be done?
probe.wrong_answer: No, nobody can find out who it is.

root_belief: hiding one clue hides everything

subject: general
concept: What to do if bullied online: save proof, block, tell an adult
statement: If someone bullies me online, I should reply in anger or stay silent and handle it alone.
why: Students fear being blamed or think replying will end it.
fix: Do not reply. Save screenshots as proof, block the person, report it on the app and tell a trusted adult. You can also use the helpline 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in.

probe.question: You get nasty messages every day. What is the best first step?
probe.wrong_answer: Send angry replies, or hide it and tell nobody.

root_belief: problems must be solved alone without help

subject: general
concept: Think before you post or forward
statement: Forwarding someone's embarrassing photo is fine because I did not create it.
why: Students feel responsible only for what they make, not what they pass on.
fix: Sharing it spreads the harm and makes you part of the bullying. Do not forward it, and report it instead.

probe.question: A classmate's embarrassing photo reaches you. Is it okay to forward it to friends?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, I did not take it so I am not responsible.

root_belief: only the starter is responsible, not those passing it on

subject: general
statement: Reporting an online fraud is useless because money lost can never be reported or recovered.
why: Students think reporting is pointless after the damage is done.
fix: Report quickly on helpline 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in and inform the bank. Fast reporting can help freeze or recover money.

probe.question: Money was fraudulently taken through UPI an hour ago. Should you report it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the money is gone and nothing can be done.

root_belief: once something has happened, it cannot be changed

subject: general
concept: Two-step verification adds a second lock
statement: If I use OTP login, I do not need a strong password.
why: Students think the OTP is a complete replacement for the password.
fix: Two-step verification uses both. A strong password adds a layer, and if the OTP is stolen, the password still protects you.

probe.question: An account has OTP login. Can its password be '1234'?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the OTP will protect it anyway.

root_belief: one protection removes need for others

subject: general
concept: Most AI is a program, not a robot body
statement: Artificial intelligence always means a robot that looks and walks like a human.
why: Films and cartoons usually show AI as humanoid robots.
fix: Most AI is software inside phones, websites and computers. It has no body at all, like the program that suggests videos or translates text.

probe.question: Is the spam filter in your email an example of AI?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is not a robot.

root_belief: the popular picture of a thing is all of it

subject: general
concept: Normal programs follow fixed rules; AI learns its rules from data
statement: Any program that runs on a computer is artificial intelligence.
why: Students hear 'smart' and 'AI' used for every digital gadget.
fix: A normal program only follows fixed steps written by a person, like a calculator. AI is different because it learns patterns from data.

probe.question: A calculator app always adds numbers using fixed rules. Is it AI?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a computer program.

root_belief: everything in a broad group is the same kind

subject: general
concept: Normal programs follow fixed rules; AI learns its rules from data
statement: Programmers type in the answer to every possible question before an AI is used.
why: Students think computers only repeat what people stored in them.
fix: Programmers do not write all answers. They give the AI many examples, and it learns patterns to answer new questions.

probe.question: How can an AI recognise a handwritten digit it has never seen before?
probe.wrong_answer: Programmers had already stored that exact digit in it.

root_belief: output must be stored in advance, not produced
source_hint: studies of students' ideas about machine learning and computers in school computing education

subject: general
concept: Many varied examples help an AI learn better
statement: Showing an AI thousands of examples of only one kind always makes it better at everything.
why: Students believe more data is always better, ignoring variety.
fix: The examples must be varied and cover the cases the AI will meet. Many photos of only one kind of cat will not help it recognise other animals.

probe.question: An AI is trained on 10,000 photos of only white cats. Will it recognise black cats well?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because 10,000 is a lot of photos.

root_belief: more of something always means better results
source_hint: research on training data representativeness in machine learning education

subject: general
concept: AI finds patterns in data; it does not understand meaning
statement: If an AI gives a correct answer, it must understand the meaning like a person does.
why: Fluent, correct answers look like understanding.
fix: AI finds patterns in the data it was trained on. It can give right answers without knowing what the words or pictures mean.

probe.question: An AI labels a photo 'dog' correctly. Does it know what a dog is like we do?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it understands dogs just as we do.

root_belief: a correct output proves real understanding
source_hint: studies of children's and learners' anthropomorphic ideas about intelligent machines

subject: general
concept: Labelled examples tell the AI the right answer while training
statement: An AI can learn to recognise cats without anyone ever showing it examples.
why: Students think computers are born knowing things or learn by themselves like magic.
fix: An AI learns only from the data it is given, such as many photos marked 'cat' or 'not cat'. Without examples it learns nothing.

probe.question: Can an AI sort photos into 'cat' and 'dog' if it was never given any photos to learn from?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it will work it out by itself.

root_belief: knowledge appears without any input

subject: general
concept: A trained AI makes guesses on new inputs using learned patterns
statement: Once an AI is trained, its answers on new inputs are always correct.
why: Students treat computer output as exact like a calculator.
fix: A trained AI only makes a best guess from patterns, so it can be wrong, especially on cases unlike its training data.

probe.question: A trained face-unlock AI fails in dim light. Is that impossible for a trained AI?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a trained AI never makes mistakes.

root_belief: machines never make mistakes
source_hint: studies of learners' trust in algorithmic output

subject: general
concept: Chatbots write by predicting likely next words
statement: A chatbot finds a ready-made answer on the internet and copies it out.
why: Students compare chatbots with search engines.
fix: A chatbot builds its reply by predicting which words are likely to come next, based on patterns it learned from lots of text. It does not just copy a stored answer.

probe.question: How does a chatbot produce a poem you asked for that nobody wrote before?
probe.wrong_answer: It searched and copied that poem from the internet.

root_belief: answers are always looked up, never produced

subject: general
concept: A confident-sounding answer is not necessarily correct
statement: If a chatbot sounds sure and writes neatly, its answer must be correct.
why: Fluent, confident language is how people usually recognise knowledgeable speakers.
fix: A chatbot can write wrong answers in a very confident tone. How sure it sounds says nothing about whether it is true.

probe.question: A chatbot confidently says Mumbai is the capital of India. Should you trust it because it sounds sure?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it sounds very sure so it must be right.

root_belief: sounding confident means being true
source_hint: research on trust and over-reliance on AI-generated text

subject: general
concept: Chatbots can make up facts, names and sources
statement: A chatbot never makes up facts or book names; it only says things that are true.
why: Students think a computer cannot lie or invent.
fix: Chatbots sometimes invent facts, names, quotes or sources that look real but do not exist. This is called hallucination.

probe.question: A chatbot gives you the title of a book and its author for your project. Is the book surely real?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, chatbots only give true information.

root_belief: machines only produce truth
source_hint: documented AI hallucination reports in language-model evaluations and media-literacy guidance

subject: general
concept: Important answers should be checked with reliable sources
statement: If two different chatbots give the same answer, it must be correct.
why: Students think agreement between sources proves truth.
fix: Chatbots may have learned from similar data and repeat the same mistake. Check important facts in a textbook or an official government source.

probe.question: Two chatbots both say a wrong date for an event. Is the date verified?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both agree so it is verified.

root_belief: agreement between sources means it is true

subject: general
concept: Unrepresentative or prejudiced data gives unfair AI results
statement: AI trained on lots of data cannot be unfair because data is just facts.
why: Students think numbers and records are neutral.
fix: Data is collected by people and can leave out some groups or show old unfair habits. An AI learns those patterns and repeats the unfairness.

probe.question: A job-selection AI is trained on past hiring records that mostly chose men. Will it treat women fairly?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, data is only facts so it will be fair.

root_belief: data and numbers are neutral facts
source_hint: documented cases of biased hiring and face-recognition systems in algorithmic fairness research

subject: general
concept: Unrepresentative or prejudiced data gives unfair AI results
statement: An AI is biased only when its programmer deliberately wants to be unfair.
why: Students think unfairness always needs a bad intention.
fix: Bias can appear by accident when the training data misses some groups or contains old prejudice, even if nobody meant harm.

probe.question: A voice AI understands boys' voices better because it was trained mostly on boys. Did a programmer plan this?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, someone must have wanted it to be unfair.

root_belief: unfair outcomes need a deliberate cause

subject: general
concept: AI is not automatically neutral or perfect
statement: Computers have no opinions, so decisions by AI are always fairer than decisions by people.
why: Machines seem emotionless and so are assumed to be impartial.
fix: AI can copy the unfairness hidden in its data, so it is not automatically fair. People need to check its results.

probe.question: Should a school fully hand over scholarship choices to an AI because machines are fair?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a machine is always fair and has no bias.

root_belief: machines are neutral and cannot be wrong
source_hint: research on automation bias and perceived objectivity of algorithms

subject: general
concept: Maps, voice assistants, spam filters and photo apps use AI
statement: An email spam filter works only from a fixed list of banned words that people typed in.
why: Students see simple rules they can imagine and miss the learning part.
fix: Modern spam filters learn from many emails marked as spam and not spam, and keep improving. They look at many patterns, not only a few words.

probe.question: How can a spam filter catch a new spam message with words never listed before?
probe.wrong_answer: It cannot; it only catches words from its fixed list.

root_belief: a rule from simple cases works everywhere

subject: general
concept: Maps, voice assistants, spam filters and photo apps use AI
statement: AI is used only in big laboratories and space missions, not in everyday phone apps.
why: AI sounds advanced and distant from daily life.
fix: Everyday apps already use AI, such as maps predicting traffic, voice assistants, translation, photo sorting and video suggestions.

probe.question: Does a phone's voice assistant that understands your speech use AI?
probe.wrong_answer: No, AI is only in laboratories.

root_belief: advanced technology is far from daily life

subject: general
concept: Recommendations are predictions from your past activity and others' data
statement: A video app shows the same recommended videos to every user.
why: Students think an app is one fixed list like a TV channel.
fix: Recommendations are predicted separately for each user from their watching history and what similar users liked, so two people see different videos.

probe.question: You and your friend open the same video app. Will you see the same recommended videos?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the app shows everyone the same list.

root_belief: everyone gets the same output from a system

subject: general
concept: Recommendations are predictions from your past activity and others' data
statement: Whatever an app recommends is the best and most true choice for me.
why: Personalised suggestions feel like expert advice.
fix: Recommendations only predict what you may keep watching or buying from past data. They may be repetitive, miss better options or push you towards one kind of content.

probe.question: A shopping app recommends a product. Does that prove it is the best one for you?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the AI knows what is best for me.

root_belief: what is shown is the best or true choice

subject: general
concept: AI has no feelings, wishes or awareness
statement: A chatbot feels hurt or happy when you scold or praise it.
why: Chatbots speak in a friendly human way and say 'I feel'.
fix: A chatbot has no feelings or awareness. It produces words that look like feelings because it learned from human text.

probe.question: A chatbot writes 'I am sad you are leaving'. Does it really feel sad?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it feels sad like a person.

root_belief: speaking like people means feeling like people
source_hint: research on anthropomorphism of conversational agents and children's ideas about machine minds

subject: general
concept: Each AI is good only at the narrow task it was trained for
statement: An AI that plays chess better than any person can also drive a car or write stories well.
why: Students think intelligence is one general ability that carries across tasks.
fix: Most AI is built and trained for one narrow job. A chess AI has not learned to drive or write.

probe.question: A champion chess AI is put in a car. Can it drive safely?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a clever AI can do any task.

root_belief: skill in one area carries over to all
source_hint: studies of student conceptions of machine intelligence and narrow versus general AI

subject: general
statement: Artificial intelligence means a machine that is as clever as a human in everything.
why: The word 'intelligence' is taken in its everyday human meaning.
fix: In everyday technology, AI means programs that do specific tasks, like recognising speech or predicting, by learning from data. They are not all-round human minds.

probe.question: Is a photo app that sorts pictures of faces AI, even though it cannot do anything else?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is not as clever as a human.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: general
statement: AI thinks and decides what it wants on its own, just like a human mind.
why: Films and news present AI as having its own will.
fix: AI has no wishes or goals of its own. It follows patterns learned from data and the goals people set for it.

probe.question: Can a chatbot decide by itself to start working on a goal that nobody gave it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it thinks and wants things like a person.

root_belief: anything that acts like us is like us
source_hint: studies of learners' anthropomorphic and science-fiction-influenced ideas about AI

subject: general
statement: A chatbot always knows the latest news from today.
why: Students think it is connected live to everything on the internet.
fix: A chatbot learns from data collected up to a certain date, so it can miss recent events unless it is connected to a live search tool.

probe.question: Will a chatbot trained last year surely know yesterday's cricket match score?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it always knows the latest news.

root_belief: a tool knows everything up to this moment

subject: general
concept: Phones send signals as radio waves
statement: Phones send voice through wires hidden in the air or the ground.
why: Old landline telephones used wires, so students assume all calls need a wired path.
fix: A phone changes your voice into a signal and sends it as radio waves through air to a tower. Wires are used only after the tower.

probe.question: How does your voice leave the phone and reach the tower?
probe.wrong_answer: Through thin wires under the ground from the phone.

root_belief: old technology rules apply to new technology

subject: general
concept: Phones send signals as radio waves
statement: Radio waves are sound waves, so they need air to travel.
why: Both are called waves and both carry voice and music.
fix: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves and can travel through vacuum, while sound needs a medium. Radio waves carry the voice as a signal.

probe.question: Can phone signals travel in empty space?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because they are sound waves and need air.

root_belief: things that do similar jobs are the same kind
source_hint: studies of students confusing sound and light or electromagnetic waves

subject: general
concept: Radio waves travel at speed of light
statement: Radio waves from phones travel slowly, like sound.
why: Students link voice with sound, which they know travels slowly.
fix: Radio waves travel at the speed of light, about 3 lakh km per second, far faster than sound.

probe.question: Which is faster, a phone signal or sound in air?
