why: Most students see UPI only through smartphone apps.
fix: UPI can also work on basic phones through services like *99# and UPI 123PAY, without a smartphone app.

probe.question: Can a person with a basic keypad phone make a UPI payment?
probe.wrong_answer: No, UPI needs a smartphone and internet.

root_belief: what I commonly see is the only way

subject: general
concept: UPI ID is a public payment address
statement: If someone knows my UPI ID, they can take money out of my account.
why: Students treat every detail of the account as a password.
fix: A UPI ID is like an address for receiving money. Taking money out needs your UPI PIN, so sharing the ID is safe.

probe.question: You give your UPI ID to a friend so they can pay you back. Is it dangerous?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they can now take money from my account.

root_belief: knowing information means having access

subject: general
concept: UPI PIN is private and needed to send money
statement: The UPI PIN is the same as my ATM card PIN or phone lock code.
why: All three are short numeric codes and are used for similar-sounding security.
fix: The UPI PIN is set separately for UPI. It can be different from the ATM PIN and the phone lock code, and must be kept secret like them.

probe.question: You forgot your UPI PIN. Can you use your phone lock code instead?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the UPI PIN is the same as the phone lock code.

root_belief: similar-looking things are the same thing

subject: general
concept: UPI PIN is private and needed to send money
statement: A bank or UPI app employee may sometimes need my PIN to fix a problem.
why: Students believe officials need complete access to help them.
fix: No bank or UPI app staff will ever ask for your PIN. Anyone who asks for it is a fraudster.

probe.question: A caller says they are from your bank and need your UPI PIN to reverse a failed payment. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Give the PIN, since they are from the bank.

root_belief: an official helper needs full access
source_hint: RBI and NPCI public awareness campaigns on digital fraud; surveys of fraud victims

subject: general
concept: OTP is a one-time code that is never shared
statement: An OTP is safe to tell someone if they say they are from my bank.
why: Students trust anyone who claims authority and think OTPs are harmless numbers.
fix: An OTP is meant only for you. Never share it with anyone, including people who say they are from the bank.

probe.question: A caller from 'the bank' asks for the OTP you just received to cancel a wrong payment. Should you tell it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they are from the bank.

root_belief: people claiming authority can be trusted
source_hint: RBI public awareness material on OTP fraud; studies of vishing victims

subject: general
statement: A caller who knows my name and bank details must be genuine.
why: Students think only a real bank could know such personal details.
fix: Fraudsters collect names and details from leaks and social media. Knowing your details does not prove a caller is genuine.

probe.question: A caller says your name, bank and last four account digits and asks for your OTP. Is the caller real?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they know my details so they must be from the bank.

root_belief: knowing personal details proves identity
source_hint: cyber-safety awareness research on social engineering and impersonation scams

subject: general
statement: Installing an app a helpful caller asks for is harmless as long as I do not say my PIN.
why: Students think a secret is only given away by saying it aloud.
fix: Screen-sharing or remote-access apps let a stranger watch your screen and see your PIN and OTP. Never install them on a stranger's advice.

probe.question: A caller asks you to install a screen-sharing app 'to fix your refund' but says not to tell the PIN. Is it safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, since I am not telling the PIN.

root_belief: a secret is only lost if I say it

subject: general
concept: UPI PIN, OTP and ATM PIN are different things
statement: The OTP that arrives on my phone is my UPI PIN.
why: Both are secret numeric codes used for approving money matters.
fix: A PIN is a fixed secret you create and remember. An OTP is a new code sent for one use only and expires quickly.

probe.question: Is your UPI PIN the number that comes by SMS each time?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the SMS number is the PIN.

root_belief: similar-looking things are the same thing

subject: general
concept: Receiving money never needs a PIN
statement: To receive money by UPI I must enter my PIN.
why: Students copy the sending steps and assume every money step needs a PIN.
fix: A PIN is needed only to send money. Receiving money never needs your PIN, so anyone asking for it to 'send you money' is cheating.

probe.question: A buyer says: 'Enter your PIN to receive my payment.' What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Enter the PIN because receiving needs it.

root_belief: every step of a process needs the same checks
source_hint: RBI and NPCI awareness advisories on receive-money and marketplace scams

subject: general
concept: A QR code only carries payee details
statement: Scanning a QR code sent by a buyer will make money come into my account.
why: Students think scanning always means taking and not giving.
fix: Scanning a QR code and entering a PIN sends money out of your account. You never need to scan anything to receive money.

probe.question: A buyer sends you a QR code to scan so they can pay you. What happens when you scan and enter your PIN?
probe.wrong_answer: I receive the money.

root_belief: the direction of an action is always inward
source_hint: NPCI and RBI fraud awareness advisories on QR code scams

subject: general
statement: Only the amount matters when paying a QR code; the name shown does not.
why: Students focus on the number they type and skip the payee details.
fix: Always read the payee name on the confirmation screen. A wrong name may mean you are paying a stranger.

probe.question: You scan a shop's QR but the name shown is a person you don't know. What should you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Pay anyway, since the amount is correct.

root_belief: only the numbers matter

subject: general
concept: A QR code only carries payee details
statement: A printed QR code at a shop is always genuine.
why: Students trust anything that looks official and printed.
fix: Fraudsters can paste fake QR codes over real ones. Check the payee name shown after scanning.

probe.question: A QR sticker is pasted at a roadside stall. Is it safe to pay without checking?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a printed QR is always genuine.

root_belief: looking official means genuine

subject: general
concept: Approving a collect request sends money
statement: Approving a collect request means I will receive money.
why: The word 'accept' sounds like receiving something.
fix: A collect request asks you to pay. Approving it and entering your PIN sends money out of your account.

probe.question: You get a collect request from a stranger. If you approve it, who gets the money?
probe.wrong_answer: I get the money.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
source_hint: NPCI and RBI awareness advisories on collect request fraud

subject: general
concept: Decline collect requests you did not expect
statement: A collect request mentioning a prize or refund is safe to approve.
why: Students believe a good-sounding message means a good purpose.
fix: Scammers use words like refund, cashback or prize to trick you. Decline any collect request you did not expect.

probe.question: A collect request says 'Cashback Rs 500, approve to claim'. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Approve it to get the cashback.

root_belief: a nice message means a nice intention

subject: general
concept: Daily UPI limit is usually Rs 1 lakh
statement: There is no limit on how much money can be sent by UPI in a day.
why: Digital payments feel unlimited because no physical cash is handled.
fix: UPI has limits, usually Rs 1 lakh a day per account for most payments. Banks and apps may set lower limits.

probe.question: Can you send Rs 5 lakh to a friend through UPI in one day?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, UPI has no limit.

root_belief: digital things have no limits

subject: general
concept: Daily UPI limit is usually Rs 1 lakh
statement: Using two different UPI apps gives me a separate daily limit on each.
why: Students think each app keeps its own count.
fix: Limits are set on the bank account, so using more apps does not add more limit for the same account.

probe.question: Your limit is Rs 1 lakh a day. Can you send Rs 1 lakh from one app and Rs 1 lakh from another for the same account?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, each app has its own limit.

root_belief: separate containers have separate limits

subject: general
concept: Ordinary UPI payments are free for users
statement: Every UPI payment costs the sender a fee.
why: Students assume digital services always charge, like card or transfer fees.
fix: Ordinary UPI payments between people and to shops are free for users.

probe.question: Do you pay a fee to send Rs 100 to a friend by UPI?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, UPI always charges a fee.

root_belief: every service must charge a fee

subject: general
statement: Once money is sent through UPI to a fraudster, nothing can be done.
why: Students think digital payments cannot be undone.
fix: Report immediately to your bank and call 1930 or use cybercrime.gov.in. Quick reporting can help freeze the money.

probe.question: You were cheated of Rs 2000 by UPI. What is the point of reporting?
probe.wrong_answer: No point, money sent is gone forever.

root_belief: what is done digitally cannot be undone

subject: general
statement: I should wait a few days before reporting a UPI fraud to be sure.
why: Students feel unsure and hope the money may return.
fix: Report within minutes or hours. Faster reporting gives a better chance to stop the money from being withdrawn.

probe.question: You notice a fraud payment. When should you report it?
probe.wrong_answer: After a few days when I am sure.

root_belief: waiting is harmless

subject: general
concept: SI = P x R x T / 100
statement: Simple interest does not depend on how long the money is kept or borrowed.
why: Students focus on principal and rate, the 'visible' numbers, and treat time as just a label.
fix: Simple interest grows with time: double the years and the interest doubles, since SI = P x R x T / 100.

probe.question: What is the simple interest on Rs 2000 at 5% per year for 1 year, and for 3 years?
probe.wrong_answer: Rs 100 in both cases

root_belief: only the main quantity matters, not duration

subject: general
statement: The simple interest on a loan is the total money you pay back at the end.
why: The words interest and amount are used loosely in daily talk about money owed.
fix: Interest is only the extra money; the amount to repay is principal plus interest.

probe.question: Rs 1000 is borrowed at 10% simple interest per year for 2 years. How much must be repaid?
probe.wrong_answer: Rs 200

subject: general
statement: Compound interest means the interest rate itself keeps increasing every year.
why: Students hear that money 'grows faster' and assume the rate rises, instead of seeing that the same rate applies to a growing balance.
fix: The rate stays the same. Interest is calculated each period on a bigger amount (principal plus earlier interest), so the rupee interest grows.

probe.question: Rs 1000 is invested at 10% per year compound interest. What rate applies in the second year?
probe.wrong_answer: More than 10%, because it is compound interest.

root_belief: Growth in interest amount means growth in rate

subject: general
concept: CI equals SI for the first period, then exceeds it
statement: Compound interest is always larger than simple interest, even for the first year.
why: Students overgeneralise 'CI beats SI' without noticing that no earlier interest exists in the first period.
fix: For the first period (one year with annual compounding) CI and SI are equal. CI becomes larger only from the second period onward.

probe.question: For Rs 2000 at 5% per year for 1 year, is CI more than SI?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, CI is more than SI even for one year.

root_belief: Compound always beats simple from the start

subject: general
concept: Half-yearly compounding: halve the rate, double the periods
statement: For half-yearly compounding, you halve the rate but keep the number of years the same.
why: Students remember 'halve the rate' but forget that the number of periods doubles.
fix: Half-yearly compounding means 2 periods per year at half the annual rate, so n years gives 2n periods.

probe.question: Find the amount on Rs 1000 for 2 years at 10% per year compounded half-yearly. How many periods and what rate per period?
probe.wrong_answer: 2 periods at 5% each.

root_belief: Only the rate changes with compounding frequency

subject: general
concept: Convert months or days to years before using the formula
statement: For 6 months, you put T = 6 in the formula SI = PRT/100.
why: Students plug the number given without converting units, since the formula only shows 'T'.
fix: Rate is per year, so convert time to years: 6 months = 6/12 = 0.5 year before using the formula.

probe.question: Find SI on Rs 1000 at 10% per year for 6 months.
probe.wrong_answer: Rs 600

root_belief: Use time number as given, ignoring units

subject: general
concept: Rate is per year unless stated otherwise
statement: A rate such as 2% means 2% per month unless it says per year.
why: Everyday talk of monthly money lenders' rates and monthly pocket-money or EMI payments makes students assume a monthly default.
fix: Unless stated otherwise, an interest rate in problems is per annum (per year). A monthly rate must be stated as 'per month'.

probe.question: Rs 5000 is lent at 2% simple interest. Time is 1 year. What is the interest, assuming the rate is per year?
probe.wrong_answer: Rs 1200, taking the rate as 2% per month.

root_belief: Rates default to the payment period

subject: general
statement: An EMI is just the loan amount divided equally by the number of months.
why: Students think of repayment as splitting the borrowed sum evenly and ignore the interest.
fix: EMI includes interest as well as principal repayment, so it is more than loan amount divided by months.

probe.question: A Rs 1,20,000 loan is repaid in 12 EMIs with interest. Is each EMI exactly Rs 10,000?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, Rs 1,20,000 divided by 12 is Rs 10,000.

root_belief: Repayment equals principal split into parts

subject: general
concept: Longer tenure lowers EMI but raises total interest
statement: A longer loan tenure means you pay less in total because each EMI is smaller.
why: Students focus on the smaller monthly payment and overlook the extra months of interest.
fix: A longer tenure lowers each EMI but interest accrues for more months, so total interest paid is higher.

probe.question: Which costs less overall: a 5-year loan or a 10-year loan for the same amount at the same rate?
probe.wrong_answer: The 10-year loan, because the EMI is smaller.

root_belief: Smaller payment means lower total cost

subject: general
statement: A flat rate of 8% and a reducing-balance rate of 8% cost the borrower the same.
why: Students see the same percentage and assume the same cost, overlooking what it is charged on.
fix: A flat rate charges interest on the original principal for the whole tenure, while reducing-balance interest is charged only on the outstanding balance. So a flat rate costs more; its effective rate is higher.

probe.question: Loan A is 8% flat and Loan B is 8% reducing balance, same amount and tenure. Which costs more?
probe.wrong_answer: Both cost the same because both are 8%.

root_belief: Same quoted percentage means same cost

subject: general
concept: Fees and charges add to the loan cost
statement: If the interest rate is low, the loan has no other costs to worry about.
why: Students treat the advertised interest rate as the entire price of the loan.
fix: Processing fees, late-payment charges and prepayment charges add to the cost. Compare the total cost, not just the interest rate.

probe.question: Bank A offers 9% with a 2% processing fee. Bank B offers 9.2% with no fee. Which is surely cheaper because of the lower rate?
probe.wrong_answer: Bank A, since 9% is lower than 9.2%.

root_belief: Interest rate alone defines loan cost

subject: general
concept: Interest-free period needs full bill payment on time
statement: A credit card's interest-free period applies even if you pay only part of the bill.
why: Students hear 'interest-free' and assume any payment within the period avoids interest.
fix: The interest-free period usually applies only when the full bill is paid by the due date. Otherwise interest is charged on the unpaid amount, often from the purchase date.

probe.question: You spent Rs 10,000 on a credit card and pay Rs 6,000 by the due date. Is the remaining Rs 4,000 free of interest?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, you paid within the interest-free period.

root_belief: Partial payment keeps the free period

subject: general
concept: Lottery and prize scams ask for a fee first
statement: If a message says I won a prize, I must pay a small fee first to get it, and that is normal.
why: Students think fees like taxes or courier charges are part of every genuine prize.
fix: A real prize never needs you to pay money in advance. Asking for a fee to release a prize is the main sign of a lottery scam.

probe.question: A message says you won Rs 10 lakh but must pay Rs 5,000 as processing fee. What should you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Pay the fee because it is small compared to the prize.

root_belief: paying a little first is the normal price of gains

subject: general
concept: You cannot win a contest you never entered
statement: If a message has my name and mobile number, the lottery win must be real.
why: Students think only a real organiser could know their personal details.
fix: Scammers get names and numbers from leaks and lists. Having your name does not make a message genuine, and you cannot win a draw you never entered.

probe.question: You get an SMS with your name saying you won a lucky draw you never joined. Is it real?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has my name, so they must know me.

root_belief: personal details prove something is genuine

subject: general
concept: You cannot win a contest you never entered
statement: It is worth replying just to check, because replying cannot cause any harm.
why: Students think only paying money or clicking can hurt, not a simple reply.
fix: Replying shows your number is active and invites more targeted scam attempts. It is safest to ignore, block and report such messages.

probe.question: An unknown number says you won a prize. Is it safe to reply 'who are you?'
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, replying is harmless; only paying causes loss.

root_belief: harm needs a big visible action

subject: general
statement: If a caller says they are from my bank and know my name, I can trust them and share details to update KYC.
why: Students think a caller who sounds official and knows basic facts must be genuine.
fix: Banks never ask for OTP, PIN or card details by phone or link. KYC is updated at the branch or through the bank's own app or website.

probe.question: A caller says your account will be blocked unless you tell the OTP to update KYC. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Tell the OTP so the account does not get blocked.

root_belief: sounding official means being genuine

subject: general
statement: KYC must be updated within hours by clicking the link sent by SMS, otherwise the account closes immediately.
why: Scare messages with deadlines make students believe the threat is a real bank rule.
fix: Banks give written notice and ample time and do not close accounts through sudden SMS links. Go to the branch or official app instead.

probe.question: An SMS says click this link in 2 hours to update KYC or the account closes. Should you click?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, click quickly to save the account.

root_belief: a deadline means the threat is real

subject: general
concept: Phishing uses fake messages, links and sites
statement: Phishing happens only through emails, not through SMS, WhatsApp or phone calls.
why: The word is usually explained with email examples in books.
fix: Phishing can come through email, SMS, WhatsApp, calls and social media. Any message that tricks you into sharing details or clicking a fake link is phishing.

probe.question: A WhatsApp message has a link to 'claim your electricity refund'. Can it be phishing?
probe.wrong_answer: No, phishing is only done by email.

root_belief: a word means only the first example learned

subject: general
concept: Phishing uses fake messages, links and sites
statement: A phishing link can only harm me if I type my password or pay money on the page.
why: Students think only entering details counts as danger.
fix: Some fake links install harmful apps or steal data once opened or downloaded. Do not open or download from unknown links at all.

probe.question: You get a link from an unknown sender. If you only open it and enter nothing, is it always safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is only dangerous if I type my password.

root_belief: harm needs a big visible action

subject: general
concept: Ponzi scheme pays old investors from new money
statement: A scheme that has been paying its members regular returns for months must be genuine.
why: Students think that seeing payments received proves the business really earns profit.
fix: A Ponzi scheme pays early investors using money from newer investors, so it works until new members stop joining. Then it collapses and most people lose their money.

probe.question: A company paid your neighbour 10% every month for a year. Does this prove it is real?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, getting paid regularly proves it earns real profit.

root_belief: what I have seen working will keep working
source_hint: studies of investor behaviour and regulatory reports on Ponzi and chain-money schemes

subject: general
concept: Ponzi scheme pays old investors from new money
statement: Bringing more friends into a scheme is a safe way to earn, because everyone gains.
why: Referral rewards look like a normal business or marketing method.
fix: In schemes that pay members for recruiting others, money only comes from new joiners, so the later ones lose. Such money circulation schemes are illegal in India.

probe.question: A scheme says join and earn more by adding 3 friends. Is everyone sure to gain?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, more members means more earnings for all.

root_belief: more people joining means more gain for all

subject: general
statement: Police or CBI can put a person under 'digital arrest' on a video call until they pay money.
why: News and films show arrests, so scary video calls from uniformed people seem real.
fix: There is no such thing as digital arrest in Indian law. No agency demands money or arrests people over video call; hang up and call 1930.

probe.question: A video caller in uniform says you are under digital arrest and must transfer money to be cleared. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Obey, because police can arrest anyone on a video call.

root_belief: authority figures must always be obeyed

subject: general
concept: Too-good-to-be-true returns are a red flag
statement: If a scheme promises high returns with a written guarantee, it is safe.
why: Students trust anything that is written down and looks official.
fix: Genuine investments carry risk, and higher returns usually mean higher risk. A guarantee of very high fixed returns is a classic fraud sign.

probe.question: A firm guarantees 30% profit every month with no risk. Is it safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a guarantee means no loss.

root_belief: a promise or paper guarantees the outcome
source_hint: financial literacy surveys and regulator investor-awareness material on high-return fraud

subject: general
concept: Too-good-to-be-true returns are a red flag
statement: Earning 20% a month is just a good business skill, and banks give low interest only because they are lazy.
why: Students compare bank interest with large offers without thinking how profit is produced.
fix: Bank interest is low because it is safe and based on real lending. Very high steady returns cannot come from any real business, so they signal a scam.

probe.question: Bank gives 7% a year; a scheme gives 20% a month. Which is more trustworthy?
probe.wrong_answer: The scheme, since it gives more money.

root_belief: bigger number means a better deal
source_hint: studies of numeracy and financial literacy in investment decisions

subject: general
concept: Urgency and secrecy are pressure tricks
statement: If an offer says 'only for today', I should act fast so I don't miss it.
why: Shops use limited-time sales, so urgency seems normal.
fix: Scammers create urgency so you cannot think or ask someone. A genuine offer survives a pause to check it.

probe.question: A caller says pay in 10 minutes or lose the offer. What is the best step?
probe.wrong_answer: Pay immediately so the offer is not lost.

root_belief: a rule from familiar settings works everywhere

subject: general
concept: Urgency and secrecy are pressure tricks
statement: If someone asks me to keep the deal secret from my family, it is only to protect my special chance.
why: Secrecy feels like trust and being chosen.
fix: Scammers ask for secrecy so no one can warn you. Always tell a trusted adult about any money deal.

probe.question: A person says do not tell your parents about this earning offer. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Keep it secret, since it is my special chance.

root_belief: being chosen means being trusted

subject: general
statement: Messages from unknown people are safe if they come from a number that looks like a normal 10-digit mobile number.
why: Students think scammers use strange numbers or foreign codes only.
fix: Scammers use ordinary mobile numbers and can even fake caller names. Judge the request, not how the number looks.

probe.question: A normal-looking mobile number offers a part-time job paying Rs 5,000 daily for liking videos. Is it safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a normal Indian number.

root_belief: looks normal means it is safe

subject: general
concept: Never share OTP, PIN, CVV or password
statement: It is fine to share an OTP with a bank employee because the bank sent it.
why: Students see that the OTP comes from the bank, so they think the bank may ask for it.
fix: An OTP is a secret only for you to enter yourself. No bank or company employee ever needs to ask for it.

probe.question: A caller says they are from your bank and asks for the OTP just received. Should you tell?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the bank sent it so they can have it.

root_belief: the source of a thing decides who may know it

subject: general
concept: Never share OTP, PIN, CVV or password
statement: The 3-digit CVV and the card PIN can be shared if I am also sharing the card number, because they are the same kind of information.
why: Students treat all card numbers as just numbers printed or set for the card.
fix: The PIN, CVV, OTP and password are secret codes that must never be shared with anyone. Together with the card number they let others take money.

probe.question: A caller asks only for your CVV 'to cancel a wrong charge'. Is that okay?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, CVV is only a small number on the card.

root_belief: short or small things carry little risk

subject: general
concept: Receiving money never needs your PIN
statement: To receive money by UPI I must enter my PIN, so a person asking me to enter my PIN to get a refund is correct.
why: Students mix up the actions of paying and receiving, as both use the same app screens.
fix: You enter the UPI PIN only to send money, never to receive it. If a request asks for a PIN to give you money, it is a scam.

probe.question: A buyer says: scan this QR and enter your PIN to receive Rs 2,000. Should you?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the PIN is needed to receive money.

root_belief: two similar actions work the same way

subject: general
concept: Check the web address before entering details
statement: If a website shows a padlock sign or starts with https, it is surely genuine and safe.
why: Safety lessons mention the padlock as a good sign, so it is taken as complete proof.
fix: A padlock only means the connection is encrypted, and fake sites can have it too. Check the full address spelling and use official apps or sites.

probe.question: A fake-looking bank site has a padlock. Is it safe to enter details?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the padlock shows it is genuine.

root_belief: one good sign proves something fully safe
source_hint: cybersecurity user-awareness studies on misreading padlock and https indicators

subject: general
concept: Verify through an official channel yourself
statement: To check if a call is genuine, I should call back the number given by the caller or in the message.
why: Calling back feels like a proper check, so students assume it works.
fix: The number given by the scammer leads to the scammer. Find the real number on your card, passbook or the bank's official website.

probe.question: A message says call 98xxxxxx to confirm your bank alert. How do you verify it?
probe.wrong_answer: Call that number and ask if it is real.

root_belief: checking with the same source gives proof

subject: general
statement: A scheme with a nice office, ID cards and a certificate is a registered, legal investment.
why: Students link buildings, papers and staff to legitimacy.
fix: Check that the company or adviser is registered with a regulator such as SEBI or RBI on its official website. Offices and certificates can be faked.

probe.question: A firm has a big office and a certificate. Is that enough to trust its deposit scheme?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a real office means it is legal.

root_belief: looking professional means being legitimate

subject: general
statement: Cyber fraud can only be reported by going to a police station, and 1930 is for other emergencies.
why: Students link all crime reporting only with the police station and general emergency numbers.
fix: Call the national cyber crime helpline 1930 or file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in from home. You can also visit the police station.

probe.question: Someone has just cheated you of money by UPI. Which number or website can you use?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the police station; 1930 is not for this.

root_belief: one familiar route is the only route

subject: general
concept: Report quickly so money can be frozen
statement: If the money is already gone, there is no use reporting, so I can wait and see.
why: Students feel transferred money cannot be traced or brought back.
fix: Reporting quickly, ideally within the first hours, helps banks and police freeze the money before it moves on. Waiting lowers the chance of getting it back.

probe.question: You lost money to a scam yesterday. Should you still report?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is already gone and cannot come back.

root_belief: what is done cannot be undone, so don't try

subject: general
concept: Tell the bank and block cards or UPI at once
statement: If I tell the bank about the fraud it is enough, and I need not block my card or UPI myself.
why: Students think the bank will automatically do everything once told.
fix: Block the card, UPI and net banking at once through the bank helpline or app, change passwords, and also report on 1930. Both steps matter.

probe.question: Your card details were shared with a scammer. What steps should follow?
probe.wrong_answer: Just wait; the bank will fix it later.

root_belief: one step by one authority solves everything

subject: general
concept: Anyone can be fooled; tell a trusted adult
statement: Only careless or foolish people get cheated, so I should hide it if it happens to me.
why: Students link fraud with stupidity and fear being blamed or laughed at.
fix: Scammers are skilled at tricking even educated and careful people. Telling a trusted adult and reporting quickly is the right and brave step.

probe.question: A friend lost money to a fake KYC call. What should they do?
probe.wrong_answer: Hide it, because only foolish people get cheated.

root_belief: bad things happen only to careless people
source_hint: research on victim blame and under-reporting of fraud

subject: general
statement: Only educated people or people who own property can vote.
why: Old rules in many countries and some village talk linked voting to schooling or land.
fix: Every Indian citizen aged 18 or above can vote, whether rich or poor, educated or not, man or woman, of any caste or religion.

probe.question: Ramesh is 40, cannot read, and owns no land. Can he vote in the Lok Sabha election?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because he is not educated and owns no property.

subject: general
statement: Election officials can see which candidate each person voted for.
why: Students see officials handling the machine and the voter list and assume they can link a name to a vote.
fix: The voter list and the EVM votes are kept separate. Votes are counted only in total for each candidate, so no one can tell how any one person voted.

probe.question: After you vote, can the polling officer find out whom you voted for?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the officer can check the machine and see my choice.

root_belief: Officials can link voters to their votes
source_hint: Election Commission of India voter education material

subject: general
concept: EVM is a standalone machine, not online
statement: EVMs are connected to the internet or Wi-Fi, so they can be hacked from far away.
why: Students think all digital devices are online, and social media rumours repeat this.
fix: Indian EVMs are standalone machines. They have no internet, Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, and run a one-time programmed chip, so they cannot be controlled remotely.

probe.question: How is an EVM connected to the counting centre during voting?
probe.wrong_answer: It is connected through the internet and sends the votes online.

root_belief: Every electronic device is networked online
source_hint: Election Commission of India EVM FAQs

subject: general
concept: EVM has a control unit and a ballot unit
statement: The EVM is one single unit where the voter presses a button and the vote is counted inside the same box.
why: Students picture a simple machine with buttons and miss that there are two parts.
fix: The EVM has a Ballot Unit, where the voter presses the button, and a Control Unit, which stays with the polling officer and records the votes. A cable joins them.

probe.question: How many main parts does an EVM have and which one does the voter use?
probe.wrong_answer: One part only, and the voter uses it as well as the officer.

root_belief: EVM is a single undivided device

subject: general
concept: VVPAT slip lets the voter verify the vote
statement: The VVPAT slip is given to the voter to take home as proof of the vote.
why: Students think a printed slip is like a receipt and should be carried away.
fix: The voter sees the slip through a glass window for about 7 seconds. It then drops into a sealed box and is not handed over, which also keeps the vote secret.

probe.question: What happens to the VVPAT slip after you see it?
probe.wrong_answer: I take it home with me as a receipt.

root_belief: A printed slip is a receipt to keep
source_hint: Election Commission of India VVPAT guidelines

subject: general
concept: NOTA means None of the Above, a valid choice
statement: A NOTA vote is a wasted or invalid vote, like leaving the ballot blank.
why: Students think that voting for none of the candidates means the vote is not counted.
fix: NOTA is an option on the EVM and a NOTA vote is a valid vote that is counted and recorded. It lets a voter say they reject all candidates.

probe.question: If 500 people press NOTA, are those votes counted as valid votes?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are wasted votes and not counted.

root_belief: Rejecting all candidates makes a vote invalid

subject: general
concept: NOTA does not decide the winner
statement: If NOTA gets the most votes, the election is cancelled and held again.
why: Students think the largest share of votes always decides the outcome, even if it is NOTA.
fix: Even if NOTA gets the most votes, the candidate with the most votes among the actual candidates is declared the winner. NOTA does not cause a re-election.

probe.question: In a seat NOTA gets 5,000 votes and the best candidate gets 4,000. What happens?
probe.wrong_answer: NOTA wins so the election is cancelled and held again.

root_belief: NOTA has power to cancel elections
source_hint: ECI clarification on NOTA; news explainers

subject: general
statement: The Election Commission is part of the ruling government and takes orders from the Prime Minister.
why: Students see ministers and officials together and assume the commission works under the government of the day.
fix: The Election Commission is an independent constitutional body under Article 324. It conducts elections without taking orders from the government.

probe.question: Who controls the Election Commission's decisions during elections?
probe.wrong_answer: The Prime Minister and the ruling party control it.

root_belief: All official bodies work under the government

subject: general
concept: Code applies from announcement until results
statement: The Model Code of Conduct applies only on the polling day.
why: Students link elections only to the day of voting and miss the campaign period.
fix: The Model Code of Conduct starts when the Election Commission announces the election schedule and stays in force until the results are declared.

probe.question: For how long does the Model Code of Conduct apply?
probe.wrong_answer: Only on the day people vote.

root_belief: Election rules apply only on voting day
source_hint: Election Commission of India MCC manual

subject: general
concept: Code stops misuse of government power and resources
statement: The Model Code of Conduct is a law and breaking it sends a candidate straight to jail.
why: Students treat any official rule for elections as a criminal law with fixed punishments.
fix: The Model Code is a set of guidelines agreed by parties, not a separate law. Its aim is to stop ruling parties from misusing government power, such as announcing new schemes or using official vehicles for campaigns. The Commission can warn or censure, and some acts also break other laws.

probe.question: Can a minister use a government vehicle for campaigning during the code period?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a minister can use it freely because they are in government.

root_belief: Rules are either full law or no rule

subject: general
statement: A candidate must get more than half of all votes to win a seat.
why: Students carry over the idea of a majority from class votes and think winning needs 50 percent.
fix: In Indian Lok Sabha and Assembly elections, the candidate who gets the most votes wins, even with less than half of the total. This is called first past the post.

probe.question: Four candidates get 30%, 28%, 22% and 20% of the votes. Who wins?
probe.wrong_answer: Nobody wins because no one has more than 50 percent.

root_belief: Winning always needs an absolute majority

subject: general
concept: Voters elect their MP or MLA, not the PM directly
statement: Voters directly vote for the Prime Minister on the EVM.
why: Media talk about leaders and party faces makes students think the PM's name appears on the ballot.
fix: Voters choose a candidate for their own constituency to be MP. The party or alliance with a majority of MPs chooses the Prime Minister.

probe.question: Whose name do you find on the EVM in a Lok Sabha election?
probe.wrong_answer: The name of the Prime Minister candidate.

root_belief: People directly elect the head of government

subject: general
concept: Voting is a right and duty, not compulsory
statement: Voting is compulsory in India and a person who does not vote is punished.
why: Students hear that voting is a duty and assume it is legally required, like attending school.
fix: Voting is a right and an important duty, but it is not compulsory in India and there is no punishment for not voting.

probe.question: What happens to a citizen who does not vote in India?
probe.wrong_answer: They are fined or punished by the government.

root_belief: Civic duty means legally compulsory

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: UN is not a world government and cannot make laws for countries
statement: The UN is a world government that makes laws all countries must obey.
why: The name 'United Nations' and news of UN 'orders' sound like a ruling authority.
fix: The UN is an organisation of sovereign countries that work together. It cannot pass laws over a country; countries agree to its decisions and treaties.

probe.question: Can the UN pass a law that India must obey like a Parliament law?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, UN laws are above every country's laws.

root_belief: a big organisation at the top must rule everyone
source_hint: research on students' ideas about international organisations in civics education

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: UN is not a world government and cannot make laws for countries
statement: The UN President rules the world.
why: Students map the idea of a country's President or PM onto the UN.
fix: The UN has a Secretary-General who is the chief administrator and voice of the UN, not a ruler. Member countries decide policies.

probe.question: Who is the head ruler of all countries in the UN?
probe.wrong_answer: The UN President.

root_belief: every organisation has a single ruler like a country

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: UN has no army of its own; peacekeepers are lent by members
statement: The UN has its own big army that it sends to fight wars.
why: Films and news show blue-helmet soldiers and 'UN forces'.
fix: The UN has no standing army. Peacekeeping troops come from member countries on loan for each mission.

probe.question: Where do UN peacekeeping soldiers come from?
probe.wrong_answer: From the UN's own permanent army.

root_belief: visible uniform means a permanent owned force

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: UN is not a world government and cannot make laws for countries
statement: If the UN says a country must stop, that country is forced to stop.
why: Students assume international bodies have police power like a state.
fix: The UN can only appeal, impose sanctions or authorise action through the Security Council; it cannot directly force a country, so some countries ignore it.

probe.question: Why did a country continue an action despite a UN call to stop?
probe.wrong_answer: Impossible; the UN can force any country to obey.

root_belief: authority always has power to enforce

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: UN was formed in 1945 after World War II to maintain peace
statement: The UN was formed to fight wars and punish countries.
why: Its link with war news makes it seem like a military alliance.
fix: The UN was set up in 1945 to prevent wars through talks, law and cooperation, and also to help development and human rights.

probe.question: What was the main aim of forming the UN in 1945?
probe.wrong_answer: To fight wars against aggressive countries.

root_belief: peace organisations work mainly through force

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: UN has 193 member states and HQ in New York
statement: The UN headquarters is in Geneva or Delhi, and only a few big countries are members.
why: Students confuse UN offices in Geneva with the headquarters and assume only powerful states join.
fix: The UN headquarters is in New York, with other offices in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi. Almost every country, 193 in all, is a member.

probe.question: Where is the UN headquarters?
probe.wrong_answer: Geneva.

root_belief: a famous place of work is the main centre

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: UN agencies like WHO, UNICEF, UNESCO do development work
statement: The UN only deals with wars and security, not health or education.
why: News highlights the Security Council more than UN agencies.
fix: Most UN work is on health, children, food, education and climate through agencies like WHO, UNICEF, FAO and UNESCO.

probe.question: Which UN body works for children's health and education?
probe.wrong_answer: None; the UN only handles wars.

root_belief: an institution has one function only

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: UN agencies like WHO, UNICEF, UNESCO do development work
statement: WHO, UNICEF and UNESCO are separate organisations unrelated to the UN.
why: They have their own names and logos.
fix: They are specialised agencies or programmes within the UN system, funded and run with member countries.

probe.question: Is WHO part of the UN system?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is an independent organisation.

root_belief: different names mean unrelated things

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: General Assembly: every member has one equal vote
statement: In the General Assembly, bigger or richer countries get more votes.
why: Students assume power in the world is mirrored in voting rights.
fix: In the General Assembly each member country, large or small, has one vote.

probe.question: How many votes does India have compared with Bhutan in the General Assembly?
probe.wrong_answer: India has many more votes.

root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
source_hint: studies of students' ideas on voting and equality in civics

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: International Court of Justice settles disputes between states
statement: The International Court of Justice can punish individual criminals and leaders directly.
why: Students mix up courts for countries with criminal courts.
fix: The ICJ settles legal disputes between countries only, and gives advice to UN organs; it does not try individuals.

probe.question: Does the ICJ try individual leaders as criminals?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it jails them.

root_belief: all courts work the same way

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: Security Council has 5 permanent and 10 elected members
statement: All 15 Security Council members are permanent and have equal power.
why: Students think all members of a council share equal rank.
fix: Only 5 members (US, UK, France, Russia, China) are permanent. 10 others are elected for two-year terms.

probe.question: How many permanent members does the Security Council have?

root_belief: members of a group are all equal

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: Security Council has 5 permanent and 10 elected members
statement: The five permanent members are the five most populous countries.
why: Students guess that size decides a place.
fix: They are the main winners of World War II, chosen in 1945. India, the most populous country, is not one of them.

probe.question: Why is China, but not India, a permanent member?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it has the most people.

root_belief: size or population decides status

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: A veto by any permanent member blocks a resolution
statement: A resolution passes if most of the 15 members vote yes, even if one permanent member says no.
why: Students apply simple majority rule from class elections.
fix: A veto by any one of the five permanent members blocks a resolution even if all others agree.

probe.question: 14 members vote yes and 1 permanent member votes no. What happens?
probe.wrong_answer: The resolution passes.

root_belief: majority rule works in every vote
source_hint: civics education research on majority rule assumptions

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: Security Council resolutions are binding; Assembly's are recommendations
statement: Everything the UN General Assembly decides is binding on all countries.
why: Students think a vote of nearly all countries must be a command.
fix: General Assembly resolutions are recommendations; only Security Council decisions are legally binding on members.

probe.question: Is a General Assembly resolution legally binding?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, every country must obey it.

root_belief: a decision by many becomes a compulsory law

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: Peacekeepers need consent of the host country and keep peace, not fight wars
statement: UN peacekeepers go anywhere and fight to defeat one side.
why: Students think soldiers always fight wars.
fix: Peacekeepers go only with the consent of the host country, stay neutral, and use force mainly in self-defence or to protect civilians.

probe.question: What is the main role of UN peacekeepers?
probe.wrong_answer: To defeat the aggressor in battle.

root_belief: soldiers exist to fight

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: G20 is a forum of 19 countries plus the EU (and AU from 2023)
statement: G20 means 20 countries are members.
why: The number 20 in the name is read literally.
fix: G20 has 19 countries plus the European Union, and the African Union joined in 2023, so 21 members.

probe.question: How many countries are in the G20?
probe.wrong_answer: Exactly 20 countries.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: G20 members hold about 85% of world GDP and discuss economy, not make binding laws
statement: The G20 is a part of the UN and can make laws.
why: Students lump all global bodies together.
fix: The G20 is an informal forum of major economies, separate from the UN, and has no power to make binding laws.

probe.question: Can the G20 pass laws binding its members?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a UN body that makes laws.

root_belief: all global bodies are one system

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: G20 members hold about 85% of world GDP and discuss economy, not make binding laws
statement: The G20 includes almost every country in the world.
why: Students think 'world summit' means everybody attends.
fix: The G20 has only about 20 members, but they have around 85 percent of world GDP and two-thirds of the world population.

probe.question: Is Nepal a G20 member?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all countries are members.

root_belief: a world event includes everyone

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: India held G20 presidency in 2023; summit in New Delhi in September
statement: The G20 summit in India was held in 2023 in Mumbai.
why: Students link big events to well-known cities like Mumbai.
fix: India held the G20 presidency in 2023, and the leaders' summit was held at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi in September 2023, with meetings across many cities.

probe.question: In which city was the 2023 G20 leaders' summit?
probe.wrong_answer: Mumbai.

root_belief: the biggest known city hosts big events

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: African Union became a permanent G20 member at Delhi summit
statement: India became a permanent G20 member in 2023 because it was host.
why: Hosting is confused with membership.
fix: India was already a member; the presidency rotates among members. In 2023 it was the African Union that was added as a permanent member.

probe.question: Which group joined the G20 at the 2023 Delhi summit?
probe.wrong_answer: India.

root_belief: hosting something means owning it

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: Theme: One Earth, One Family, One Future (Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam)
statement: The G20 2023 theme was about only trade and money.
why: Students think the G20 is a purely financial meeting.
fix: The theme 'One Earth, One Family, One Future' covered climate, health, digital public infrastructure, and development along with the economy.

probe.question: What did the G20 2023 theme 'One Earth, One Family, One Future' stress?
probe.wrong_answer: Only trade and money.

root_belief: an institution has one function only

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: Treaties and agreements are voluntary commitments by countries
statement: Once a country signs an international treaty, no one can ever stop it from breaking it, so treaties are meaningless.
why: Students see news of countries violating agreements.
fix: Treaties are voluntary, and countries follow most of them because of trust, trade and diplomatic cost; some have mechanisms like sanctions or courts.

probe.question: Why do countries usually follow treaties they have signed?
probe.wrong_answer: They do not; treaties have no effect.

root_belief: if rules are broken sometimes they never work

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: India is not a permanent member of the Security Council
statement: India is a permanent member of the UN Security Council.
why: India's big role and population make it seem permanent.
fix: India is not a permanent member. It has been elected non-permanent member several times and seeks permanent reform of the Council.

probe.question: Does India have veto power in the Security Council?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, India is a permanent member with veto.

root_belief: importance in a field means formal status

topic: The UN, G20 and India in the world
subject: general
concept: India is a founding member of the UN and a major peacekeeping contributor
statement: India joined the UN only recently, after becoming a big economy.
why: Students link global roles to recent economic news.
fix: India was a founding member in 1945, even before independence, and has sent peacekeepers to many UN missions.

probe.question: When did India become a UN member?
probe.wrong_answer: In the 1990s after liberalisation.

root_belief: present importance means recent beginning

subject: general
concept: Solar cells convert sunlight into electricity
statement: Solar panels work by trapping the Sun's heat to boil water and turn turbines.
why: Students link solar with heat from the Sun and with steam turbines in thermal plants.
fix: Solar photovoltaic cells directly change light into electricity without heat or moving parts. Only solar thermal systems use heat.

probe.question: How does a solar panel on a roof make electricity?
probe.wrong_answer: It heats water to steam which spins a turbine.

root_belief: all electricity comes from spinning turbines

subject: general
concept: Solar cells convert sunlight into electricity
statement: Solar panels need hot weather and give no electricity in cool weather.
why: Students mix up heat with light because the Sun gives both.
fix: Solar cells use light, not heat, and actually work slightly better when cool. Bright sunny winter days give good output.

probe.question: Will a solar panel work well on a bright, cold day in Leh?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is too cold for solar panels.

root_belief: heat and light are the same thing

subject: general
concept: Solar parks are large fields of panels
statement: Solar parks take away land only from forests, so they are always harmful to nature.
why: Large land use is easily linked with cutting forests.

probe.question: On what kind of land are many large Indian solar parks built?
probe.wrong_answer: Cleared forest land.

root_belief: one example represents all cases

subject: general
concept: Rooftop solar on homes and buildings
statement: Rooftop solar panels store the electricity for use only on that house and can never send power to the grid.
why: Students picture the panel as a self-contained battery.

probe.question: A house makes more solar power than it needs at noon. What can happen to the extra?

subject: general
concept: Rooftop solar on homes and buildings
statement: A rooftop solar system gives power at night if it is a good panel.
why: Students think panels hold energy like a battery.

probe.question: A home has rooftop panels and no battery. Does it get solar power at 9 pm?

subject: general
concept: Wind turbines turn moving air into electricity
statement: Wind turbines make wind by spinning their blades.

source_hint: Studies of student ideas on energy transfer and appearance-based reasoning

subject: general

subject: general
statement: Renewable energy means the energy can be used again and again, like recycling.

subject: general
statement: Coal and petrol will be renewed quickly by nature if we wait a few years.
why: Students do not grasp geological time.

subject: general
concept: Renewable energy has environmental costs too, but is low-carbon

probe.question: Does a solar park have any environmental impact?

subject: general
concept: Renewable energy has environmental costs too, but is low-carbon
statement: Wind turbines cause global warming by stirring the air.
why: Students link big machines with changes in weather.
fix: Wind turbines do not release greenhouse gases while working, and they help reduce global warming by replacing fossil fuels.

subject: general
concept: Target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030

subject: general

subject: general
concept: India co-founded the International Solar Alliance
statement: The International Solar Alliance is a company that sells solar panels.

probe.question: What is the International Solar Alliance?

subject: general

why: Students confuse new focus on solar with newness of all renewables.

probe.question: Which renewable source has India used for the longest time for electricity?

subject: general
concept: Solar output stops at night and falls under clouds
statement: Solar panels give no power on cloudy days.

probe.question: On a cloudy afternoon, how much electricity does a solar panel make?

subject: general
concept: Solar output stops at night and falls under clouds

why: Students notice the daytime Sun but forget night, clouds and seasons.

probe.question: What happens to a wind turbine's output when the wind drops to near zero?

subject: general
concept: Wind output varies with wind speed, with none when calm

subject: general
concept: Batteries and pumped hydro store surplus energy
statement: Batteries create new electricity from nothing, so storage makes extra energy.
why: Students think of a battery as a source.
fix: A battery stores energy that was made earlier, and some energy is lost, so it never gives more than what was put in.

probe.question: If you store 100 units in a battery, can you get back more than 100?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a battery makes extra electricity.

source_hint: Research on energy conservation and the idea of energy being produced

subject: general
concept: Mixing sources and grid connecting regions reduces the problem
statement: Intermittency is a fatal flaw, so renewables can never supply a large share of electricity.
why: Students notice the problem but not the solutions.
fix: Using solar, wind, hydro, batteries and a connected grid together balances supply. Several countries already get large shares from renewables.

probe.question: Can a grid with a lot of solar and wind be reliable?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it cannot work at all.

root_belief: one problem makes the whole idea impossible

subject: general
concept: EVs run on battery-driven motors and have no engine exhaust
statement: Electric vehicles are completely pollution-free.
why: No smoke comes from the exhaust, so students assume no pollution exists.
fix: EVs have no exhaust, but electricity and battery manufacturing can cause emissions, especially if the power comes from coal.

probe.question: Does charging an EV from a coal-powered grid cause any pollution?
probe.wrong_answer: No, EVs never cause pollution.

subject: general
concept: EVs run on battery-driven motors and have no engine exhaust
statement: An electric vehicle has an engine that burns a special fuel.
why: Students picture all vehicles with an engine and a fuel tank.
fix: An EV has a battery that powers an electric motor. No fuel is burned in it.

probe.question: What makes the wheels of an electric car turn?
probe.wrong_answer: An engine burning a clean fuel.

subject: general
concept: EV benefit depends on how the electricity is made
statement: Switching to electric vehicles alone solves India's air pollution and carbon emissions.
why: Students think of a single cause and a single fix.
fix: EVs cut tailpipe pollution, but India's total emissions also come from coal power, industry, and farming, so cleaner electricity is needed too.

probe.question: If every car in India became electric but electricity stayed coal-based, would emissions fall to zero?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all pollution would stop.

root_belief: one event has one single cause

subject: maths
concept: Multiplication and division have equal rank
statement: Multiplication always comes before division because M comes before D in BODMAS.
why: The letters in the word BODMAS are read as a strict ranking.
fix: Multiplication and division have the same rank, so we do whichever comes first from the left.

subject: maths
statement: In 8 - 3 + 2, addition must be done before subtraction, so the answer is 3.
why: Student treats A before S in BODMAS as a strict order, ignoring that addition and subtraction have equal rank.
fix: Addition and subtraction have equal rank, so work left to right: 8 - 3 = 5, then 5 + 2 = 7.

probe.question: Find the value of 8 - 3 + 2.

root_belief: Letter order in BODMAS fixes the order of operations
source_hint: research on student errors with order of operations

subject: maths
statement: In 48 ÷ 2 × 3, multiplication is done first, so the answer is 8.
why: Student believes multiplication always outranks division, ignoring left-to-right rule for equal rank.
fix: Division and multiplication have equal rank, so go left to right: 48 ÷ 2 = 24, then 24 × 3 = 72.

probe.question: Find the value of 48 ÷ 2 × 3.

root_belief: Multiplication outranks division in every expression
source_hint: studies of students' misuse of BODMAS/PEMDAS mnemonics

subject: maths
statement: In 2 × 3², you multiply 2 × 3 first and then square, so the answer is 36.
why: Student reads the expression left to right and ignores that orders (powers) rank above multiplication.
fix: Do the power first: 3² = 9, then 2 × 9 = 18.

probe.question: Find the value of 2 × 3².

root_belief: Operations are always done in written left-to-right order
source_hint: research on exponent and order-of-operations errors

subject: maths
statement: 3² means 3 × 2, so 3² equals 6.
why: Student reads the index as a multiplier instead of the number of times the base is multiplied by itself.
fix: 3² means 3 × 3 = 9; the small number tells how many times the base is used as a factor.

probe.question: Find the value of 5 + 4².

root_belief: A power means base times the index

subject: maths
statement: In brackets inside brackets, you should start with the outermost bracket first.
why: Student works from the left or outside, as they read, rather than from the innermost bracket.
fix: Simplify the innermost bracket first and then move outward step by step.

probe.question: Find the value of 20 - (3 + (2 × 4)).

root_belief: Work from outside in, following reading direction

subject: maths
statement: Curly brackets { } are always done before round brackets ( ) because they are bigger.
why: Student judges priority by the size or look of the bracket instead of by nesting.
fix: Round ( ) is cleared first, then { }, then [ ] when they are nested in that order; work from the innermost bracket outward.

probe.question: Find the value of 30 - {4 + (2 × 3)}.

root_belief: Larger-looking brackets have higher priority

subject: maths
concept: A minus sign before a bracket changes every sign inside
statement: In 10 - (3 + 2), the minus sign only changes the first number inside, so it is 10 - 3 + 2 = 9.
why: Student drops the bracket and applies the minus sign only to the first term.
fix: The minus sign applies to the whole bracket: 10 - (3 + 2) = 10 - 5 = 5, or 10 - 3 - 2 = 5.

probe.question: Remove the bracket and simplify: 10 - (3 + 2).

root_belief: A minus sign affects only the next term
source_hint: research on bracket expansion and sign errors

subject: maths
concept: A number touching a bracket multiplies the whole bracket
statement: In 4(3 + 2), the 4 touching the bracket means 4 is added to the numbers, giving 4 + 3 + 2 = 9.
why: Student ignores that a number written next to a bracket means multiplication.
fix: No sign between a number and a bracket means multiply: 4(3 + 2) = 4 × 5 = 20.

probe.question: Find the value of 4(3 + 2).

root_belief: Juxtaposition means addition, not multiplication

subject: maths
concept: Fraction bar groups numerator and denominator
statement: In (6 + 4) ÷ 2, the fraction bar in 6 + 4 over 2 divides only the 4, so the answer is 8.
why: Student does not see the fraction bar as a bracket around the numerator, so divides only the nearest number.
fix: The bar groups the whole numerator: (6 + 4)/2 = 10 ÷ 2 = 5.

probe.question: Find the value of (6 + 4)/2 written as a fraction.

root_belief: A fraction bar divides only the adjacent number
source_hint: research on hidden grouping in fractions

subject: maths
concept: Do one operation per line, copy the rest
statement: To save time, you can do all the operations in one line without copying the rest, and the answer will still be right.
why: Student combines several operations at once and loses or changes terms that were not yet worked.
fix: Do one operation per line and copy the remaining expression unchanged, so no term is dropped.

probe.question: Simplify 12 + 6 ÷ 3 - 1 step by step. What is the first line after one step?

root_belief: Skipping written steps never causes mistakes

subject: maths
concept: Scientific calculators apply BODMAS; basic ones may not
statement: A basic calculator always gives the right answer for 2 + 3 × 4 because it follows BODMAS.
why: Student trusts every calculator, not knowing basic ones may evaluate in the order keys are pressed.
fix: Scientific calculators apply BODMAS and give 14; basic ones may work left to right and give 20, so check by hand.

probe.question: A basic calculator shows 20 for 2 + 3 × 4. Is it correct?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the calculator is always correct, so 20

root_belief: All calculators follow BODMAS automatically
source_hint: research on calculator use and order of operations

subject: maths
concept: a out of b becomes a/b x 100 percent
statement: A percentage can be found only when the total is exactly 100.
why: Students hear 'out of 100' and think the total must be 100.
fix: Any part out of any total can be written as a percent by finding the equivalent fraction with denominator 100; for example 5 out of 20 is 25%.

probe.question: In a class of 20, 5 students are absent. What percent are absent?
probe.wrong_answer: Cannot be found, or just 5%

root_belief: a special case is the only case

subject: maths
concept: Same percent of different wholes gives different amounts
statement: 50% always means the same amount, whatever the whole is.
why: Students treat a percent like a fixed quantity such as 50 rupees.
fix: A percent is a fraction of the whole, so 50% of 20 is 10 but 50% of 200 is 100.

probe.question: Is 50% of a Rs 40 pen the same as 50% of a Rs 400 bag?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both are 50

subject: maths
statement: Percent is a unit of measurement like centimetres, so 20% is a fixed amount.
why: The student treats % as a unit attached to a number rather than a ratio out of 100, so the quantity it refers to is lost.
fix: Percent is a fraction with denominator 100. 20% means 20/100 of some whole, and the actual amount depends on the whole.

probe.question: A shop gives 20% off on a Rs 500 shirt. How much is the discount?
probe.wrong_answer: Rs 20

root_belief: percent is a unit giving a fixed amount

subject: maths
statement: To change a fraction like 3/5 to a percent, you just write 3/5 as 3.5%.
why: The student joins numerator and denominator as digits around a decimal point and attaches a % sign, without scaling to 100.
fix: Make the denominator 100: 3/5 = 60/100 = 60%. Or multiply the fraction by 100.

probe.question: Write 3/5 as a percent.

root_belief: percent is just fraction digits with a sign

subject: maths
statement: A fraction with a larger denominator always gives a smaller percent.
why: The student reasons only from the denominator and ignores the numerator, so 1/4 vs 3/8 or 3/4 vs 7/10 are mis-compared.
fix: Percent depends on both parts. Convert each to a percent: 3/8 = 37.5% is more than 1/4 = 25%.

probe.question: Which is greater, 1/4 or 3/8, as a percent?
probe.wrong_answer: 1/4 is greater because 4 is smaller than 8, so it is 25% against a smaller percent.

root_belief: bigger denominator always means smaller value

subject: maths
concept: Finding a percent of a number
statement: To find 25% of 80 you multiply 25 by 80.
why: The student treats 'of' as plain multiplication of the numbers and forgets that percent means per hundred.

probe.question: Find 25% of 80.

root_belief: percent of a number means multiply the numbers

subject: maths
concept: Finding a percent of a number
statement: Finding 10% of a number means dividing it by 10 only when the number is a multiple of 10, otherwise you cannot do it.
why: The student ties 10% to whole-number division and thinks answers must be whole numbers.
fix: 10% of N = N/10 for any N, and the answer may be a decimal: 10% of 45 = 4.5.

probe.question: Find 10% of 45.
probe.wrong_answer: It cannot be found because 45 is not a multiple of 10.

root_belief: percent answers must be whole numbers

subject: maths
concept: Percents greater than 100 and less than 1
statement: Percent can never be more than 100, so 150% is not possible.
why: The student has only met percent as a part of a whole, and a part cannot exceed the whole.
fix: Percent above 100 means more than the whole, e.g. 150% of 40 is 60. It is used for comparisons and growth.

probe.question: Ravi's savings this year are 150% of last year's Rs 400. How much are they now?
probe.wrong_answer: This is not possible because percent cannot be more than 100.

root_belief: percent is always between 0 and 100
source_hint: research on rational number and percent understanding

subject: maths
statement: 0.5% is the same as 0.5, or 50%.
why: The student ignores the % sign when a decimal is attached and does not divide by 100.

probe.question: Write 0.5% as a decimal.

root_belief: percent sign can be ignored with decimals

subject: maths
statement: If a price goes from Rs 80 to Rs 100, the percent increase is 20% because the difference is 20.
why: The student treats the numerical difference as the percent, as if the original were 100.
fix: Percent change = change/original x 100 = 20/80 x 100 = 25%.

probe.question: A price rises from Rs 80 to Rs 100. What is the percent increase?

root_belief: the difference itself is the percent change

subject: maths
concept: Increase then decrease by same percent does not return the original
statement: A 10% rise followed by a 10% fall brings you back to the original price.
why: The student believes opposite changes of equal size cancel, forgetting the base changes after the first step.
fix: The 10% fall is taken on the new, larger price. Rs 100 becomes 110, then 99, so it is not the original.

probe.question: A price of Rs 100 rises by 10% and then falls by 10%. What is the final price?
probe.wrong_answer: Rs 100

root_belief: equal increase and decrease cancel out

subject: maths
concept: A percentage point is the difference between two percents
statement: If a rate goes from 8% to 12%, it has increased by 12 percent.
why: The student confuses the difference in percentage points with a percent increase, or reads the new value as the change.
fix: The difference is 4 percentage points. The relative increase is 4/8 x 100 = 50%.

probe.question: A bank's interest rate rises from 8% to 12%. By how many percentage points did it rise?
probe.wrong_answer: 12 percentage points

root_belief: percentage points and percent change are the same
source_hint: research on percent vs percentage points

subject: maths
concept: Identify the digit in the rounding place
statement: To round to the nearest hundred I round the tens digit.
why: Students pick the digit just to the right of the place, which is the deciding digit, and treat it as the place to change.
fix: For the nearest hundred, the hundreds digit is the place being rounded. The tens digit only tells you whether to keep it or increase it by one.

probe.question: Round 7,468 to the nearest hundred.

root_belief: the digit I look at is the digit I change

subject: maths
concept: Only the next digit decides: 5 or more rounds up
statement: I can round one digit at a time from the right, and each new 5 makes me round up again.
why: Students treat rounding like a step-by-step carry process starting at the last digit.
fix: Look only at the single digit right after the rounding place. Rounding 1,449 to the nearest hundred gives 1,400 because 4 is less than 5.

probe.question: Round 1,449 to the nearest hundred.

root_belief: repeat a step from the end until done
source_hint: research on double rounding errors in students' estimation and rounding work

subject: maths
concept: Only the next digit decides: 5 or more rounds up
statement: If the digit in the rounding place is 5 or more, round up.
why: Students remember the 5-or-more rule but apply it to the wrong digit.
fix: The rule applies to the digit just to the right of the rounding place. In 3,748 to the nearest hundred, the tens digit 4 is below 5, so the answer is 3,700.

probe.question: Round 3,748 to the nearest hundred.

root_belief: a rule applies to the digit I am standing on

subject: maths
concept: Only the next digit decides: 5 or more rounds up
statement: Rounding always means going up to the next ten.
why: In everyday speech 'rounding up' or 'rounding off' is heard as making a number bigger or neat.
fix: Rounding means moving to the nearest ten, which can be below or above. 42 is nearer to 40 than 50, so it rounds down to 40.

probe.question: Round 42 to the nearest ten.

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

subject: maths
concept: Keep digits up to the chosen decimal place and drop the rest
statement: Rounding to a decimal place just means chopping off the extra digits.
why: Students see 'fewer digits' and cut the number without checking whether the last kept digit should go up.
fix: After keeping the digits up to the place, look at the next digit. If it is 5 or more, increase the last kept digit by one.

probe.question: Round 2.68 to 1 decimal place.

root_belief: dropping the extra part is the same as approximating
source_hint: research on students confusing truncation with rounding of decimals

subject: maths
concept: Keep digits up to the chosen decimal place and drop the rest
statement: Rounding to the nearest tenth is the same as rounding to the nearest ten.
why: The words tenth and ten sound alike and students link them.
fix: Tenth is the first place after the decimal point and ten is a whole-number place. 47.36 to the nearest tenth is 47.4, but to the nearest ten it is 50.

probe.question: Round 47.36 to the nearest tenth.

root_belief: words that sound alike name the same thing
source_hint: research on confusion between tens/tenths place value names

subject: maths
concept: Rounding a 9 up carries to the next place (4.95 to 5.0)
statement: When a 9 is rounded up, I write 10 in that place.
why: Students add one to the digit and write the result without carrying.
fix: There is no digit 10. 9 plus 1 gives 0 with a carry of 1 to the next place, so 3.96 to 1 decimal place is 4.0.

probe.question: Round 3.96 to 1 decimal place.

root_belief: a place can hold any number, not just a digit

subject: maths
concept: Rounding a 9 up carries to the next place (4.95 to 5.0)
statement: A 9 cannot be rounded up, so it stays 9.
why: Students think 9 is the biggest digit and cannot go any higher.
fix: Rounding up a 9 makes it 0 and adds 1 to the digit on its left. So 7.96 to 1 decimal place is 8.0.

probe.question: Round 7.96 to 1 decimal place.

root_belief: the biggest symbol cannot go any higher

subject: maths
concept: Halfway values such as 0.5 and 2.5 round up
statement: A number exactly halfway, like 2.5, rounds down.
why: Students feel a tie is neither up nor down and choose the smaller number.
fix: By the usual rule, a digit 5 rounds up. So 2.5 rounds to 3 and 0.5 rounds to 1.

probe.question: Round 2.5 to the nearest whole number.

root_belief: when unsure, choose the smaller

subject: maths
concept: A trailing zero after rounding shows the place kept (7.0)
statement: After rounding, 7.0 and 7 are not both needed, so I can leave out the zero.
why: Students know 7.0 equals 7 and think the zero adds nothing.
fix: The zero shows that the number was rounded to 1 decimal place. When a question asks for 1 decimal place, write 7.0.

probe.question: Round 6.96 to 1 decimal place.

root_belief: a zero adds nothing so can be left out

subject: maths
statement: Every digit written counts as significant, including zeros at the start of a decimal.
why: Students count all digits they can see.
fix: Zeros that only show where the decimal point is are not significant. 0.0045 has 2 significant figures, 4 and 5.

probe.question: How many significant figures are in 0.0045?

root_belief: every written symbol counts
source_hint: research on student errors with significant figures in science and mathematics education

subject: maths
concept: Zeros between non-zero digits are significant
statement: Zeros between other digits are not significant because zero means nothing.
why: Students think zero is nothing, so it cannot add to precision.
fix: A zero between non-zero digits is significant because it holds a place. 3007 has 4 significant figures.

probe.question: How many significant figures are in 3007?

root_belief: zero means nothing
source_hint: research on student errors with significant figures in science and mathematics education

subject: maths
concept: Significant figures differ from decimal places
statement: Rounding to 2 significant figures is the same as rounding to 2 decimal places.
why: Both phrases ask for 'two digits' and students treat them as one idea.
fix: Decimal places count from the decimal point. Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit. 0.04567 to 2 s.f. is 0.046, but to 2 d.p. it is 0.05.

probe.question: Round 0.04567 to 2 significant figures.

root_belief: two ways of counting digits are the same
source_hint: research on confusion between significant figures and decimal places

subject: maths
statement: Estimating means guessing a number without working anything out.
why: In everyday speech an estimate is a guess, so students skip the rounding steps.
fix: An estimate is found by rounding the numbers and then calculating. 487 + 312 is about 500 + 300 = 800.

probe.question: Estimate 487 + 312.
probe.wrong_answer: About 1,000

root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
